rows: Bashiru Rashid Omar (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a Tanzanian national. At the time of filing the Application, he was incarcerated at the Institute of Education for Offenders in Zanzibar, in the United Republic of Tanzania, awaiting the execution of the death sentence by hanging following his trial, conviction, and sentencing for the offence of murder. He alleges that his rights were violated during proceedings before the domestic courts.

The Application is filed against the United Republic of Tanzania (hereinafter referred to as “Respondent State”) which became party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 10 February 2006. Furthermore, on 29 March 2010, the Respondent State deposited the Declaration prescribed under Article 34(6) of the Protocol, by which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications filed by individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations. On 21 November 2019, the Respondent State deposited, with the African Union Commission, an instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration. The Court has held that this withdrawal has no bearing on pending cases and new cases filed before the withdrawal comes into effect, one year after the deposit, that is, on 22 November 2020.

It emerges from the record that, on 29 August 2003, the Applicant killed his son after the child’s mother attempted to deny the Applicant access to his child. The Applicant has confirmed the murder in his Application, but has alleged that he was not of a sound mental state at the time of the killing.
On 28 September 2016, the High Court of Zanzibar convicted the Applicant of murder and mandatorily sentenced him to death by hanging.
On 13 December 2018, the Court of Appeal of Tanzania, sitting at Zanzibar, dismissed the Applicant’s appeal against his conviction and sentence.
The Application, together with a request for provisional measures and legal aid, was received by the Court, on 21 November 2020.

The Application was served on the Respondent State on 2 December 2020, which was granted 15 days to file its observations on the request for provisional measures and 90 days to respond to the Application.
On 11 December 2020, the Court approved the Applicant’s request to be provided with legal aid and appointed Advocate Alphonse Van as his pro bono counsel.

On 4 February 2021, the Respondent State filed its Response to the Applicant’s request for an order for provisional measures staying the execution of the death penalty. The Court served this Response on the Applicant on 9 February 2021.
On 26 February 2021, the Court issued an ruling on provisional measures and ordered a stay of the Applicant’s death sentence pending the outcome of this Application.
On 26 March 2021, the Applicant filed supplementary pleadings which were served on the Respondent State on 30 June 2022.
On 13 April 2023, the Respondent State applied for an extension of time to filing its Response. The Court granted a 30 day extension of time on 6 October 2023.
On 20 December 2023, the Respondent State filed its Response which was served on the Applicant on 27 February 2024.

On 10 December 2024, the Court wrote to the Applicant to remind them to file a Reply to the Response and provided, suo motu, a thirty (30) day extension to the deadline for filing a Reply. The Applicant did not submit a Reply to the Response.
Pleadings were closed on 6 May 2026 and the parties were duly notified.

Rule 46(3) of the Rules provides that “the Court has the discretion to determine whether or not to reopen pleadings”. The Court notes that pursuant to Rule 90 of the Rules, “Nothing in these Rules shall limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to adopt such procedure or decisions as may be necessary to meet the ends of justice.”

Furthermore, the Court notes that Rule 55 of the Rules provides as follows: i. The Court may, of its own accord or at the request of a party, obtain any evidence which in its opinion may provide clarification of the facts of a case. The Court may decide to hear a witness, an expert or any other person whose evidence, assertions or statements it deems likely to assist it in carrying out its task. ii. The Court may, for purposes of obtaining information, request any person or institution of its choice to express an opinion or submit a report to it on any specific point. iii. The Court may, at any time during the proceedings, assign one or more Judges to conduct an enquiry, carry out a visit to the scene or take evidence in any other manner, including to take testimony on oath using appropriate means.

The Court observes that neither the Applicant nor the Respondent State have filed copies of the judgments handed down by the domestic courts, or submitted evidence that explains the delay in the Applicant being tried and convicted.

Considering that the Applicant has alleged that his right to a fair trial has been violated by the Respondent State, including his right to be tried within a reasonable time, the Court, suo motu, has decided to reopen pleadings in order for the Parties to file copies of the judgments issued by the domestic courts, and submit further evidence that explains the delay in the Applicant being tried and convicted.

Therefore, the Court holds that it is in the interests of justice to reopen pleadings, and orders that, within 30 days of this order being notified to the parties: (i) the Parties file a copy of the judgment handed down by the High Court of Zanzibar on 28 September 2016, together with any transcript of the proceedings before that court; (ii) the parties to file a copy of the judgment handed down by the Court of Appeal of Tanzania on 13 December 2018, together with any transcript of the proceedings before that court; (iii) the Parties to file a copy of any other judgment, order, or transcript of court proceedings that relate to the Applicant’s conviction and sentencing; and (iv) the Parties be permitted to each submit further evidence that explains the delay in the Applicant being tried and convicted.

For these reasons: THE COURT Unanimously i. Orders that the proceedings in Application 045/2020 – Bashiru Rashid Omar v. United Republic of Tanzania are hereby reopened. ii. Orders the Parties to file a copy of the judgment handed down by the High Court of Zanzibar on 28 September 2016, together with any transcript of the proceedings before that court. iii. Orders the Parties to file a copy of the judgment handed down by the Court of Appeal of Tanzania on 13 December 2018, together with any transcript of the proceedings before that court. iv. Orders the Parties to file copies of any other judgment(s), order(s), or transcript(s) of court proceedings that relate to the Applicant’s conviction and sentencing. v. Orders the Parties be permitted to each submit further evidence that explains the delay in the Applicant being tried and convicted. vi. Orders the Parties to file the information requested by the Court under (ii), (iii), (iv), (v) above, within thirty (30) days from the date of notification of this Order.

Mr Jean Roger M’BA (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a national of Cameroon. At the time of filing the present Application, he was serving a life sentence at the Ouagadougou Remand and Correctional Centre, having been tried and convicted for murder, aggravated robbery, forgery and the use of forged public documents on 16 June 2011. He alleges violation of his rights in connection with the proceedings before Burkinabe courts.

The Application is filed against Burkina Faso (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “‘the Charter”‘) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter “the Protocol”) on 25 January 2004. It also deposited, on 28 July 1998, the Declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepts the Court’s jurisdiction to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

It emerges from the Application that the Applicant was sentenced to death for murder, aggravated robbery, forgery and the use of forged public documents by the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Appeal of Bobo- Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, by Judgment No. 7 of 16 June 2011.

The Applicant avers that he appealed the said judgment before the Cassation Court on 20 June 2011. He further avers that he filed supplementary pleadings on 9 January 2012 but the appeal was dismissed by judgment of the Criminal Chamber of the Respondent State’s Cassation Court rendered on 24 January 2013.

The Applicant alleges violation of the following rights: i. The right to life, protected by Article 4 of the Charter; ii. The right to respect for human dignity, protected by Article 5 of the Charter; iii. The right to have one’s case heard, protected by Article 7 of the Charter.

The Application was filed on 23 April 2019. It was served on the Respondent State on 4 June 2019 with a request to submit the names of its representatives and to file its Response within 30 and 60 days respectively.
On 16 July 2019, the Respondent State submitted the list of names and contact details of its representatives.
On 22 June 2019, the Respondent State requested a one-month extension of time to file its Response.
On 20 January 2020, the Registry requested the Applicant to submit, within eight days, a certified copy of the judgment of the Cassation Court. The Applicant did not respond.

On 26 February 2024, pursuant to Rule 42(5)(b) of the Rules, the Registry transmitted the Application to the Republic of Cameroon requesting it to indicate, within 30 days, whether it wanted to intervene in the case, given that the Applicant was a national of that State. The Republic of Cameroon did not respond.

On 16 April 2026, the Registry drew the Respondent State’s attention to Rule 63 of the Rules of Court concerning the Court’s power to render a judgment in default and granted it an additional 45 days to file its Response.

On 27 May 2026, the Permanent Mission of Burkina Faso to the African Union in Addis Ababa acknowledged receipt of the notice regarding Rule 63 of the Rules and requested that the said documents in the record be sent to it for onward transmission to the Judicial Agent of the State.

By email dated 13 May 2026, the Registry transmitted the Application and procedural documents to the Permanent Mission of Burkina Faso in Addis Ababa, together with the acknowledgement of receipt issued by the Respondent State’s legal representative in respect of the Application. The Respondent State did not file a Response.
Pleadings were closed on 20 August 2026 and the Parties were duly informed.

The Applicant prays for an order compelling the Respondent State to: i. Grant him a presidential pardon; ii. Commute his death penalty and that of all persons sentenced to the same penalty to prison sentence; iii. Grant him parole; iv. Repatriate him to his country of origin; v. Grant him Amnesty; vi. Grant him an out-of-court settlement; vii. Pay him financial compensation for the harm he suffered as a result of the ‘unjust’ judicial decisions handed down against him.
The Respondent State did not make any submission.

Rule 63(1) of the Rules provides: Whenever a party does not appear before the Court, or fails to defend its case within the period prescribed by the Court, the Court may, on the Application of the other party, or on its own motion, enter judgment in default after it has satisfied itself that the defaulting party has been duly served with the Application and all other documents pertinent to the proceedings.

The Court emphasises that the aforementioned Rule 63(1) sets out three requirements for rendering a judgment in default, namely: (i) the application and procedural documents have been served on the defaulting party, in this case the Respondent State; (ii) absence of representation or a Response from the Respondent State; and (iii) a request made by the adverse party or a decision taken by the Court on its own initiative.

With regard to the first requirement, the Court recalls, as stated in paragraph 6 above, that on 4 June 2019, the Application and the procedural documents were served on the Respondent State for its Response within 60 days. The Respondent State did not comply. On 16 April 2026, the Registry drew the Respondent State’s attention to the effects of Rule 63 of the Rules and resent the Application and the procedural documents, giving it additional 45 days to file its Response. The first requirement under Rule 63 is, therefore, met.

With regard to the second requirement, the Court notes that, although the Respondent State received the Application and the procedural documents, it failed to defend the case. The Court therefore finds that the Respondent State defaulted.

As for the third requirement, the Court emphasises that the Applicant has not submitted any request seeking a judgment in default. However, it decides, on its own motion, in the interests of justice, to enter a judgment in default.
In view of the foregoing, the Court considers that the requirements under Rule 63(1) of the Rules are met and decides to deliver a decision in default.

The Court notes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.
Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “The Court shall ascertain its jurisdiction … in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
Based on the aforementioned provisions, the Court, in every application, must conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on any objections thereto, if any.
As the Respondent State failed to defend its case, no objection to the Court’s jurisdiction is on record.

Having found that there is nothing in the record to suggest that it lacks jurisdiction, the Court considers that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges violation of human rights protected by the Charter, which is a human rights instrument to which the Respondent State is a Party; ii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred after the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol; iii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State deposited the Declaration; iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations took place on the territory of the Respondent State, which is a Party to the Protocol.
In view of the foregoing, the Court considers that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides: The Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.

Under Rule 50(1) of the Rules, which essentially restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors, even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter, c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union, d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged, f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter

As the Respondent State failed to defend its case, no objection has been raised to the admissibility of the Application. Nevertheless, the Court must satisfy itself that all admissibility requirements under Article 6(2) of the Protocol and Rule 50(1) of the Rules are met.
The Court notes, from the record, that the Applicant has clearly stated his identity, in accordance with Rule 50(2)(a) of the Rules.

The Court observes that the Applicant’s requests seek to protect his rights guaranteed by the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Indeed, one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act, as set out in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. Furthermore, there is nothing in the Application that is incompatible with the said Constitutive Act. Consequently, the Court considers that the Application meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Court further notes that the language in which the Application is drafted is neither disparaging nor insulting to the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union, so that it complies with Rule 50(2) of the Rules.

Furthermore, the Court considers that the Application complies with Rule 50(2)(d) of the Rules insofar as it is not based on news reports disseminated in the mass media, but rather on judicial documents issued by the courts of the Respondent State.

With regard to the exhaustion of local remedies, the Court recalls its jurisprudence that the remedies to be exhausted in order to comply with the requirement of Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules are judicial remedies, unless it is clear that they are unduly prolonged. These remedies must be available, effective and satisfactory.

The Court emphasises that, within the meaning of Article 127(1) of the Respondent State’s Constitution, the Cassation Court is the highest court in the judicial system. Furthermore, the Court has consistently held that, in the Burkinabe judicial system, in criminal matters, a Cassation appeal is a remedy that must be exhausted, as it is available, effective and satisfactory.

In the present case, the Court notes that, following his conviction by the Criminal Division of the Bobo Dioulasso Court of Appeal by judgment of 16 June 2011, the Applicant filed a cassation appeal on 20 June 2011. On 9 January 2012, he filed supplementary pleadings in support of his appeal. By judgment of 24 January 2013, the Cassation Court of the Respondent State dismissed the appeal.
In view of the foregoing, the Court considers that the Applicant exhausted local remedies and that, consequently, the requirement under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules is met.

As regards the requirement that an application be filed within a reasonable time from the exhaustion of local remedies or from the date set by the Court as the start of reasonable time under Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules, the Court notes that neither the Charter, the Protocol, nor indeed the Rules, specify the time limit for filing an application. Accordingly, it has consistently held that the reasonableness of the time-limit for filing an application depends on the specific circumstances of each case and must, therefore, be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

In this regard, the Court has held that, in assessing the reasonableness of the time taken to bring a case before it, it takes into account certain factors. These factors include, by way of example, whether the applicant is literate, has access to legal aid, or is incarcerated with restricted movement and limited access to information.

The Court emphasises, in this regard, that whilst it is true that Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules allows applicants sufficient time to consider the appropriateness of bringing proceedings before the Court, the fact remains that the Rule seeks to ensure that “the authorities and other concerned persons are not kept in a situation of uncertainty for a protracted period”.

The Court reiterates that it is for the Applicant to prove that the time it took him to file his Application is reasonable. In the absence of such proof, the Court has held in several cases brought by detained applicants that the delays of five years and eleven months, five years and four months, and five years and six months were not reasonable. It follows that incarceration is not, in and of itself, a justification in the present matter.

In the present case, the Court notes that, as local remedies were exhausted following the Cassation Court’s judgment of 24 January 2013, the start date for assessing reasonable time for bringing the case before it must be that date. Between that date and 23 April 2019, when the present proceedings were brought, six years, two months and 29 days elapsed. The question is, therefore, whether this time limit is reasonable within the meaning of Article 56(5) as restated in Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules.
In the instant Application, the Applicant does not state the reasons why he waited six years, two months and 29 days to bring his case before it.

The Court notes that the record shows that although the Applicant was assisted by Counsel, he himself submitted a ‘statement’ in support of his appeal before the Respondent State’s Cassation Court. This shows that he is not illiterate.
Furthermore, it does not emerge from the record that the Applicant was unaware of the Court’s existence or that he was indigent.

It follows from the foregoing that not only does the Applicant fail to justify the delay of six years, two months and 29 days, but also that there is nothing on the record to suggest that this delay is reasonable, having regard to the Court’s jurisprudence.

The Court, therefore, considers that the period of six years, two months and 29 days from the exhaustion of local remedies to the filing of the present Application is not reasonable. Consequently, the requirement under Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules is not met.
Having found that the Application was not filed within a reasonable time after exhaustion of local remedies, the Court considers it unnecessary to examine the other admissibility requirements.
Consequently, the Court declares the Application inadmissible for not being filed within a reasonable time.
The Applicant does not make any submissions on costs.
The Respondent did not make any submissions with regards to costs. ***
Under Article 32(2) of the Rules: “Unless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.

In the present case, the Court considers that nothing in the circumstances of the case warrants a departure from this provision and therefore orders that the Applicant bear his own costs. Accordingly, the Court decides that each Party shall bear its costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, The Respondent State having defaulted, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Finds that the Application was not filed within a reasonable time; iii. Consequently, declares the Application inadmissible. On costs iv. Orders each Party to bear its own costs.

Mr. Babarou BOCOUM (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a Malian national. At the time of filing the present Application, he was an entrepreneur and Political Affairs Secretary of the African Democracy and Independence Solidarity Party (SADI), a political party registered in the Republic of Mali. He alleges, in particular, violation of his right to vote during the 29 March 2020 parliamentary elections.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Mali (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 20 June 2000. The Respondent State also deposited, on 19 February 2010, the declaration Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepts the Court’s jurisdiction to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

The Applicant avers that, as a citizen of the Respondent State, he is captured in the biometric database of the Respondent State’s civil registry and enjoys his civil and political rights, since he is not subject to any disqualification or prohibition under the law. He further avers that, due to the failure to update the voter register – in violation of the law – he was not included on it, an omission which deprived him of his status as a voter and, consequently, of his right to vote in the 29 March 2020 parliamentary elections.

The Applicant further contends that the failure to update the voter register also undermined the integrity of the electoral process. In his view, Decree No. 2020-0010/PRM of 22 January 2020 setting the date for elections was issued contrary to the requirements of the Elections Act, as it was based on a voter register that was not duly updated.

The Applicant further argues that this illegality persisted with the connivance of the Constitutional Court, the judgment of which validated the electoral process, insofar as it upheld the elections despite the alleged failure to update the voter register.

The Applicant therefore maintains that the parliamentary elections were held in violation of the Respondent State’s international obligations, in particular those arising from the human rights instruments to which it is a Party.

The Applicant alleges violation of the following rights and obligations: i. The right to equality before the law and to equal protection under the law, protected by Article 3 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter “the Charter”), Article 10(3) of the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance (hereinafter “ACDEG”), Article 3 of Protocol A/SP1/12/01 on Democracy and Good Governance of ECOWAS (hereinafter “the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy”), Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (hereinafter “the UDHR”); ii. The right to participate freely in the government of one’s country, protected by Article 13(1) of the Charter; iii. The obligation to establish an independent, neutral and credible electoral dispute resolution mechanism, protected by Article 17 of the ACDEG and Articles 3 and 7 of the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy; iv. The obligation to establish an independent and impartial electoral body, protected by Article 17 of the African Charter on Democracy and Articles 3 and 6 of the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy; v. The obligation to organise elections on the dates or within the timeframes provided for in the Constitution and the Electoral Law, under Article 2(2) of the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy.

On 16 June 2020, the Application together with a request for provisional measures were filed with the Registry. The Application and the request for provisional measures were served on the Respondent State for its Responses within 90 days and 72 hours respectively.
On 5 August 2020, the Respondent State filed its Response to the request for provisional measures, which was served on the Applicant.
On 1 September 2020, the Respondent State filed its Response to the Application, which was served on the Applicant on 4 September 2020.

On 21 September 2020, the Applicant filed his Reply, which was notified to the Respondent State. In the Reply, he prayed the Court to declare his request for provisional measures seeking the necessary steps to safeguard his electoral rights and the suspension of any legislative activity inconsistent with the provisions of Articles 1(b) and 2(2) of the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy moot. In support of his request, he argued that, following mass protests and the intervention of the armed forces, the President of the Republic dissolved the National Assembly and subsequently resigned.
On 23 October 2020, the Court declared the request for provisional measures moot. The Ruling was served on the Parties the same day.
Pleadings were closed on 30 June 2022, and the Parties were duly informed.

The Applicant prays the Court to order the Respondent State to: i. Annul the parliamentary elections organised pursuant to Decree No. 2020-0010/PRM of 22 January 2020 calling elections and setting the dates for the opening and closing of the election campaign for the 29 March 2020 election, as well as Judgment No. 2020-04/CC-EL of 30 April 2020 of the Constitutional Court announcing the final results of the first and second rounds of the parliamentary elections; ii. Update the voter register, in accordance with the applicable provisions of domestic law, in order to ensure the effective participation of Malian citizens in the exercise of universal suffrage, and to complete all subsequent procedures necessary for the organisation of elections in compliance with legal requirements; iii. Take the necessary constitutional and legislative measures to amend: Article 92 of the Constitution of Mali; Organic Law No. 97-010 of 11 February 1997 on the rules governing the structure and functioning of the Constitutional Court and the procedure to be followed before it, as amended by Law No. 02-011 of 5 March 2002; Law No. 2016-048 of 17 October 2016, as amended by Law No. 2018-014 of 23 April 2018 on elections; as well as the Constitutional Court’s Rules of Procedure of 28 August 2002, in order to ensure their compliance with the treaty obligations relating to the establishment of a credible electoral dispute resolution mechanism, as provided for by Article 17 of ACDEG, Articles 3 and 7 of the ECOWAS Protocol A/SP1/12/01, as well as the guarantees under the principle of equality before the law and equal protection under the law, enshrined in particular in Article 3 of the Charter, Article 1 of the UDHR and Article 26 of the ICCPR; iv. Amend Electoral Law No. 06-044 of 4 September 2006, as amended by Laws No. 2011-085 of 30 December 2011 and No. 2016-017 of 21 May 2016, in order to ensure its compliance with the obligations arising from Articles 3 and 6 of the ECOWAS Protocol A/SP1/12/01 and Article 17(1) of the CAD, in particular by establishing an independent National Electoral Commission, in line with international legal standards on democratic governance and the integrity of electoral processes; v. Pay him the sum of 100,000,000 CFA francs as reparation for all the harm suffered, in particular financial, material and moral harm, and to order the Respondent State to bear costs and expenses.
In its Response, the Respondent State prays the Court to: i. Declare that the Application is unfounded; and ii. Order the Applicant to bear all costs.

The Court notes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.
Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “[t]he Court shall ascertain its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
Based on the aforementioned provisions, the Court, in every application, must conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on any objections thereto, if any.

In the present case, the Respondent State does not contest the Court’s jurisdiction. However, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, the Court must ensure that the requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction are met.

Having found that there is nothing in the record to suggest that it lacks jurisdiction, the Court considers that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges violation of human rights protected by the Charter, the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy and the ICCPR, human rights instruments to which the Respondent State is a Party; ii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State is a Party to the Protocol and has deposited the Declaration on 19 February 2010, as indicated in paragraph 2 of this Judgment; iii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the violations alleged by the Applicant occurred after the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol. iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred on the territory of the Respondent State, which is a Party to the Charter and the Protocol.
In the light of the foregoing, the Court considers that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides: The Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.
Under Rule 50(1) the Rules, The Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an Application filed before it in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6 (2) of the Protocol and these Rules.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which essentially restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Law of the African Union and with the Charter, c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union, d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged, f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date the Court is seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that the Respondent State does not raise any objection to the admissibility of the Application. However, in accordance with Rule 50(1) of the Rules, the Court must satisfy itself that the requirements under the aforementioned provisions are met.
The Court observes that it emerges from the record that the Applicant is clearly identified by name, in compliance with Rule 50(2)(a) of the Rules.

The Court notes that the Applicant’s requests seek to protect his fundamental rights guaranteed by the Charter and other international human rights instruments. It notes, in fact, that one of the objectives of the Constitutive Law of the African Union, as set out in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. Furthermore, there is no evidence in the record that it is inconsistent with the Constitutive Law of the African Union. The Court therefore considers that the Application meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Court further notes that the language in which the Application is drafted is neither disparaging nor insulting to the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union, so that it is in compliance with Rule 50(2)(c) of the Rules.

The Court also notes that the Application is not based exclusively on news disseminated in the mass media, but on judicial documents issued by the domestic courts of the Respondent State. The Court therefore considers that the Application complies with Rule 50(2)(d) of the Rules.

With regard to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, the Court notes that the non-registration of the Applicant in the voter register is the main grievance that led to the present Application to which the other claims are ancillary or derivative. It is therefore preliminary to assess compliance with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies in respect of the Applicant’s non-registration in the voter register.

The Court recalls its jurisprudence that the remedies to be exhausted in order to comply with the requirement of Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules are judicial remedies, unless same are unavailable, ineffective or unsatisfactory, or the related proceedings are unduly prolonged.

The Court notes that the Applicant alleges that he was not registered in the voter register due to the Respondent State’s failure to revise the said register, in violation of the electoral law, and that, having thus been deprived of his status as a voter, he was unable to vote in the first and second rounds of the 29 March 2020 parliamentary elections.

The Court notes that the Applicant contends that no local remedy exists against Decree No. 2020-0010/PRM of 22 January 2020 setting the date for elections and setting the start and end dates of the election campaign for the parliamentary elections, as the decree is an act of the Government not subject to judicial review. He further submits that he lacked standing to bring legal proceedings against the said Law because it did affect him personally and directly.

The Applicant further submits that local remedies against the Constitutional Court’s Judgments No. 2020-03/CC-EL of 9 April 2020 and No. 2020- 04/CC-EL of 30 April 2020, by which it announced the disputed final results, are not available.

The Court notes that pursuant to Law No. 2016-048 of 17 October 2016 on the Electoral Code, as amended by Law No. 2018-014 of 23 April 2018, a complaint regarding an omission from the voter register is subject to procedures that reflect its individual nature. Indeed, Article 54 of the aforementioned law provides that every complaint must be recorded in a register and must include the last name, first name, and address of each complainant, as well as the grounds on which the complaint is based. It follows from these procedures that this remedy must be exercised by the person concerned. It was therefore for the Applicant – who contends that the failure to update the voter register resulted in his exclusion therefrom – to personally exercise this remedy in order to have the omission rectified prior to filing the present Application with the Court.

The Court notes that, pursuant to Articles 55 through 60 of the Malian Electoral Law, Law No. 2018-014, any voter whose name does not appear on the voter register may request to be registered before the register is definitively closed. To that end, the person concerned may file a complaint with the Administrative Commission, which may grant the request and proceed to register the complainant on the voter register.

Where the request for registration is rejected, Article 55 of the Electoral Law requires the Administrative Commission to notify the applicant of its reasoned decision within five days and to inform the applicant of his/her right to bring the matter before a civil court within ten days of such notification. A civil court, ruling at first instance, may either uphold the Administrative Commission’s decision or overturn it by recognizing the complainant’s right to be registered on the voter register. The civil court must render a decision within ten days.
The civil court’s decision, which must be served within seven days, is subject to appeal, and the Court of Appeals must render a decision within 15 days.

The Court notes that the effectiveness and adequacy of these remedies stem from the fact that they allow a citizen whose name does not appear on the voter register to be registered on the final voter register, which must be exhibited no later than seven days before the election.

The Court notes that these provisions avail voters judicial remedies to challenge their registration, non-registration, or removal from the register. The Court considers that, under these circumstances, the Applicant had adequate local remedies available to challenge his electoral status if he believed his right to vote was violated.

The Court notes, however, that there is nothing on the record to establish that the Applicant pursued the available local remedies to challenge the alleged failure to update the voter register, which alleged violation is the main ground of the Application and from which, in particular, his noninclusion on said register is said to stem. Accordingly, the Court finds that the Applicant did not meet the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

Having found that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies and given that the admissibility requirements are cumulative, the Court considers it unnecessary to examine the last two admissibility requirements under Rule 50(2)(f) and (g) of the Rules.
In light of the foregoing, the Court declares the Application inadmissible.
The Applicant prays that the Respondent State be ordered to bear costs.
For its part, the Respondent State prays the Court to dismiss the prayer.
The Court notes that under Rule 32(2) of the Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.

The Court observes that, whilst the Parties request that costs be borne by the opposing Party, they do not demonstrate the existence of any special circumstances warranting a departure from the principle that each party bears its own costs. It also points out that proceedings before it are free of charge.
Consequently, the Court considers that, in the present case, there is no reason to depart from the principle that each party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Declares the Application inadmissible for non-exhaustion of local remedies. ABOUD, Judge; Dumisa B. NTSEBEZA, Judge; Modibo SACKO, Judge; Dennis D. ADJEI, Judge; Duncan GASWAGA, Judge; and Robert Eno, Registrar. Done at Arusha, on the Thirteenth Day of November in the year Two Thousand and Twenty-Six, in French and English, the French version being authoritative.

Mr Patroklos Tsaperas (hereinafter referred to as the “Applicant”) is a national of the Republic of South Africa. He is also a director of Malawi Mobile Limited (hereinafter referred to as “MML”), in which he holds shares through Finanz Capital Management. He alleges violation of his rights in relation to the proceedings before the Malawian courts.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Malawi (hereinafter referred to as “Respondent State”), which became a party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 23 February 1990. On 9 October 2008, the Respondent State became a party to the Protocol and deposited the Declaration prescribed under Article 34(6) of the Protocol, by which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications filed by individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations (hereinafter “the Declaration”).

The record indicates that on 19 April 2002, MML, a company of which the Applicant is a director, entered into a licence agreement with the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (MACRA) to provide mobile telecommunications services in the Respondent State for a period of 15 years upon payment of an annual licence fee of United States Dollars One Hundred Thousand (USD 100,000).

Under this agreement, MML was required to roll out the services in Malawi within 12 months. However, by January 2005, MML had not rolled out the services but had apparently engaged third parties to facilitate the roll-out. The Applicant claims that on 27 January 2005, MML sought an extension of time up to 31 October 2005 to effect the roll-out.

On 9 February 2005, MACRA notified MML that its licence had been revoked and demanded payment of outstanding licence fees and penalties. On 21 March 2005, MML sent another request for extension of time to MACRA for the roll-out.

The Applicant alleges that, on 29 March 2005, MML and MACRA concluded a further agreement extending the roll-out period until 31 October 2005, subject to specified conditions. He further avers that on 4 April 2005, the Attorney General of Malawi suspended MACRA’s board of directors and invalidated all its resolutions from 24 March 2005, including the decision to extend MML’s roll-out period.

According to the Applicant, MML, relying on the extension of time given by MACRA, made two payments for the licence fee of United States Dollars One Hundred Thousand (USD 100,000) each on 19 and 20 April 2005.

The Applicant claims that following the suspension of the Board of Directors of MACRA, he was arrested along with the Chairman of MACRA and its counsel, Mr Khuze Kapeta, Senior Counsel, for allegedly uttering a false document, obtaining a document by false pretence, and perjury. However, they were subsequently released, and the criminal proceedings against them were discontinued. Furthermore, Mr Kapeta served a notice of intention to sue the Attorney General for malicious prosecution, but this claim was settled amicably.
On 12 May 2005, MML instituted a civil case against the Respondent State before the High Court of Malawi alleging breach of contract and the tort of inducement.

The Applicant alleges that on 13 June 2005, the former Chairman of MACRA’s board, Mr Abdul Pillane, filed a constitutional claim before the High Court of Malawi challenging both the suspension of the MACRA’s Board of Directors and the resolutions that they had made. According to the Applicant, on 3 February 2006, the High Court of Malawi found in favour of Mr Pillane, holding that the decision of the Attorney General was “unconstitutional and unlawful, and therefore null and void”. The Applicant also alleges that the Attorney General did not appeal this decision.

The Applicant avers that MML’s case was referred to arbitration on 1 October 2010. The arbitration was terminated on 17 February 2011, and the case was referred back to the High Court. By judgment of 20 April 2012, the High Court found in favour of MML and awarded damages of United States Dollars Sixty-Six Million, Eight Hundred and Fifty Thousand (USD 66,850,000) together with costs.

The Respondent State appealed to the Malawi Supreme Court of Appeal (MSCA), and MML filed a cross-appeal before the same Court as it was not satisfied with the amount of damages awarded. On 10 March 2015, judgment was delivered in the Respondent State’s favour as the MSCA found that there was no breach of contract and thus set aside the decision of the High Court and dismissed the MML’s cross appeal.

Following the MSCA’s judgment of 10 March 2015, MML, on 15 May 2015, instituted proceedings before the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa Court of Justice (hereinafter referred to as “COMESA CJ”). The Respondent State objected to the jurisdiction of the said Court. On 20 November 2015, the First Instance Division of the COMESA CJ dismissed the Respondent State’s preliminary objection to its jurisdiction.

The Respondent State thus appealed the ruling on jurisdiction to the Appellate Division of the COMESA CJ. On 27 April 2017, the Appellate Division of the COMESA CJ held that it lacked jurisdiction and dismissed the reference. Being dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Division, MML filed a petition for review, which was dismissed on 17 September 2021.

The Applicant alleges violations of the following: i. Right to property under Article 14 of the Charter and Article 17 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR); ii. Freedom from discrimination under Article 2 of the Charter and Article 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR); iii. Right to equal protection of the law under Article 3 of the Charter and Article 14 of the ICCPR; iv. Right to be recognised as a person under Article 16 of the ICCPR; and v. Right to have one’s cause heard under Article 7(1) of the Charter.

The Application was filed on 17 October 2022 and served on the Respondent State on 28 January 2023. The Respondent State was granted 30 days to submit its list of representatives and 90 days to file its Response. It filed its Response on 18 August 2023, and the Response was transmitted to the Applicant on 29 August 2023 for his Reply.
On 9 October 2023, the Applicant filed his Reply, which was transmitted to the Respondent State for information.
Pleadings were closed on 3 December 2023, and the Parties were notified.

The Applicant prays the Court for the following: i. Compensation for loss of income/revenue and pecuniary/material damage in the sum of $133,700,000 as assessed by the uncontroverted evidence of expert…; ii. The sum of $400,000 being reimbursement of the license fees paid by MML to MACRA; iii. Compensation for non-pecuniary/moral damage (to be assessed by the African Court); iv. Satisfaction (publication of the Court’s judgment); v. Rehabilitation (withdrawal of the defamatory and disparaging material concerning the 1 Applicant on the internet); vi. US$ 1,200,000 being reimbursement of the inevitable expenditure and costs (Lawyer’s fees in domestic courts and in the African Court, transport and sojourn expenses); vii. A Declaration that the acts and/or omissions of the Respondent complained herein amount to a violation of the provisions of the African Charter.

The Respondent State prays the Court that: i. The Application should be dismissed as: a. No contract to extend the network roll existed; b. There was no breach of contract by MACRA; c. Malawi Government did not induce breach of contract as no contract existed; d. Neither did Malawi Government interfere with any contract since none existed; e. Malawi Government and MACRA are not liable at all to MML; f. MML does not deserve any award of damages as they have not proved a contract or its breach or any loss or damage. ii. Malawi Government and MACRA should be awarded costs.

The Court notes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides as follows: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and Application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.
The Court further notes that pursuant to Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it “…shall conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction…in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules.”
On the basis of the above-cited provisions, the Court must conduct a preliminary assessment of its jurisdiction and dispose of any objections thereto.

The Court observes that the Respondent State does not challenge its jurisdiction. However, being cognisant of Rule 49(1) of the Rules, the Court must satisfy itself that all aspects of its jurisdiction are established before proceeding to determine the Application.

With respect to its personal jurisdiction, as stated in paragraph 2 of this Ruling, the Respondent State became a party to the Protocol on 9 October 2008 and deposited the Declaration with the African Union Commission on the same day. Consequently, the Court finds that it has personal jurisdiction.

The Court notes that the Applicant alleges violations of his rights guaranteed under Articles 2, 3 and 14 of the Charter and Articles 14 and 16 of the ICCPR, treaties to which the Respondent State is a party. Accordingly, the Court finds that it possesses material jurisdiction to entertain this Application.

As to temporal jurisdiction, the Court notes that the alleged violations began in 2005 with the Attorney General’s breach of contract, which predates the Respondent State’s accession to the Protocol. However, the Applicant alleges that the MSCA violated his rights to property and to a fair trial in 2012, that is, after the Respondent State became a party to the Protocol. The Court thus finds that it has temporal jurisdiction.
The Court also notes that it has territorial jurisdiction as the alleged violations occurred in the territory of the Respondent State, which is a party to the Charter and the Protocol.
In light of the foregoing, the Court holds that it has jurisdiction to hear this Application.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides that “the Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.”

Pursuant to Rule 50(1) of the Rules, “[t]he Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an Application filed before it in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol and these Rules.”

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which in substance restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides as follows: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity; b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seised with the matter; and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of the African Union, or the provisions of the Charter.

The Respondent State raises two objections to the admissibility of the Application. The Court will, therefore, consider the said objections before examining other conditions of admissibility, if necessary.

The Respondent State raises two objections to the admissibility of the Application: (i) that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies and (ii) that the Application was not filed within a reasonable time. The Court will consider the objections sequentially.

The Respondent State contends that the objective of the requirement to exhaust local remedies is for victims of human rights violations first to seek redress for their grievances through national bodies, up to the highest judicial authority, before submitting the case to an international body. The Respondent State further submits that the condition of exhaustion of local remedies underscores that international bodies are subsidiary to state institutions and should thus “not get involved unless human rights violations cannot be resolved at the national level”.

According to the Respondent State, an international judicial body must not be made a court of first instance; therefore, the Applicant must pursue all appeals at the national level before approaching an international court.

The Respondent State argues that, in the present case, the “issues litigated upon in the domestic courts” related to a breach of contract by MACRA and an alleged tort of inducement to commit a breach of contract. It thus submits that no human rights violations were pleaded. According to the Respondent State, the issues raised before the national courts had no relevance to the Charter, the Protocol or any other relevant instrument that it has ratified.

It is the Respondent State’s view that the Applicant has brought to this Court “a totally different set of remedies which were not litigated upon in the domestic courts in Malawi”. Furthermore, the Respondent State contends that the Court derives its jurisdiction from the Charter and should, therefore, adhere to the Charter’s provisions.
Consequently, the Respondent State submits that the Application should be declared inadmissible for the Applicant’s failure to exhaust local remedies. *

Citing the Court’s decision in African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights v. Kenya, the Applicant submits that a matter brought before this Court need not have been previously raised before domestic courts by the same applicants. Rather, what is required is that the Respondent State was afforded a genuine opportunity to address the grievance through its national legal processes. In this regard, he avers that Mr Abdul Pillane filed a case before the High Court of Malawi, which implicated the Respondent State.

Furthermore, the Applicant avers that the Application raises, in substance, the same issues that were litigated before the Constitutional Court of Malawi pertaining to the conduct of the Attorney General in seeking to dissolve the Board of MACRA and set aside its resolutions, including the resolution purporting to extend the roll-out period of the MML network. The Applicant argues that local remedies were exhausted, since the Attorney General did not appeal the decision of the Constitutional Court.

According to the Applicant, MML separately instituted proceedings before the High Court against the Respondent State, seeking damages for loss of profit arising from breach of contract. Judgment was delivered in favour of MML on 20 April 2012. He asserts that the Respondent State challenged the High Court’s decision, while MML cross-appealed in respect of the damages awarded. On 10 March 2015, the MSCA reversed the High Court’s judgment, allowed the Respondent State’s appeal, and dismissed MML’s cross-appeal. He thus submits that the MSCA’s decision marked the exhaustion of local remedies.

The Applicant avers that the burden lies with the Respondent State to prove that he has not exhausted domestic remedies with regard to “the question of the alleged tort of inducement and the breach of contract”. The Applicant also asserts that “there is no available or effective remedy with respect to human rights violations”. ***

Article 56(5) of the Charter, whose provisions are restated in Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, provides that any application filed before the Court shall fulfil the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies, unless such remedies are unavailable, ineffective and insufficient or the domestic proceedings thereof are unduly prolonged.

The Court underscores that the objective of the rule of exhaustion of local remedies is to provide States with the opportunity to resolve cases of alleged human rights violations within their jurisdiction before an international human rights body is called upon to determine the State’s responsibility for the same, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity.

Furthermore, for local remedies to be exhausted, an applicant must have presented before domestic courts the claims that he raises before this Court. The Court further recalls that exhaustion of local remedies is assessed as at the time the application is filed before it, and compliance with this requirement entails that applicants must await the outcome of pending domestic proceedings before seising the Court. The exceptions to this rule are where the applicable remedy is unavailable, ineffective or insufficient, or where the domestic proceedings are unduly prolonged.

In the instant case, the Applicant alleges the violations of the right to property, right to non-discrimination, right to be recognised as a person, right to equal protection of the law and the right to have one’s cause heard. The Court will thus determine whether he exhausted local remedies in relation to each of the claims.
The Applicant argues that he exhausted all local remedies when the MSCA delivered its decision on 10 March 2015.

For its part, the Respondent State contends that the “issues litigated upon in the domestic courts” related to a breach of contract by MACRA and an alleged tort of inducement to commit a breach of contract. It thus argues that no human rights violations were pleaded. ***

With regard to the Applicant’s claim on the right to property, the Court must determine whether the evidence provided by the Applicant concerning the cases decided by the national courts satisfies the requirements of exhaustion of local remedies in accordance with Article 56(5) of the Charter.

The Court has held that, in determining whether proceedings instituted by a company may be attributed to an individual applicant for the purposes of Article 56(5) of the Charter, regard must be had to the link between the Applicant and the company whose interests form the basis of the claim before the Court.

The Court also observes that limited liability companies constitute legal vehicles through which investors pool and deploy capital, while the shareholder’s proprietary interest is embodied in his shares. Section 43(1) of the Malawi Companies Act 1984 expressly recognised that “the shares or other interest of any member in a company shall be personal estate and movable property”. Although the company’s assets are legally distinct from those of its shareholders, the value of a shareholder’s proprietary interest is necessarily affected by the economic position of the company in which the shares are held.

Thus, conduct which materially diminishes the assets, business or value of the company may correspondingly prejudice the shareholder’s own property interest in his shares. The Court, therefore, recognises the economic and proprietary connection between the company’s fortunes and the value of the shareholder’s investment.

In the present case, MML may accordingly be regarded, for the limited purpose of establishing the requisite nexus between the domestic proceedings and the Applicant’s claim, as the corporate vehicle through which the Applicant’s economic and proprietary interests were invested.

Applying these principles to the facts of the present case, the Court finds that the Applicant has established a sufficient link to MML through his indirect shareholding. The domestic proceedings instituted by MML placed before the national courts the substance of the dispute arising from the impugned measures attributable to the Respondent State, and were pursued through the domestic judicial hierarchy up to the MSCA. Those proceedings consequently afforded the Respondent State the opportunity to examine and, where appropriate, remedy the underlying matters now brought before this Court.

To require the Applicant, notwithstanding his established proprietary connection with MML and the adjudication of the substance of the dispute by the domestic courts, to institute separate proceedings raising substantially the same underlying grievance would elevate the formal identity of the domestic litigant over the substantive purpose of the exhaustion requirement. As a consequence, in the circumstances of the present case, the domestic proceedings pursued by MML satisfy the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies in respect of the Applicant’s claim.
The Court accordingly finds that the Applicant has exhausted local remedies with regard to the claim on the right to property.

With regard to the allegation that the MSCA was inquorate when it delivered its judgment of 10 March 2015, the Court notes that the Applicant has not submitted any proof of exhaustion of local remedies. Rather, the Applicant argues that the remedies are ineffective.

In this regard, the Court recalls that it has consistently held that it is not enough for the Applicant to cast aspersions on the effectiveness of the Respondent State’s local remedies. It is incumbent on him to take all necessary steps to exhaust, or at least attempt to exhaust, all local remedies.
The Court therefore finds that the Applicant has not exhausted local remedies with regard to the claim that the MSCA was inquorate.

The Applicant’s claims in relation to his rights to equality before the law and equal protection of the law relate to the alleged non-execution of the Constitutional Court’s judgment. In this regard, the Applicant has not pointed to any specific domestic proceedings, whether before the High Court, the Constitutional Court, or the MSCA, in which he initiated execution proceedings as the decree holder.
The Court therefore finds that the Applicant has not exhausted local remedies with regard to the claim on the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law.

With regard to the Applicant’s claim that he was discriminated against on grounds of nationality and race despite having complied with all legal requirements for the roll-out of the mobile services, the Court notes that he has neither adduced any evidence of exhaustion of local remedies nor shown that any of the exceptions to that rule apply.
The Court therefore finds that he has not exhausted local remedies with regard to these claims.

In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Applicant exhausted local remedies only in respect of the claim concerning the right to property. Accordingly, it dismisses the Respondent State’s objection on this ground but upholds the objection in respect of the other three claims.

Citing the decisions of Anudo Ochieng Anudo v. Tanzania and Alex Thomas v. Tanzania, the Respondent State avers that the Court’s assessment of whether an application was filed within a reasonable time depends on factors such as the status of the applicant and the conduct of the Respondent State or its officials.

The Respondent State contends that the reasonableness of time is assessed on the basis of “objective considerations”. It further submits that the decision of the MSCA was delivered on 10 March 2015, while the final decision of the COMESA CJ was delivered on 23 April 2021. The Respondent State therefore asserts that more than one year elapsed from the time the COMESA CJ delivered its final decision to the time the Applicant seised the Court.

The Respondent State contends that the Applicant was neither imprisoned nor subject to restrictions on his freedom of movement; that he is not indigent; and that he has enjoyed continuous legal representation. In those circumstances, the Respondent State submits, the Applicant must be presumed to have been aware of the Court’s existence. The Respondent State further argues that the Applicant has advanced no sufficient justification for the delay in instituting the present proceedings.
According to the Respondent State, the Application should be declared inadmissible for not having been filed within a reasonable time.

The Applicant avers that a delay of one year cannot be considered inordinate given the complexity of the case and the time needed to prepare the Application “after lengthy protracted proceedings in pursuit of judicial remedies”.
The Applicant argues that the violations are continuing and they “renew themselves day by day as long as they remain unsettled”.

The Court notes that Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules, which in substance restates the contents of Article 56(6) of the Charter, requires an application to be filed within a reasonable time after exhaustion of domestic remedies or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seised with the matter.
As the Court has previously held, “… the reasonableness of the timeframe for seizure depends on the specific circumstances of the case and should be determined on a case-by-case basis.”

In the instant case, the Court observes that the Application was filed on 17 October 2022, that is, seven years, seven months and seven days after the MSCA’s decision of 10 March 2015, which marked the exhaustion of local remedies. The Court will therefore determine whether this period is reasonable within the meaning of Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules.

The Court also observes that although the Applicant exhausted local remedies on 10 March 2015, he subsequently pursued litigation before the COMESA CJ for six years. However, the proceedings before the COMESA CJ cannot form part of the exhaustion of domestic remedies, as that Court is a regional tribunal operating within a distinct legal order. Accordingly, the Court will calculate the reasonable time period starting from the date of the final domestic court’s ruling, namely, 10 March 2015, when the MSCA rendered its decision.

The Court observes that the Applicant seized the Court after a period of seven years, seven months and seven days. Such a period is significantly longer than that considered acceptable and, in the absence of compelling justification, weighs decisively against the reasonableness of the Applicant’s conduct in the present case.
The Court thus finds that the period of seven years, seven months and seven days which elapsed after the exhaustion of local remedies constitutes unjustified excessive delay.

The Court accordingly upholds the objection of the Respondent State and finds that the Application was not filed within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of local remedies, and finds the Application inadmissible.

Having found that the Application does not satisfy the requirement of Article 56(6) of the Charter as restated under Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules, the Court does not need to rule on the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56(1), (2), (3), (4) and (7) of the Charter as restated in Rule 50(2)(a), (b), (c), (d) and (g) of the Rules, as the admissibility requirements are cumulative.
The Applicant does not make any submissions on costs. The Respondent State prays that the costs be borne by the Applicant.
The Court observes that Rule 32(2) of the Rules provides that “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each Party shall bear its own costs, if any.”

The Court recalls that proceedings before it are free of charge. Furthermore, although the Respondent State prays that the costs be borne by the Applicant, it has not demonstrated that it incurred any such costs. Accordingly, the Court sees no reason to depart from the above provision and decides that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Dismisses the objection to the admissibility of the Application in relation to the non-exhaustion of local remedies on the alleged violation of the right to property; iii. Upholds the objection to the admissibility of the Application in relation to the non-exhaustion of local remedies on the alleged violations of the rights to equality before the law and equal protection of the law, to non-discrimination, to be recognised as a person before the law, and to a fair trial; iv. Upholds the objection to the admissibility of the Application for failure to file the Application within a reasonable time; and v. Holds that the Application is inadmissible. On costs vi. Orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

Mrs Ida Afiavi AJAVON, Nee GOUDJO, Ms Ludmila Isis Ayelé AJAVON and Ms Evaëlle Jonella Noémie Ayoko AJAVON, and Mr Ronald K. Steeven Karen Ayité AJAVON (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicants”), are all nationals of Benin, residing in Paris, France, and are political refugees. They allege the violation of their right to property and the right to have their cause heard.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Benin (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights establishing an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 22 August 2014. Furthermore, on 8 February 2016, the Respondent State deposited the Declaration under Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepted the Court’s jurisdiction to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations. On 25 March 2020, the Respondent State deposited with the African Union Commission (AUC) an instrument of withdrawal of its Declaration. The Court has held that the withdrawal of the Declaration has no effect either on pending cases or new cases brought before the Court prior to its entry into force one year after the deposit of the relevant instrument, in this case, on 26 March 2021.

The Applicants allege that the Respondent State violated their property rights in connection with the conviction of Mr. Sébastien Germain Marie Aikoué Ajavon, director and shareholder of the company COMON SA, for drug trafficking offenses by judgment dated 18 October 2018, of the Court for the Suppression of Economic Offenses and Terrorism (CRIET).

In this regard, they aver that their personal bank accounts were unlawfully seized; as shareholders of COMON SA, they were adversely affected by abusive acts and measures taken by the Respondent State against the said company. They also allege that the Respondent State deliberately refused to implement the decisions of this Court rendered in Application No. 013/2017.
The Applicants allege violation of their right to property and the right to have their cause heard, as protected by Articles 14 and 7 of the Charter respectively.

The Application was filed on 29 November 2019. On 14 January 2020, the Registry received a supplementary amended Application. On 17 January 2020, the two Applications were served on the Respondent State, with a request to submit the names and addresses of its representative and its Response on the applications within 30 and 60 days respectively.

On 16 March 2020, the Respondent State submitted the name and address of its representative. On 7 May 2020, after a 60-day extension of time, the Respondent State filed its Responses, which were transmitted to the Applicants on 20 May 2020 for their Replies within 30 days of notification.
On 28 May 2020, the Applicants filed their Reply, which was transmitted to the Respondent State on 8 June 2020 for its observations within 30 days of receipt. The Respondent State did not respond.
Pleadings were closed on 21 August 2026, and the Parties were duly informed.

In their Application, the Applicants pray the Court to: i. Declare that it has jurisdiction; ii. Declare the Application admissible; iii. Find that the Respondent State violated their right to property protected by Article 14 of the Charter; iv. Hold that the Respondent State violated their fundamental rights; v. Rule that the said violations committed against them caused them irreparable prejudice warranting reparation; vi. Order the Respondent State to pay each of them the sum of One Hundred and Seventy Million (170,000,000) CFA francs as damages; vii. Order the Respondent State to bear costs;

In their amended and supplementary Application of 7 January 2020, the Applicants pray the Court to: i. Order the Respondent State to pay each of them compensation proportionate to their shareholdings in COMON SA, in respect of the loss of opportunity arising from the partnership with PHILIA; ii. Order the Respondent State to pay to Ronald K. Steeven, Karen Ayité Ajavon and Ludima Isis Ayélé Ajavon the sums of: - 2,928,285,906 CFA francs in respect of loss of profits as COMON SA shareholders ; - 1,214,037,112 CFA francs in respect of the depreciation of their shares in COMON SA; - 209,206,534 CFA francs in respect of the depreciation of their shares in SOCOTRAC; - 20,000,000,000 CFA francs for loss of business opportunities in relation to the oil project.

The Respondent State prays the Court to: i. Find that the Applicants do not allege any specific violation of the right to property; ii. Find that the Application is incompatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter; iii. Consequently, to declare that it lacks jurisdiction; iv. Note that there are available and effective remedies in Benin against acts constituting human rights violations; v. Note that the Applicants did not bring their cases before the domestic courts; vi. Consequently, declare the Application inadmissible for non-exhaustion of local remedies; vii. Note that the judgment on reparations of 28 November 2019 (Application No. 013/2017) addressed all the requests in the present case; viii. Find, therefore, that the Application is moot; ix. Consequently, declare it inadmissible ; x. Note that the decisions in Application No. 013/2017 are binding on the Parties and cannot inure to the benefit of the applicants; xi. Find that the Applicants’ requests are unfounded and, consequently, dismiss them; xii. Find that the Respondent State did not commit any violation causing the Applicants prejudice; xiii. Find that the Applicants fail to prove the alleged prejudice suffered as a result of the Respondent State’s actions; xiv. Rule that there is no basis for reparation; xv. Declare that the Application lacks merit.

Article 3(1) of the Protocol provides that: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

In accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules of Court, “the Court shall conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction […]”. Based on the aforementioned provisions, the Court must, in every application, conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on objections thereto, if any.

The Court notes that the Respondent State raises (A) an objection to the Court’s material jurisdiction, which it will examine before ruling, if necessary (B) on the other aspects of its jurisdiction which are not in contention.

The Respondent State raises an objection to Court’s material jurisdiction based on two grounds, firstly, (i) on the Application being incompatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the Charter and, secondly, (ii) on the absence of any human rights violation.

The Court recalls that, within the meaning of Article 56(2) of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules of Court, the compatibility of the Application with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or with the Charter is an admissibility requirement, not a matter related to the Court’s material jurisdiction. The Court will therefore address this objection at the admissibility stage.
Consequently, the Court will rule at this stage solely on the ground relating to the absence of allegations of human rights violations.

The Respondent State draws attention to Rule 34(4) of the Rules of Court, which provides that “[t]he application shall specify the alleged violation”. It contends that the exercise of the Court’s material jurisdiction is predicated on a specific and well-founded case of human rights violation being brought before it.
The Respondent State contends that the Applicants claim to have suffered violation of their right to property based solely on their status as shareholders of COMON SA.

The Respondent State argues that the mere fact of natural persons holding shares in a commercial company does not constitute a human rights violation attributable to a State. It concludes that the Court lacks material jurisdiction, as there has been no substantive violation of human rights.

The Applicants aver that Rule 34(4) of the Rules does not lay out criteria for material jurisdiction but rather sets out other ancillary admissibility requirements.
