They emphasise that material jurisdiction is assessed in the light of Article 3(1) of the Protocol, read in conjunction with Rule 26(1) of the Rules, which confers on the Court jurisdiction to hear all cases and disputes relating to the interpretation or application of the Charter, the Protocol and any relevant instrument ratified by the States concerned.

The Applicants further assert that they expressly stated and characterised the violation of their right to property guaranteed under Article 14 of the Charter, through personal, concrete and ongoing violations. They therefore submit that the Court has material jurisdiction, and that the objection be dismissed.

The Court emphasises, first of all, that Rule 34(4) of the Rules – now Rule 41(1)(f) of the Rules – relied upon by the Respondent State, is a requirement relating to the form and content of the Application. It does not require the applicant to fully demonstrate the merits of their claims at this stage of the proceedings, but merely requires that the alleged violations be set out with sufficient clarity to enable the Respondent State to understand the nature of the complaints raised and to respond to them effectively.
The Court emphasises that its material jurisdiction is assessed in the light of the provisions of Articles 3 and 7 of the Protocol, and Rule 29(1)(a) of the Rules of Court.

Recalling its established jurisprudence, the Court reaffirms that it has material jurisdiction, provided that the application before it concerns allegations of human rights violations and that, in such cases, it is sufficient that the application alleges violation of the rights guaranteed by the Charter or by any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the States concerned.

In the present case, the Court notes that the Applicants allege violation of their right to property and the right to have their cause heard, protected by Articles 14 and 7 of the Charter respectively.
In view of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Respondent State’s objection lacks merit.
Consequently, the Court dismisses the objection and declares that it has material jurisdiction in the present case.

There is no contention regarding the Court’s personal, temporal, and territorial jurisdiction. Nevertheless, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, the Court must satisfy itself that all requirements relating to these aspects of its jurisdiction are met.

The Court confirms that the requirement relating to personal jurisdiction is met insofar as the Respondent State is a Party to the Protocol and had deposited the Declaration at the time the Application was filed. In this regard, the Court reiterates its previous holding that the Respondent State’s withdrawal of its Declaration on 25 March 2020 has no effect on the present Application, insofar as the said withdrawal took effect after the Application had been filed with the Court.
The Court finds that it has temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations were committed after the Respondent State had become a Party to the Protocol.
The Court declares that it has territorial jurisdiction insofar as the facts of the case and the alleged violations took place on the Respondent State’s territory.
In view of the foregoing, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.

The Respondent State raises (A) objections to admissibility not provided for either in the Charter or the Rules, and (B) objections based on admissibility requirements provided for by the instruments referenced. In line with its jurisprudence, the Court will examine the said objections sequentially, if necessary.
The Respondent State contends that the Application is (i) moot and (ii) that it is, furthermore, foreclosed by the principle of res judicata.

The Respondent State contends that, by its judgment on reparations of 28 November 2019 in Application No. 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin, the Court already fully redressed the prejudice allegedly suffered by COMON SA, of which the Applicants are shareholders.

It argues that, in that judgment, the Court, inter alia, awarded the Applicants the sum of 4,359,661,765 CFA francs as reparation for the loss of profits suffered by COMON SA, 1,960,526,692 CFA francs for the depreciation of the Applicant’s shares in COMON SA and SOCOTRAC SARL, and 30,000,000,000 CFA francs for the loss of investment opportunities in the oil sector.
The Respondent State contends that the Court also expressly awarded the Applicants reparation for moral prejudice.

It considers that the Applicants have therefore already been ‘compensated’ by the Court in respect of their relationship with COMON SA and Mr AJAVON, such that a separate action seeking reparation for prejudice arising from the same situation lacks merit.
Consequently, the Respondent State prays the Court to declare the present Application moot and dismiss it.

The Applicants aver that the judgment of 28 November 2019 redressed the prejudice suffered by Mr Sébastien Germain AJAVON, in particular in respect of loss of profits and the depreciation of his shares in COMON SA and SOCOTRAC SARL.

They aver that the said judgment did not take into account the full extent of the prejudice suffered by COMON SA, given that this Court, as a human and peoples’ rights court, can in principle only hear cases concerning violations of the rights of individuals, groups of individuals or peoples, upon referral by the entities and persons enumerated under Article 5 of the Protocol. Therefore, it cannot adjudicate violations of the rights of other legal persons governed by private or public law.

The Applicants allege that the Court has yet to award them reparation for the loss of profits and the depreciation of the shares in COMON SA and SOCOTRAC Sarl, companies of which they are shareholders. They aver that the Court instead awarded them reparation for moral prejudice.

The Applicants argue that, under international law, the term “moral prejudice” encompasses the suffering and prejudice caused to the direct victim, the distress caused to their relatives, and the change in the living conditions of the victim and their family, whilst the victim is still alive.
They assert that moral prejudice does not include prejudice resulting in financial loss, so that the present Application is fully meritorious. They therefore argue that the objection be dismissed.

The Court recalls that in its judgment on reparations of 28 November 2019 in Application No. 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin, it found several violations of Mr. Sébastien Germain Ajavon’s rights, whereupon it awarded him reparation for loss of profits and the depreciation of shares personally, in his capacity as the applicant in Application No. 013/2017. The said compensation cannot be interpreted as having remedied the financial losses specific to all other COMON SA shareholders.

The Court notes in the present case that the Applicants, in their individual capacities, contend that their rights guaranteed by Articles 7 and 14 of the Charter were violated, due in particular to the depreciation of their own shares in COMON SA, the alleged loss of profits by that company, the seizure of their personal bank accounts, and the failure to implement the judgment in question.

The instant Application therefore raises a separate issue concerning the possible existence of specific financial harm suffered by persons other than Mr. Sébastien Ajavon, who allege a separate violation of their property rights resulting from measures taken by the Respondent State.

The Court therefore finds that the Applicants have a legal interest to have their claims based on the alleged violations examined and, if necessary, to seek reparation for any financial harm that they may have personally suffered.

Consequently, the Court finds that the judgment of 28 November 2019 in Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. the Republic of Benin neither exhausted the autonomous property rights invoked by the Applicants nor repaired the full extent of the prejudice they claim to have personally suffered.

The present Application therefore has its own distinct subject-matter, separate from the subject-matter of the judgment on reparations in Application No. 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin.
Accordingly, the Court dismisses the objection to admissibility based on the Application being moot.

The Respondent State contends that the Applicants request the Court to also grant them reparation for the prejudice allegedly suffered by Mr Sébastien Ajavon, so that the effects of the decisions rendered in that case inure to their benefit.

It contends that, under international law, judicial decisions carry the authority of res judicata, which, however, is relative. Res judicata authority means that states are obliged to comply with final judgments delivered in disputes to which they were parties, and only in respect of matters that have actually been decided. Citing the judgment of the European Court of Human Rights of 8 July 1980 in X v. Switzerland, the Respondent State contends that the Court’s decisions, although rendered as a court of last resort, only affect the parties to the proceedings.

The Respondent State argues that in the present case, the Applicants seek to rely on the Court’s judgment of 28 November 2019 on the Application No. 013/2017 – Ajavon v. Benin. However, that judgment, which is subject to relative res judicata, cannot benefit them as they were not parties to the proceedings. It concludes that the Application is inadmissible.

The Applicants aver that they do not request the Court to automatically accord them the benefits accruing from the operative part of the judgment in Ajavon v. Benin, nor to make them beneficiaries of the reparations awarded in 2019 in lieu of Mr Ajavon.

They assert that the human rights violations committed against Mr Ajavon, as established by the judgment on the merits of 29 March 2019 and the judgment on reparations of 28 November 2019, led to the demise of COMON SA.

They submit that COMON SA’s bankruptcy affected their own economic interests as shareholders. They therefore rely on the judgments handed down in Application 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin as factual and legal particulars establishing the international liability of the Respondent State and the causal link between the violations already found and the financial losses inflicted on them.

They aver that whilst res judicata effect is relative as regards the obligation to implement the operative part of the judgment, the interpretative and normative scope of the Court’s judgments may nevertheless be taken into account in other cases involving the same State, provided that the applicant establishes direct and personal prejudice.

Finally, they contend that the Respondent State’s failure to implement the judgments rendered in favour of Mr Ajavon exacerbated COMON SA’s situation and, consequently, their own situation, so that they were entitled to file a separate application with the Court for violation of their rights.

The Court recalls its settled jurisprudence that the principle of res judicata is predicated on the fulfilment of three cumulative requirements, namely, identity of the parties, identity of claims, and the existence of a prior decision on the merits.
In the present case, the Court notes that the Applicants in the present Application and those in Application 013/2017 are not the same.

In view of the cumulative nature of the requirements, and without it being necessary to examine the requirements relating to the identity requests and the existence of a prior decision on the merits, the Court finds that the objection lacks merit. Consequently, the Court dismisses it.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides that “the Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter”.
Rule 50(1) of the Rules provides, “the Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an application filed before it in accordance with the Charter, […] the Protocol and these Rules”.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which essentially restates Article 56 of the Charter, provides that: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter, c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union, d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged, f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter.

The Respondent State raises three objections to the admissibility of the Application based on the Application being incompatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the Charter (i), the failure to exhaust local remedies (ii), and failure to file the Application within a reasonable time (iii). The Court will examine these objections successively before ruling on the other admissibility requirements, if necessary.

The Respondent State submits that the Court has jurisdiction to hear only applications that clearly allege violations of the rights enshrined in the Charter. It considers that an application which fails to do so is incompatible with the Charter, having regard to the African Commission’s Communication No. 13/88 of 7 April 1994 and Communication No. 35/89 of 27 April 1994.

It contends that, in the present case, the Applicants merely hold themselves out as shareholders of a company of which Mr Sébastien Ajavon was the managing director and seek to be accorded the benefits of a decision made in favour of the latter. They do not in any way allege violation of their human rights by the Respondent State.

The Respondent State asserts that the present Application does not contain any specific allegations of human rights violations attributable to the Respondent State, but rather concerns a mere private dispute between shareholders, so that the Court should decline jurisdiction.
The Applicants pray the Court to dismiss the objection, seeing as, in their Application, they allege violation of their rights protected by the Charter.

The Court notes that the Respondent State’s objection to jurisdiction based on the Application being incompatible with the African Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union suggests that the Application concerns claims, rights or situations that are not covered by the Charter and the mechanisms under the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

The Court notes in the present case that the Applicants’ requests seek to protect their rights guaranteed by the Charter. Furthermore, one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, as set out in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. Furthermore, the Application does not contain any request that is incompatible with the Constitutive Act.
The Court therefore considers that the Application is consistent with the Constitutive Act and the Charter and that it meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Respondent State contends that, in line with the principle of subsidiarity, an applicant must have exhausted available local remedies before bringing a case before an international human rights court, by first raising, in substance, before domestic courts the complaints which he intends to bring before an international court. In this regard, it cites the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights in Guzzardi v. Italy, Azinas v. Cyprus, Selmouni v. France, Kudła v. Poland.

The Respondent State argues that this requirement seeks to afford the sovereign state the opportunity to prevent or remedy the violations alleged within its domestic legal system, before being called to account at the international level.

The Respondent State contends that the Commission has already clarified the scope of the rule of exhaustion of local remedies, which applies where judicial remedies exist, are effective and are not subject to the discretion of public authorities. It emphasises, in this regard, that in the case of Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania, the Commission clarified that this requirement is intended, in particular, to apprise the State concerned of the violations alleged so that it may remedy them.

The Respondent State further submits that, in line with the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, in particular in the case of Portu Juanenea and Sarasola Yarzabal v. Spain of 13 February 2018, applicants must make normal use of the available and sufficient legal remedies to obtain redress.

The Respondent State asserts that, in the present case, the Applicants merely claim that the Respondent State’s failure to implement the judgments delivered by the African Court in Application No. 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin constitutes irrefutable proof that there is no available and effective local remedy capable of redress.

In its view, article 114 of the Benin Constitution establishes the Constitutional Court as the highest court in matters of fundamental rights and civil liberties, such that it is a relevant, accessible and effective local remedy for human rights protection.
The Respondent State observes, however, that the Applicants did not bring any of the complaints they now raise before this Court before any Beninese court.
Consequently, the Respondent State prays the Court to declare the Application inadmissible.
The Applicants aver that the exhaustion of local remedies implies, in particular, that the available legal remedies must be effective.

The Applicants assert that the Respondent State’s persistent failure to comply with this Court’s judgments in Application No. 013/2017 – Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin is a perfect illustration that an appeal to the Constitutional Court stands no chance of affording them redress for the prejudice suffered.
They pray the Court to dismiss the objection.

The Court recalls that, under Article 56(5) of the Charter, applications are admissible provided that they “are sent after exhaustion of local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged”. Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules of Court restates this requirement.

The Court has held, with regard to the exhaustion of local remedies, that the mere existence of a remedy does not automatically meet the requirements of the rule; the remedy must also be effective, sufficient and offer prospects of success or be capable of remedying the situation in dispute.

The Court also emphasizes, with regard to the effectiveness of local remedies, that it is the Applicant’s responsibility to take all necessary steps to exhaust, or at least attempt to exhaust, local remedies. It is not sufficient for an applicant, without evidence, to merely cast doubt on the effectiveness of such remedies.
The Court further notes that the determination of whether all remedies were exhausted is made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the circumstances of each case.

In the present case, the Court notes that the Applicants allege violation of their property rights as a result of, on the one hand, their status as COMON SA shareholders and, on the other hand, the seizure of their personal bank accounts.
The Court will determine whether local remedies were available and effective with respect to these two aspects.

With regard, first, to the harm that the Applicants claim to have personally suffered as a result of the Respondent State’s actions against COMON SA, the Court observes that the Respondent State’s domestic law on liability, specifically Articles 1382 and 1383 of the Civil Code as applicable to the facts of the case, avails persons who consider themselves injured by the acts of a third party, whether a private individual or the State, an avenue to bring an action for reparations before a competent civil court.

The Court further notes that, from a procedural standpoint, Law No. 2008- 07 of 28 February 2011, establishing the Code of Civil, Commercial, Social, Administrative, and Accounting Procedure, which was applicable at the time of the events, expressly provides for such an action in article 48, which stipulates that a claim for reparations for damages may be brought before the court of the jurisdiction where the harmful incident occurred.

The Court observes that such a remedy, available to any natural or legal person who claims to have suffered harm, including in his or her capacity as a shareholder of a company whose interests may have been affected by the actions of the Respondent State, is an ordinary judicial remedy capable, if successful, of repairing the alleged harm.

The Court finds that it was therefore incumbent upon the Applicants to bring such an action before the competent court of first instance, which they do not show that they did, or even attempted to do.

Second, with regard to the seizure of their personal bank accounts, the Court notes that the Uniform Act on the Organization of Simplified Collection Procedures and Enforcement Measures of 10 April 1998 (AUPSRVE), which is binding on the Respondent State as a State Party to the Treaty on the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa (OHADA Treaty), establishes a specific remedy available to any person who considers that his/her assets have been unlawfully seized.

The Court notes that, under Article 49 of the said Uniform Act, any dispute concerning an enforcement measure or a provisional seizure falls within the jurisdiction of a judge hearing emergency matters, or a judge delegated by the same for that purpose, whose decision is itself subject to appeal within fifteen days.

With regard more specifically to the seizure of bank accounts, the Court notes that article 170(1) entitles a debtor whose assets have been seized to contest the seizure, by way of a summons, before a competent court within one month of being notified of the seizure; such an objection may specifically seek to have the contested measure lifted by a judge.
The Court considers that the procedures set forth in the OHADA Uniform Act are integrated in the judicial system of the Respondent State and therefore constitute local remedies.

The Court notes that this remedy seeking to lift the seizure, which is automatically available to any individual whose bank accounts have been seized, is both available and accessible and, if successful, is likely to vacate the disputed measure.

The Court notes, however, that the Applicants neither demonstrate that they filed cases before the competent court to have the seizure of their personal bank accounts lifted, nor do they provide specific reasons that prevented them from doing so.

It follows from the foregoing that the Applicants were afforded available and effective local remedies—both with regard to the violations related to their status as COMON SA shareholders and with regard to the seizure of their personal bank accounts, which remedies they neither exhausted nor even attempted to exhaust.

In light of the foregoing, the Court finds it unnecessary to examine the Respondent State’s objection to admissibility based on non-exhaustion of local remedies, in particular, the remedy before the Constitutional Court.
Consequently, the Court finds that the Applicants did not exhaust the available local remedies, so that the Application does not meet the requirement of Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

Having found that the Application does not comply with Article 56(5) of the Charter restated in Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, and recalling that the admissibility requirements are cumulative, the Court finds that there is no need to rule on the other admissibility requirements under Article 56 of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50(2) (a), (c), (d), (f), and (g) of the Rules.
Accordingly, the Court declares the Application inadmissible.
The Applicants pray the Court to order the Respondent State to bear the costs. *
The Respondent State does not submit on costs. ***
Under Rule 32(2) of the Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.
In the present case, the Court notes that proceedings before it are free of charge.

Furthermore, the Applicants do not produce proof in support of the costs they claim to have incurred in the present proceedings. The cheques and flight tickets in the name of Moustafa Issiaka, their Counsel, that were submitted do not conclusively establish a link with the present case.
In the circumstances, the Court considers that there is no reason to depart from the principle laid down in the aforementioned provision and therefore orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction: i. Dismisses the objection to material jurisdiction; ii. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility: iii. Upholds the objection to admissibility and finds that the Application does not meet the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules; iv. Declares the Application inadmissible. On costs: v. Declares that each Party shall bear its own costs.

Mr. Brahim Ben Mohamed Ben Brahim Belgeith (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”), is a Tunisian national and a lawyer residing in France with his office in Montfleury, Tunisia. He alleges violation of the fundamental rights of Tunisians by the Republic of Tunisia, following its withdrawal of the Declaration filed in accordance with Article 34(6) of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”).

The Application is filed against the Republic of Tunisia (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as the “Charter”) on 16 March 1983, and to the Protocol on 21 August 2007. It deposited, on 16 April 2017, the Declaration under Article 34(6) of the Protocol by virtue of which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive cases from individuals and Non- Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”). On 7 March 2025, the Respondent State deposited, with the African Union Commission, an instrument withdrawing the said Declaration. The Court has held that this withdrawal has no bearing on pending cases and new cases filed before 8 March 2026, which is the day on which the withdrawal took effect, being a period of one year after its deposit.

The Applicant alleges that the President of the Respondent State, Mr. Kais Saied, invoked the exceptional circumstances based on Chapter 80 of the Respondent State’s Constitution of 2014, in particular, Presidential Decree No. 117/2021 by virtue of which the President assumed a position above the Constitution and seized the executive and legislative powers. According to the Applicant, this Court has ruled that the exceptional measures taken were unconstitutional and it issued a decision nullifying those measures, ordered a return to constitutional democracy, and the establishment of a constitutional Court.

The Applicant also alleges that the Respondent State has not complied with the decision of this Court but instead it has issued more orders that undermine the democratic process. It is also alleged that the Respondent State promulgated a new constitution in 2022 which consolidated the authority of the President of the Respondent State.

The Applicant also alleges that the Respondent State withdrew the Declaration of acceptance of the jurisdiction of this Court, as provided for under Article 34(06) of the Protocol, which constitutes a violation of number of human rights as outlined in his Application before this Court.
The main Application, together with a request for provisional measures, were filed on 7 July 2025.

On 21 July 2025, the main Application, together with the request for provisional measures, were served on the Respondent State, which was granted 45 days to respond to the request for provisional measures and 90 days to respond to the main Application. At the expiration of these deadlines, the Respondent State had not filed any Responses.
On 3 December 2025, the Respondent State was reminded of the expiration of the deadlines and was granted an additional 30 days to file its Responses but it did not do so.
Pleadings were closed on 25 February 2026, and the Parties were duly informed.
On 6 July 2026, the Court issued an order dismissing the Applicant’s request for provisional measures.
On 18 September 2026, the Respondent State filed its Response to the Main Application. IV.

None of the Parties request for the reopening of pleadings. The Respondent State filed its Response to the Main Application out of time, without however expressly requesting for reopening of pleadings. ***

Rule 46(3) of the Rules provides that “The Court has the discretion to determine whether or not to reopen pleadings”. Furthermore, Rule 90 of the Rules provides that “Nothing in these Rules shall limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to adopt such procedure or decisions as may be necessary to meet the ends of justice”.
The Court considers that, in the present case, the interests of justice require that the Respondent State be permitted to submit its Response to the Main Application.

Accordingly, in the exercise of its discretionary power and in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the Court considers that it is proper to deem the Respondent State’s Response as having been duly filed. The Court therefore decides to reopen the proceedings and to serve the Respondent State’s Response on the Applicant, granting him a period of 45 days to submit his Reply thereto, should he so wishes.

For the above reasons, THE COURT Unanimously, i. Decides to reopen pleadings in Application No. 004/2025 – Brahim Ben Mohamed Ben Brahim Belgeith v. Republic of Tunisia; and ii. Orders the Applicant to submit his Reply to the Respondent State’s Response, if he so wishes, within 45 days of receipt of this Order.
Whilst I agree with all the grounds and the operative part of the above judgment, I nevertheless disagree on one point, namely, the right to be triedwithin a reasonable time.

I regret that I am unable to endorse the majority’s holding that the Republic of Malawi did not violate the Applicants’ (Kambeyo Ka-Kaunda and Emmie Chenda Mkandawire) right to be tried within a reasonable time, a right guaranteed by Article 7(1)(d) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (‘the Charter’). Indeed, in paragraph (v) of the operative part, the Court: Holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to a fair trial with respect to the right to be tried within a reasonable time as provided under Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter

I would like to emphasise upfront that I agree with the Court’s observation that the assessment of whether proceedings were conducted within a reasonable time: requires an examination of the entire record of domestic proceedings, including the sequence of hearings, adjournments, and procedural steps taken by the parties. This assessment must be carried out on a case-by-case basis as: The Court’s analysis takes into account, in particular, the complexity of the case or of the proceedings relating to it, the conduct of the parties themselves and that of the judicial authorities in order to determine whether the latter “has been passive or clearly negligent.

This approach is consistent with the Court’s established jurisprudence, notably in the judgments in Mariam Kouma and Ousmane Diabaté v. Republic of Mali, Beneficiaries of the late Norbert Zongo and Others v. Burkina Faso, and Wilfred Onyango Nganyi and 9 Others v. United Republic of Tanzania.

I shall focus on two issues presently, namely, (I) the manifestly unreasonable length of the proceedings in light of the requirements of a fair trial, on the one hand, and (II) the State’s responsibility for judicial malfunctions and the effectiveness of the right to be tried within a reasonable time, on the other.

I disagree with the majority as to how these principles apply to the facts of the present case. In my view, proceedings which took more than nine years to reach a conclusion in a relatively straightforward land dispute, and which, from the time they were brought until their final resolution, spanned a period of nearly twelve years, cannot be regarded as having been conducted within a reasonable time in the absence of particularly serious and concrete justification. I therefore find a violation of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter.
Neither (A) the nature of the dispute nor (B) the circumstances thereof can justify such a delay.

Article 7(1) of the Charter provides that “Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard”. This guarantee expressly includes, in subparagraph (d), “The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal”. The reasonableness of the time is therefore not an administrative or secondary consideration. It is unequivocally a treaty guarantee of a fair trial.

The Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Aid in Africa, adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights in 2003, confirm this requirement. They provide, amongst the essential elements of a fair hearing, a person’s right to have his/her rights and obligations determined ‘without undue delay’ and with adequate notice and the grounds for decisions. These Principles and Guidelines were specifically drafted to reinforce the guarantees of the Charter, in compliance with international standards on fair trial.

This requirement is of particular importance in civil proceedings. The right to a fair trial would be considerably undermined if a person were able to bring a case before a court but had to wait forever before their rights and obligations were finally determined.

Delayed justice may, in practice, lose a substantial part of its effectiveness. In a land dispute such as the one in the present case, prolonged uncertainty over the title to the property directly affects the legal certainty of the Parties. It may also have significant economic and financial consequences. The right to be tried within a reasonable time is specifically intended to prevent litigants from remaining in this state of unduly prolonged uncertainty.

The Court rightly points out that there is no standard duration which, on its own, would lead to a finding of a violation of Article 7(1)(d). It is nevertheless important to distinguish between two non-equivalent propositions. The first is that a specific duration does not automatically constitute a violation. The second would be to consider that an exceptionally long period remains reasonable if the applicant cannot precisely identify the cause of each period of inactivity.

I do not believe that the Court’s jurisprudence supports this second proposition. The absence of a numerical threshold does not mean that the duration of the proceedings is of no legal effect. On the contrary, the longer the duration, the more convincing the justification required from the State for same must be.

Proceedings lasting a few months may be reasonable in almost all circumstances. Proceedings lasting several years already call for closer scrutiny. Proceedings lasting more than nine years in a relatively straightforward case require, in my view, a particularly rigorous justification. This is not a matter of introducing an automatic nine-year threshold into the Court’s jurisprudence.

It is about recognising an obvious principle arising from the very requirement of ‘reasonableness’: an exceptional duration calls for an exceptional justification. In the present case, such justification has not been provided.

The first relevant criterion is the complexity of the case. The judgment itself describes the case as a ‘straightforward land dispute’ and acknowledges that the duration of nine years, five months and twenty-nine days ‘appears to be too long’ given the nature of the case. This finding should, in my view, have led to a more rigorous examination of the time taken. Nothing in the evidence submitted to the Court establishes that the case involved exceptional factual or legal complexity that might account for its duration.

This was not a case involving a very large number of parties, an exceptional volume of evidence, particularly complex expert reports or novel legal issues of exceptional difficulty. It essentially entailed determining the respective rights of the Parties in respect of a piece of land.

The nature of the dispute therefore constitutes a factor that strongly supports a finding of an unreasonable delay. It is worth recalling here the approach taken by the European Court of Human Rights in Zimmermann and Steiner v. Switzerland. In that case, the Court considered that nearly three and a half years before one level of jurisdiction already constituted a considerable length of time warranting careful scrutiny. It noted that the case was not particularly complex and that the applicants did not contribute to the delay. More significantly still, in Baggetta v. Italy, the European Court declined to accept that structural difficulties within the judicial system could justify a duration exceeding nine years.

This jurisprudence is obviously not a benchmark directly applicable to the Charter. It nevertheless illustrates a widely held view of what constitutes a reasonable time: where a straightforward case remains pending for a particularly long period, the State must provide a convincing explanation. In the present case, we are faced with a duration more than twice as long as that which had already been deemed considerable at a single level of jurisdiction.

The dates set out in the judgment are particularly significant. Proceedings before the High Court were brought on 20 April 2010 and the said court rendered its judgment on 9 June 2014, that is, a period of four years, one month and twenty days. The appeal to the Supreme Court of Appeal was lodged on 22 July 2015 and the apex court rendered its judgment on 2 August 2016, that is, a period of one year and eleven days.

As regards the review application, it was filed in December 2017 and received by the Supreme Court of Appeal in June 2019, whilst the final review judgment was not delivered until 6 April 2022. In all, it took nine years, five months and twenty-nine days. However, it should also be noted that the Court’s own temporal jurisdiction is defined in the judgment as running from 20 April 2010 to 6 April 2022. This period corresponds to nearly twelve years.

I do not dispute that there may be delays between certain procedural stages which should not be attributed to the State. However, these periods of delay must be identified and justified; they cannot simply be omitted from the calculation on the grounds that their cause cannot be determined from the record.

In my view, herein lies one of the main difficulties with the majority’s reasoning. The absence of information regarding the cause of a delay does not render that delay legally irrelevant. It means, precisely, that the Court does not know why the delayed occurred.
However, when faced with such exceptionally lengthy proceedings, this uncertainty should not be resolved to the detriment of the right guaranteed by Article 7(1)(d).

The Applicants stated that the High Court adjourned the case on eleven occasions and that the Supreme Court of appeal adjourned the hearing on thirteen occasions. I recognise that these assertions must be treated with caution where they are not supported by the full court records. However, they cannot simply be ignored. Their significance must be assessed in conjunction with the overall duration of the proceedings.

Eleven adjournments at first instance and thirteen on appeal constitute, at the very least, a serious indication requiring an explanation. If these adjournments were attributable to the Applicants, it was for the State to establish this. If they resulted from circumstances beyond the Parties’ control, it was also incumbent on the State to explain their nature. If they resulted from difficulties inherent in the functioning of the courts, such difficulties then fall within the State’s institutional responsibility. In none of these scenarios does the mere absence of any mention in the record allow the conclusion that the duration was reasonable.

The judgment partly justifies the unduly prolonged proceedings by noting that the Applicants and the State exhausted all domestic legal remedies. I do not consider that this circumstance, in itself, justifies the delay.
The exercise of local remedies is a procedural guarantee afforded to individuals. It cannot subsequently be used to subvert the protection afforded them under Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter.

A distinction must be drawn between the existence of multiple-layered jurisdiction and the slowness of proceedings at each of those levels. The fact that a case may be heard by several courts explains why it may involve several decisions. It does not explain why each of those decisions takes several years.

In other words: the exhaustion of legal remedies explains the existence of multiple decisions; it does not explain the slowness with which each of these decisions is delivered. A person who brings a legal action provided for under domestic law does not, in so doing, waive their right to have that action examined within a reasonable time. Moreover, a contrary interpretation would create a paradoxical effect: the more a litigant makes use of the judicial mechanisms made available to them by the State, the greater the risk that they would lose the benefit of the guarantee of a reasonable time. Such an approach would be difficult to reconcile with the right to an effective remedy.

The African Commission’s decision in Odjouoriby Cossi Paul v. Benin is particularly relevant. This case concerned a civil dispute relating to property. The African Commission expressly reiterated that Article 7(1)(d) guarantees the right to be tried within a reasonable time and found that the proceedings before the court of appeal had been unduly prolonged. It concluded that the delay was contrary to Article 7(1)(d) and called on Benin to take the necessary measures to ensure that the appeal was heard as quickly as possible, as well as to pay compensation for the damages resulting from the unduly delayed proceedings.

The decision referenced is of particular significance in the present case for two reasons. Firstly, it confirms that the requirement of a reasonable time fully applies to civil and property proceedings. Secondly, it confirms that undue prolongation of legal proceedings in itself constitutes a violation of Article 7(1)(d), irrespective of the final outcome of the dispute.

The jurisprudence of this Court is consistent with this approach. In Wilfred Onyango Nganyi and 9 others v. the United Republic of Tanzania, the Court found a violation of the right to be tried within a reasonable time and ordered the State to take all necessary measures to expedite and conclude the judicial proceedings in question. In that case, the Court placed particular emphasis on the conduct of the judicial authorities and their duty of diligence. It follows from this jurisprudence that the decisive criterion is not simply whether proceedings ultimately resulted in a decision but more importantly whether they were concluded within a timeframe that meets with the requirements of a fair trial.

In the present case, the Applicants cannot be faulted for (A) the shortcomings of the national judicial system. Furthermore, (B) the effectiveness of the guarantee of a reasonable time and the need to find a violation of Article 7(1)(d).

The judgment appears to consider that the absence of court records and procedural documents prevents a determination as to whether the delays are attributable to the State. I consider that this approach confuses two distinct issues: establishing the facts and assignment of individual responsibility.
Assigning the State’s international responsibility does not require the Court to identify the specific judge, court registrar, administrative department or authority responsible for each day’s delay.

This principle is clearly illustrated by the judgment of the European Court in Zimmermann and Steiner v. Switzerland. In that case, the Strasbourg Court expressly stated that it was not required to determine which specific national authority was responsible for the violation: the only relevant determination was that of the State’s international responsibility.

This approach strikes me as particularly relevant in the context of the present case. The right guaranteed by Article 7(1)(d) is a right of the individual vis-à-vis the State as a whole. The individual need not know whether his or her case was left unresolved in a judge’s chambers, at the court registry, in a court division, in the pre-trial preparation office or within the judicial administration. What matters from the point of view of international responsibility is that the State’s judicial system failed to ensure that his or her case was determined within a reasonable time.

Whether the time taken is reasonable is therefore not measured solely by the ability to identify individual fault; it is measured by the objective capacity of the judicial system to deliver justice within a timeframe consistent with the nature and stakes of the dispute.

This, in my view, is the most problematic aspect of the reasoning set out in the judgment. It notes that the Applicants did not produce all the internal files, in particular the records of adjournments and the procedural timetables. It concludes from this that it is unable to verify the precise causes of the delays or whether they are attributable to the State.

However, the documents in question are precisely those emanating from the internal workings of domestic courts. There is therefore an objective asymmetry between the Parties. The Applicants are the users of the judicial system. The State is its organiser.

Court registers, adjournment orders, court schedules and administrative documents relating to the handling of cases are, by their very nature, documents that are primarily under the control of national judicial institutions.

It would therefore be excessively formalistic to require the Applicants to establish, by means of documents to which they do not necessarily have access, every period of inactivity within the judicial system.

I am not proposing to reverse the burden of proof as a general rule in all cases concerning reasonable time. I consider, however, that where an applicant establishes an exceptionally long duration in a straightforward case, and where the State fails to provide any explanation to justify that delay, the absence of internal documents should not automatically lead to the rejection of the complaint.

The opposite line of reasoning would create a paradoxical situation: the more incomplete or inaccessible court records are, the more difficult it would become to demonstrate a violation resulting precisely from the functioning of the judicial system. This would amount to treating the inadequacy of court records as a mitigating circumstance for the State. Such a consequence does not, in my view, appear compatible with the object and purpose of Article 7(1)(d).

This consideration is reinforced by a circumstance specific to the present case: the Respondent State does not advance any arguments on the merits. The judgment expressly notes this. The State’s failure to do so certainly does not preclude the Court from examining the Applicants’ allegations rigorously.
Neither should it be regarded as legally irrelevant when the State is precisely the party best placed to explain the functioning of its own judicial system.

The State could have provided an explanation for the many years that elapsed between the various stages of the proceedings. It could have set out the reasons for the adjournments. It could have established that certain delays were due to the Applicants’ conduct. It could have invoked particular complexity, a temporary and exceptional backlog in the courts, procedural difficulties or any other objective circumstance. It did not do so.

There is therefore no explanation in the record from the State that would allow an objectively exceptional duration to be regarded as reasonable. In these circumstances, I consider that the Court was required to assess, taken together, the State’s silence, the overall duration, the simplicity of the dispute and the available information concerning the adjournments.

Another consideration strikes me as essential. Even where a delay is linked to an overload on the courts, lack of resources, poor organisation of the court registries or administrative difficulties, it does not cease to be attributable to the State under international law.

In the Zimmermann and Steiner judgment referred to above, the ECHR specifically examined the argument concerning the court’s excessive workload. It concluded that the difficulties encountered by the court could not, after a certain period, be regarded as temporary and could not deprive the applicants of their right to be tried within a reasonable time. It also emphasised that it was not for it to determine which national authority was responsible: the relevant responsibility lay with the State.

This approach is particularly important for international human rights courts. International law does not permit the State to shirk its treaty obligations by invoking the organisational failings of its own institutions. The State must organise its judicial system in such a way as to enable the courts to meet the requirements arising from fundamental rights.
A litigant cannot be forced to endure for years the consequences of the shortcomings of the judicial system on which they rely to have their rights determined.

I also consider that excessive fragmentation of the proceedings should be avoided. The Court must, of course, examine the various stages of the proceedings. However, such an analysis is only meaningful if it enables an assessment of the overall duration of the justice administered to the litigant.

The judgment itself states that the assessment must cover the case as a whole, including the sequence of hearings, adjournments and procedural steps. This holistic approach must also be applied to the conclusion. It is therefore not sufficient merely to note that each level of jurisdiction operated in accordance with its own rules and procedures.

Compliance with procedural rules does not, in itself, justify the time taken to implement them. A procedure may be legally sound at every stage and yet excessively lengthy overall. Procedural regularity and judicial promptness are two distinct requirements of a fair trial. One cannot override the other.

The duration of the review proceedings is of particular importance. The Applicants exercised a remedy provided for under domestic law. This circumstance cannot be used against them. The review proceedings nevertheless dragged on for several years, until 6 April 2022.

It should also be noted that the Applicants alleged that they did not receive a signed or certified copy of certain decisions and neither did they receive a legible or official version of the 6 April 2022 decision. The judgment echoes these concerns, as well as the requirements of national procedural rules regarding the formalisation and certification of decisions. This is not merely a formal matter. The reasonable time limit must be assessed in light of the litigant’s actual ability to obtain an effective and intelligible determination of their rights.

A delayed decision, the grounds for which are not made available to the litigant in an official and intelligible form, does not fully produce the effect expected of a judicial decision. On the contrary, it prolongs legal uncertainty.
The various international sources cited in the judgment converge on the same principles.

At the African level, Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter expressly guarantees the right to be tried within a reasonable time. The African Commission, in the case of Odjouoriby Cossi Paul v. Benin, ( ) applied this guarantee to a civil dispute and found a violation due to the undue prolongation of the appeal proceedings.
The Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and to Legal Aid in Africa also enshrine the right to a determination of rights and obligations ‘without undue delay’.

At the level of the African Court, the judgment in Wilfred Onyango Nganyi confirms that the conduct of the judicial authorities and their diligence are determining factors in assessing what constitutes a reasonable time.

At the European level, the Grand Chamber judgment in Frydlender v. France established the classic criteria relating to the complexity of the case, the applicant’s conduct, the conduct of the authorities and what is at stake for the person concerned.

In the judgment in Zimmermann and Steiner v. Switzerland, the European Court held that nearly three and a half years before a single court already was a considerable length of time warranting thorough scrutiny, and found a violation despite the difficulties encountered by the court.

These treaty systems are certainly not identical. Nevertheless, they reflect a common fundamental principle: the right to a fair trial requires the State to organise its judicial system in such a way that the rights of litigants are determined within a timeframe that remains compatible with the nature and stakes of the dispute.
If we apply the criteria established by the Court’s jurisprudence, the outcome seems clear to me.
Firstly, the complexity of the case. There is nothing to suggest that the land dispute is sufficiently complex to justify proceedings of this duration.

Second is the conduct of the Applicants. There is nothing in the record to suggest that they engaged in delay tactics or that they were responsible for a substantial part of the delay. The judgment itself notes that there is no evidence to suggest that the parties deliberately obstructed the proceedings.

Thirdly, the conduct of the judicial authorities. The proceedings lasted four years before the High Court, over a year before the Supreme Court at the initial stage, and several further years during the review stage. Added to this is the significant number of adjournments alleged by the Applicants.

Fourthly, the subject matter of the dispute. The case concerned the determination of property rights in respect of a plot of land, meaning that the prolonged uncertainty was not without consequences for the Applicants.
Fifthly, the justification for the delay. The Respondent State does not state any grounds to explain the length of the proceedings.
Taken together, these factors clearly point to a finding of a violation.

I am particularly concerned about the potential implications of the reasoning adopted in this judgment. If, in a straightforward case that lasted more than nine years, the Court refuses to find a violation on the grounds that the Applicant does not produce all the documents necessary to explain each period of delay, the threshold of protection afforded by Article 7(1)(d) risks becoming excessively high.
This risk is all the greater given that the documents required to reconstruct the timeframes accurately are often produced and held by the State’s judicial institutions.

Article 7(1)(d) must not be interpreted in such a way as to make it practically impossible to establish a violation in cases where institutional failings result, precisely, in the poor preservation or limited accessibility of court documents.

On the contrary, an interpretation consistent with the effective purpose of the Charter requires that the Court be able to assess the overall duration of proceedings based on all the available evidence.
Where proceedings are found to have been exceptionally lengthy and there is no convincing explanation thereof, the Court must be able to draw the necessary treaty conclusions.
I recognise that there is not, and should not be, an automatic numerical threshold beyond which any proceedings become contrary to Article 7(1)(d).

However, the absence of such a threshold cannot lead to a duration of more than nine years in a relatively straightforward case being accepted as reasonable without requiring the State to provide a particularly convincing justification.

In the present case, the proceedings began on 20 April 2010 and were not finally resolved until 6 April 2022. The judgment itself records a cumulative duration of nine years, five months and twenty-nine days.

The judgment acknowledges that this duration may seem excessive for a simple land dispute. However, in my view, there are no exceptional circumstances to explain this duration. It has not been established that the Applicants caused the delays. The number of alleged adjournments is significant. The State does not provide any justification.
The documents that might explain the delays in detail are, for the most part, documents relating to the functioning of the domestic courts.
Finally, the exercise of legal remedies cannot be used to justify exceptionally lengthy proceedings.

The issue before the Court is therefore, in my view, less a question of whether each day’s delay can be attributed to a specific individual than whether, taken as a whole, the State’s judicial system administered justice to the Applicants within a reasonable time.

My answer is in the negative. For all these reasons, I consider that the duration of the domestic proceedings — nine years, five months and twentynine days according to the timelines set out in the judgment — was manifestly excessive in view of the nature of the dispute, its relative simplicity, the absence of evidence of delay tactics on the part of the Applicants, the significant number of alleged adjournments and the lack of justification provided by the Respondent State.

Above all, I consider that the absence, in the record submitted to the Court, of evidence enabling each period of delay to be precisely attributed cannot be used to exonerate the State when such evidence relates primarily to its own judicial system and when the Applicants themselves encountered difficulties in obtaining the relevant court documents.

The right to a fair trial would be deprived of part of its substance if a State were able to rely on the shortcomings of its own system for the preservation of and access to court records to evade liability arising from excessively lengthy proceedings.

In my view, Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter requires the State not only to provide access to a judge, but also to ensure that a judicial decision is delivered within a timeframe that is compatible with the requirement of effective justice. Judge Rafaâ Ben Achour Done at Arusha, this Twenty Fourth Day of September in the Year Two Thousand and Twenty-Six, the French text being authoritative.

The First Applicant, Kambeyo Ka-Kaunda, was a property consultant in Blantyre, Malawi, while the Second Applicant, Emmie Chenda Mkandawire was his business associate and a retired primary school teacher. The First and Second Applicants (hereinafter jointly referred to as “the Applicants”) are nationals of Malawi. They allege violations of the rights to a fair trial and property.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Malawi (hereinafter referred to as “Respondent State”). The Respondent State became party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 23 February 1990. Furthermore, the Respondent State became a party to the Protocol and deposited the Declaration required under Article 34(6) of the Protocol, accepting the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications filed by individuals and Non-Governmental Organizations with Observer Status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”) on 9 October 2008.

The Applicants aver that for over a period of 12 years they suffered violations of their rights arising from a property dispute in Blantyre. They allege that they assisted an associate, Profera Mtambalika, to obtain a title to land known as “Tittle number Ndirance 26”, and to register it in his name. In return for which Mtambalika was to transfer to them a portion of 2.2 hectares of that land. The Applicants submit that when Mtambalika breached the agreement by refusing to transfer the portion to them, they sought specific performance before the High Court of Malawi, on 20 April 2010.

The Applicants submit that on 9 June 2014, the High Court of Malawi dismissed their case in its entirety, even though neither Mtambalika nor his lawyer appeared at the hearings. Furthermore, the High Court of Malawi held that “there can be no specific performance where contracts are declared invalid due to the plaintiff’s misrepresentation”.

Dissatisfied with the High Court’s judgment, the Applicants on 22 July 2015, appealed to the Malawi Supreme Court of Appeal (MSCA) which, on 2 August 2016, dismissed the appeal with costs. The Applicants aver that despite multiple written requests to the Chief Justice, they never received a signed copy of the MSCA’s judgment.

On 30 October 2016, the Applicants filed a Notice of Motion for Review of the MSCA’s judgment. The MSCA dismissed the application for review on 6 April 2022. The Applicants submit that they never received the official copy of the review judgment despite several requests to the MSCA’s Registry. Eventually, the MSCA’s Registry provided them with illegible handwritten notes purporting to be a copy of the review judgment. In addition, they complain that the review proceedings were marred by procedural irregularities.
The Applicants filed the Application before this Court after their request to restore their case to the cause list of the MSCA remained unanswered for six months.

The Applicants allege the following violations: i. Article 7 on the right to a fair trial under the Charter, Article 2 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) on the following aspects: a. The right to due process: legal certainty; b. The right to a fair and public hearing; c. The right to defence; and d. The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court; ii. The right to property as guaranteed under Article 14 of the Charter.
On 17 October 2022, the Applicants filed the Application together with a request for legal aid.
On 2 December 2022, the Court granted the Applicants’ request for legal aid in accordance with Rule 31(2) of the Rules and assigned PALU to represent them.
On 21 March 2023, PALU submitted that the Applicants raised concerns about the First Applicant’s health and requested for a speedy consideration of the matter.

On 19 April 2024, PALU filed an amended Application, which was transmitted to the Respondent State on 3 May 2024, requesting it to file its list of its representatives and its Response by 2 June 2024 and 1 August 2024, respectively. At the expiry of these deadlines, the Respondent State did not respond.

On 19 and 21 August 2024, the Parties were informed that the Court had decided suo motu to grant an extension of time for the Respondent State to file its Response, failing which, the Court would proceed with the matter and render a judgment in default. At the expiry of this deadline, the Respondent State had neither filed its Response nor its list of representatives.

On 27 January 2026, the Applicants filed a request for expedited procedure substantiated with medical reports and a request for a judgment in default to be rendered at the 82 Ordinary Session of the Court.
Pleadings were closed on 20 March 2026, and the Parties were duly notified.

On 1 June 2026, the Parties were informed that the Court decided to reopen pleadings suo motu and transmitted the Applicants’ requests for expedited procedure and judgment in default to the Respondent State for its observations. The Respondent State had not filed any observations by the lapse of the deadline.
Pleadings were closed again on 24 June 2026, and the Parties were duly notified.

During its 82 Ordinary Session, having considered the request for expedited procedure on the ground of illness of the First Applicant, the Court decided to prioritise the consideration of this Application.

The Applicants pray the Court to make the following orders: i. A DECLARATION that the Respondent State violated Articles 7 and 14 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights; ii. A DECLARATION that the Respondent State violated Articles 2 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; iii. A DECLARATION that the Respondent State violated Articles 10 and 17 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; iv. AN ORDER requiring the Respondent State to compensate as follows: a. the sum of USD 1.6 million for material damages; and b. the sum of USD 5.6 million for moral damages; v. AN ORDER requiring the Respondent State to adopt constitutional, legislative, administrative, and other measures to remedy the violations of the rights of the Applicants, including presenting a signed version of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Appeal of 2 August 2016 and the formal decision of the Supreme Court of Appeal, dismissing Applicants’ application for review on 6 April 2022; vi. AN ORDER that the Respondent State make all necessary reforms/amendments/changes to ensure that cases are tried within a reasonable time, that the court records and judgments are accessible, and that the legal framework is clear and certain; vii. AN ORDER for costs in favour of the Applicants.
The Respondent State did not file any pleadings in respect of this Application and, therefore, did not make any prayers.
The Applicants filed various requests for a judgment in default. *
The Respondent State did not file any pleadings in this Application. ***

Rule 63(1) of the Rules provides as follows: Whenever a party does not appear before the Court or fails to defend its case within the period prescribed, the Court may, on the application of the other party, or on its own motion, enter a decision in default after it has satisfied itself that the defaulting party has been duly served with the Application and all other documents pertinent to the proceedings.

Rule 63(1) of the Rules sets out three conditions on which the Court may render judgment in default, namely: (i) the failure of one of the parties to appear before the Court or to defend its case within the prescribed time; (ii) the notification to the defaulting party of the application and all other documents pertinent to the proceedings; and (iii) a request made by the other party or the discretion of the Court.

With respect to the first condition relating to a party’s failure to appear or defend its case, the Court observes that on 3 May 2024, the Registry transmitted the Application to the Respondent State, which was granted 90 days to file its Response and 30 days to file the list of its representatives. Although the Respondent State acknowledged receipt of the Application on 21 August 2024, it did not file its Response despite two reminders sent on 19 and 21 August 2024. The Registry, in the two reminders, informed the Respondent State that should it fail to file its Response, the Court would decide the matter in default. The Court, therefore, finds that the first condition is satisfied.

With respect to the second condition that the defaulting party should be notified about the application and all pleadings, the Court observes that on 3 May 2024, the main Application and all supporting documents were duly served on the Respondent State, which acknowledged receipt by a letter dated 21 August 2024. The Respondent State was granted 90 days to file its Response, which it failed to do. Thereafter, the Respondent State was granted an additional 45 days to file its Response to the main Application, failing which the Court would render a judgment in default.

Furthermore, on 1 June 2026, the Registry transmitted the Order on the reopening of pleadings, the Applicants’ request for a judgment in default and for an expedited procedure, directing the Respondent State to file its response within 15 days. The Respondent State did not file any response.
In light of the above, the Court finds that the second condition is met given the Respondent State failed to file a defence despite being served with the Application and other pleadings on file.

Lastly, with regard to the third condition, namely, that the judgment in default is rendered either through a request by the other party or suo motu by the Court, the Court observes that the Applicants filed requests for judgment in default on several occasions in letters dated: 18 October 2024; 27 November 2024; 10 February 2025; 26 June 2025 and 27 January 2026, arguing that the Respondent State had been given sufficient time to defend itself. The Court therefore finds that the third condition is equally satisfied.
Based on the foregoing, the Court finds that the requirements under Rule 63 of the Rules are met, and accordingly decides to render the Judgment in default.

Pursuant to Article 3 of the Protocol: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instruments ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

Furthermore, Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “The Court shall conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction … of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules,” and rule on any objections thereto, if necessary.

Having found that there is nothing on the record to indicate that it lacks jurisdiction, the Court finds that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicants allege violations of human rights protected by Article 7 and 14 of the Charter; Article 2 and the ICCPR, instruments to which the Respondent State is a party. ii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State has ratified the Protocol and deposited the Declaration required under Article 34(6) of the Protocol. iii. Temporal jurisdiction, as the proceedings that led to the alleged violations occurred between 20 April 2010, when the Applicants filed a case before the High Court and 6 April 2022, when the MSCA rendered its decision on review. The alleged violations therefore took place after the Respondent State had become a party to the Protocol, on 9 October 2008. iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred in the territory of the Respondent State, which is a Party to the Charter and the Protocol.
Based on the foregoing, the Court holds that it has jurisdiction to hear this Application.
Pursuant to Article 6(2) of the Protocol, “the Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter”.

In accordance with Rule 50(1) of the Rules, “the Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an Application filed before it in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol and these Rules.”

The Court notes that Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which in substance restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides as follows: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter requests anonymity; b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter; and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of African Union or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes, from the record, that the Application’s compliance with the requirements in Article 56 of the Charter, which are reiterated in Rule 50(2) of the Rules, is not in contention between the Parties. Nevertheless, it must ascertain that these requirements have been fulfilled.
The Court finds that the requirement laid down in Rule 50(2)(a) of the Rules is met since the Applicants have indicated their identities.

The Court also finds that the claims made by the Applicants seek to protect their rights guaranteed under the Charter. It further notes that one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, as stated in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. The Application also does not contain any claim or prayer that is incompatible with the said provision of the Act. Therefore, the Court considers that the Application meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Court further finds that the Application does not contain any disparaging or insulting language regarding the Respondent State or its institutions, which makes it consistent with the requirement of Rule 50(2)(c) of the Rules.

Regarding the condition stated in Rule 50(2)(d) of the Rules, the Court observes that the Application is not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, but it is derived from court records. The Court accordingly finds that the Application complies with this condition.

As far as the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies set out under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules is concerned, this Court observes that, on 2 August 2016, the MSCA, which is the highest court of the Respondent State, dismissed the appeal that had been instituted against the Judgment of the High Court of 9 June 2014. The requirement to exhaust local remedies has, therefore, been met. The Court accordingly finds that the Application complies with this condition.

Regarding the condition stated in Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules, the Court notes that the Rule provides that applications must be filed “… within reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter”.
The Court recalls that in assessing the reasonableness of time, to file an application should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

The Court notes that the MSCA rendered its decision on 2 August 2016, and on 3 October 2016, the Applicants filed an application for review, which was dismissed on 6 April 2022. The Applicants then filed the Application before this Court on 2 September 2022.

This Court has previously held that a review procedure is an extraordinary remedy that the Applicants need not exhaust. The Court has also held in Nguza Viking and Johnson Nguza v. Tanzania that even if the review process is an extraordinary remedy, the time spent by the applicant in attempting to exhaust the said remedy should be considered when assessing reasonableness within the meaning of Article 56(6) of the Charter.

The Court emphasizes that, pursuant to Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules, it has discretion to determine commencement of time for its seizure. In the present Application, given that the Applicants decided to pursue the review procedure, the Court cannot ignore the time they spent in attempting to do so. In this regard, the reasonableness of time should be computed from 6 April 2022 being the date of the MSCA decision on review. A period of six months and 11 days had elapsed between the said date and when the present Application was filed, which is on 17 October 2022. Such period is relatively short, and is deemed manifestly reasonable as per the jurisprudence of this Court. The Court accordingly finds that the Application complies with the condition set out under Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules.

Finally, with respect to the requirement laid down in Rule 50(2)(g) of the Rules, the Court finds that the present Application does not concern a case which has already been settled by the Parties in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union, or the provisions of the Charter. The Application, therefore, meets this condition.

In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Application fulfils all the admissibility requirements set out under Article 56 of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50 of the Rules, and accordingly declares the Application admissible.

The Applicants allege that the Respondent State has violated their right to a fair trial guaranteed under Article 7 of the Charter; Articles 2 and 14 of the ICCPR; and the right to property guaranteed under Article 14 of the Charter.
The Court will address these allegations successively.

The alleged violation of the right to a fair trial is made in respect of four specific rights, namely: the right to due process; the right to a fair and public hearing; the right to defence; and the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court. Given that the right to due process and the right to a fair and public hearing fall under (i) the right to have one’s cause heard, the Court will deal with them jointly before examining (ii) the alleged violations of the right to defence and (iii) the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court.

The Applicants’ allegations regarding the right to have one’s cause heard are two-fold: (a) alleged violation of fair and public hearing in relation to the availability of courts’ decisions; and (b) alleged violation of due process owing to the composition of the bench and competency of the MSCA.

The Applicants aver that their right to a fair trial was violated because the purported decision of the MSCA, dated 6 April 2022, dismissing their review application, is not legible. Furthermore, they allege that the record of proceedings and subsequent court decisions should be accessible and legible. They buttress their allegation by citing the provisions of the Principles and Guidelines on the Rights to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (herein after referred to as the Commission’s Fair Trial Guidelines).
