The Applicants further allege that they were unable to ascertain the grounds on which their application was dismissed due to the lack of access to the court proceedings and because MSCA’s review judgment of 6 April 2022 was purported illegible. *
The Respondent State did not file a response. ***
Article 7(1) of the Charter provides that: Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard.

Article 14(1) of the ICCPR provides that: … In the determination of any criminal charge against him, or of his rights and obligations in a suit at law, everyone shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law. …

Principles D(b) and (c) of the Commission’s Fair Trial Guidelines provide that States Parties have the duty to maintain effective systems for recording and storing all proceedings before judicial bodies, storing such information and making it accessible to the public. They should also publish the decisions throughout the country.

The Court recalls its jurisprudence that “… the right to acquire knowledge of the record of proceedings is also an important aspect of the right to a fair trial and is related to the right to defence, more particularly the principle of equality of arms between the parties. Courts therefore have an obligation to strike a fair balance between the parties with a view to enabling them to be aware of and comment on all the evidence tendered by the adverse party”. In Alex Thomas v. Tanzania, this Court also examined the right to receive documents and held that it behoves on the Respondent State to provide applicants with the record required to pursue an appeal.

In the present Application, the Applicants allege violation of their right to have one’s cause heard owing to the Respondent State’s failure to provide them with legible copies of the domestic courts’ decisions and pleadings. The Court notes from the record that, in support of this allegation, the Applicants made several attempts to obtain certified copies of the records and decisions of domestic courts but were unsuccessful. Although the domestic courts provided copies of the decisions, these were either unsigned, illegible or handwritten, which are not in line with the obligations of the Respondent State expounded on earlier in this Judgment.

The Court observes that once the Applicants have adduced evidence of due diligence to obtain the required documents, the burden of proof shifts to the Respondent State whose judicial bodies rendered the said decisions. However, the Respondent State did not file a response. The Court also notes that the Respondent State did not act diligently to address the complaints of the Applicants to receive the signed decisions of the MSCA’s judgments of 2 August 2016, and the review of 6 April 2022.
The Court thus observes that the Applicants were not informed of the grounds of dismissal of their applications before domestic courts.

In the circumstances, the Court finds that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ rights to be heard, protected under Article 7(1) of the Charter as read jointly with Article 14(1) of the ICCPR in respect of the rights to a fair and public hearing and availability of courts’ decisions.

The Applicants aver that the MSCA Rules (hereinafter referred to as “the MSCA Rules”) 29 and 34 do not specify the applicable law, procedural requirements, and processes for review. However, according to the Applicants, the said Rules only refer to “the practice of the Court of Appeal in England”, which they aver creates legal uncertainty and violates their right to due process.

In substantiating this claim, the Applicants contend that during the review hearing of 26 October 2021, before the MSCA, “counsel for the Respondent State” informed the court that the quorum was not reached because only two judges were in attendance. Resultantly, the case was deferred to 6 April 2026. Notwithstanding their objection, the Applicants claim that the case was eventually heard by two judges who dismissed it with costs. According to the Applicants, a composition of two judges did not meet the quorum of nine Justices of Appeal and was therefore in contravention of the provisions of Chief Justice’s Practice Direction No. 1 of 2018 (hereinafter referred to as “Practice Directions), thereby rendering the judgment void. *
The Respondent State did not file a response. ***

The Court notes that the Applicants allege violations of both Articles 7 of the Charter and 14 of the ICCPR, however, the Court observes that the claims made regarding the violation of the competence of the MSCA’s review bench and its composition are covered under Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter. The Court will therefore consider the allegation solely based on the Charter.

Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter provides that: Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force.

The Court observes that the right to have one’s cause heard, as enshrined under Article 7(1) of the Charter, bestows upon individuals a wide range of entitlements pertaining to due process of law, including the right to be given an opportunity to express their views on matters and procedures affecting their rights, the right to file a petition before appropriate judicial and quasijudicial authorities for violations of these rights and the right to appeal to higher judicial authorities when their grievances are not properly addressed by the lower courts. Additionally, the right to be heard requires that a mechanism to review such findings should be put in place.

In considering the question of the composition and competence of the MSCA’s review bench and whether its procedures contravene the law, the Court refers to the caselaw of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). In this regard, the ECtHR has undertaken such assessment based, among others, on the principle of “manifest breach of domestic law”, under which it examines whether the domestic court clearly violated its own national statutory laws regarding composition, bench size, or quorum requirements.

In assessing observance of the first requirement stated above, the Court observes that Section 105 of the Constitution of Malawi, provides that “[w]hen the Supreme Court of Appeal is determining any matter, other than an interlocutory matter, it shall be composed of an uneven number of Justices of Appeal, not being less than three”. On the other hand, the Practice Directions stipulate that the composition of the review bench should not be less than seven judges in determining any matter other than an interlocutory matter. In the instant case, the Court finds that the quorum of two judges who presided over the review hearing did not comply with the provisions of the Respondent State’s Constitution or the Practice Directions of the MSCA.
The Court observes that given the MSCA review bench was not properly constituted, it was thus incompetent to hear the review hearings in 2021 and 2022.

Accordingly, the Court finds that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ right to a fair trial under Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter with respect to the composition and competency of the MSCA’s review bench.

The Applicants submit that due to the illegibility of the MSCA’s judgment of 6 April 2022, they were unable to ascertain the legal grounds for the dismissal of their application, thereby rendering them unable to protect their interests effectively.

They argue that the violation was further compounded by the procedural irregularities during the review hearing of 6 April 2022. They also aver that their legal representative was unable to attend the hearing due to circumstances beyond his control and he allegedly informed the court of his unavailability verbally. They aver that the First Applicant was present but was denied the opportunity to speak. On the converse, counsel of Mtambalika was present during the hearing and was asked some questions by the judges, which he responded to. According to the Applicants, this clearly indicates that the case was not yet decided and that it was still possible for the parties to provide additional information, clarify statements, and to participate fully in the proceedings.

The Applicants further aver that they filed their affidavits and skeleton arguments before the High Court, using Originating Summons, however, the High Court decided that they should have filed a Writ of Summons. Nevertheless, it still accepted the affidavits filed by Mtambalika. Furthermore, the Applicants’ aver that they were deprived of the opportunity to challenge the affidavits filed by Mtambalika, who did not attend any hearing, even though those affidavits were decisive to the outcome of the case, as is evident from the reasoning in the High Court decision of 9 June 2014 and the unsigned Judgment of the MSCA of 2 August 2016. *
The Respondent State did not file a response. ***

The Court observes that the Applicants raise two claims that: (i) due to the illegibility of the MSCA’s judgment dated 6 April 2022, they were unable to ascertain the legal grounds for the dismissal of their application, thereby rendering them unable to protect their interests effectively and (ii) they were not granted opportunity to be heard during the review proceedings before the MSCA.

The Court notes that the issue of illegibility raised by the Applicants was already determined under the alleged violation of the right to a fair and public hearing and availability of courts’ decisions. The Court will therefore determine the alleged violation of the claim to be heard during the review proceedings before the MSCA.

The Court observes that Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter provides that: Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (c) the right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice…

While the Applicants cite Article 14 of the ICCPR, the Court is of the view that the right is covered under Article 7 of the Charter; and will therefore consider the allegation solely on the basis of the Charter.

Regarding the right to defence, the Court has previously held in Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Republic of Benin, that “the right to defence as set out in Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter is a key component of the right to a fair trial and reflects the potential of a judicial process offering the parties the opportunity to express their claims and submit their evidence.”

The Court also recalls that domestic courts enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in terms of assessing the probative value of evidence before it. This, however, does not preclude it from evaluating proceedings of the domestic courts to assess whether the same are in consonance with the Charter and international human rights standards.

The Court observes that the Applicants were represented by counsel at some stages of the proceedings before the domestic courts, for instance during the review hearing at the Court of Appeal on 6 April 2022. Their advocate had allegedly notified the MSCA of his unavailability to attend the hearing owing to reasons beyond his control.

The Court notes that Rules 20 and 21 of the MSCA Rules, Order III, provide for procedure for non-representation before it. Specifically, Rule 20 of the said Rules provides that: At any time before hearing of the appeal any party to the appeal may file a declaration in writing that he does not wish to be present in person or by a legal representative on the hearing of the appeal together with four copies of such arguments as he desires to submit to the Court and serve a copy of such declaration and arguments upon every other party who has led an address for service and thereupon the appeal shall be dealt with as if the party had appeared.

Rule 21 of the same Rules provides that: (1) If the appellant fails to appear when his appeal is called on for hearing and has not taken action under Rule 20 of this Order, the appeal may be struck out or dismissed with or without costs. (2) When an appeal has been struck out owing to the nonappearance of the appellant, the Court may, if it thinks fit, and on such terms as for costs or otherwise as it may deem just, direct the appeal to be re-entered for hearing.

Considering these provisions, the Court observes that the legal representative of the Applicants, Barrister E. B. Sitolo, allegedly notified the court verbally about his inability to attend the review hearing. Under the Respondent State’s laws, namely Rules 20 and 21 of the MSCA Rules, Order III, counsel was obliged to file a declaration in writing indicating that he would be absent for the hearing, together with four copies of arguments that he desires to submit to the court and upon every other party to the case. In the alternative, counsel should have notified the Applicants about the procedures in good time to enable them to comply with the requirements under MSCA Rules 20 and 21.

Additionally, the Court notes that there is nothing on record to indicate that the Applicants were denied an opportunity or hindered in any way to be heard or to present their case. Furthermore, both the Applicants’ and the Respondent’s affidavits were accepted by the High Court. This disproves the allegations made by the Applicants that it was only the affidavits of Mtambalika that were considered by the High Court and were decisive of the outcome of the case.

Therefore, the Court is of the opinion that the Parties were treated equally in the domestic proceedings under consideration, and the Applicants were not placed at a disadvantage. Accordingly, the claim that the Applicants were deprived of the opportunity to challenge evidence and to defend themselves is unfounded.
Consequently, the Court finds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to a fair trial regarding the right to defence as guaranteed under Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter.

The Applicants submit that their right to be tried within a reasonable time under Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter was violated due to excessive and unjustified delays in the determination of their case from the time the Application was filed at the High Court up to the delivery of the judgment of the MSCA on the review application. They further submit that the proceedings were adjourned 11 times before the High Court, and 13 times before the MSCA.

They aver that the proceedings, which commenced by Originating Summons on 20 April 2010 before the High Court of Malawi, were only heard by the MSCA and judgment rendered on 6 April 2022, nearly 12 years later. It is the Applicants’ submission that the review proceedings, where their Notice of Motion filed on 30 October 2016 was only determined on 13 June 2019, more than two and a half years later.

The Applicants further submit that such prolonged delays are inconsistent with established jurisprudence of the African Commission, which has held that undue prolongation of proceedings violates Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter, as affirmed in Odjouoriby Cossi Paul v. Benin. In that case, even a significantly shorter delay was found to be unreasonable. Citing the wellestablished three-factor test in Wilfred Onyango Nganyi & 9 Others v. United Republic of Tanzania, namely: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the Applicants, and the conduct of judicial authorities, the Applicants aver that their “dispute was a straightforward land dispute without complexities and at times they acted diligently and did everything within their power to assist the court in the smooth running of the procedure”. They submit that these unjustified delays are solely attributed to the judicial authorities.

The Applicants also argue that the prolonged proceedings caused legal uncertainty and denied them procedural fairness, particularly as they were never provided with a signed or certified copy of the MSCA decision of 2 August 2016, despite clear procedural requirements under Order III Rules 27 and 28 of the Supreme Court of Appeal Rules that judgments be formally pronounced and certified. Additionally, the Applicants aver that they were not furnished with a readable or official version of the decision of 6 April 2022, leaving them uncertain of the reasons for the dismissal of their review application, thereby further compounding the violation of their right to a fair and timely determination. *
The Respondent State did not file any response to this Application. ***

Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter provides that “[e]very individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This right comprises: (a) [...]; (d) the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial tribunal.”

The Court recalls its jurisprudence that “determination as to whether the duration of the procedure in respect of local remedies has been normal or abnormal should be carried out on a case-by-case basis depending on the circumstances of each case”. Additionally, the Court’s analysis takes into account the complexity of the case or of the proceedings relating to it, the conduct of the parties and that of the judicial authorities in order to determine whether the latter “has been passive or clearly negligent.”

The Court observes that the assessment of whether proceedings were conducted within a reasonable time requires an examination of the entire record of domestic proceedings, including the sequence of hearings, adjournments, and procedural steps taken by the parties.

In the present case, although the Applicants annexed the judgments of the High Court and the MSCA which were unsigned, they did not provide the complete record of proceedings from the High Court to the MSCA, such as records of adjournments or procedural timelines. Instead, they rely largely on their own summaries of the proceedings.

Based on the information provided by the Applicant, the Court can establish that the duration of the trial at the High Court from the commencement on 20 April 2010 to the delivery of judgment on 9 June 2014 was four years, one month and 20 days.
Similarly, the judgment of the MSCA shows that the appeal was filed on 22 July 2015, and decided on 2 August 2016, a period of one year and 11 days.

The record indicates that the petition for leave to review of the judgment of the MSCA was filed on 7 December 2017 and granted by the MSCA on 12 June 2019, however, judgment was only rendered on 6 April 2022. Therefore, a period of two years, nine months and 23 days had elapsed between the time when the Applicants filed the Application for review on 12 June 2019, and when the judgment on review was delivered on 6 April 2022.

The Court observes that it took the Respondent State’s courts a cumulative period of nine years, five months and twenty-nine days to finalise the Applicants’ case. Notably, the proceedings lasted four years at the High Court, one year at the initial stage before the MSCA and two years at the review stage before the same court. While the cumulative period of nine years, five months, and 29 days to finalise the Applicants’ case appears to be too long to consider a straightforward land dispute, the time must be contextualised since the Applicants and the Respondent State pursued the available judicial remedies at the national courts.

The Court notes that there is no evidence to show that the conduct of the Parties resulted in the delay. In the absence of such primary material evidence, the Court is unable to verify the precise causes of delay or determine whether such delay is attributable to the Respondent State either through procedural developments, adjournments, or other factors attributable either to the parties or to the judicial authorities. Thus, the Court cannot find a violation. The Court also observes that judicial proceedings before each of the concerned courts involved different rules, practices and processes which require some time to be observed or completed.

From the foregoing, the Court finds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to a fair trial, as provided under Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter in respect of the right to be tried within a reasonable time.
The Applicants submit that the Respondent State violated their right to property by failing to safeguard their right to fair trial and by ruling that they were not the rightful owners of the land.

Citing the jurisprudence of the ECtHR, Kotov v. Russia and Anheuser- Busch Inc. v. Portugal, the Applicants aver that the State has a positive obligation to establish an effective legal and judicial framework for the protection of property rights, including ensuring access to fair and effective judicial procedures for the determination and enforcement of such rights. *
The Respondent State did not file any response in this Application. ***

Article 14 of the Charter provides: The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws.

The Court recalls its jurisprudence that the right to property as guaranteed under Article 14 of the Charter includes the right to use one’s property (usus), the right to enjoy its fruits (fructus) and the right to dispose of it, including the right to sell it (abusus).

In the present case, the Applicants have not established that they held a valid and legally recognised proprietary right over the land in question. As reflected in the domestic proceedings before the High Court, the ownership of the land in question was contested and the High Court judge held on 9 June 2014 that “the purported agreements herein are invalid, the defendant’s signature having been secured through misrepresentation. The contracts can, therefore, not be enforced and are invalid. I so order. There can be no specific performance whereas in this matter, the contracts are declared invalid, due to the plaintiff’s misrepresentation, the plaintiff’s originating summons is therefore dismissed in its entirety.” This decision was contested by the Applicants on appeal before the MSCA which dismissed the appeal with costs on 2 August 2016.

In the absence of a proven property right, the Court finds that the Applicants cannot successfully invoke the full scope of Article 14, including usus, fructus, and abusus, as these protections attach to an established legal entitlement. The Court notes that the domestic judicial system provided a forum in which the Applicants’ claim to property was heard and determined. From the pleadings on record, it is evident that the Applicants were able to present their case before the High Court, including reliance on the alleged sale agreements and supporting affidavits. The existence of such judicial proceedings demonstrates that the Applicants were afforded an opportunity to prove their property claim before competent domestic courts.
As a consequence, the Court dismisses the Applicants’ allegation and holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to property, protected under Article 14 of the Charter.

In relation to reparations, the Applicants pray the Court to: i. Order the Respondent State to pay to them the sum of USD 5.6 Million, as compensation for the moral damage (emotional suffering, psychological trauma, anguish and grief, distress, and frustration) they have suffered; ii. Order the Respondent State to pay to them the sum of money equivalent to the current market value of the land (2.2 hectares) that they have lost as a result of the mishandling and/or nonhandling of their case; iii. Order the Respondent State to pay them the sum of USD 1.6 Million, as material damages; iv. Order the Respondent State to pay them a sum of money, as compensation for the loss of their income, other business opportunities, travel expenses to the national courts for 12 years, legal expenses, etc.; v. Order the relevant officials of the Respondent State to sign the Judgment of the Supreme Court of Appeal of 2 August 2016 and to provide the formal decision of the Supreme Court of Appeal, dismissing the Applicants’ application for review on 6 April 2022; vi. Order the Respondent State to make all necessary reforms/amendments/changes to ensure that cases are tried within a reasonable time (e.g., enough capacity), that the court records and judgments are accessible (e.g., electronically), and that the legal framework (ref. Practice Directions) is clear and certain. *
The Respondent State did not file any response in this Application. ***

The Court notes that Article 27 of the Protocol provides that: If the Court finds that there has been violation of a human or peoples’ right, it shall make appropriate orders to remedy the violation, including the payment of fair compensation or reparation.

The Court recalls its previous judgments on reparation and reaffirms that, in considering claims for compensation for damage resulting from human rights violations, it takes into account the principle that the State found to be the author of an internationally wrongful act is under an obligation to make full reparation for the consequences so as to cover all the damage suffered by the victim. The Court also takes into account the principle that there must be a causal link between the violation and the alleged harm and that the burden of proof rests with the Applicant, who must provide the information to justify his or her claim.

The Court also established that “reparation must, as far as possible, erase all the consequences of the unlawful act and re-establish the state that would probably have existed had the unlawful act not been committed.” In addition, reparation measures may include: restitution, compensation, rehabilitation of the victim and measures to ensure that the violations are not repeated.
Furthermore, the Court recalls that, as it has already established, reparation measures for harm resulting from human rights violations must consider the circumstances of each case.

The Court reiterates that the onus is on the applicant to provide evidence to justify his prayers, particularly for material damages. With regard to moral damages, the Court has held that it is presumed when violations are established. The Court further underscores that it cannot order reparation measures based on claims where no human rights violation has been established.

In the instant case, the Court has established that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ right to a fair trial regarding the right to due process as guaranteed by Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter as read together with Article 2(3)(b) of the ICCPR. Additionally, the Court found that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ right to a fair and public hearing as guaranteed under Article 7(1) of the Charter. The Court shall thus proceed to determine the appropriate reparations.

The Applicants seek reparations for material and moral prejudice that they suffered and for moral prejudice suffered by the indirect victims. The Court notes that the prayers of the Applicants are in relation to the right to property and legal expenses incurred in domestic proceedings for which this Court did not find any violation. As such, the Court dismisses these prayers.
In respect of moral prejudice, the Court notes that the Applicants pray for reparations regarding prejudice related to the right to due process and to a fair and public hearing.

The Applicants request that this Court orders the Respondent State to pay them the sum of USD 5.6 million as compensation for the moral damage (emotional suffering, psychological trauma, anguish and grief, distress, and frustration) that they have suffered. They further aver that the violations have also affected their families. They argue that this delay and injustice allegedly made Applicants unfit to work, which resulted in a loss of income, thus undermining their children’s education. ***

The Court recalls its previous jurisprudence that moral prejudice suffered by victims of human rights violations is presumed when violations are established. In the instant case, the Court has found that the violation of the Applicants’ right to a fair trial with regard to due process and the right to a fair and public hearing.

With regard to the Applicants’ compensation for moral damages occasioned by the violation of the right to due process and the right to a fair and public hearing, the Court considers that these violations caused the Applicants moral prejudice. In the circumstances, and in the exercise of its discretion, the Court awards each one of them a sum of Five Hundred Malawi Kwacha (MK 500) for prejudice suffered as compensation for the moral damages.

In relation to the compensation of the Applicants’ family members, the Court has previously held that compensation is granted only when there is proof of marital status for the spouses or filiation with the applicant with regard to children, including their birth certificates. The Court notes that the Applicants have not provided any evidence to establish marital status or filiation, such as marriage certificates or birth certificates. Accordingly, the Court finds that the claim is unsubstantiated.
In view of these circumstances, the Court finds that the claim for moral prejudice suffered by the families of the Applicants as indirect victims is unjustified and is therefore dismissed.

The Applicants pray the Court to grant them non-pecuniary reparations in the form of restitution and guarantee of non-repetition measures. Furthermore, the Applicants request that this Court orders the Respondent State to provide them with a signed copy of the judgment of the MSCA of 2 August 2016 and the formal decision of the MSCA, dismissing the Applicants’ application for review on 6 April 2022. ***
Given its findings in this Judgment, the Court does not deem it necessary to grant any restitution measures. The prayer for restitution is therefore dismissed.

Conversely, in light of the violations established regarding due process and legal certainty, fair and public hearing, the Court considers it appropriate to order the Respondent State to take the necessary measures to immediately furnish the Applicants with official copies of the judgment of the MSCA of 2 August 2016 and the formal decision of the review judgment of the MSCA of 6 April 2022.

The Applicants also pray the Court to order the Respondent State to make all necessary reforms to ensure that cases are tried within a reasonable time (e.g., enough capacity), that the court records and judgments are accessible (e.g., electronically), and that the legal framework (ref. Practice Directions) is clear and certain. ***

The Court observes that while guarantees of non-repetition generally apply in cases of systemic violations, these remedies would also be relevant in individual cases where the violations will not cease, are likely to recur, or are systemic or structural in nature. In the present case, the Court does not deem it necessary to issue an order regarding non-repetition of the violations of the Applicants’ rights, since there is no possibility of such violations being repeated with respect to the Applicants. Additionally, there is nothing on record to demonstrate that the violations are systemic to warrant such a prayer. The Applicants’ prayer in this regard is therefore dismissed.
The Applicants do not make specific prayers in respect of implementation and reporting. ***
Even so, the Court notes that the order relating to reporting on the measures taken by a Respondent State is a matter of judicial practice.

The Court therefore finds it appropriate to order the Respondent State to submit within six months of notification of this judgment, periodic reports on the implementation thereof, indicating the measures taken to comply with this Judgment, in accordance with Article 30 of the Protocol.
The Applicants pray for costs. *
The Respondent State did not file any Response to the Application. ***
The Court notes that under Rule 32(2) of its Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any.”
The Court also notes that the proceedings before it are free of charge and while the Applicants pray for costs, they do not provide any evidence to support this prayer.
In the present case, the Court finds that there is no reason to depart from the principle laid down in that provision. Accordingly, each party must bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously On the request for a judgment by default i. Grants the Applicants’ prayer to render this judgment in default; ii. Renders this judgment by default. On jurisdiction iii. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility iv. Declares that the Application is admissible. On merits v. Holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to defence as guaranteed under Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter; By a majority of nine (9) Judges for, and one (1) Judge against, Rafaâ BEN ACHOUR dissenting, vi. Holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to be tried within a reasonable time as provided under Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter; Unanimously, vii. Holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicants’ right to property, protected under Article 14 of the Charter; viii. Holds that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ right to have one’s cause heard guaranteed under Article 7(1) of the Charter as read jointly with Article 14(1) of the ICCPR, in respect of a fair and public hearing, and availability of courts’ decisions; ix. Holds that the Respondent State violated the Applicants’ right to have one’s cause heard as guaranteed by Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter in respect of the composition and competency of the bench of the Malawi Supreme Court of Appeal during the review hearing. On reparations x. Dismisses the Applicants’ prayers for pecuniary reparations in respect of material prejudice; xi. Dismisses the Applicants’ prayer for restitution; xii. Grants the Applicants’ prayers for moral prejudice suffered as compensation and awards each one of them a sum of Five Hundred Malawi Kwacha (MK 500); xiii. Orders the Respondent State to pay the amount indicated above free from taxes within six months, effective from the notification of this judgment; xiv. Orders the Respondent State to take the necessary measures to immediately furnish the Applicants with official and accessible copies of the judgment of the Malawi Supreme Court of Appeal of 2 August 2016 and the formal decision of the review judgment of the Malawi Supreme Court of Appeal, of 6 April 2022; xv. Orders the Respondent State to submit, within six months of notification of this Judgment, periodic reports on the implementation thereof, indicating the measures taken to comply with this Judgment, in accordance with Article 30 of the Protocol. On costs xvi. Orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

Mr Mohamed AL BOUSIFI (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a Libyan national who used to live in Niger. He alleges violation of his right to property as a result of Judgement N°009/2023 of 23 February 2013 issued by the Niamey Special High Court Court (TGI) relating to a registered undeveloped property located in Niamey, Niger.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Niger (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 July 1986, and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 26 June 2004. On 7 April 2022, the Respondent State deposited the declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”) by virtue of which it accepts the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples Rights.

It emerges from the Application that, pursuant to a notarial deed dated 15 February 2010, the Applicant acquired from EAPAD Sarl an undeveloped plot of land measuring 55 hectares located in Niamey, Niger, covered by land title (LT) No. 17625 RN. After the LT had been transferred to his name, he deposited it as collateral with the Libyan Peoples Investment Office in Niger (BIPLN) for the purpose of obtaining a loan, after which he travelled to Libya.

The Applicant avers that, in February 2015, while passing through Niamey, he discovered that, at the request of the Public Prosecutor of the Niamey Special High Court Court (TGI), the Land Registry Office had parcelled out and transferred his property to third parties, including Mr Jalaoui ALKABOUSS. According to him, the property was parcelled out and transferred pursuant to confirmation Judgment No. 009/2023 of 27 February 2013 delivered by the Niamey Special High Court Court, approving a judicial settlement reached between Mr ALKABOUSS and BIPLN (Confirmation Judgment No. 009/2023 of 27 February 2013 by the Niamey Special High Court Court). He contends that he was never informed of those proceedings.

The Applicant further avers that in an effort to have the dispossession set aside, he instituted proceedings before the Niamey Special High Court against Mr ALKABOUSS, BIPLN, and EAPAD, while the Respondent State was joined to the proceedings before that court by a writ dated 17 February 2016.
The Applicant alleges violation of his right to property protected by Article 14 of the Charter.

The Application was filed with the Registry on 15 June 2022. It was served on the Respondent State with a request to submit the names of its representatives and to file its Response within thirty (30) and ninety (90) days, respectively.
In a request dated 3 January 2023, the Applicant sought legal aid. On 9 March 2023, the Registry informed him that his request had been rejected.
The Parties filed all pleadings and procedural documents within the prescribed time limits.

On 29 April 2026, the Registry notified the Application to State of Libya for its intervention if it so wished, in accordance with Rule 42(5)(b) of the Rules (hereinafter referred to as “the Rules), and granted it thirty (30) days to respond. Upon expiry of that period, the State of Libya did not file a Response.
Pleadings were closed on 22 June 2026, and the Parties were duly informed.

On 16 September 2026, the Applicant requested the reopening of pleadings in order to make oral observations online, or at the very least, to submit additional written pleadings. On 23 September 2026, the Court rejected this request. The Registry informed the Applicant on the same day.

The Applicant prays the Court to: i. Hold that he was not a Party to the conciliation report of 27 February 2013; ii. Declare that Judicial Settlement Approval Judgment No. 009/2013 of 27 February 2013 is unenforceable against him; iii. Hold and declare that the said report does not constitute a valid ownership rights transfer instrument attached to Land Title No. 17625, in accordance with the law; iv. Annul the parcelling out of 35 hectares carried out pursuant to the report of 1 March 2013 concerning Land Title No. 17625, together with all subsequent acts, for violation of the law; v. Hold and declare that the 55-hectare plot of land situated in Niamey, Route Dosso, covered by Land Title No. 17625, remains the property of the Applicant; vi. Order the Land Registry to proceed with the full and immediate restitution of Land Title No. 17625 to the Applicant; vii. Order the Respondent State to pay the Applicant the sum of Two Hundred Million (200,000,000) CFA francs in damages for all the prejudice suffered; viii. Order the Respondent State to pay costs.

For its part, the Respondent State prays the Court to: Primarily i. Note that the Republic of Libya makes no admission in the present case; ii. Declare Mr Mohamed Al BOUSIFI’s Application inadmissible; In the alternative, iii. Dismiss in their entirety all the requests, prayers and submissions of Mr Mohamed Al BOUSIFI; iv. Order Mr Mohamed Al BOUSIFI to pay costs.

Article 3 of the Protocol provides that: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

Furthermore, under Rule 49(1) of the Rules of Procedure: The Court shall conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules.
In light of the aforementioned provisions, the Court, in every application, must conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on objections thereto, if any.

The Court notes that the Respondent State does not raise any objection to its jurisdiction. Nonetheless, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it must ensure that all requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction are met before proceeding to hear the Application.

The Court observes that there is nothing in the record to indicate that it lacks jurisdiction in the present matter. Consequently, it considers that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges the violation of a right protected under the Charter an instrument ratified by the Respondent State; ii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State deposited the Declaration on 7 April 2022; iii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged facts occurred after 25 June 2004, the date on which the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol; and iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged facts took place on the Respondent State’s territory.
In the light of the foregoing, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides: The Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.
Under Rule 50(1) of the Rules: The Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an Application […] in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol and these Rules.

Furthermore, under Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which essentially restates Article 56 of the Charter: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date the Court is seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that the Respondent State raises an objection to admissibility based on non-exhaustion of local remedies. The Court will rule on this objection before examining the other admissibility requirements, if necessary.

The Respondent State submits that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies insofar as he did not bring before domestic courts any claim relating to recovery of the property covered by Land Title No. 17625, of which he claims he was unlawfully dispossessed.

According to the Respondent State, the only proceedings initiated by the Applicant consisted of a liability action arising from the “freezing of funds allocated to Aigle de l’Afrique SARL by the Libyan Arab Bank from abroad under the credit agreement of 27 January 2003”, and sought the “release of those funds” for the continuation of the Aigle de l’Afrique SARL investment project, which had been halted as a result thereof, the total amount involved being CFAF 1,749,667,500”.
The Respondent State contends that the Applicant, therefore, fails to provide evidence that he exhausted local remedies. It thus prays that the Application be declared inadmissible. ***

The Applicant prays the Court to dismiss the Respondent State’s objection. In this regard, he argues that a remedy can only be exhausted to the extent that it is available and effective. He contends that it was virtually impossible to exhaust local remedies during the Libyan revolution and the massive, arbitrary and unjustified expulsion of investors.
The Applicant further submits that, by writ dated 17 February 2016, he instituted proceedings against the BIPLN, Mr ALKABOUSS, and EAPAD Sarl and joined the Respondent State thereto.

In addition, the Applicant produced Judgment No. 320 of 13 June 2012 delivered in the case between Aigle de l’Afrique Sarl, of which he was the Managing Director, and representative of the BIPLN. In the said Judgment, the Niamey Special High Court dismissed his liability action arising from the freezing of funds allocated to Aigle de l’Afrique SARL by the Libyan Arab Foreign Bank under the 27 January 2003 credit agreement, and his request for the release of the sum of CFAF 1,749,667,500. The Applicant also submitted confirmation Judgment No. 009/2023 of 27 February 2013, delivered by the Niamey Special High Court, recording the judicial settlement reached between the BIPLN and Mr ALKABOUSS, pursuant to which the latter was allocated a 35-hectare plot carved out from his 55- hectare property. He maintains that he was never informed of those proceedings. ***

The Court recalls that, in accordance with Article 56(5) of the Charter and Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, applications must be filed after exhaustion of local remedies, where such remedies exist, unless it is obvious that the procedure thereof has been unduly prolonged.

The Court emphasises that the remedies to be exhausted are judicial remedies. Such remedies must be available, in the sense that they can be exercised by the Applicant without impediment, and effective, in that they are “capable of redressing the complaint or of remedying the situation in dispute”.

The Court recalls its established jurisprudence that it is not sufficient for the Applicant merely to cast doubt on the effectiveness of local remedies. It is incumbent upon the Applicant to take all necessary steps to exhaust, or at least attempt to exhaust, local remedies.
The Court further notes that the exhaustion of local remedies presupposes that the matter brought before it is, at least in substance, identical to the matter previously submitted to domestic courts.

In the present case, the Court will assess the exhaustion of local remedies in light of the Parties’ submissions and the documents in the record, namely: (i) the difficulties allegedly encountered in exhausting local remedies during the Libyan revolution; (ii) Judgment No. 320 of 13 June 2012 delivered by the Niamey Special High Court; (iii) the Judicial Settlement Approval Judgment No. 009/2013 of 27 February 2013 delivered by the Niamey Special High Court; and (iv) the writ of summons dated 17 February 2016 before the Niamey Special High Court.
The Court emphasises that the Applicant is not required to seize Libyan courts since Libya is not a party to these proceedings.
Consequently, the Court dismisses the argument relating to the difficulty in exhausting local remedies due to the Libyan revolution.

The Court recalls, as stated above, that the exhaustion of local remedies requires that the matter before it be, at least in substance, the same as that which was previously brought before domestic courts.

The Court notes that Judgment No. 320 of 13 June 2012 was delivered by the Niamey Special High Court in proceedings between the Applicant, acting in his capacity as Managing Director of l’Aigle de l’Afrique SARL, and BIPLN. The court that delivered the said judgment was seised of a liability action arising from “the freezing of funds allocated to Aigle de l’Afrique SARL by the Libyan Arab Bank from abroad under the credit agreement of 27 January 2003”, by which the Applicant sought “the release of the said funds” and the payment of various sums of money as compensation for the damage allegedly suffered.
The Court notes that this action differs fundamentally from the one brought before it. The Applicant cannot, therefore, rely on same to justify the nonexhaustion of local remedies.
Consequently, the Court dismisses the Applicant’s argument on this point.

The Court recalls that the Applicant asserts that he was dispossessed of his property was based on Judicial Settlement Approval Judgment No. 009/2013 delivered on 27 February 2013 by the President of the Niamey Special High Court Court. He explains that he was never informed of those proceedings.

The Court notes that under Article 550 of the Civil Procedure Code (CCP) of the Respondent State: “a third-party appeal seeks to have a judgment set aside where it adversely affects the rights of a person who was not a party thereto. It is available to all third parties where neither they, nor their principals, nor those they represent were, summoned to the proceedings”.

Having never been informed of these proceedings, as he himself claims, the Applicant had the avenue of filing a third-party appeal to have that judgment set aside. However, he did not avail himself of that remedy provided for under Article 550 of the Respondent State’s Civil Procedure Code.
Consequently, the Court considers that the Applicant failed to exhaust that remedy.

The Court recalls that the Applicant claims that by writ dated 17 February 2016, he instituted proceedings before the Niamey Special High Court Court against the BILPN, Mr ALKABOUSS and EAPAD, with the Respondent State joined thereto.

The Court notes, however, that the Applicant does not produce the said writ, and neither does he indicate its subject matter. In the circumstances, the Court is unable to assess , whether the subject matter of those proceeding was, in substance, the same as that of the present Application. Furthermore, the Applicant does not demonstrate that those proceedings resulted in a judgment or, in the absence of a judgment, that the proceedings were unduly prolonged.
It follows that the Court cannot conclude, solely on the strength of the allegation regarding the writ of 17 February 2016 before the Niamey Special High Court, that local remedies were exhausted.

In conclusion, the Court finds that the Applicant fails to establish that he brought an action before domestic courts in respect of his landed property rights, namely, a civil action falling within the jurisdiction of the High Court, pursuant to Articles 64 and 73 of Organic Law 2004-50 of 22 July 2004 on the organisation and jurisdiction of courts in the Republic of Niger, and Article 43 of the Respondent State’s Civil Procedure Code.

Consequently, the Court upholds the Respondent State’s objection based on non-exhaustion of local remedies and finds that the Application does not meet the requirement under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

Having found that the Application does not meet the requirement under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, and in view of the cumulative nature of the admissibility requirements, the Court need not rule on the other admissibility requirements under Article 56 (1), (2), (3), (4), (6) and (7) of the Charter, restated in Rule 50(2)(a)(b)(c)(d)(f) and (g) of the Rules.
Accordingly, the Court declares the Application inadmissible.
Each Party prays the Court to order the other to pay the costs. ***
Article 32(2) of the Rules provides that “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.

The Court notes that proceedings before it are free of charge and that, as a general rule, each party bears its own costs. In the present case, none of Parties demonstrates the existence of circumstances warranting a departure from the provisions of Rule 32(2) of the Rules.
Accordingly, the Court orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Upholds the Respondent State’s objection based on nonexhaustion of domestic remedies; iii. Declares the Application inadmissible. On costs iv. Orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

Fea Charles, Gueu Louapou Christian, Diomande Aboubakar Sidiki, Traoré Aboulaye, Adae Tano Alain Christian, Kpea Albert Damas, are all Ivorian nationals while Badiène Moussa is a national of Burkina Faso. They are jointly referred to hereinafter as (“the Applicants”). At the time of filing the present Application, Fea Charles, Gueu Louapou Christian, Diomande Aboubakar Sidiki, Traoré Aboulaye and Adae Tano Alain Christian were serving a twenty (20)-year prison sentence for criminal conspiracy, armed robbery and unlawful possession of firearms, whilst Kpea Albert Damas and Badiène Moussa had been acquitted of these charges on appeal. They allege violation of their human rights in connection with proceedings before domestic courts.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 31 March 1992, and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 25 January 2004. The Respondent State also deposited, on 23 July 2013, the Declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights. On 29 April 2020, the Respondent State deposited with the Chairperson of the African Union Commission the instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration. The Court ruled that the said withdrawal has no bearing on pending or new applications filed before the withdrawal took effect one year after the deposit of the instrument thereof, in this case, on 30 April 2021.

The Applicants aver that they were arrested and held in police custody in connection with investigations conducted in 2012 into armed robberies committed in hotels in certain neighbourhoods of the Yopougon municipality of Abidjan. They were subsequently brought before the Public Prosecutor at the Yopougon Court of First Instance who requested the investigating judge to open a judicial investigation against them for armed robbery, criminal conspiracy and unlawful possession of firearms. According to the Applicants, the investigating judge charged them with the aforementioned offences and, having concluded the investigation, committed them to trial before the Yopougon Court of First Instance.

On 6 July 2012, the Yopougon Court of First Instance found the Applicants guilty as charged and sentenced them to twenty (20) years’ imprisonment each. The Applicants appealed the said judgment before the Abidjan Court of Appeal.

By judgment of 3 July 2013, the Abidjan Court of Appeal upheld the convictions of Fea Charles, Gueu Louapou Christian, Adae Tano Alain Christian, Diomandé Aboubacar Sidiki and Traoré Abdoulaye. It however quashed the judgment in respect of Badienne Moussa and Kpea Albert Damas, and acquitted them.

The Applicants allege violation of the following rights: i. The right not to be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment, protected by Article 5 of the Charter; ii. The right to liberty and security of the human person, protected by Article 6 of the Charter; iii. The right to a fair trial, in particular: a. the right to an appeal to competent national courts against any acts violating the fundamental rights recognised and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force, protected by Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter; b. the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty by an impartial court, protected by Article 7(1)(b) of the Charter; c. the right to defence, including the right to be assisted by counsel of one’s choice, protected by Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter; d. the right to respect for the principle of adversarial proceedings, as provided for in Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter the “ICCPR”).; e. the right to respect for the principle of proportionality of penalties, as provided for in Article 15(1) of the ICCPR; iv. The right to protection of the dignity of detainees, in accordance with Article 10(1) of the ICCPR.
On 22 July 2019, Fea Charles, Badienne Moussa, Gueu Louapou Christian and Albert Damas filed their Applications with the Registry.
On 16 September 2019, Diomandé Aboubakar Sidiki, Traoré Aboulaye and Adae Tano Alain Christian filed their Applications with the Registry.
On 2 December 2019, the Court issued an order consolidating the Applications.
The Respondent State filed its Response on 29 January 2020
Pleadings were closed on 30 June 2022 and the Parties were duly notified.

The Applicants pray the Court to: i. Declare that the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire violated their fundamental rights; ii. Order the Respondent State to grant them a presidential pardon or parole; iii. Award pecuniary reparations for the harm suffered as a result of their unlawful imprisonment.

The Court notes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.
Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “The Court shall ascertain its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
In light of the aforementioned provisions, the Court must, in every application, conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on any objections thereto, if any.

The Court notes that the Respondent State does not raise any objection to its jurisdiction. However, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it must ensure that all requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction are met.

Having found that there is nothing on the record to suggest that it lacks jurisdiction, the Court finds that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicants allege violation of human rights protected by the Charter and the ICCPR, human rights instruments to which the Respondent State is a Party. ii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State deposited the Declaration on 23 July 2013, as indicated in paragraph 2 above. On 29 April 2020, it deposited the instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration. In this regard, the Court reiterates its jurisprudence cited above, that the withdrawal of the Declaration has no retroactive effect and has no bearing on cases pending prior to the withdrawal, or on new cases filed before the withdrawal takes effect, one year after the deposit of the instrument thereof, in this case, on 30 April 2021. The present Application, having been filed on 19 February 2021, that is, two months and eleven days before the withdrawal of the Declaration took effect, is therefore not affected by it. iii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the violations alleged by the Applicants occurred after the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol. iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred on the territory of the Respondent State.
In the light of the foregoing, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides: The Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.
Under Rule 50(1) the Rules, The Court shall ascertain the admissibility of any Application […] in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol and these Rules.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that, in the present case, the Respondent State raises an objection to admissibility of the Application based on non-exhaustion of local remedies. The Court will rule on this objection before examining the other admissibility requirements, if necessary.

The Respondent State raises an objection to the admissibility of the Application based on failure by the Applicants to exhaust local remedies, arguing that it was not afforded the opportunity to remedy the alleged violations insofar as the matter was never brought before its courts. It emphasises that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies allows its higher courts to rectify the errors of lower courts.

The Respondent State specifically contends that the Applicants were required to file a cassation appeal before the Cassation Court to challenge the judgment of the Abidjan Court of Appeal, in accordance with Article 571 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP).

The Respondent State further argues that the Applicants failed to seek legal aid at both the trial and appeal stages, thereby undermining their argument that they were unaware of the right to appeal the impugned judgment before the Cassation Court.

The Applicants aver that they did not pursue further remedies for reasons beyond their control, including the lack of legal aid which, they claim, prevented them from being apprised of the existence of the appellate remedy, thereby effectively barring access thereto. They further contend that, in any event, such an appeal was bound to fail as it is not effective. ***

The Court notes that, under Article 56(5) of the Charter as restated in Rule 50(2) of the Rules, applications brought before it must be filed after exhaustion of local remedies where such remedies exist, unless the proceedings thereof are unduly prolonged.

The Court observes that the remedies to be exhausted are judicial remedies. They must, furthermore, be effective and sufficient, in the sense that they are capable of remedying the situation in question. It is settled jurisprudence that this requirement is waived only where the remedies fall short or where they are unduly prolonged.

The Court further notes that it has consistently held that it assesses the exhaustion of local remedies in the light of the specific circumstances of each case, taking into account the remedies available under the judicial system of the Respondent State.

In the present case, the Court observes that the Applicants concede that they did not file a cassation appeal against the judgment of the Abidjan Court of Appeal. They advance, in justification thereof, that they did not benefit from the services of a legal counsel, ; therefore, they were ignorant of the existence of the said remedy. They further contend, in the alternative, that the remedy would have been neither effective nor sufficient.

The Court observes that it has consistently held that, within the judicial system of the Respondent State, a cassation appeal before the Cassation Court is an available, effective and sufficient remedy.

The Court further reiterates, in line with its established jurisprudence, that the lack of legal representation or awareness of the existence of a remedy cannot justify the failure to exhaust that remedy, as “ignorance of the law is not a defence”. The Court further notes that an applicant cannot merely allege that a remedy is ineffective but must, at least, attempt to exhaust it.

In view of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Applicants did not exhaust local remedies and consequently, that the Application does not meet the admissibility requirement under Article 56(5) of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

The Court recalls that the admissibility requirements are cumulative, such that if any one of them is not met, the Application is inadmissible. Having found that the Applicants did not exhaust local remedies, the Court considers it superfluous to rule on the other admissibility requirements under Article 56(1)(2)(3)(4)(6) and (7) of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50(2)(a)(b)(c)(d)(f)(g) of the Rules.
In view of the foregoing, the Court declares the Application inadmissible.
The Applicants pray the Court that the costs should be borne by the Respondent State.
The Respondent State does not submit on costs. ***
Under Rule 32(2) of the Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.
The Court notes that, although the Applicants pray that the Respondent State bear the costs of the proceedings, they did not adduce any proof of having incurred such costs.

Consequently, the Court considers that there is nothing in the present case to warrant a departure from the provisions of Rule 32(2) of the Rules and therefore decides that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that is has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Upholds the Respondent State’s objection to admissibility based on non-exhaustion of local remedies; and iii. Declares the Application inadmissible. On costs iv. Orders that each Party shall bear its own costs.

Mr Goore Bi Youzan Jean (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a national of the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire. At the time of filing this Application, he was serving a ten-year prison sentence for indecent assault with violence on a 15-year-old minor. He alleges violation of his rights in connection with proceedings before domestic courts.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”), on 31 March 1992, and to the Protocol to the Charter Establishing an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 25 January 2004. The Respondent State also deposited, on 23 July 2013, the declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications from individuals and Non- Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”). On 29 April 2020, the Respondent State deposited with the Chairperson of the African Union Commission the instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration. The Court has ruled that the said withdrawal has no effect, either on pending cases or on new cases filed before the withdrawal takes effect one year after the deposit of the relevant instrument, in this case, on 30 April 2021.
It emerges from the Application that the Applicant was charged with indecent assault with violence on a 15-year-old minor.
On 16 November 2011, he was convicted and sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment by the Criminal Division of the Yopougon Court of First Instance.
The Applicant appealed the said judgment before the Abidjan Court of Appeal which, by Judgment No. 608 of 18 July 2012, upheld the judgment of the Court of First Instance.
The Applicant avers that both at the trial court and the appeal court he admitted to having sexually touched the victim but denied the act of penetration of which he was accused.

The Applicant avers that “for reasons beyond his control”, he did not appeal the judgment of the Abidjan Court of Appeal before the Cassation Court, since, having not been assisted by counsel “in limine litis”, he was unaware of the existence of the cassation appeal remedy. He notes that, in any event, the appeal “would be futile under the current legal and judicial system of the State in question”.

The Applicant alleges violation of his right to a fair trial, as follows: i. The right of access to a judge and to justice provided for in Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the UDHR”), including the right to bring before the competent national courts any act that violates fundamental rights recognised and guaranteed by the conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force, protected by Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter; the right to the presumption of innocence, protected by Article 7(1)(b) of the Charter; the right to defence, protected by Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter; and the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court, protected by Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter; ii. The right to an effective remedy provided for in Article 8 of the UDHR. iii. The right to reasoned decisions in criminal proceedings; iv. The right to protection of the dignity of a person in custody, protected under Article 10(1) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the ICCPR”); v. The right to equality of arms and the adversarial principle; vi. The right to respect for the principle of proportionality of penalties.

The Application was received by the Registry on 22 July 2019 and served on the Respondent State on 14 August 2019 with a request to submit the names of its representatives and to file its Response within 30 and 60 days respectively.

On 25 September 2019, the Respondent State submitted the names of its representatives. On 18 March 2020, the Respondent State filed its Response, which was transmitted to the Applicant on the same day.
The Parties filed their other pleadings and supporting documents within the time limits set by the Court.
Pleadings were closed on 28 October 2021, and the Parties were duly notified.

The Applicant prays the Court to order the following measures: i. A presidential pardon; ii. Formal commutation of his 10-year determinate prison sentence to a lesser sentence; iii. Parole; iv. An out-of-court settlement; v. Financial compensation for the harm suffered as a result of the unjust judicial decisions handed down against him.

The Applicant further prays the Court to order the Respondent State to pay him the following sums as reparation for the harm suffered: i. 3,000,000 CFA francs as pecuniary reparation for legal damage; ii. 3,000,000 CFA francs as pecuniary reparation for material damage; iii. 4,000,000 CFA francs as pecuniary reparation for moral damage.

The Respondent State prays the Court to: i. Declare the Application inadmissible for breach of Article 6(2) of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and Article 56 of the Charter; or ii. Declare the Application unfounded and, consequently, dismiss it.

The Court notes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “The Court shall conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
In light of the aforementioned provisions, the Court must, in every application, conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on objections thereto, if any.

The Court notes that in the present case, the Respondent State does not raise any objection to its jurisdiction. Nonetheless, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it must ensure that all requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction are met.

Having found that there is nothing in the record to suggest that it lacks jurisdiction, the Court considers that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges violation of human rights protected by the Charter and the ICCPR, instruments to which the Respondent State is a Party. ii. Personal jurisdiction, since, as indicated in paragraph 2 of this Ruling, the Respondent State deposited the Declaration on 23 July 2013. Although on 29 April 2020, it deposited the instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration, the Court reiterates that the withdrawal of the Declaration has no retroactive effect and has no bearing on cases pending at the time of the deposit of the instrument of withdrawal or on new cases filed before the withdrawal takes effect, in this case, on 30 April 2021. The present Application, having been filed on 22 July 2019, that is, prior to the withdrawal of the Declaration, is thus not affected by it. iii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred after the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol. iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations took place on the Respondent State’s territory.
In light of the foregoing, the Court declares that it has jurisdiction to hear the present Application.
Under Article 6(2) of the Protocol, “[t]he Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases, taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter”.

Rule 50(1) of the Rules provides that “[t]he Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an application filed before it in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol, and these Rules”.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which essentially restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides as follows: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity, b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter; and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that, in the present case, the Respondent State raises three objections to admissibility based on the use of disparaging and insulting language, failure to exhaust local remedies, and the Application not being filed within reasonable time. The Court will rule on these objections before examining the other admissibility requirements, if necessary.

The Respondent State argues that the Application is inadmissible on account of the use of disparaging and insulting language against it. According to the Respondent State, describing the judicial decisions handed down against the Applicant as “unjust”, as well as the assertion that “even if he had lodged the aforementioned appeal, the outcome would have been unsuccessful under the current legal and judicial system of the Respondent State”, constitute disparaging language.
The Respondent State contends that, by making these remarks, the Applicant “brings shame and discredit upon its institutions, particularly its judicial system”. *

For his part, the Applicant maintains that the language ”unjust decisions”, which the Respondent State describes as disparaging or insulting, is not so. According to the Applicant, in this case, the said language suggests that the decisions in question are illegitimate, unfair and biased, given the total disregard for the rules of a fair trial. ***

The Court notes that under Article 56(3) of the Charter, restated in Rule 50 of the Rules, “…Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: (c) Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union”.

The Court recalls its jurisprudence that disparaging or insulting language is that which is generally intended to undermine the dignity, reputation, or integrity of a person, in particular public authorities, and the person using such language must provide evidence in support of his allegations.

The Court notes that the question arising here is whether the language referenced above by the Respondent State is disparaging or not, within the meaning of Rule 50 of the Rules. In this regard, the Court has, in the past, shared the Commission’s view that for a remark or language to be disparaging or insulting, it must be: aimed at unlawfully and intentionally violating the dignity, reputation and integrity of a judicial official or body and whether it is used in a manner calculated to pollute the minds of the public or any reasonable man to cast aspersions on and weaken public confidence on the administration of justice. The language must be aimed at undermining the integrity and status of the institution and bring it into disrepute.

In the present case, the Court considers that the Applicant’s assertions that the decisions of the domestic courts were “unjust” or that bringing a case before them would be “futile” cannot be regarded as intended to undermine the dignity, reputation, or integrity of the Respondent State’s authorities or institutions. This is not language that can be characterised as disparaging or insulting within the meaning of Rule 50(2)(c) of the Rules.
Consequently, the Court dismisses the objection to the admissibility of the Application based on the use of disparaging and insulting language.
