The Respondent State argues that the Application is inadmissible for nonexhaustion of local remedies, contending that it was not afforded the opportunity to remedy the alleged violations, insofar as the alleged violations were never brought before its domestic courts.
The Respondent State further submits that the Applicant did not pursue the appropriate remedies and is therefore not entitled to bring the matter before this Court. *
For his part, the Applicant prays that the objection be dismissed, arguing that the rule of exhaustion of local remedies is not absolute and must be interpreted flexibly.

The Applicant states that he appealed the judgment of the Yopougon Court of First Instance, but declares that, “for reasons beyond his control”, he did not appeal the judgment of the Abidjan Court of Appeal before the Cassation Court. However, he argues that, as he was not assisted by Counsel, he was unaware of the existence of the cassation appeal remedy and that, in any event, filing an appeal before the Court of Cassation “would be entirely futile within the current legal and judicial system of the State in question”. ***

The Court notes that under Article 56(5) of the Charter, restated in Rule 50(2) of the Rules, applications brought before it must be filed after exhaustion of local remedies, where such remedies exist, unless it is manifest that the proceedings thereof are unduly prolonged.

The Court emphasises that the remedies to be exhausted are judicial remedies. They must be available, that is, they must be capable of being exercised without hindrance. They must, furthermore, be effective and satisfactory in the sense that they are capable of remedying the situation in dispute. In line with the Court’s established jurisprudence, this requirement is waived only where the remedies fall short or where they are unduly prolonged.

Furthermore, the Court has consistently held that it assesses the exhaustion of local remedies in the light of the specific circumstances of each case and taking into account the remedies available under the judicial system of the Respondent State.

In the present case, the Court notes that the Applicant concedes that he did not appeal the judgment of the Abidjan Court of Appeal before the Cassation Court because he was not represented by Counsel and was unaware of the existence of the remedy, which, in any event, is ineffective.
The Court notes that it has consistently held that, within the Respondent State’s judicial system, a cassation appeal before the Cassation Court is an available, effective and satisfactory remedy.

The Court further reiterates, in line with its established jurisprudence, that the fact of not being assisted by Counsel or being unaware of the existence of a remedy cannot justify the failure to exercise that remedy. The Court further considers that an applicant cannot merely allege that a remedy is ineffective but must, at the very least, attempt to exercise it.
In view of the foregoing, the Court considers that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies and that, consequently, the Application does not meet this admissibility requirement.
Consequently, the Court upholds the Respondent State’s objection and holds that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies.

Having upheld the objection based on non-exhaustion of local remedies, the Court considers that there is no need to examine the objection based on the Application not being filed within a reasonable time.

Having found that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies, the Court considers it superfluous to rule on the other admissibility requirements under Article 56(1), (2), (3), (4), (6) and (7) of the Charter and Rule 50(2)(a), (b), (c), (d), (f) and (g) of the Rules.
Consequently, the Court declares the Application inadmissible.
Neither Party made submissions on costs. ***
The Court recalls that under Rule 32(2) of the Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.
The Court considers that, in the present case, there is no reason to depart from this provision.
Consequently, the Court decides that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Upholds the Respondent State’s objection based on nonexhaustion of local remedies; iii. Declares the Application inadmissible. On costs iv. Orders each Party to bear its own costs.

Mr Souleymane Camara (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a Malian national and businessman. He alleges violation of his rights in connection with judicial proceedings in domestic courts relating to a dispute between himself and his former business partner.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Mali (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986, and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 20 June 2000. The Respondent State also deposited, on 19 February 2010, the declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepts the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

It emerges from the Application that in 2010, the Applicant and one Mr Baba Moulaye Haïdara entered into a real estate and agribusiness partnership by pooling their expertise and capital. However, trust between the two business partners subsequently broke down, leading to the termination of their contractual relationship.

Following a complaint lodged by Mr Baba Moulaye Haïdara contesting the authenticity of an acknowledgement of debt submitted by the Applicant in the amount of Twenty-Five Million (25,000,000) CFA francs, criminal proceedings were initiated against the latter. By Judgment No. 47 of 7 September 2020 (hereinafter “the Judgment of 7 September 2020”) delivered in absentia, the Bamako Assize Court found the Applicant guilty of forgery and use of forged documents, and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment.

The Applicant alleges that he filed a motion to set aside the said judgment. According to him, that motion resulted in Judgment in Default No. 48 of 8 April 2021 (hereinafter referred to as “the Judgment of 8 April 2021”), by which the Bamako Assize Court upheld the sentence of ten years’ imprisonment imposed by the Judgment of 7 September 2020. The said court further imposed a ten-year prohibition on residence and ordered the Applicant to pay Mr Baba Moulaye Haïdara the sum of ten million (10,000,000) CFA Francs in damages. The Applicant avers without further detail, that as at the date of filing the present Application his appeal against the Judgment of 8 April 2021 had not yet been determined.

The Applicant alleges that in the course of the aforementioned proceedings, the domestic courts violated his fundamental rights protected under the Charter and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

The Applicant alleges violation of the following rights: i. The right to equality before the law and the right to equal protection by the law, protected by Article 3(1) and (2) of the Charter; ii. The right to dignity, protected by Article 5 of the Charter; iii. The right to have one’s cause heard, protected by Article 7(1) of the Charter; and iv. The rights protected by Articles 14(1), (2), (3)(d) and (e), 16, 19 and 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).
The Application, together with a request for legal aid, was filed on 20 April 2021.

On 18 June 2021, the Registry informed the Applicant that the Court had decided to grant him legal aid and had appointed Mr Mamadou Diarra, a member of the Malian Bar, to represent him. On the same date, the Registry forwarded the case file to the appointed counsel.

On 26 July 2021, the Application was served on the Respondent State, with a request to submit the names of its representatives and to file its Response within 30 days and 90 days respectively from the date of receipt of the notification.

Following the extension of time accorded on 18 August 2023 and 25 March 2024, the Respondent State filed its Response on 29 April 2024. The Response was notified to the Applicant with a request to file his Reply within 45 days from the date of receipt.
On 9 October 2024, the Applicant filed his Reply, which was notified to the Respondent State on 16 October 2024.
Pleadings were closed on 21 May 2025, and the Parties duly were informed.

The Applicant prays the Court to: i. Declare that it has jurisdiction; ii. Declare the Application admissible; iii. Declare that the Respondent State violated the Protocol, the Charter and other human rights instruments; iv. Order the Respondent State to pay him the sum of Eight Hundred And Fifty Million (850,000,000) CFA francs as damages for serious violation of his honour and dignity; v. Order the Respondent State to pay costs.

The Respondent State prays the Court to: i. Declare the Application inadmissible for lack of standing; ii. Find and hold that it did not violate the provisions of the Protocol or the Charter; iii. Declare the Application without merit and dismiss it; iv. Order the Applicant to pay the costs.

The Court observes that Article 3 of the Protocol provides: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “[T]he Court shall conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
In light of the aforementioned provisions, the Court must, in every application, conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on objections thereto, where applicable.

The Court notes that there’s no contention between the Parties with regards to its material, personal, temporal or territorial jurisdiction. Nevertheless, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it must ensure that all requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction have been fulfilled.
The Court finds that it has material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges violation of rights protected by the Charter and the ICCPR, instruments to which the Respondent State is a Party.
The Court further finds that it has personal jurisdiction insofar as the Respondent State is a Party to the Protocol and has deposited the Declaration.
As regards its temporal jurisdiction, the Court finds that this is established insofar as the alleged violations occurred after the Protocol had entered into force in respect of the Respondent State.
The Court also finds it has territorial jurisdiction insofar as the facts of the case and the alleged violations took place on the Respondent State’s territory.
Accordingly, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction to hear the Application.

The Court notes that the Respondent State raises an objection to the admissibility of the Application on the ground that the Applicant lacks standing to bring the matter before the Court, a requirement which is not expressly provided for in the Charter or the Rules.

In line with its established jurisprudence, the Court is required to examine this preliminary objection before determining if the admissibility requirements expressly prescribed by its constituent instruments are met.

The Respondent State raises an objection to the admissibility of the Application on the ground that the Applicant lacks standing to file the Application. It contends that the Applicant merely invokes international human rights instruments vaguely, without establishing any personal and direct injury. Consequently, the Respondent State prays the Court to declare the Application inadmissible.

The Applicant prays the Court to dismiss the said objection, arguing that he has victim status in this Application. In this regard, he submits that he is personally and directly affected by the alleged violations committed by the Respondent State, thereby establishing a sufficient causal link entitling him to bring the matter before this Court.

The Court recalls its established jurisprudence according to which “[a]rticles 5(3) and 34(6) of the Protocol do not require individuals or NGOs to demonstrate a personal interest in an application in order to have access to the Court”. Consequently, the Court has consistently held that, as a principle, applicants are not required to establish standing as a condition for filing an application before it.

However, the Court notes that, in the present case, the debate concerning the Applicant’s standing is pointless. Indeed, it emerges from the record that the violations alleged by the Applicant arose in connection with criminal proceedings brought against him. His standing cannot therefore be contested, since he is directly and personally affected by the judicial measures of which he complains.
Consequently, the Court dismisses the objection.
Article 6(2) of the Protocol provides: “[T]he Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases taking into account the provisions of article 56 of the Charter”.
Under Rule 50(1) of the Rules, “The Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an Application […] in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, Article 6(2) of the Protocol and these Rules”.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which substantially restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides as follows: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity; b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date the Court is seized with the matter, and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that the Respondent State does not raise any objection to admissibility based on requirements provided for in the aforementioned provisions. Nonetheless, the Court is duty-bound to ensure that those requirements are met.
In this regard, the Court finds that, in accordance with Rule 50(2)(a) of the Rules, the Applicant has clearly indicated his identity.

The Court also notes that the Applicant’s requests seek to protect his rights guaranteed by the Charter. Furthermore, one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, as set out in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. In addition, there is nothing on the record to suggest that the Application is incompatible with any provision of the Constitutive Act. The Court therefore finds that the Application is compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the Charter, and accordingly finds that it meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Court further notes that the Application does not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union, as required by Rule 50(2)(c) of the Rules.

The Court further finds that the Application meets the requirement under Rule 50(2)(d) of the Rules, insofar as it is not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media but rather concerns judicial decisions rendered by the Respondent State’s domestic courts.

The Court recalls that, pursuant to Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, the local remedies to be exhausted are judicial remedies. Such remedies must not only be available, that is, accessible to the Applicant without impediment, but must also be effective and sufficient, in the sense that they must be capable of directly redressing the impugned situation.

In the present case, the Court notes that the alleged violations arise from criminal proceedings brought against the Applicant for forgery and the use of forged documents. It further observes that, by a judgment in absentia delivered on 7 September 2020, the Bamako Assize Court found the Applicant guilty and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment.

The Court further notes that following the appeal filed by the Applicant against the said judgment, the Bamako Assize Court, by Judgment in repeated default of 8 April 2021, confirmed the ten-year prison sentence, and added a ten-year prohibition on residence, and ordered him to pay ten million (10,000,000) CFA francs in damages to the civil party. The Applicant submits that he lodged an appeal against that decision, which was pending at the time of filing of the present Application.

The Court observes that, in the present case, the remedy available against the 8 April 2021 Judgment of the Bamako Assize Court was an appeal before the Supreme Court, the highest judicial authority of the Respondent State. That remedy is expressly provided for under Article 505 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) and is instituted by means of a notice filed with the registry of the court that delivered the impugned decision.
In this regard, the Court has consistently held that, within the Respondent State’s judicial system, an appeal before the Supreme Court is an available remedy that must be exhausted.

The Court notes that, although the Applicant claims to have appealed the Judgment of 8 April 2021, he does not produce any evidence on record, such as a copy of the notice of appeal on points of law or an acknowledgement of filing, capable of demonstrating that he effectively exercised that remedy.
Consequently, the Court finds that the Applicant did not exhaust available local remedies.
It follows that the Application does not satisfy the admissibility requirement under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

Having found that the Application does not satisfy the requirement under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, and recalling that the admissibility requirements are cumulative, the Court observes that there is no need to determine whether the Application meets the other requirements under Article 56 of the Charter, as restated in Rule 50(2) (a), (b), (c), (d), (f) and (g) of the Rules.
The Court therefore declares the Application inadmissible.
Each Party prays the Court to order the other Party to bear costs. ***

The Court notes that proceedings before it are free of charge and that, as a general rule, each party bears its own costs. In the present case, none of Parties demonstrates the existence of circumstances warranting a departure from the provisions of Rule 32(2) of the Rules.
The Court therefore orders that each party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Finds that the Application does not meet the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules; iii. Declares the Application inadmissible. On costs iv. Orders that each party shall bear its own costs.

Mr Ibrahim Touré (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a Malian national and a civil servant. He alleges violation of his rights in connection with deductions made from his salary in respect of mandatory health insurance scheme, which he considers unlawful.

The Application is filed against the Republic of Mali (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986, and to the Protocol to the Charter Establishing an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 20 June 2000. The Respondent State also deposited, on 19 February 2010, the Declaration provided for under Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”), by virtue of which it accepts the jurisdiction of the Court to receive applications from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations with observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights.

As it emerges from the record, the Respondent State established a mandatory health insurance scheme (hereinafter “AMO”) pursuant to Law No. 09-015 of 26 June 2009 (hereinafter “the AMO Law”), to cover the health care costs of insured persons and their dependents. The administration of this scheme was entrusted to the National Health Insurance Fund (hereinafter “CANAM”), a public institution established under Law No. 09- 016 of 26 June 2009 (hereinafter “the CANAM Law”).

The Applicant avers that since 2009, deductions have been consistently made from his salary in respect of AMO contributions and paid to CANAM, without his prior consent. He further submits that he made several requests to CANAM to cease the deductions on the grounds that he was not a member of the scheme, but to no avail.

The Applicant further submits that on 24 January 2018, he petitioned the Minister for Higher Education and Scientific Research, as well as the Minister for Social Development and Solidarity, seeking his withdrawal from AMO and the refund of the monies deducted. The Applicant avers that he did not receive any response to his petition.

The Applicant asserts that in the wake of these implied rejections, on 12 June 2018, he filed a case before the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court which, by Judgment No. 193 of 5 March 2020, dismissed it.

The Applicant alleges violation of the following rights: i. The right to respect for inherent dignity and not to be subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment, protected by Article 5 of the Charter and Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR); ii. The right to non-discrimination, protected by Article 2 of the Charter, Article 26 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and Article 2 of the UDHR; iii. The right to equality before the law and the right to equal protection of the law, protected by Article 3 of the Charter and Article 7 of the UDHR.
The Application was filed on 7 August 2020. On 4 September 2020, the Registry requested the Applicant to refile his application using the form prescribed by the Rules of Court.

On 29 September 2020, the Applicant refiled a handwritten Application using the prescribed form. On 30 September 2020, 30 March 2021 and 14 July 2023, the Registry wrote to the Applicant requesting him to submit a legible and duly signed Application, but the Applicant did not comply.

On 23 August 2023, the Application was served on the Respondent State together with a request to submit the list of its representatives and file its Response within 30 and 90 days of notification, respectively.

Following extensions of time granted on 2 April 2024 and 19 August 2024, the Respondent State filed its Response on 10 September 2024. The response was transmitted to the Applicant on 13 September 2024 for his Reply within 45 days of receipt.
By email dated 1 April 2025, the Applicant informed the Registry that he would not be filing a Reply.
Pleadings were closed on 27 May 2025, and the Parties were duly informed.

The Applicant prays the Court to: i. Declare his claims admissible and well-founded, and grant the requests; ii. Order the cessation of the unjustified and unlawful deductions, subject to a penalty of One Hundred Thousand (100,000) CFA francs per month of delay from the date of the judgment; iii. Order the full refund of the said deductions, in addition to the interest legally due in the amount of Two Million Five Hundred Thousand (2,500,000) CFA francs; iv. Order his unequivocal withdrawal from the imposed AMO; v. Order compensation in the amount of Three Million (3,000,000) CFA francs for general damages; and vi. Order the Respondent State to pay all costs.
The Respondent State prays the Court to: i. Rule as appropriate on the admissibility of the Application; ii. Dismiss the Application as unfounded; and iii. Order the Applicant to pay all costs.

Article 3 of the Protocol provides that: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant Human Rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules, “[t]he Court shall conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and the admissibility of an Application in accordance with the Charter, the Protocol and these Rules”.
In light of the aforementioned provisions, the Court must, in every application, conduct a preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and rule on objections thereto, if any.

The Court notes that, in the present case, the Respondent State does not raise any objection to its jurisdiction. Nonetheless, in accordance with Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it must ensure that all requirements relating to all aspects of its jurisdiction are met before proceeding to hear the Application.

The Court considers that there is nothing in the record to suggest that it lacks jurisdiction, and therefore finds that it has: i. Material jurisdiction, insofar as the Applicant alleges violation of his rights protected under Articles 2, 3 and 5 of the Charter, Article 26 of the ICCPR, and Articles 1, 2 and 7 of the UDHR, instruments to which the Respondent State is a Party; ii. Personal jurisdiction, insofar as the Respondent State is a Party to the Protocol and has deposited the Declaration; iii. Temporal jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged violations occurred after the Respondent State became a Party to the Protocol; and iv. Territorial jurisdiction, insofar as the alleged facts and violations occurred on the Respondent State’s territory.
In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction to hear the Application.
Under Article 6(2) of the Protocol, “[t]he Court shall rule on the admissibility of cases taking into account the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.”

Rule 50(1) of the Rules provides that “the Court shall ascertain the admissibility of an application filed before it in accordance with Article 56 of the Charter, and Article 6(2) of the Protocol. and the Rules of Court”.

Rule 50(2) of the Rules, which restates the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter, provides that: Applications filed before the Court shall comply with all of the following conditions: a. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity; b. Are compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and with the Charter; c. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the African Union; d. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; e. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; f. Are submitted within a reasonable time from the date local remedies were exhausted or from the date set by the Court as being the commencement of the time limit within which it shall be seized with the matter; and g. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Constitutive Act of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the Charter.

The Court notes that the Respondent State does not raise any objection to the admissibility of the Application. Nonetheless, the Court must ensure that all admissibility requirements under the aforementioned provisions are met before proceeding to examine the Application.
In this regard, the Court observes that the Applicant has clearly identified himself and that the Application therefore complies with Rule 50(2)(a) of the Rules.

The Court also notes that the Applicant’s requests seek to protect his rights guaranteed by the Charter. Furthermore, one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, as set out in Article 3(h) thereof, is the promotion and protection of human and peoples’ rights. Moreover, the Application contains no allegations that are incompatible with the Constitutive Act. The Court therefore finds that the Application is compatible with the Constitutive Act and the Charter, and that it meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(b) of the Rules.

The Court notes that the Application is written in language that is neither disparaging nor insulting to the Respondent State and its institutions, nor to the African Union, so that it complies with Rule 50(2)(c) of the Rules.

The Court further finds that the Application meets the requirement of Rule 50(2)(d) of the Rules, insofar as it is not based exclusively on news disseminated in the mass media, but rather concerns the legislative and regulatory provisions of the Respondent State.

As regards the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules, the Court reiterates that every application brought before it must meet the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies, unless such remedies are unavailable, ineffective or insufficient, or the proceedings thereof are unduly prolonged.

In the present case, the Court notes that under Section 232 (2), (3) and (4) of Law No. 2016-046 of 23 September 2016 establishing the Organic Law on the organisation, the rules of operation, and the procedure followed by the Supreme Court (hereinafter referred to as “the Organic Law of 23 September 2016”), the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear petitions for misuse of power against express or implicit dismissal decisions issued by public authorities.

The Court further notes that the Applicant petitioned the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court challenging the implicit dismissal decisions pursuant to Article 232(2) of the Organic Law of 23 September 2016, owing to the fact that the Minister for Higher Education and the Minister for Social Development and Solidarity did not respond to his petition . The Administrative Division of the Supreme Court dismissed the petition by Judgment of 7 August 2020.

The Court also observes that, in the Respondent State’s judicial system, the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court is the highest court of the land in accordance with Article 111 of the Organic Law of 23 September 2016. Thus there is no remedy against the decision of the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court on the misuse of power.
The Court, therefore, finds that the Applicant exhausted local remedies, such that the Application meets the requirements of Rule 50(2)(e) of the Rules.

Regarding the requirement under Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules relating to the filing of the Application within a reasonable time after exhaustion of local remedies or from the date determined by the Court as the starting point for the time limit for its seizure, the Court notes that it has adopted a case-bycase approach in assessing the reasonableness of the time within which it is seized. However, the Court has held that the time limit for filing an application before it is manifestly reasonable where it is relatively short.

In the present case, the Court has found that local remedies were exhausted through the Judgment of the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court of 7 August 2020. The reasonable time limit will be calculated from that date, within the meaning of Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules. In the present case, the Application was filed with the Court on 29 March 2021, that is, seven months and 22 days after the exhaustion of local remedies. The Court considers that this time limit is manifestly reasonable. Consequently, the Application complies with Rule 50(2)(f) of the Rules.

Finally, the Court finds that the present Application does not concern a matter previously settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the provisions of the Charter and therefore complies with Rule 50(2)(g) of the Rules.

In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Application meets all the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the Charter and restated in Rule 50(2) of the Rules. Accordingly, it declares the Application admissible.

The Court recalls that the Applicant alleges violations of his right to inherent dignity, protected by Article 5 of the Charter and Article 1 of the UDHR; his right to non-discrimination, protected by Article 2 of the Charter and Article 26 of the ICCPR; and his right to equality before the law and to equal protection of the law, protected by Article 3 of the Charter and Article 7 of the UDHR.

The Court will examine each of the Applicant’s allegations successively. However, the Court notes that notwithstanding the fact that the Applicant relies, in addition to the Charter, on the ICCPR and the UDHR to support his allegations, it will, in line with its jurisprudence, consider the said allegations solely in light of the corresponding provisions of the Charter, which is the principal instrument it applies.
The Applicant avers that the Respondent State violated his right to inherent dignity, as protected by Article 5 of the Charter and Article 1 of the UDHR.
In this regard, he argues that since 2009, regular deductions have been made from his salary, without his consent, and paid to CNAM as compulsory health insurance contributions.

He further submits that those deductions, consequent losses and deprivation of income suffered over the past 12 years, have caused him and his family significant psychological distress. According to the Applicant, this psychological distress constitutes an act of torture, thereby violating his right to dignity.

In response, the Respondent State contends that the application of a duly adopted and enacted law does not constitute any fault, a violation of rights or an abuse of power in any country in the world.

The Respondent State submits that it cannot be held at fault given that the Applicant, like all civil servants, is subject to the AMO scheme and that the corresponding contributions are deducted from his salary in accordance with Decree No. 10-601/P-RM of 18 November 2010, which establishes the contribution rates applicable to the AMO scheme.

The Respondent State contends that, in May 2010, in the quest to ease the social tensions caused by the AMO law, the Government, in agreement with the major workers’ trade union organisations, authorized workers who did not wish to join AMO to submit individual requests for exemption no later than 15 December 2011. The decision was announced through a statement in the Essor newspaper on 21 May 2011 and on subsequent dates.

The Respondent State argues that workers who failed to submit a request for exemption before the aforementioned deadline could no longer withdraw from the AMO scheme, as the law makes membership mandatory. It further contends that the Applicant’s request was not received by CANAM until March 2017, that is, six years and three months after the deadline for submitting requests for exemption had elapsed.
The Respondent State therefore submits that it did not violate the Applicant’s rights protected by Article 5 of the Charter and Article 1 of the UDHR.

Article 5 of the Charter, whose violation is alleged by the Applicant, provides that: “Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited”.

The Court notes that the violation alleged by the Applicant is anchored on two arguments: first, that the deductions were made without his consent and, second that the deductions caused psychological suffering amounting to torture.

The Court recalls that human rights are an indivisible whole, in the sense that all rights, whether civil, political, economic, social or cultural, are interdependent and of equal importance. They cannot be ranked or dissociated, as the violation of one right may affect the enjoyment of others.

In this regard, the Court notes that although the Applicant alleges violation of his right to inherent dignity due to deductions effected on his salary without his consent under a health insurance scheme, the matter also relates to the right to health provided for in Article 16 of the Charter, which enshrines the right of every individual to “enjoy the best attainable state of physical and mental health” and its corollary, namely the obligation on each “State Party to the Charter […] to take the necessary measures to protect the health of their people and to ensure that they receive medical attention when they are sick”.

The Court notes that mandatory national health insurance established by law enables the State to guarantee the effective enjoyment of the right to health, insofar as it ensures the pooling of risks for the target population, irrespective of income or health status, thereby making health care accessible and rendering the right practical and effective.

The Court observes that, where such insurance scheme is established, insured persons must necessarily pay contributions to ensure the proper functioning and sustainability of the protection system put in place, so that such contributions serve the purpose of social protection for the insured. It follows that the principle of national solidarity and the State’s obligation to protect the community takes precedence over the individual consent of an employee.
Moreover, such salary deductions, when used to fund a universal health care system, contribute to the preservation of collective human dignity by providing individuals free or affordable health care.

The Court emphasises, however, that this principle cannot be general and absolute, since the amount deducted may become incompatible with human dignity where it reduces individuals to a state of deprivation such that they can no longer meet essential needs.
The Court notes in this case, based on the Applicant’s August 2017 payslip, that the amount deducted in respect of AMO corresponds to 3% of his net salary.
The Court finds that the amount deducted in respect of AMO cannot, clearly, undermine the Applicant’s right to a dignified and decent life.
The Court therefore considers that this argument is not well founded.
The Court recalls the Applicant’s claim that the deductions from his salary caused him and his family psychological distress amounting to torture.

The Court recalls its position that deductions from the Applicant’s salary does not, per se, amount to torture nor does it violate his right to dignity, but rather contribute to give effect to his right to health.

The Court notes that the Applicant does not provide any evidence that would enable it to assess the existence and severity of the psychological suffering he claims to have endured. Nor does any such evidence emerge from the record. Consequently, the Court finds that the argument is unsubstantiated.
The Court therefore dismisses the Applicant’s allegation and finds that the Respondent State did not violate Article 5 of the Charter.
The Applicant alleges that the Respondent State violated his rights guaranteed by Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter, Article 26 of the ICCPR, and Articles 2 and 7 of the UDHR.

He submits that the AMO law enacted by the Respondent State is discriminatory and violates his right to equality before the law insofar as it does not apply to all citizens, but only to salaried workers. *

The Respondent State contends that it did not violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter. It submits that the AMO law is generally applicable and thus applies to all employees in both the private and public sectors within the meaning of the Labour Code. ***

The Court notes that Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter provide that: Article 2: Every individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as race, ethnic group, colour, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status. Article 3 1 Every individual shall be equal before the law. 2 Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law.

The Court notes that the Applicant alleges discrimination arising from the AMO law, as he considers that it establishes a distinction between nonsalaried citizens and salaried workers in both the private and public sectors, and that, as a result, the Respondent State is in violation of the principle of equality of citizens before the law.
The Court notes in line with its established jurisprudence that the right to non-discrimination is linked to the right to equality before the law and to equal protection of the law.

The Court has also held that the principle of equality before the law does not necessarily require equal treatment in all circumstances. It may also allow for differential treatment of individuals or groups in objectively different situations, provided that such treatment pursues a legitimate aim, and is proportionate to the aim sought.

In the present case, the Court must determine whether the application of the AMO law to a specific category of citizens, namely, salaried employees in the private and public sectors, constitutes discrimination and a violation of equality in relation to other categories of citizens not subject to that law.

Regarding the first criterion, the Court notes that the contested law concerns a specific regime applicable to salaried private and public sector employees. By virtue of their relationship of subordination and the nature of remuneration, such employees are in a different legal and economic situation from that of self-employed or unemployed persons. The circumstances of persons subject to the AMO law justify a distinct legislative approach adopted by the Respondent State in the exercise of its regulatory powers.

In this regard, the Court notes that legislature enjoys a “wide margin of discretion”. The Court therefore observes that the Respondent State acted within the limits of that margin in defining the scope of the AMO law, as the distinction between non-salaried citizens and salaried employees in both the private and public sectors is a classic and universally recognised distinction in social law.

As regards the second criterion, the Court observes that the organisation of a legal regime or its application to specific sectors of activity does not, in itself, constitute discrimination, provided that the inclusion or exclusion criteria are informed by technical and objective factors. In this regard, the Court notes that the difference in situation established in the preceding paragraph constitutes sufficient objective basis for the legislature to enact specific rules applicable exclusively to private and public sector employees.

Finally, regarding the proportionality criterion, the Court emphasises that the general aim of a mandatory national health insurance scheme is to guarantee universal access to health care while protecting individuals against the financial risks associated with illness. In the present case, Section 2 of the law on mandatory health insurance provides insured persons and their dependents health care costs coverage for illness and maternity, in return for a modest financial contribution by way of salary deductions. As such, the automatic application of the law to persons falling within the targeted categories cannot be regarded as disproportionate in relation to the objective pursued.

Consequently, the Court finds that the distinction established by the AMO law is based on an objective and reasonable ground linked to the management of workers in the Republic of Mali. The law is therefore not discriminatory in nature and does not contradict the principle of equality before the law.
In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that the Respondent State did not violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter.

The Applicant prays the Court to order the Respondent State to cease all unjustified and unlawful deductions from his salary, subject to a penalty of One Hundred Thousand (100,000) CFA francs per month of delay from the date of the judgment, the full refund of the said deductions together with legally due interest, his unequivocal withdrawal from the mandatory AMO scheme, and compensation in the amount of Two Million (2,000,000) CFA francs for all prejudice suffered. *
The Respondent State generally prays that the Applicant’s requests be dismissed, without making any specific submissions on reparations.

The Court notes that, under Article 27(1) of the Protocol, “if the Court finds that there has been violation of a human or peoples’ right, it shall make appropriate orders to remedy the violation, including the payment of fair compensation or reparation”.
The Court reiterates that it has found that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicant’s rights. There is, therefore, no basis for ordering reparations.
The Court therefore dismisses the Applicant’s requests for reparations.
The Applicant makes no submissions on costs.
The Respondent State, for its part, requests that the Applicant bear the costs.
Under Rule 32 of the Rules, “[u]nless otherwise decided by the Court, each party shall bear its own costs, if any”.

The Court notes that proceedings before it are free of charge and that, although the Respondent State requests that the costs be borne by the Applicant, it does not demonstrate that it incurred any costs.
The Court finds, in the present case, that there are no grounds warranting a departure from the principle laid down in that provision.
Consequently, the Court decides that each Party shall bear its own costs.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, On jurisdiction i. Declares that it has jurisdiction. On admissibility ii. Declares the Application admissible. On the merits iii. Holds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicant’s right to inherent dignity, protected in Article 5 of the Charter; iv. Finds that the Respondent State did not violate the Applicant;s right to non-discrimination and equality before the law, protected by Articles 2 and 3 of the Charter. On reparations v. Dismisses the requests for reparations. On costs vi. Orders each Party to bear its own costs.

The Application is filed by Chief Festus A. Ogwuche and 24 others (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicants”) who are nationals of various member States of the Economic Community of West African States (hereinafter referred to as “the ECOWAS”). They allege violation of their rights due to the proposal to amend Protocol A/P.1/7/91 on the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice.

The Application is filed against the following six States (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent States”): i. Burkina Faso, which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 25 January 2004. Burkina Faso deposited the Declaration required under Article 34(6) of the Protocol (hereinafter “the Declaration) on 28 July 1998 thereby accepting the jurisdiction of the Court to accept cases from individuals and NGOs with observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter “the Commission”). ii. The Republic of the Gambia, which became a Party to the Charter on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 25 January 2004. It deposited the Declaration on 3 February 2020. iii. The Republic of Ghana, which became a Party to the Charter on 1 March 1989 and to the Protocol on 16 August 2005. It deposited the Declaration on 10 March 2011. iv. The Republic of Guinea Bissau, which became a Party to the Charter on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 2 November 2021. It deposited the Declaration on 2 November 2021. v. The Republic of Mali, which became a Party to the Charter on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol on 25 January 2004. It deposited the Declaration on 19 February 2010. vi. The Republic of Niger, which became a Party to the Charter on 21 October 1986, and to the Protocol on 26 June 2004. On 7 April 2022 it deposited the Declaration.

The Applicants allege that following an extraordinary summit of the ECOWAS Heads of State and Government, the Chief Justices of ECOWAS member States, acting in their capacity as the “Community’s Judicial Service Commission”, proposed an amendment to Protocol A/P.1/7/91 on the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice (hereinafter referred to as “the ECOWAS Court”) to incorporate the requirement for exhaustion of domestic remedies as a prerequisite for the admissibility of cases before the ECOWAS Court.

The Applicants contend that the proposal to incorporate the requirement for the exhaustion of domestic remedies would procedurally and substantively deprive them of their fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter and other international human rights instruments.

The Applicants also assert that the establishment, and expanded jurisdiction of the ECOWAS Court, was driven by the recognition that domestic courts had largely failed to guarantee the protection and enforcement of individuals’ rights. They assert that the ECOWAS Court was created to serve the people of the region, not the interests of member States against whom those people frequently bring claims of rights violations. Consequently, the Applicants argue that any decision affecting the functioning and accessibility of the ECOWAS Court cannot be legitimately made without consulting the very individuals for whose benefit the Court was established.

In the main Application, the Applicants allege that the Respondent States’ conduct violates the following rights and obligations: i. The obligation of States to recognize and implement the rights, duties, and freedoms enshrined in the Charter, as provided under Article 1 of the Charter; ii. The right to have one’s cause heard, including the right to appeal, presumption of innocence, legal defence, and trial within a reasonable time, as provided under Article 7 of the Charter; iii. The right to self-determination and to freely determine political status and economic, social, and cultural development, as protected under Article 20(1) of the Charter; iv. The right of colonized or oppressed peoples to free themselves from domination, as provided under Article 20(2) of the Charter; v. The right of oppressed peoples to receive assistance in their liberation struggle against foreign domination, as protected under Article 20(3) of the Charter; vi. The right to self-determination, as protected under common Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter “the ICCPR”) and the International Covenant on Economic Social and Cultural Rights (hereinafter the “ICESCR”); vii. The obligation of States to adopt necessary legislative or other measures to give effect to recognized rights, as provided under Article 2(2) of the ICCPR; viii. The right to an effective remedy for violations of fundamental rights, as provided under Article 3 of the ICCPR; ix. The right to an effective remedy for acts violating fundamental rights, as protected under Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (hereinafter “the UDHR”); x. The right to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal guaranteed under Article 10 of the UDHR; xi. The right to a social and international order in which rights and freedoms can be fully realized enshrined under Article 28 of the UDHR and; xii. The prohibition against engaging in activities that undermine the rights and freedoms in the Declaration, as enshrined under Article 30 of the UDHR.

The Applicants also allege, without specifying the particular provisions thereof, that the Respondent States’ conduct violates the ECOWAS Protocol on Democracy, Elections and Good Governance, the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa.
The Application, together with a request for provisional measures, was filed as against all 15 member States of the ECOWAS on 10 May 2024.
On 28 July 2024, the Registry informed the Applicants of the registration of the Application and requested them to provide further information in relation to the decision(s) complained of.

On 9 October 2024, the Applicants filed “documentary materials” that they alleged were in support of their Application. They also informed the Court that “appropriate applications for regularization of our processes” would be filed later.

In a Ruling dated 17 June 2025, the Court struck out one of the Applicants, being a Non-Government Organisation, for not having observer status before the Commission. Additionally, the Court found that some of the Respondent States included by the Applicants were not Parties to the Protocol, while others had deposited instruments withdrawing their Declarations, which had already taken effect. Accordingly, the Court struck them out from being parties to the Application.

The Application was served on the Respondent States on 27 June 2025. They were requested to submit the list of their representatives within 30 days and to file their Responses to the request for provisional measures and the main Application within 30 and 90 days of receipt, respectively.
On 12 July 2025, the Republic of Niger filed its Response to the Application.
On 2 October 2025, the Republic of Ghana filed its Response to the request for provisional measures.
On 10 October 2025, Burkina Faso filed its Response to both the request for provisional measures and the main Application.
On 6 November 2025, the Republic of Ghana filed a request for extension of time for filing the Response. Filed together with this request for extension of time was a copy of its Response.

On 13 March 2026, the request for extension of time by the Republic of Ghana was served on the Applicants and the other Respondent States who were all given fifteen (15) days, from the date of notification, to file any observations on the request.
On 19 March 2026, the Court dismissed the request for provisional measures and reserved its determination of the main Application.
By an Order dated 23 April 2026, the Court granted Ghana leave to file its Response out of time and deemed the Response duly filed. Ghana’s Response was transmitted to the parties on 17 June 2026.

On 26 May 2026, the Republic of Mali filed, electronically, a request for an exceptional extension of time to file its Response. A copy of its Response was attached to the electronic communication. The signed hard copies were, subsequently, filed on 11 June 2026.

On 18 June 2026, the Registry acknowledged receipt of the request by the Republic of Mali and transmitted the same to the Applicants and the Respondent States inviting them to file observations on the request within 15 days of receipt.

The Republic of Niger acknowledged receipt of the request by the Republic of Mali on 18 June 2026 and informed the Registry that it endorsed the additional factual and legal arguments advanced by the Republic of Mali.
None of the other Parties to the Application filed any observations to the request by the Republic of Mali.

In its request, the Republic of Mali acknowledges that it failed to file its Response within the prescribed time but submits that its failure was not borne out of disrespect for the Court. It explains that changes within the Direction Générale du Contentieux de l’État, together with other official commitments connected to the particular situation of the country, disrupted the ordinary performance of administrative tasks and prevented filing within time. It thus prays for the Court to extend time for filing its Response. *

In so far as the time limit for filing pleadings is concerned, the Court considers that Rules 44(5) and 44(6) of the Rules are relevant. These Rules provide as follows: 44(5) Any further extension of time may only be granted by decision of the Court taking into account the particular circumstances of the case. 44(6) The decision to extend time is at the discretion of the Court.
The Court notes that a combined reading of Rules 44(5) and 44(6) confirms that it has the discretion to determine whether or not to reopen pleadings.

The Court also notes that Rule 90 of the Rules stipulates that “nothing in these Rules shall limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to adopt such procedure or decisions as may be necessary to meet the ends of justice.”
Ultimately, therefore, it lies within the discretion of the Court to decide whether or not to extend time for filing pleadings.

In the instant Application, the Court observes that no objection to the request for extension of time has been registered by the Applicants or any other party to the proceedings. In the circumstances, the Court holds that, for the proper administration of justice, the request by the Republic of Mali must be granted.
Given that the Republic of Mali already filed a copy of its Response, the Court thus holds that the Response be deemed to have been properly filed.

The Court, in the circumstances, orders that the Response filed by the Republic of Mali be served upon the Applicants and the other Respondent States in this Application. The Applicants and the other Respondent States are given 30 days, from the date of notification of this Order, to file a Reply, should they so wish.

For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, i. Grants the request by the Republic of Mali to file its Response out of time; ii. Holds that the Response filed by the Republic of Mali be deemed to have been duly filed; iii. Orders that the Response by the Republic of Mali be served on the Applicants and other Respondent States, who shall file a Reply, if any, within 30 days from the date of notification of this Order.

Mr. Brahim Ben Mohamed Ben Brahim Belgeith (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”), is a Tunisian national and a lawyer residing in France with his office in Montfleury, Tunisia. He alleges violation of the fundamental rights of Tunisians by the Republic of Tunisia following its withdrawal of the Declaration filed in accordance with Article 34(6) of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter “the Protocol”).

The Application is filed against the Republic of Tunisia (hereinafter referred to as “the Respondent State”), which became a Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as the “Charter”) on 16 March 1983, and to the Protocol on 21 August 2007. It deposited, on 16 April 2017, the Declaration under Article 34(6) of the Protocol by virtue of which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive cases from individuals and Non-Governmental Organisations having observer status before the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Declaration”). On 7 March 2025, the Respondent State deposited, with the African Union Commission, an instrument withdrawing the said Declaration. The Court has held that this withdrawal has no bearing on pending cases and new cases filed before 8 March 2026, which is the day on which the withdrawal took effect, being a period of one year after its deposit.

The Applicant alleges that the President of the Respondent State, Mr. Kais Saied, invoked the exceptional circumstances based on Chapter 80 of the Respondent State’s Constitution of 2014. In particular, the President assumed a position above the Constitution and seized the executive and legislative powers. According to the Applicant, this Court has ruled that the exceptional measures taken were unconstitutional and it issued a decision nullifying those measures, ordered a return to constitutional democracy, and the establishment of a constitutional Court.

The Applicant also alleges that the Respondent State did not comply with the decision of this Court, issued more orders that undermined the democratic process, and further promulgated a new constitution in 2022, which consolidated the authority of the President of the Republic.

The Applicant cites some of the presidential orders and decrees previously issued by the President of the Respondent State as follows: - Decree-Law No. 2022-11 on the High Judicial Council, under which the President of the Republic and the executive branch intervene in the appointment and dismissal of members of the High Judicial Council, and amend its composition. - Presidential Decree No. 2022-35, which grants the President of the Respondent State the authority to dismiss judges and prosecutors without disciplinary or administrative procedures and also without the right to challenge such decision by exercising their right to defence. - Presidential Decree No. 2022-516, in relation to the dismissal of 54 judges without due procedures. The judges who obtained a stay of execution from the President of the Administrative Court were unable to resume their duties. Four of them resorted to this Court, which issued an order of provisional measures to suspend the implementation of Decree 35/2022 and Order 516/2022 pending consideration of the merits of the case. However, the Respondent State did not comply with the decision of the Court. - Organic Law No. 2014-16, relating to elections and referenda, which was amended to allow the President of the Respondent State to appoint and dismiss members of the Independent High Electoral Commission and control the course and outcome of elections; - Decree No. 2022-54 on combating cybercrime and “false information” online, particularly in chapter 24, which is used in prosecuting journalists, activists, and critics. This decree is a subject of a case before this Court, Application No. 006/2022 – Salaheddine Kchouk v. Republic of Tunisia.
The Applicant also alleges that the Respondent State withdrew the Declaration, which constitutes a violation of a number of human rights as outlined in his Application before this Court.

The Applicant alleges the violation of the following rights: i. The right to have one’s case heard, guaranteed by Articles 1 and 7 of the Charter, 5 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter referred to as “ICCPR”), Articles 5(3), 34(6) and 35 of the Protocol and articles 31(3), 26 and 60(1) of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (hereinafter referred to as “VCLT”); ii. The right to participate freely in the public affairs of one’s country as provided for in Articles 13(1) of the Charter and Article 25(a) of the ICCPR; iii. The right to information guaranteed in Article 9(1) of the Charter.
The main Application, together with a request for provisional measures, were filed on 7 July 2025.

On 21 July 2025, the main Application, together with the request for provisional measures, were served on the Respondent State, which was granted 45 days to respond to the request for provisional measures and 90 days to respond to the main Application. At the expiration of these deadlines, the Respondent State had not filed any Responses.
On 3 December 2025, the Respondent State was reminded of the expiration of the deadlines and was granted an additional 30 days to file its Responses but it did not do so.

Article 3 of the Protocol provides as follows: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol, and any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the States concerned. 2. In the event of a dispute as to whether the Court has jurisdiction, the Court shall decide.

The Court recalls that, pursuant to Rule 49(1) of the Rules, it “shall preliminarily ascertain its jurisdiction ….” However, as regards requests for provisional measures, it is not necessary at this stage of the proceedings for the Court to satisfy itself that it has jurisdiction to examine the merits of the Application. The Court must only satisfy itself that it has prima facie jurisdiction in the matter.
In the instant case, the Court observes that the Applicant alleges violation of rights protected under the Charter and the ICCPR, instruments to which the Respondent State is a party.

The Court further notes that, as stated in paragraph 2 of this Ruling, the Respondent State became a party to the Charter on 16 March 1983, and to the Protocol on 21 August 2007, and deposited the Declaration on 16 April 2017. On 7 March 2025, the Respondent State deposited, with the African Union Commission, an instrument withdrawing the said Declaration. The Court had held that this withdrawal has no bearing on pending cases and new cases filed before 8 March 2026, which is the day on which the withdrawal took effect, being a period of one year after its deposit. This Application having been filed on 7 July 2025 is thus not affected by the withdrawal of the Declaration.
In the circumstances, the Court finds, therefore, that it has prima facie jurisdiction to consider the Request for provisional measures.

The Applicant prays the Court to order the Respondent State to: i. Put on hold the decision of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs filed with the African Union Commission on the withdrawal of the Declaration of the Court’s jurisdiction under Article 34(6) of the Protocol pending a decision on the merits of the case is rendered. ii. If the court deems it necessary not to make an order, to suspend the withdrawal of the Declaration of jurisdiction, order the entry into force of the withdrawal from 8 March 2026, by any other means the court deems appropriate.

In substantiating the first request, the Applicant argues that the Respondent State’s withdrawal of the Declaration would result in Tunisians being deprived of their right to access justice, which is serious and dangerous reality in light of the continuing human rights violations in Tunisia as well as the Respondent State’s failure to comply with the Court’s previous rulings and orders.

The Applicant alleges that it is certain that the entry into force of the withdrawal of the Declaration on 8 March 2026 would deny Tunisians the means of litigation guaranteed under Articles 7 of the Charter and 14 of ICCPR. He emphasises that this is especially the case because of the absence of domestic remedies and continued violations under Tunisia’s current decrees, some of which this Court ordered to be revoked.

The Applicant avers that the extreme gravity and urgency of the matter is documented in international reports submitted to international bodies, highlighting the deterioration of the human rights situation in the Respondent State. He further submits that at the domestic level, there are a number of legal instruments in force that have led to the violation of the independence of the judiciary, and of the principle of separation of powers, and supremacy of the constitution.

It is also the Applicant’s contention that the decision to withdraw the Declaration will deprive the Tunisians of the right to be heard before this Court after the expiry of a one-year period. According to the Applicant, with the elapsing of the deadline before the determination of the main Application in the present matter, individuals and non-governmental organisations will no longer have the right to seize this Court, which constitutes irreparable harm to them.

The Applicant also alleges that the situation of extreme gravity and urgency justifies the issuance of provisional measures and that rejecting the request would be tantamount to not providing assistance to those who are in danger.

He reiterates that this Court is the last resort for Tunisians, specifically with regard to the serious violations of the Tunisian Constitution and other laws that affect the independence of the judiciary, as there is no other competent body to consider such violations.

With regard to the second request for provisional measures, the Applicant prays the Court, should it not grant an order for provisional measures, to suspend the decision to withdraw the Declaration and to delay the entry into force of the withdrawal to any other time as it may deem fit. *
The Respondent State did not file any submissions. ***

Pursuant to Article 27(2) of the Protocol, the Court may, at the request of a party, or on its own accord, in case of extreme gravity and urgency and where necessary to avoid irreparable harm to persons, adopt such provisional measures as it deems necessary, pending determination of the main Application.
In light of the above, the Court has the discretion to order provisional measures only in cases of extreme gravity and urgency and in order to prevent irreparable harm to individuals.

The Court recalls that urgency, which is consubstantial with extreme gravity, means that “irreparable and imminent risk will be caused before it renders its final judgment.” The Court further recalls that the risk referred to must be real, which excludes the purely hypothetical risk and justifies the need to remedy it in the immediate future.
With respect to irreparable harm, the Court considers that there must be a “reasonable probability of occurrence” having regard to the context and the Applicant’s personal situation.
In light of the above, the Court can order provisional measures only if the requirements of extreme gravity, urgency and irreparable harm to persons are met.

The Court emphasizes, however, that it is only required to ascertain the existence of these basic conditions if it is established that the measures sought do not prejudge the merits of the main application.

The Court recalls that the merits of an application are prejudged by a request for provisional measures when the measures sought are identical to those requested in the main application or if they seek to achieve the same result, or if the request for provisional measures addresses matters which the Court necessarily must decide when considering the merits of the Application.

In the instant case, the Court notes that the Applicant seeks provisional measures aiming at ordering the Respondent State to put on hold the decision to withdraw the Declaration, pending the Court’s ruling on the merits of the main Application. The Applicant alternatively prays that should the Court deem it necessary not to order the suspension of the withdrawal of the Declaration, it should order the delay of entry into force of the withdrawal from 8 March 2026 to any other date that it finds appropriate.

The Court also notes that in the main Application, the Applicant prays the Court, among others, to suspend or extend the date of entry into force of the withdrawal of the Declaration and find that it violates human rights.

The Court finds that it cannot examine the provisional measures requested without discussing the merits of the main Application. As such, granting the measures requested would amount to prejudging the merits of the main Application. In the circumstances, the Court cannot order the provisional measures requested by the Applicant.
The Court, therefore, dismisses the Applicant’s request for provisional measures.

For the avoidance of doubt, the Court reiterates that this Ruling is interlocutory in nature and shall not be taken to prejudice or determine its eventual findings in respect of its jurisdiction, the admissibility of the Application, or the merits thereof.
For these reasons: THE COURT, Unanimously, i. Hold that it has prima facie jurisdiction; ii. Dismisses the Request for provisional measures.

Saif Eddine Makhlouf (hereinafter referred to as “the Applicant”) is a national of Tunisia, a lawyer and a Member of Assembly of the Representatives of the People. He alleges the violation of his rights during the proceedings before the national courts.

The Respondent State became party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Charter”) on 21 October 1986 and to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (hereinafter referred to as “the Protocol”) on 5 October 2007 and deposited the Declaration required under Article 34(6) of the Protocol by which it accepted the jurisdiction of the Court to receive cases from individuals and Non-Governmental Organizations on 2 June 2017. On 7 March 2025, the Respondent State submitted to the African Union Commission an instrument of withdrawal of the said Declaration. The Court decided that this withdrawal would have no effect on pending cases and new cases filed before 8 March 2026, the date on which the withdrawal took effect, that is, one year after its submission.

It emerges from the Application that, on 15 March 2021, the Applicant, acting in his capacity as a Member of the Assembly of the Representatives of the People and as legal counsel, proceeded to Tunis-Carthage International Airport to assist a woman who had been prevented from travelling. A confrontation ensued with airport staff and security union members, leading to a criminal investigation of the Applicant and his referral to the Tunis District Court in a case publicly known as “the airport case”.

The Applicant alleges that on 30 July 2021, the Secretary-General of the National Union of Internal Security Forces also submitted a complaint to the Military Prosecutor concerning the Applicant’s confrontation with the airport staff and the security union members. A subsequent separate and parallel military investigation led to the Applicant’s referral to the Permanent Military Court of Tunis.
On 21 March 2022, the Tunis District Court convicted the Applicant of insulting a public official in the course of the performance of his duty and sentenced him to three-month imprisonment.

On 16 May 2022, the Permanent Military Court of Tunis convicted him of undermining the dignity and morale of the national army and insulting a public official, for which he received a suspended sentence of one year imprisonment.

The Applicant appealed the decision of the Tunis District Court before the Court of First Instance of Tunis, sitting as an appellate court, which, on 25 May 2022, upheld the conviction while suspending the custodial sentence. The Applicant did not submit further information with regard to this procedure.

With regards to the procedure before the Military Court, both the Prosecution and the Applicant appealed the decision of the Permanent Military Court and on 20 January 2023, the Criminal Chamber of the Military Court of Appeal upheld the guilty verdicts of the Military Court of First Instance and issued a more severe sentence to the Applicant of one year and two months’ imprisonment for “disturbing the public peace with the aim of committing an offence or opposing the execution of a law and insulting public officials while on duty”. The Applicant served eight months in prison. Upon further appeal, a military appellate judgment on 22 October 2024 confirmed the conviction and custodial sentence.

The Applicant appealed against the decision of the Military Court of Appeal to the Court of Cassation, which quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the Military Court of Appeal for rehearing. On 13 June 2023, the Military Court of Appeal set aside the conviction for undermining army morale but upheld the offence of insulting a public official by words and threats, sentencing the Applicant to one-month imprisonment and a twoyear ban from legal practice, without suspension. On 1 July 2024, the Court of Cassation declared a subsequent appeal inadmissible.

Subsequently, the Applicant fled to Algeria, where he was convicted for unlawful entry and sentenced to three-month imprisonment. He sought asylum from the Annaba Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (hereinafter referred to as “UNHCR”) and was placed under UNHCR protection. Despite the preliminary approval by the United Kingdom for family reunification, he was surrendered by the government of Algeria to Tunisia on 18 January 2025, allegedly in violation of the Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees. The Applicant provided no further information regarding events between 18 January 2025 and 4 February 2026, when he filed the present Application.

In the main Application, the Applicant alleges the violation of the following: i. The right to equality and equal protection of the law; ii. The right not to be tried twice for the same offenses; iii. The right to a competent and independent court and the prohibition of trying civilians before military courts; iv. The right to defense, as a right of a fair trial; v. The right to the presumption of innocence and liberty; vi. The right to the legality of crimes and punishments; vii. The right to freedom of movement and to leave the country; viii. The right not to be extradited; and ix. The right to enjoy the human rights enshrined in the Charter and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
On 4 February 2026, the Applicant filed the main Application together with a request for provisional measures.

The Application was served on the Respondent State on 6 March 2026 for its responses within 45 days for the request on provisional measures and, 90 days for the main Application. The Respondent State did not respond to the request for provisional measures within the timeframe allocated.

Article 3(1) of the Protocol provides that: The jurisdiction of the Court shall extend to all cases and disputes submitted to it concerning the interpretation and application of the Charter, this Protocol and any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the States concerned.

Under Rule 49(1) of the Rules of the Court “the Court shall conduct preliminarily examination of its jurisdiction…”. However, with respect to the provisional measures, the Court need not satisfy itself that it has jurisdiction on the merits of the case, only that it has prima facie jurisdiction.

In the instant case, the Applicant alleges the violations of rights protected under Articles 1, 3, 7(1)(a), 7(1)(c), 7(1)(d), 7(2) and 12(2) of the Charter and Article 14(7) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter referred to as “ICCPR”) to which the Respondent State is a party. The Court further notes, as indicated at paragraph 2 of the present Ruling, the Respondent State is a party to the Protocol and had filed the Declaration.
