The Complainant requests the Commission to: a. Consider the referral of the Communication to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Court) pursuant to Article 118.3 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure, the case being one of many cases of serious human rights violations and in particular cases of torture committed during this period in Burundi; b. Declare the Communication admissible; c. Find that the facts before the Commission disclose violations by the State Party of Articles 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 18(1) and 26 read together with Article 1 of the African Charter. d. Order the Respondent State to provide appropriate reparation to the victim, including measures of financial compensation for the material and non-material harm caused, measures of psychological, economic, social and judicial rehabilitation as well as measures of satisfaction, in particular through public apologies addressed to the victim accompanied by a strong message condemning such acts and their impunity; e. Request the Respondent State to adopt all necessary measures so that such facts do not recur; f. Request the Respondent State to publish the Commission's findings; g. Order the Respondent State to report, within a period of 3 months, on the follow-up it has given to the Commission's conclusions.
The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission on 18 June 2019. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 2 July 2019.

During the 26th Extraordinary Session, held from 16 to 30 March 2019, the complaint was seized, satisfying all the requirements of Rule 93(2) of the 2010 Rules. On that same occasion, the Commission decided to defer to a later date the consideration of the request for referral of the case to the Court.

On 5 August 2019, the parties were informed of the seizure of the complaint and the Complainant was requested to submit his arguments and evidence on admissibility within two (2) months, in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure of 2010.
On 14 March 2024, the Complainant was granted an additional period of thirty (30) days to submit his arguments on admissibility, failing which the complaint would be closed.

The Commission notes that after the seizure of the complaint, the Complainant was requested to submit his arguments and evidence on the admissibility of the communication within two (02) months of receipt of the notification.

The Commission notes that the Complainant did not submit his arguments and evidence on admissibility within the two (2) months following notification of the seizure of the complaint, nor did he do so within the additional thirty (30) days granted to him.

The Commission finds that a total of more than 5 years, 6 months days elapsed between the notification of the seizure of the complaint and the start of the present session. Moreover, more than 10 months have elapsed between the end of the additional 30-day period and the start of the present session.
The Commission observes that the Complainant has not shown any interest in pursuing the present Communication.

The Commission recalls, in this regard, its jurisprudence, in particular in Communications 594/15 Mohammed Ramadan Mahmoud Fayad Allah v. Arab Republic of Egypt; 612/16 Ahmed Mohammed Ali Subaie v. Arab Republic of Egypt; 412/12 Journal Echos du Nord v. Republic of Gabon and Communication 387/10 Kofi Yamagnane v. Togo, which were dismissed for lack of diligence.

In view of the foregoing, and having regard to the lack of diligence shown by the Complainant in pursuing the present Communication, the Commission decides to order its striking out. Adopted at the 82nd Ordinary Session of the African Commission, held virtually from 25 February to 11 March 2025.

Le Secrétariat de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu, le 5 novembre 2018, une Communication déposée par la World Service Authority (la Représentante), agissant au nom de la population Ogoni déplacée (la Plaignante).
La plainte est dirigée contre la République du Bénin (l'État défendeur), État partie à la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte Africaine).

La Plainte note que la population Ogoni a fui le Nigéria en 1999 en raison de persécutions alléguées et de l'absence de protection de la part du gouvernement, de l'inexistence de statut juridique en tant que population et de la crainte de menaces de mort après la destruction de leurs maisons.

La Plainte indique que les victimes sont arrivées et ont demandé l'asile dans le camp de réfugiés de Kpomasse au Bénin, d'où elles ont été refoulées le 16 septembre 1999 et contraintes de se réinstaller dans les camps de Lebou et Ouidah, au Bénin.
La Plainte soutient qu'après leur refoulement, les victimes se sont installées dans des tentes et des structures temporaires, où elles vivent depuis vingt ans.

La Plainte note en outre que les victimes sont confrontées à un obstacle linguistique important, car elles parlent une langue différente de celles utilisées au Bénin. De plus, en raison de leur situation irrégulière, elles ne bénéficient d'aucune aide publique, ce qui entraîne une insécurité alimentaire alarmante.

La Plainte souligne en outre valoir que l'État défendeur n'a pas fourni d'éducation aux enfants, ni un environnement de travail sûr et une assistance médicale, soulignant que l'accès à un médecin leur a été refusé au cours des vingt dernières années. En outre, il est allégué que la population Ogoni dépend de médicaments obtenus auprès de sources non officielles et de remèdes maison à base de plantes locales.

La Plainte affirme qu'en 2001, l'Ambassadeur du Nigéria au Bénin a fourni aux victimes de la nourriture empoisonnée, qui a causé la mort d'une grande partie de leurs animaux domestiques. De plus, il est allégué que les représentants diplomatiques nigérians au Bénin ont tenté d'entraver la demande d'asile des Ogoni, qui a été rejetée à chaque fois, ne leur accordant pas le statut de réfugiés ni l'accès à une assistance juridique.

La Plainte affirme en outre que les rapports des victimes ont mis en évidence l'existence de menaces de mort proférées par des fonctionnaires nigérians au Bénin. Par conséquent, la population Ogoni craint des représailles à son arrivée si elle choisit de retourner dans son pays d'origine (le Nigéria).

La Plainte affirme en outre que les victimes ont fait état de menaces d'arrestation et d'expulsion de la part du Ministère de l'Intérieur et de la Commission nationale d'aide aux réfugiés (CNAR). Toutefois, il est également allégué qu'un seul témoin peut témoigner, le pasteur Monday Ngbenenee, qui réside dans le camp de Lebou et a été témoin des conditions qui y règnent ainsi que des interactions entre les Ogonis et les étrangers.

La Plainte soutient que, selon les victimes, l'État défendeur a manqué à son obligation de les protéger compte tenu de ses relations diplomatiques avec le Nigéria, ce qui a conduit à leur ostracisme, à leur discrimination et à leur persécution.
La Plaignante allègue la violation des articles 2, 3, 5, 12 (3), 16, 17 et 18 (3) de la Charte Africaine.

La Plaignante demande à la Commission de : Veiller à ce que la population Ogoni obtienne réparation pour les souffrances endurées au cours des vingt (20) dernières années ; Rendre une décision ordonnant à l'État défendeur d'accorder l'asile aux victimes ou ; Veiller à ce que les victimes trouvent un refuge sûr où elles ne vivront plus dans la peur permanente.

Le Secrétariat a reçu la plainte le 5 novembre 2018 et en a accusé réception le 11 janvier 2019. Dans cette lettre, il a été aussi demandé à la Plaignante des précisions afin de savoir si la plainte était dirigée contre le Nigéria, le Bénin ou les deux États et quelles mesures avaient été prises pour épuiser les recours internes. Le Secrétariat a reçu les réponses le 17 janvier et le 6 avril 2019.
La plainte a été admise lors de la 68ème session ordinaire tenue à Banjul, en Gambie, du 14 avril au 4 mai 2021.

Le 8 octobre 2021, les parties ont été informées de l'admission de la plainte et la Plaignante a été invitée à soumettre ses observations sur la recevabilité et le fond dans un délai de soixante (60) jours, conformément à la règle 116((1) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission de (2020). Le Secrétariat a également demandé à la Plaignante des précisions si le camp des réfugiés en cause était officiel ou pas.

Le 13 août 2024, le Secrétariat a envoyé un rappel à la Plaignante relative à lettre lui demandant de soumettre ses observations sur la recevabilité et lui a demandé d'indiquer si 'elle souhaite toujours poursuivre l'affaire, faute de quoi, la Commission pourrait procéder à la radiation de la Communication pour défaut de poursuite diligente. Le même jour, la Plaignante informe la Commission qu'elle était toujours intéressée à poursuivre l'affaire et qu'elle cherchait des informations pour répondre aux questions posées par la Commission dans la lettre d'admission.
Le 23 aout 2024, la Plaignante a informé la Commission que le camp de réfugiés en cause n'est pas officiel et a confirmé que la plainte est introduite aussi contre le Nigéria.
Malgré le rappel du 13 aout 2024, la Plaignante n'a pas soumis ses observations sur la recevabilité et le fond de la Communication.

La règle 116(1) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission (2020) dispose que lorsque la Commission est saisie d'une plainte, elle demande à la Plaignante de présenter des preuves et des arguments sur la recevabilité et le fond de la Communication dans un délai de soixante (60) jours à compter de la réception.

Dans la présente Communication, la Plaignante a été invitée, par une lettre datée du 8 octobre 2021, à présenter des preuves et des arguments sur la recevabilité et le fond de la Communication dans un délai de soixante (60) jours à compter de la notification. Cependant, la Plaignante ne l'a pas fait. Le délai prescrit de soixante (60) jours a expiré le 5 décembre 2021, mais aucune preuve ni aucun argument n'ont été présentés dans le délai imparti.

Le 13 août 2024, le Secrétariat a adressé une lettre de rappel à la Plaignante, réitérant la demande de présenter des preuves et des arguments sur la recevabilité et le fond de la Communication et l'informant que l'absence de réponse pourrait constituer un motif de radiation de la Communication.
Près de quatre (4) ans se sont écoulés depuis l'expiration du délai, et aucun élément de preuve ni argument n'a été présenté par la Plaignante sur la recevabilité et le fond de la Communication.
Compte tenu de ce qui précède, la Commission estime que la Plaignante n'a pas manifesté son intérêt à donner suite à la Communication .

Compte tenu de ce qui précède, la Commission décide de radier la présente Communication pour défaut de procédure diligente, en application de la règle 124(2) de son Règlement intérieur de 2020. Adoptée lors de la 84 session ordinaire de la Commission africaine, tenue virtuellement du 21 au 30 juillet 2025 à Banjul, Gambie.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received, on 5 November 2018, a Communication submitted by the World Service Authority (the Representative), acting on behalf of the displaced Ogoni population (the Complainant).
The complaint is brought against the Republic of Benin (the Respondent State), a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complaint notes that the Ogoni population fled Nigeria in 1999 on account of alleged persecution and the lack of protection from the government, the absence of legal status as a population, and fear of death threats after the destruction of their homes.

The Complaint states that the victims arrived and sought asylum in the Kpomasse refugee camp in Benin, from where they were pushed back on 16 September 1999 and forced to resettle in the Lebou and Ouidah camps, in Benin.
The Complaint contends that, after their removal, the victims settled in tents and temporary structures, where they have been living for twenty years.

The Complaint further notes that the victims face a significant language barrier, as they speak a language different from those used in Benin. Moreover, because of their irregular situation, they receive no public assistance, which results in alarming food insecurity.

The Complaint further alleges that the Respondent State has not provided education for the children, nor a safe working environment and medical assistance, stressing that access to a doctor has been denied to them over the past twenty years. In addition, it is alleged that the Ogoni population relies on medicines obtained from unofficial sources and on home remedies made from local plants.

The Complaint states that in 2001, the Ambassador of Nigeria to Benin provided the victims with poisoned food, which caused the death of a large part of their domestic animals. Moreover, it is alleged that Nigerian diplomatic representatives in Benin attempted to obstruct the asylum application of the Ogoni, which was rejected each time, without granting them refugee status or access to legal assistance.

The Complaint further states that the victims' accounts revealed the existence of death threats made by Nigerian officials in Benin. Consequently, the Ogoni population fears reprisals on arrival should it choose to return to its country of origin (Nigeria).

The Complaint further states that the victims reported threats of arrest and expulsion from the Ministry of the Interior and the National Commission for Assistance to Refugees (CNAR). However, it is also alleged that only one witness can testify, Pastor Monday Ngbenenee, who lives in the Lebou camp and has witnessed the conditions there as well as the interactions between the Ogonis and outsiders.

The Complaint contends that, according to the victims, the Respondent State failed in its obligation to protect them in view of its diplomatic relations with Nigeria, which led to their ostracism, discrimination and persecution.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 2, 3, 5, 12(3), 16, 17 and 18(3) of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission to: Ensure that the Ogoni population obtains reparation for the suffering endured over the past twenty (20) years; Render a decision ordering the Respondent State to grant asylum to the victims or; Ensure that the victims find a safe refuge where they will no longer live in permanent fear.

The Secretariat received the complaint on 5 November 2018 and acknowledged receipt on 11 January 2019. In that letter, the Complainant was also asked to clarify whether the complaint was directed against Nigeria, Benin or both States, and what steps had been taken to exhaust local remedies. The Secretariat received the replies on 17 January and 6 April 2019.
The complaint was seized at the 68th Ordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 14 April to 4 May 2021.

On 8 October 2021, the parties were informed of the seizure of the complaint and the Complainant was requested to submit its observations on admissibility and the merits within sixty (60) days, in accordance with Rule 116((1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2020). The Secretariat also asked the Complainant to clarify whether the refugee camp in question was official or not.

On 13 August 2024, the Secretariat sent a reminder to the Complainant concerning the letter requesting it to submit its observations on admissibility, and asked it to indicate whether 'it still wishes to pursue the case, failing which the Commission may proceed to strike out the Communication for lack of diligent prosecution. On the same day, the Complainant informed the Commission that it was still interested in pursuing the case and that it was seeking information to answer the questions put by the Commission in the letter of seizure.
On 23 August 2024, the Complainant informed the Commission that the refugee camp in question is not official and confirmed that the complaint is also brought against Nigeria.
Despite the reminder of 13 August 2024, the Complainant has not submitted its observations on the admissibility and merits of the Communication.

Rule 116(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2020) provides that when the Commission is seized of a complaint, it requests the Complainant to submit evidence and arguments on the admissibility and merits of the Communication within sixty (60) days of receipt.

In the present Communication, the Complainant was requested, by a letter dated 8 October 2021, to submit evidence and arguments on the admissibility and merits of the Communication within sixty (60) days of notification. However, the Complainant did not do so. The prescribed period of sixty (60) days expired on 5 December 2021, but no evidence or arguments were submitted within the time allowed.

On 13 August 2024, the Secretariat sent a reminder letter to the Complainant, reiterating the request to submit evidence and arguments on the admissibility and merits of the Communication and informing it that failure to respond could constitute grounds for striking out the Communication.
Almost four (4) years have elapsed since the expiry of the time limit, and no evidence or arguments have been submitted by the Complainant on the admissibility and merits of the Communication.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission considers that the Complainant has not shown an interest in pursuing the Communication.

In view of the foregoing, the Commission decides to strike out the present Communication for lack of diligent prosecution, pursuant to Rule 124(2) of its Rules of Procedure of 2020. Adopted at the 84th Ordinary Session of the African Commission, held virtually from 21 to 30 July 2025 in Banjul, The Gambia.

The Arab Republic of Egypt (Egypt) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter), ratified on 3 April 1984.

In accordance with Article 62 of the African Charter, Egypt presented its initial Periodic Report at the 11 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission), held from 2 to 9 March 1992, in Tunis, Tunisia.

Subsequently, the 7 - 8 Periodic Report was considered by the Commission during its 37 Ordinary Session held in Banjul (The Gambia) from 27 April to 11 May 2005 and the 9 – 17 Periodic Report (2001-2017) during the 64 Ordinary Session of the African Commission, held from 24 April to 14 May 2019 in Sharm El Sheikh, Arab Republic of Egypt. The relating Concluding Observations were adopted at the 31 Extraordinary Session, held virtually from 19 to 25 February 2021.

Egypt submitted its 18 - 19 Combined Periodic Report under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights 2019-2024 (the Report under review) in May 2025. The same was reviewed on 25 and 27 October 2025, during the 85 Ordinary Session of the African Commission, held in Banjul from 21 to 30 October 2025.

A high-level Egyptian Delegation led by H.E. Ambassador Khaled Elbakly, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs, Chair of the Technical Committee for Human Rights, represented the State Party during the review, which was marked by a frank and constructive dialogue with the members of the Commission.
At the end of the interactive dialogue, the Egyptian Delegation undertook to provide the Commission with more information in writing and sent a written contribution on 1 December 2025.
The Commission wishes to commend the State Party for its strong engagement in State Reporting, under Article 62 of the African Charter.

The Commission takes note with appreciation of the participatory and inclusive process that led to the preparation of the Periodic Report under review, through the Permanent High Commission for Human Rights, established in 2020 by a decision of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, which includes all Ministries and Government agencies concerned with human rights, under the leadership of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (paragraph 2).

Whilst appreciating the State Periodic Report, the present Concluding Observations reflect positive aspects and factors limiting the enjoyment of human rights in Egypt. They also highlight the areas of concern identified through the review of the Report and the additional information provided subsequently.

Finally, the Commission presents recommendations to Egypt on measures necessary to strengthen the enjoyment of human rights by all Egyptians as guaranteed by the African Charter, as well as other relevant regional and international instruments. Recommendation: Egypt should: Continue the State Party's commitment to the submission of Periodic Reports, in accordance with the relevant ACHPR Guidelines on State Reporting. Ratifications
The Commission takes note that Egypt did not ratify any African or international human rights instrument during the period under consideration.

The Delegation has stated that accession to international instruments is an act of sovereignty, whereby each State has the right to determine its position on such treaties, in accordance with its specific circumstances, and the legal and societal consultation that may be required for some of their provisions.

The Commission believes that international treaties, negotiated and concluded by the States themselves, reflect a collective desire to promote human rights. Their ratification, while it is indeed a matter of sovereignty, remains a fundamental step for the promotion and protection of human rights at the national and international levels.

The Commission notes with appreciation that executive measures have recently been taken to accede to the Protocols to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons and on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Strengthen its efforts to finalise the ratification of the Protocols to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons and on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. - Engage consultations on the ratification of the following instruments: • At the African Union level: o The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; o The AU Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (Kampala Convention); o The AU Convention on Ending Violence Against Women and Girls; o The African Charter on the Values and Principles of Decentralisation, Local Governance and Development; o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol); o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights; o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security; o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Specific Aspects of the Right to a Nationality and the Eradication of Statelessness in Africa; o The Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights. • At the United Nations level: o The Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance; o The 1954 United Nations Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons; o The 1961 United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. o The Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture; o The two Optional Protocols to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; o The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; o The Optional protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; o The Optional Protocols to the Convention on the Rights of the Child; o The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. National Human Rights Framework

Article 5 of the 2014 Egyptian Constitution states that “The political system is based on political and partisan pluralism, (…), and respect for human rights and freedoms, as stated in the Constitution”.

The Commission welcomes the first National Human Rights Strategy (2021-2026) launched in September 2021,with a consultative approach involving all ministries and government agencies, and non-governmental organisations, drawing on international experiences and best practices in many countries around the world (paragraph 3). The Delegation stated that the Strategy has reached 90% of its objectives by 2026.

The Delegation recognises that the lifting of the state of emergency in October 2021 has contributed to the promotion of a range of rights and freedoms, foremost among them the right to a fair and equitable trial. It also contributed to the promotion of public freedoms and facilitated national dialogue among political components. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue its efforts to extend and reformulate the National Human Rights Strategy (2021-2026) for the coming period and provide sufficient human and financial resources for the implementation of its targets. - Continue strengthening the capacity and mandate of the High Permanent Committee for Human Rights. - Continue its efforts to popularise and disseminate the African Charter and other relevant regional human rights instruments. - Regardless of articles 151 and 93 of the Constitution, consider adopting national legislation to domesticate international human rights treaty provisions, to contribute to a better protection and promotion of human rights. Non-discrimination (Article 2)

Non-discrimination is provided for in Articles 4, 9, 11, 53 of the Egyptian Constitution. Egypt ratified the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination on 1 May 1967.

The Commission takes note of the provisions aiming at preventing and combatting discrimination in the Egyptian legislation, inter alia Law No. 14 of 2025 enacting the Labor Law (Article 4), the Penal Code (Article 161 bis), Sports Law No. 71 of 2017, Law No. 10 of 2018 on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, etc. However, the State Party’s attention is drawn to recent allegations on acts of discrimination from Sudanese and Eritrean refugees. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Consider adopting a specific law on preventing and combatting discrimination. - Ensure that the specific law prohibits discrimination in all spheres, including direct and indirect discrimination and discrimination on ethnic affiliation, religion, disability, albinism, socio-economic status, HIV/AIDS, political opinions or other status. - Pursue efforts to combat eventual discriminatory practices under any customary law. - Pursue efforts in raising awareness on and combatting discrimination. - Investigate the recent allegations of discrimination provided recently by Sudanese and Eritrean refugees. Right to Freedom of Conscience (Article 8)
The Commission takes note that the right to freedom of conscience is provided for in articles 3, 53 and 64 of the Egyptian Constitution (paragraph 30).
The Delegation stated that the Egyptian Government is considering lifting its reservation on article 8 of the African Charter. The Commission welcomes this positive development.

The Commission takes note with appreciation that the practice of religious activities shall not be prohibited or suspended for any reason whatsoever in Egypt, including in unlicensed church buildings. The number of churches and related service buildings that have been legalised rose from 1,800 churches and buildings in January 2021 to 3,613 churches and buildings in October 2025, an increase of nearly 70%. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Continue efforts to promoting inter-religious dialogue. - Pursue its efforts of church restoration and legalisation, according to Law No. 80 of 2016 on the regulation, construction, and restoration of churches. Right to Participate in Public Affairs / Government (Article 13)

The Report informs that, during the period under review, Elections for the House of Representatives held in October 2020, with the election of 165 women (27% of the members of the House), 123 young people under the age of 40, 9 persons with disabilities, 8 Egyptians living abroad and 38 Christians.

The Delegation stated that the Egyptian Supreme Administrative Court shall have jurisdiction to rule on appeals against the decisions of the National Elections Authority related to referendums, presidential, and parliamentary elections and their results, while appeals against local elections shall be brought before the Administrative Court.

A Short-Term Joint African Union / COMESA Election Observation Mission was deployed to Egypt to observe the 10-12 December 2023 presidential election. The Mission noted with satisfaction the peaceful atmosphere in which the presidential election was held. However the Commission notes that the Observer Mission did not underscore the importance of Civic Education in the election preparatory process. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue the measures aiming at strengthening confidence in the electoral processes, in particular through the effective implementation of Law No. (45) of 2014 on the exercise of political rights. - Redouble efforts to implement the AU Joint Election Observation Mission recommendations, in particular regarding the need to provide clear identification to polling officials and candidates’ agents, the continuous training for polling officials on closing and counting procedures to enhance their proficiency and the efficiency in the issuance of accreditation badges to allow for timely deployment of observers. - The Commission encourages the State Party to ensure that an inclusive Civic education program is part of future election processes. National Human Rights Institution and other institutions (Art 26)

The Report under review mentions Presidential Decree No. 616 of December 2021 which restructured the National Council for Human Rights (NCHR). The NCHR is a member of the Network of African National Human Rights Institutions and enjoys the ACHPR affiliate Status. It is accredited with “A” status by the Global Alliance of NHRI.

The Commission takes note of the detail on the nomination of the NCHR Members provided by the Delegation. 6 The Joint African Union (AU) and Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) Election Observation Mission to the 10–12 December 2023 Presidential Elections in the Arab Republic of Egypt - Preliminary Statement. 7 https://www.nanhri.org/members-egypt/ 8 Granted at the 73rd Ordinary Session, held in Banjul – Oct/Nov 2022 https://achpr.au.int/en/nhris/national-council-human-rights-arab-republic-egypt 9 https://ganhri.org/membership/ Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue its efforts to strengthen the independence and effectiveness of the NCHR in delivering its mandate. - Pursue its efforts to strengthen the human and financial resources of the NCHR, in line with national and regional standards. - Involve the National Council more closely in the monitoring and the follow-up on the regional and international human rights organs' recommendations. Cooperation with the Commission

The African Commission wishes to reiterate and extend its appreciation to the GoE for having hosted the ACHPR 64 Ordinary Session from 24 April to 14 May 2019 in Sharm el-Sheikh. Additionally, the Commission is grateful for the GoE for having received Hon. Dr. Litha Musyimi-Ogana, the Country Rapporteur for Egypt at the ACHPR, in December 2024.

However, the Delegation did not provide updates on the measures taken to implement decisions on communications adopted by the Commission during the reporting period. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue its commendable cooperation with the ACHPR. - Take concrete measures to implement decisions adopted by the Commission on communications 344/07 (adopted at the 66th Ordinary Session in August 2020), 396/11 (adopted at the 66th Ordinary Session in August 2020) and 424/12 (adopted at the 75th Ordinary Session in May 2023). Specific recommendations Mandate of the Working Group on the Death Penalty and Extrajudicial, Summary or Arbitrary killings and Enforced Disappearances in Africa Article 4: Right to Life
The Commission notes the main safeguards established by the Egyptian law for the imposition of the death penalty provided by the Report as well as the written answers of the Delegation.

Reports inform that, in 2024, 509 individuals, including 49 women, were under sentence of death, with 13 executions, including 2 women, carried out by hanging. Egypt did not ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR, and consistently opposed the UN General Assembly Resolution calling for a universal moratorium on the use of the death penalty, from 2007 to 2024.
During the period under review, the Commission expressed several times its concerns about the persistence of the application of the death penalty in Egypt.

The Commission notes the legal and institutional arrangements and frameworks in place to prevent extrajudicial killings in Egypt; inter alia the legal framework governing the use of force by law enforcement officials. Recommendations: Egypt should: - The Commission reiterates its recommendation to Egypt to adopt a moratorium on the death penalty and eventually move towards its de jure abolition. - Disseminate the Commission's General Comment No. 3 of 2016 on the Right to Life. - Consider commuting the death sentences on individuals currently on death row to life imprisonment. - Explore the possibility of invoking Presidential pardon in exceptional cases. - Ensure that investigations and prosecutions are initiated concerning all allegations of summary or arbitrary executions. - Pursue its efforts, in the framework of the National Human Rights Strategy, to reduce the scope of application of death penalty to the most serious crimes. - Ratify the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance. - Ensure that the Egyptian legislation identifies enforced disappearance as an autonomous offence and provides for the non-derogability of the prohibition of enforced disappearance under any exceptional circumstances. - Ensure effective prosecution / conviction / reparation for cases / victims of enforced disappearances. - Disseminate the Commission’s Guidelines for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance in Africa. - Support the draft Protocol to the African Charter on the Abolition of the Death Penalty in Africa. Mandate of the Committee for the Prevention of Torture in Africa Article 5: Prohibition of Torture, Cruel, Inhuman and Degrading Treatment

Egypt ratified the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment in June 1986. Article 52 of the Egyptian Constitution explicitly prohibits torture in all its forms and manifestations, identified as a crime that is not subject to a statute of limitations.

The Commission takes note of the detailed information provided by the Delegation on the national efforts aiming at preventing and combatting torture (prohibition of torture according to the principles of absolute and non-derogable prohibition, the principle of non-applicability of statutory limitations, the principle of non-discrimination and the principle of exclusion of evidence obtained through torture, the State's action plan to prevent torture, the establishment and modernisation of a number of correctional and community rehabilitation centres (prisons) in all regions of the country and training to law enforcement agents).

The Delegation did not provide information about the implementation of the Commission’s Decisions on communications, which concluded that Egypt violated Article 5 of the African Charter, and ordered the Egyptian Government to pay compensation and to issue a public apology to victims. 12 https://achpr.au.int/fr/documents/2022-10-25/lignes-directrices-protection-personnes-disparitions-forcees- afrique 13 For instance: Communication 396/11, Mohammed Abderrahim El Sharkawi (represented by EIPR and OSJI) v Egypt and Communication 344/07, George Iyanyori Kajikabi v Egypt. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Provide in its next periodic Report information on the implementation of the Commission’s Decisions on communications, which concluded that Egypt violated Article 5 of the African Charter. - Consider ratifying the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture. - Continue efforts to prevent and punish police brutality, excessive use of force and the culture of impunity. - Ensure that investigations / convictions are led on cases of torture, legal aid is provided and reparations are granted for victims, in accordance with Resolution ACHPR/Res.303 (LVI) 2015, on the right to rehabilitation of torture victims. - Take steps to ensure that none of the equipment that has any legitimate purpose for maintaining law and order (such as direct contact with electric shock weapons, whips or restraint devices such as thumb handcuffs, weighted handcuffs or wall/floor fixtures) is currently in use by law enforcement, including prison authorities. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Prisons, Conditions of Detention and Policing in Africa
The Report informs that Article 52, 94, 96 and 97 of the Egyptian Constitution provide that all persons are equal before the law and have the right to enjoy its protection.

The Commission welcomes the entry into force of Law No. 1/24 introducing amendments to the Code of criminal procedure, in order to address issues of regulating pretrial detention and reducing its duration, ensuring immediate release upon reaching the maximum duration, introducing mechanisms for appealing pretrial detention decisions, compensating those who have suffered material and moral damage in cases of wrongful pretrial detention, and emphasizing the application of alternatives, all under judicial oversight at various levels.

The Commission acknowledges the efforts made by the Egyptian Government, and in particular the Ministry of Justice, to implement the comprehensive plan to modernize the system, with an emphasis on training for the judiciary.

On the other hand, the Commission expresses some concern about the maintenance of the minimum age of criminal responsibility in Egypt at 15 years of age, as well as the lack of information on a considerable age group of children, from 12 to 14 years and 11 months of age, who may come into conflict with the law.

The Delegation provided a list of crimes for which civilians may be tried before military courts in Egypt. The Delegation also provided some information on the existing legal aid system, without presenting statistics on the received requests / granted legal aid during the reporting period.

The Commission welcomes the country's change of philosophy towards strengthening the rights of persons deprived of their liberty, in accordance with the new designation. However, the Delegation did not provide statistical data on prison infrastructure, now referred to as rehabilitation centers, and the respective prison population in the country.

Although the Delegation enumerated measures taken by Egyptian authorities to improve health service and living conditions in detention, the Commission remains concerned about the number of detainees died in Egypt’s prisons, mainly due to heat and difficult conditions. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Strengthen the existing legal aid system to give a concrete expression to Article 98 of the Egyptian Constitution which guarantees the right to defend oneself or to be defended by a representative. - Provide in its next periodic Report statistics on the prison infrastructure and the respective prison population in the country. - - Ensure that the use of preventive detention is considered an exceptional measure. - Promote a change in philosophy in the daily practice of those deprived of their liberty, improving sanitation conditions, vocational and academic training, and visiting and recreation programs. - Strengthen the use of alternative or non-custodial sentences for minor offences, where deprivation of liberty may be a measure of last resort. - Strengthen efforts to disseminate the instruments adopted by the ACHPR, such as the Luanda Guidelines, the Mandela Rules and the Principles on the decriminalisation of minor offences and the study on the use of firearms and the Guidelines on Policing Assemblies. - Strengthen the prison health circuit, in terms of: Medical assistance, clinical examinations, medication assistance, including for chronically ill and mentally ill persons, improvement of hygiene conditions and water supply. - Strengthen efforts in training law enforcement officials at the national level in areas related to the promotion and protection of human rights, mainly with the rights of persons deprived of liberty. - Increase the number of magistrates and pursue efforts to create decent conditions enabling people working in the justice system to perform their work with dignity. - Continue efforts to ensure that vocational training and leisure programs for prisoners in the country are respected and implemented. - Demonstrate in its next periodic report that the quality of life for prisoners in Egypt is comparable to the “Badr Prison” model. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa

The Egyptian Constitution, in its Articles 67 and 68, provides that information, data, statistics, and official documents belong to the people, and obliges the State to disclose them and make them available.

The Delegation stated that Law No. 356 of 1954 regulates freedom of access to official documents held in the National Library and Archives and permits scholars and researchers to freely access and photocopy these documents. It also establishes the Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics, entrusted with the production, publishing, and analysis of high quality official statistical data. The Commission also notes the Supreme Council for Media regulation, established by Law 180-2018.

Furthermore, the Commission takes note of the Egyptian media landscape (580 registered newspapers, more than 74 licensed satellite channels, more than 247 licensed websites, and more than 14 radio stations).

The Delegation has emphasised that the authority to block websites is exclusively vested in the judiciary, according to articles 6 and 7 of Law No. 175 of 2018 on combatting information technology crimes.

The Commission expressed during the period under review concerns about restrictions on freedom of expression and access to information in Egypt. The Delegation provided information on the case of Hossam El-Din Mohamed Bahgat. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Consider updating Law No. 356 of 1954 regulating freedom of access to official documents, to address the broader scope of access to information and reflect current developments, as provided for in the National Strategy on Human Rights. - Make use of the ACHPR Model Law on Access to Information in Africa of 2013 in this regard. - Strengthen the Supreme Council for Media regulation mandate, as the national Access to Information Authority which supervises the right to access to information, and allocate sufficient human and financial resources to fulfil its mandate. - Ensure that all potential limitations on the Freedom of Expression and Access to Information observe the Principle of Justifiable limitations (Principle 9 of the ACHPR Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa). - Consider repealing criminal defamation laws which may impede freedom of speech, in accordance with the Commission’s Resolution ACHPR/Res.169(XLVIII) 10 on Repealing Criminal Defamation Laws in Africa. - Ensure better respect for the freedom of expression, including on the Internet, in the context of elections. - Prevent any judicial, political, or economic pressure that could lead to self- censorship by media professionals. - Ensure effective protection for journalists, as provided for in Resolution ACHPR/Res.468 (LXVII) 2020 on the Safety of Journalists and Media Practitioners in Africa. - Pursue its effort to adopt executive regulations for the Personal Data Protection Law. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders, Focal Point on Reprisals and Focal Point on Independence of the Judiciary in Africa

In its Article 75, the Egyptian Constitution guarantees the right to form associations on a democratic basis, granting them legal personality upon notification, and prohibiting administrative authorities from interfering in their affairs, dissolving them or their boards of directors or trustees, except by judicial ruling (paragraph 39).

The Law Regulating Civil Society Activities No. 149 of 2019 and its implementing regulations of January 2021 removed all penalties involving deprivation of liberty, facilitated the receipt of foreign funding and created an electronic platform to help civil society organisations register or regularise their status (paragraph 40).

Article 73 of the Egyptian Constitution enshrines the right to peaceful assembly or demonstration, also provided for by Law No. 107 of 2013 regulating the right to public meetings, processions, and peaceful demonstrations.

The Commission expressed, on several occasions, concerns about the situation of Human Rights Defenders in Egypt. The Commission believes that intimidation, harassment and arbitrary detention of human rights defenders, may create a climate that prevents criticism of human rights violations. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ensure effective respect on the ground of notification regime for freedom of association / assembly and peaceful demonstration. - Disseminate the African Commission’s Guidelines on Freedom of Association and Assembly in Africa. - Ensure that articles 14, 15, 19 and 45 of Law 149/2019 are implemented in a way that does not represent any kind of restriction on CSOs. - Disseminate the Guidelines for the Policing of Assemblies by Law Enforcement Officials in Africa, and use them in any legislative or institutional initiative with regards to the right to peaceful assembly or demonstration. - Strengthen awareness raising and training provided to the police force and other stakeholders on standards related to the right to peaceful assembly and the freedom of association. - The Commission reiterates its recommendation to Egypt to adopt a specific law on the protection of human rights defenders. - Strengthen measures to protect human rights defenders from reprisals, intimidation and judicial harassment. - Ratify the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights and, subsequently, and make the Declaration provided for in Article 34(6), accepting the jurisdiction of the Court to receive cases submitted by NGOs with observer status before the Commission and individuals. - Strengthen the legal and institutional guarantees for the independence of justice in Egypt. Mandate of the Working Group on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in Africa
The Egyptian Constitution states in its Article 11: “The State shall ensure the achievement of (…), economic, social, and cultural rights in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution”.

The Egyptian judiciary has issued several rulings affirming that economic, social, and cultural rights—such as the right to work, education, health, social security, adequate housing, food, and clean water—are justiciable rights. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ratify the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security. - Ratify the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Article 14 – right to property and right to housing

The Delegation stated that informal areas constituted 37.5% of the total built-up urban mass and that sixty of these areas (encompassing 468,000 beneficiary families) have been upgraded. Also, the National Strategic Urban Development Plan aims to transform Egypt into a modern and globally competitive State, with the target of doubling the country’s urbanised area from 7% to 14%. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue efforts to strengthen the right to property and the right to housing implementation, in the framework of Egypt Vision 2030 and the Egypt Housing Strategy 2020. - Pursue public-private partnerships for housing construction to address the challenges in the implementing of this right. - Continue efforts to address the problem of precarious housing and affordable rental homes. Article 15 – Right to work under equitable conditions

The Report informs that the Government has reduced the unemployment rate from 13% in 2014 to 6.4% in 2024, and has raised the minimum wage several times, in both the public and private sectors in 2019, 2023 and 2024.

The Commission notes that unemployment rate among women declined from 17.8% in 2021 to 15.8% in 2025, in the framework of the National Plan for Enhancing Gender Equality in the Workplace of 2022. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ratify ILO Convention 2011 No. 189 on domestic workers. - Continue efforts to ensure that growth and economic diversification translate into increased employment opportunities. - Extend the National Plan for Combatting the Worst Forms of Child Labor 2018- 2025. - Pursue the Government’s commendable efforts to address: work in the Informal Economy, gender-based discrimination and sexual harassment at the workplace, non-adherence of employers to work hour law, safety and health standards, and minimum wage law. Article 16 - Right to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health
The Report contains detailed information on the legal and institutional framework as well as the governmental initiatives aiming at promoting the right to health in Egypt (Pages 14-17).

The Delegation stated that public spending allocations on health increased to reach EGP 617.9 billion in the fiscal year 2025/2026, which represents an increase of EGP 544.9 billion compared to the budget for the fiscal year 2019/2020. While the Commission welcomes this positive development, it still doesn’t show the health budget proportion in the general State budget.

With regards to human resources, the physician ratio in Egypt was about 26 physicians per 10,000 inhabitants in 2024, compared to 21 physicians per 10,000 inhabitants in 2020. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue its efforts in raising the health budget proportion to meet the regional standards (15% of the general State budget according to Abuja Declaration of 2001). - Redouble its efforts to achieve 100% coverage under the health insurance umbrella by 2030. - Pursue efforts to address the quality and efficiency of healthcare facilities, access to high-quality health care and unsafe abortion. - Disseminate the Commission’s General Comment No. 7 on the obligations of States under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the context of the private provision of social services. Article 17 - Right to education

The Report provides detailed information on the implementation of the right to education in general terms (Pages 17-21). The right to education is enshrined in the Constitution of Egypt (Articles 19-23).

The Commission takes note with appreciation that the Constitution requires the State to allocate a percentage of Government spending to pre-university education receiving 4%, university education receiving 2%, and scientific research receiving 1% (total 7%) (Articles 19 to 23).

The Delegation submitted detailed information on education fees, initiatives to improve education quality, expenditure allocations for the pre-university education sector, sanctions for non-enrolment of children, school dropouts and efforts to address regional disparities in education.

The Delegation stated that dropout rates remain slightly higher among female students at the preparatory education (0.7% compared to 0.6%). Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ensure the effective implementation of the Strategic Plan for Pre-University Education Development 2014–2030, and the Education 2.0 system of 2018. - Strengthen the respect for compulsory schooling for all children of both sexes aged 6 to 16, in particular through coercive measures against offending parents/guardians. - Continue efforts in the field of human rights education. - Continue efforts to revitalise technical education and vocational training. - Adopt specific measures to address female dropouts, in particular at the preparatory education. Article 22 – Right to Economic, Social and Cultural Development

The Delegation stated about a significant reduction in poverty for the first time in 20 years, from 32.5% in 2018 to 29.7% in 2020. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Allocate adequate human and financial resources to strengthen national development and reach Egypt Vision 2030 main objectives. - Pursue its efforts to ensure that vulnerable people have income security to meet basic needs. Rights of the family and vulnerable groups Mandate of the Working Group on the Rights of Older Persons and People with Disabilities in Africa (Article 18: Rights of vulnerable groups)

The Delegation stated that Egypt is currently in the process of acceding to the African Protocols relating to the Elderly and Persons with Disabilities, pending the completion of constitutional procedures. The Commission welcomes this positive development.

In Egypt, the Qadiroun Bi-Ikhtilaf (Differently Abled, Law No. 161 of 2023) initiative has successfully facilitated the employment integration of thousands of persons with disabilities. Over 30,000 persons with disabilities have been employed over 10 years, including 14,000 since the beginning of 2023. Furthermore, nine seats have been reserved for persons with disabilities in the House of Representatives during the last elections.

The Delegation highlighted an increase in the number of elderly persons in Egypt from 9.3 million (representing 8.8% of the total population) in 2024, to approximately 9.8 million (representing 9.1% of the total population) in 2025.

However, the reference age for older persons in Egypt is 65 years, according to Article 1 of Law No. 19 of 2024 on the Rights of the Elderly, which is not in line with the Protocol's provisions. The Delegation affirms that this difference does not affect the actual enjoyment of rights by the elderly in Egypt. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ensure the effective implementation of the National Strategy for the Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, finalised recently. - Pursue efforts to promote access of persons with disabilities to employment, including through the effective implementation on the ground of the reservation of 5% of created jobs for persons with disabilities. - Take immediate and effective measures to ensure that all facilities and services open or provided to the public are accessible to persons with disabilities, in accordance with the ACHPR Resolution on accessibility for persons with disabilities - ACHPR/Res.305(EXT.OS/XVIII)2015. - Ensure that persons with disabilities and older persons are involved in the development of all initiatives to promote and protect their rights. - Amend Article 1 of Law No. 19 of 2024 on the Rights of the Elderly, to bring the reference age for older persons to 60 years instead of 65 years. - Continue to specifically target older persons in the Government’s social policies. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Refugees, Asylum Seekers, Internally Displaced Persons and Migrants in Africa

Egypt hosts more than 10 million foreign nationals, including migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers, from 62 nationalities. In October 2025, Egypt registered 104,266 refugees and 952,385 asylum seekers, among them 74.1% are women or children and 19.07% are people with special needs.

The Commission takes note of the Law No. (164) of 2024 regarding the asylum of foreigners, which has established a National Committee tasked with regulating refugee affairs and deciding on asylum applications on a case-by-case basis.
The Commission welcomes the recent amendment on the validity period of residency permits (a full-year, renewable, instead of six months).

The Delegation has provided information on measures taken to combat irregular migration and protect migrants from trafficking (the National Strategy for Combatting Irregular Migration 2026). Only a few information on the rights of migrants living in Egypt has been presented.

Furthermore, the Delegation did not provide any information on internally displaced persons, nor on the legal and institutional framework governing this topic. Also, Egypt did not ratify any of the international or regional instruments dealing with statelessness. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Pursue efforts to finalise the adoption of Executive Regulations for the Law regulating asylum, in collaboration with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). Operationalize the National Committee responsible for regulating refugee affairs as soon as possible.Ensure concrete admissibility criteria for the prompt and impartial examination of asylum applications in Egypt. - Provide for remedies and the right to appeal concerning asylum cases to a judicial or quasi-judicial independent and impartial adjudication body. - Continue efforts to combat all forms of discrimination and arbitrary detention of asylum seekers and take prompt action to investigate recent allegations particularly from Sudanese refugees. - Make use of and disseminate ACHPR Resolution on the inclusion of refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons and stateless persons in the national socio-economic systems, services and economic opportunities in Africa - ACHPR/Res.565 (LXXVI) 2023. - Consider lifting its reservations under articles 4 (members of the family) and 18 (6) (compensation) of the Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. - Adopt a human rights-based approach to the treatment of irregular migrants and involve the national human rights institution and civil society organisations in the protection and promotion of their rights. - Strengthen concrete and specific measures to prevent and combat discrimination against migrants. - Ratify the African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (Kampala Convention). - Even in the absence of cases of internal displacement, consider taking preventive measures and preparing a legal and institutional frameworks for this topic. - Ratify the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Specific Aspects of the Right to a Nationality and the Eradication of Statelessness in Africa. - Ratify the 1954 United Nations Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons and the 1961 United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. Mandate of the Committee on the Protection of Persons Living with HIV and those at Risk, Vulnerable to and Affected by HIV in Africa

The Delegation provided some additional replies stating that Egypt and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria signed a Framework Agreement in November 2024 which focuses on the national response to combat HIV and Tuberculosis.

Also, the National Strategy for Combatting HIV/AIDS was updated in December 2024, covering the period from 2024 to 2030, and introducing the concept of "Three Zeros": Zero new infections, Zero AIDS-related deaths, and Zero discrimination.

Nevertheless, reports raise concerns about the increase in the number of cases of HIV/AIDS in Egypt. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Provide in its next periodic Report disaggregated information about the HIV prevalence evolution during the reporting period. - Redouble its efforts to achieve the 95% (situation awareness), 95% (treatment) and 95% (virological suppression) targets. - Pay special attention to vulnerable /at-risk fringes in the design and implementation of public policies to combat HIV/AIDS, including people living in Prison and Correctional institutions. - Adopt concrete measures to address the negative effects of the stigma faced by persons living with HIV. - Criminalise the forced sterilisation of people with HIV, without their free, prior and informed consent, as well as the intentional/deliberate transmission of HIV. - Disseminate and implement the recommendations of the Commission's study on HIV, law and human rights in the African human rights system (2017). - Materialize the cooperation on the development of the Application (APP) for the protection of PLWHIV pledged during the December 2024 Advocacy mission by the Commission. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Women in Africa

Egypt is among the few States Parties to the African Charter that have not yet ratified the Maputo Protocol. The Report under review provided detailed information on combatting discrimination against women (Paragraphs 105-109).

Egypt ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) in September 1981. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Continue efforts to ratify the Maputo Protocol. - Consider lifting its reservations on articles 2 (non-discrimination) and 16 (matters relating to marriage and family) of the CEDAW Convention. - Consider the use of the Maputo Protocol Dashboard and Index (MPSI), published in 2022 by the Directorate of Women, Gender and Youth of the African Union Commission, for the identification and continuous monitoring of progress in the implementation of the Maputo Protocol. •

The Egyptian Constitution guarantees equality of rights, freedoms, and public duties, as well as equal opportunities for women and men without discrimination, in 22 of its articles, most notably Articles 11 and 53 (paragraph 105).

The Delegation recognises the absence of a specific law dedicated solely to gender equality. 29 https://achpr.au.int/index.php/en/special-mechanisms-reports/hiv-law-human-rights-key-challenges- opportunities-rights-based-responses 30 https://au.int/fr/node/38758 Recommendations: Egypt should: - Consider adopting a specific gender equality law enshrining, among others, a definition of discrimination against women covering direct and indirect discrimination in the public and private spheres, the principle of equality of women and men and prohibition of all forms of discrimination against women. - Provide mechanisms for monitoring and enforcing existing measures to prevent and combat discrimination against women. - Pursue its efforts in the field of raising awareness of the rights of women, particularly in rural areas.

The Commission takes note with appreciation of efforts to strengthen access of women to justice and legal aid services in Egypt, in particular the National Council for Women (NCW) which receives and studies complaints, refers them to the competent authorities, and provides legal aid and consultation to women subjected to violence, as well as the hotline service provided for reporting any violations or complaints. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ensure that women are fully aware of their right to access to legal aid. - Continue awareness-raising campaigns to encourage women to report cases of violence, and ensure their protection against possible reprisals.
The percentage of seats held by women in the current House of Representatives is unprecedented and the highest in Egypt's history, with 164 seats, representing 27.7% (paragraph 108).

The Commission takes note of the detailed information provided by the Delegation on the representation of women in decision-making institutions. However, article 11 of the Egyptian Constitution of 2014 provides that “2. The State commits to taking the necessary measures to ensure appropriate representation of women in the Houses of Parliament, in the manner specified by law”. So far, the Egyptian legislation does not specify the appropriate representation of women in Parliament. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Adopt legislative measures for specific quotas reserved for women in national or regional elective assemblies. - Continue efforts to promote women’s representation in the private sector and in leadership positions. •

In addition to the Penal Code Provisions, Egypt adopted the National Strategy for the Empowerment of Egyptian Women 2030 with a specific axis on protection from violence and an independent monitoring mechanism to follow up on the implementation of national indicators.

The Delegation provided detailed information on the concrete measures taken to combat violence against women, including the role of the National Council for Women Complaint Office and the National Standard Case Model for reporting cases of violence against women.

The Commission takes note of the National Plan for the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (2022-2026), launched by the National Committee for the Elimination of FGM. The rate of FGM in Egypt witnessed a tangible decrease, reaching 14% in 2021 compared to 21% in 2014. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ratify the African Union Convention on Ending Violence against Women and Girls (adopted in February 2025). - Disseminate and take into account the Commission's Guidelines on combatting sexual violence and its consequences in Africa, as part of the measures aiming at combatting gender-based violence. - Strengthen rehabilitation and reparation efforts for victims of sexual violence. - Prevent and punish digital violence against women, in line with the Commission Resolution on the Protection of Women from Digital violence in Africa (ACHPR/Res. 522 (LXXII) 2022). - Continue awareness-raising efforts around the prevention and punishment of gender-based violence. - Continue efforts to raise awareness of harmful practices such as female genital mutilation and domestic violence, targeting in particular rural communities where such practices may be more prevalent. - Continue to address patriarchal norms and gender inequalities, especially in rural areas. - Disseminate and use the Joint General Comment of the Commission and the African Committee of experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child on female genital mutilation (FGM). •

In Egypt, the law prohibits marriage conclusion for anyone of either sex who has not reached the age of eighteen complete years (paragraph 184). The Delegation stated that efforts of the Ministry of Interior from January 2014 to October 2023 resulted in the apprehension of 412 cases involving 609 defendants and 895 minor victims in areas of combatting the exploitation of children and child marriage. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ensure the dissemination of the Joint General Comment of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) and the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) on ending child marriage. - Continue efforts to end child marriage and ensure the dissemination of the Commission's General Comment No. 6 on the Maputo Protocol: The right to property in the event of legal separation or divorce. •

The Commission takes note of the Government’s efforts to eliminate stereotypical concepts regarding the roles of men and women in the field of education, and to provide equal curricula, examinations, school buildings, and equipment. The Commission also takes note of the National Project for the Development of the Egyptian Family and the 'Support Mother and Foetus Health' Initiative. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Ratify ILO Conventions No. 189 on domestic work, No. 190 on Violence in the Workplace, and No. 183 on Maternity Protection. - Strengthen measures to encourage women and girls to choose non-traditional fields of education and careers, including science, technology, engineering and mathematics. - Strengthen adult literacy programs for women, including women with disabilities, older women and rural women. - Strengthen young people’s access to sexual and reproductive health services and products. - Exploit and disseminate the Commission’s General Comment on Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol, which provides for access to reproductive health and rights, including medical abortion in some cases. • Rights of especially protected women’s group Recommendations: Egypt should: - Continue efforts to address the specific needs of women in prison settings, particularly pregnant and nursing mothers. - Continue to pay particular attention to women and girls with disabilities in addressing the specific needs of this category. Rights of peoples or collective rights Mandate of the Working Group on Extractive Industries, Environment and Human Rights Violations in Africa

The Constitution affirms the right of the Egyptian people to own their wealth and resources and to freely dispose of them. It stipulates that the State's natural resources belong to the people, and that the State is obligated to preserve and utilise them wisely, refrain from depleting them, and take into consideration the rights of future generations.
The right to environment is enshrined in the Egyptian Constitution which states in Article 46 that every person has the right to a healthy environment, and that its protection is a national duty.

The Commission notes the details provided by the Delegation on the main extractive activities in Egypt (petroleum and natural gas, mining and quarrying activities, which encompass the extraction of precious metals, phosphate, limestone, granite, and heavy minerals), which represent a contribution of 7,7% to GDP.

The legal framework of extractive activities in Egypt includes Mineral Resources Law No. 198 of 2014 and its Executive Regulations issued by Prime Ministerial Decree No. 108 of 2020. The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources is the government entity responsible for formulating and implementing the general policy for extractive activities in the State.
The Commission takes note of the two lawsuits filed before the Egyptian National Courts against extractive industries, including a lawsuit concerning the involvement of local communities.

In Egypt, the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) before the commencement of extractive activities is a mandatory procedure before licensing any project, pursuant to Environmental Law No. 4 of 1994. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Observe the ACHPR Guidelines on State Reporting under Articles 21 and 24 when preparing the next periodic Report. - Ensure that the National Human Rights Strategy addresses all business-related human rights concerns and align business practices with international human rights standards. - Enhance community participation in all stages of the start-up of extractive industries, within Egypt’s Vision 2030 which emphasises the importance of 37 https://achpr.au.int/en/documents/2018-05-07/state-reporting-guidelines-and-principles-articles-21-and-24- african engaging local communities, women, and rural groups in the formulation, implementation, and monitoring of developmental policies. - Strengthen the fight against corruption and illicit financial flows in the extractive industries sector. - Ensure compliance with the obligation to carry out prior environmental impact assessments in the context of extractive industries activities, with the participation of potentially affected communities and civil society organisations. - Guarantee effective compensation for those affected by environmental degradation. - Integrate the human rights dimension into the development of any policy or legislation related to extractive activities. - Continue awareness-raising campaigns among the population so that they adopt more responsible behaviour in terms of preserving the environment. Mandate of the Working Group on Indigenous Populations / Communities and Minorities in Africa

On the question whether the Government of Egypt recognises the existence of indigenous peoples and respects their cultures, languages and traditional knowledge, the Delegation stated that Egypt affirms its full support for the rights of all indigenous peoples around the world. Nevertheless, Egypt asserts that the entire Egyptian people have been the owners of the land of Egypt for thousands of years, and all Egyptians belong to one homeland, sharing a common history and a deeply rooted identity.

Accordingly, Bedouins, Nubians and Amazigh are not considered as indigenous people in Egypt. Recommendations: Egypt should: - Consider ratifying ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples of 1989. - Strengthen the legal or administrative framework that specifically protects the rights of ethnic and linguistic minorities, including their right to own, use, control and manage their ancestral lands. - Take measures for the effective participation of all communities in decision- making bodies, where necessary, through the establishment of quotas. - Strengthen and improve access for all communities to essential services, such as education and health. - Strengthen the fight against marginalisation and discrimination against people from ethnic and linguistic minorities. - Take note of the findings of the Commission‘s study on Mapping of Indigenous Peoples in Africa, on the existence and locations of Indigenous Peoples in the continent.
The consideration of Periodic Reports submitted by States Parties is an important part of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights mandate.
This procedure constitutes a relevant tool for assessing the implementation of the provisions of the Charter and other relevant instruments by States Parties.

The Commission reiterates its congratulations to the Government of Egypt for its constructive participation in the review of the State Party’s 18 - 19 Combined Periodic Report under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (2019-2024).
Egypt is now up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the Charter.
The State Party is strongly encouraged to continue its constructive engagement with the Commission in the submission of Periodic Reports.
The Commission hopes that these recommendations will be taken into account and implemented by Egypt.
