They report that these demonstrations were characterised by violent clashes between opposition supporters and law enforcement forces.

The Complainants also report that in the night of 31 August to 1 September 2016, an operation described as "violent" by the ICC was launched against the opposition headquarters by the Gabonese law enforcement forces. They indicate that in its statement of 06 September 2016 on the human rights situation in the Gabonese Republic, the Commission also noted the extremely worrying nature of the "information alleging an attack carried out against the opposition headquarters by agents of the State Security Services, while twenty-seven (27) members of the opposition were being held there".

The Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC considered that the assault carried out against the headquarters of Jean PING constituted a demonstration of excessive force in the overall context of the 2016 post-electoral violence, marked by a particularly unjustified use of force against the civilian population. The Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC thus concluded that there were serious human rights violations.

The Complainants assert that these violations include arbitrary detentions, the destruction of public and private property and harm to the integrity and life of persons. The ICC report reports mass arrests with the number of persons arrested ranging from 800 to 1100 between 31 August and 4 September 2016.

According to the same report, at least three cases of unlawful detention, four cases of torture and persecution, as well as the murder of civilians (between 3 and 8 civilians killed) were reported. Finally, the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court notes the existence of 38 to 41 injured civilians, of whom 12 "possibly having suffered other inhumane acts".

The United Nations, the African Union as well as the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights expressed their concerns at the loss of human life, the numerous injured, the mass arrests of demonstrators by the security forces and the destruction of property that occurred as a result of these events.

According to the Complainants, the Gabonese Minister of Justice himself confirmed in his letter to the Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office that he had recorded 3 deaths and 700 arrests, followed by the release of 500 persons for insufficient evidence.

The Complainants also report that on Thursday 8 September 2016, Jean PING seized the Constitutional Court of Gabon to contest the results of the presidential election of 27 August 2016. He asked the Court to authorise a recount of the votes in the Haut-Ogooué Province, the Bongo stronghold in the south-east of the country.

The Complainants observe that on 21 September 2016, the Gabonese Republic seized the ICC for the facts of crimes against humanity and incitement to the crime of genocide. Mr. Jean PING also lodged a complaint with the Prosecutor of the said Court in which he accused the government of having committed crimes against humanity. On 21 September 2016, the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC, in its report, acknowledged the existence of human rights violations despite the Court's lack of subject-matter jurisdiction to hear them and called for prosecutions at the national level.

In the night of Friday 23 to Saturday 24 September 2016, the Gabonese Constitutional Court validated the re-election of President Ali BONGO ONDIMBA, and refused to proceed with the recount of the votes and to compare the tallies before the destruction of the ballot papers.

The Complainants assert that no investigation mechanism, nor any sufficient compensation procedure, has been put in place to redress the human rights violations that occurred during the 2016 post-electoral violence. They indicate that the victims of the electoral violence have still not seen the harm suffered adequately redressed.
The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 and 20 of the African Charter.

The Complainants ask the Commission to find the violation of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 and 20 of the African Charter; and consequently to recommend that the Government of Gabon: a) Provide full reparation for the harm suffered by the victims of the 2016 post-electoral violence; a) Put in place legislation favourable to just and equitable prompt compensation of victims of human rights violations; b) Ensure the non-repetition of the human rights violations committed in 2016, in particular: i) By offering the security forces appropriate and regular training on the non-violent policing of peaceful demonstrations; ii) By granting an allocation of 50,000,000 euros to the Consortium of Gabonese Civil Society for Electoral Transparency and Democracy; iii) By putting in place procedures guaranteeing the sincerity of election results as well as the right to an effective remedy before an impartial body in the event of electoral fraud; iv) By cooperating in good faith with the relevant international authorities, if necessary by allowing them to monitor all stages of the procedure. c) Amend its legislation incompatible with the provisions of the African Charter and set a time limit for the State for the implementation of the decision that the Commission will have taken; d) Pay the costs they were compelled to incur in court as well as all costs, the total sum amounting to 20,000 euros.
The complaint was received at the Secretariat of the Commission on 15 June 2023.

The Secretariat examined the complaint in accordance with Rule 115(2) of its Rules of Procedure (2020), and it was admitted on 22 September 2023. On the same day, the Parties were informed thereof, the Complainants having been invited to submit arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits within a period of sixty (60) days in accordance with Rule 116(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure of 2020.

By letter of 04 October 2023, the Complainants provided the arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits. The Secretariat transmitted them to the Respondent State, and requested its reply within a period of sixty days, in accordance with Rule 116(2) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure.
The Respondent State did not submit a reply after receipt of the Complainants' brief.

On 12 August 2024, the Secretariat informed the parties of the expiry of the time limit granted to the Respondent State to submit its evidence on admissibility and the merits and that it would take the decision on the basis of the information available in accordance with Rule 188/2 and 120(2) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure.

According to the Complainants, the admissibility conditions as required by Article 56 of the Charter are met. The Complainants' submissions relate to the conditions stipulated in Article 56(1), (2), (5), (6) and (7) of the Charter.

As regards the requirements of Article 56(1) of the African Charter, this communication is submitted by two civil society organisations, namely the Consortium of Gabonese Civil Society for Electoral Transparency and Democracy (COTED) and the Network of Free Civil Society Organisations for Good Governance in Gabon (ROLBG), as well as Bishop Mike JOCKTANE, of Gabonese nationality. The Complainants are represented by the law firm SELASU AVOCATS PANDELON.

As regards Article 56(2), the Complainants argue that the complaint is compatible with the Charter insofar as it is directed against the Gabonese Republic, a State Party to the African Charter since 20 February 1986. Moreover, the alleged violations were perpetrated when the Gabonese Republic was already bound by the Charter.
As regards Article 56(3), the Complainants assert that the complaint does not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the AU.

As regards the requirement of Article 56(4), the Complainants maintain that the present complaint is mainly based on reports produced by the Commission, the United Nations, the European Union as well as the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC. It does not rely on the mass media.

As regards the obligation to exhaust local remedies before seizing the Commission in accordance with Article 56(5), the Complainants maintain that Mr. Jean PING seized the Constitutional Court of Gabon on 8 September 2016, requesting a recount of the votes, and that his appeal was rejected on 24 September 2016.
Furthermore, the Complainants specify that Mr. Jean PING seized the Constitutional Court on 3 November 2016 with an application for review, which was rejected on 15 November 2016.

The Complainants recall that in accordance with the jurisprudence of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, local remedies need to be exhausted only where ordinary remedies exist and are effective and available. According to the Complainants, there is in principle no requirement to exhaust local remedies where the State adopts an attitude of tolerance or passivity in the face of violations.

The Complainants deduce from this that local remedies were ineffective, and refer to its argumentation from the angle of Articles 7, 13 and 20 of the Charter (on the constitutional appeal) and from the angle of reparations (on the absence of investigation and compensation).

As regards the requirement set out in Article 56(6), although the present complaint was submitted seven years after the facts, the Complainants maintain that in international human rights law, the reasonableness of the time limit must be assessed in light of the specific circumstances of the case. In this instance, the Complainants emphasise that the general climate that prevailed in Gabon following the post-electoral violence must be taken into consideration in assessing the reasonable time criterion.

The Complainants cite the jurisprudence of the Commission to corroborate their claim. They allege that in 2003, the Commission agreed to hear facts concerning post-electoral violence that occurred in 1992 even though the complaint had been filed 11 years later. They also cite the judgment of the African Court in the case of Association pour le progrès et la défense des droits des femmes maliennes and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Mali, in which the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights declared admissible an application submitted after 4 years, 6 months and 24 days, taking into account two contextual elements to reject the objection of inadmissibility raised by the Respondent State: "[...] first, the fact that the Applicants need time to verify the conformity of the new law with the international instruments to which the Respondent State is a party; second, given the climate of fear, intimidation and threats that characterised the period [in question], it is reasonable that the applicants were affected by the situation, the country having found itself in an exceptional crisis situation [...] which, according to the Respondent State itself, could "be fatal for peace, coexistence and social cohesion""

The Complainants assert that they took the time to verify whether Gabon was complying with its international obligations before resolving to seize the Commission, which was a prerequisite for national reconciliation and Gabonese social cohesion. The Gabonese Republic partially deferred to international institutions, notably the ICC, in order to shed light on the facts and allow justice to do its work.

According to the Complainants, the time elapsed cannot be considered unreasonable, since they had given the Gabonese Republic the opportunity to investigate the human rights violations and to adequately redress the harm suffered by the victims, in accordance with the requirements of the African Charter and the principles of international human rights law. Nevertheless, the investigations carried out as well as the promises of compensation made by Gabon never led to concrete results.
The Complainants conclude that the condition set out in Article 56(6) of the African Charter is indeed fulfilled.

As regards the requirement set out in Article 56(7), the Complainants specify that, although the matter was brought before the ICC, the latter declared itself lacking jurisdiction ratione materiae. They therefore conclude that the condition set out in Article 56(7) of the African Charter is duly fulfilled.

The Commission notes that the Respondent State did not submit its arguments on admissibility in the communication. In this case, the Commission decides on the basis of the facts communicated by the Complainants in accordance with Rule 118(1) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure, which provides that "Where no observations on admissibility have been received from the Respondent State within the time limit set, the Commission shall proceed to adopt a decision by default based on the information available to it".

The admissibility of a communication before the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights is governed by Article 56 of the African Charter, which sets out seven conditions that must all be satisfied before the Commission can declare it admissible. In the absence of valid justifications, non-compliance with any one of the requirements results in the inadmissibility of the communication. The Commission will now examine in turn the Complainants' arguments in light of these requirements.
Article 56(1) of the Charter requires that a communication indicate the identity of its authors, even if the latter request anonymity.

The Commission notes that the present Communication is submitted by two civil society organisations, namely the Consortium of Gabonese Civil Society for Electoral Transparency and Democracy (COTED) and the Network of Free Civil Society Organisations for Good Governance in Gabon (ROLBG), as well as Bishop Mike JOCKTANE, of Gabonese nationality. The Complainants mandated the firm SELASU AVOCATS PANDELON, represented by Maître Gérald Pandelon.

The Commission recalls the provisions of Rule 115(2) of its Rules of Procedure (2020), which provides that Communications submitted before it must contain "the name, nationality and signature of the person or persons submitting the communication; or in cases where the complainant is a non-governmental organisation, the name and signature of its legal representative or representatives".

In the present case, the Complainants clearly identified themselves. The communication also contains the names and signatures of the lawyer to whom the Complainants gave a power of attorney signed and dated 26 May 2023. The lawyer also provided an email address for all correspondence.

While acknowledging that the denunciation of human rights violations is a characteristic feature of the system of international human rights protection, the Commission has explained that "the obvious reason justifying the opening of a broad path of access for complaints under the Charter is the practical understanding, in Africa, that victims may face various difficulties that prevent them from approaching the African Commission". The African Court adopted a similar interpretation in holding that the requirement of standing over interest to act "takes into account the practical difficulties that victims of human rights violations may encounter in bringing their complaints before the Court (...)". It emerges from this jurisprudence that Complainants acting without a mandate from the victims must demonstrate that it was reasonably impracticable to be granted the power of representation.

The Commission notes that the Complainants are not themselves victims. They allege, on the one hand, irregularities during the 2017 presidential election in which Jean Ping was the loser. However, Jean Ping did not give them a mandate to represent him. They allege, on the other hand, post-electoral violence characterised by the death of 3 to 8 civilians, the unlawful detention of 3 persons, 4 cases of torture and persecution, 38 to 41 injured, the mass arrest of demonstrators (ranging between 700 and 1100) followed by their release with the exception of 200 who were the subject of judicial proceedings, and the destruction of public and private property.

The Commission considers that the Complainants should have contacted the families of the persons killed, the persons detained, the persons injured and the owners of the private property destroyed. In the Complainants' submissions, the Commission finds no indication that the victims were unable or had difficulty in giving the Complainants a mandate of representation. Thus, in the present case, the raison d'être of the actio popularis, without a mandate from the victims, disappears.
Consequently, the Commission considers that the condition provided for in Article 56(1) is not fulfilled.

Article 56(2) provides that "communications ... received by the Commission shall be considered if they are compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter." The Commission's consistent interpretation of this provision is that the compatibility of a communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter is understood as the possibility for the Commission to hear the case before it without violating the provisions of these two instruments, as well as conformity with the four aspects of its jurisdiction, namely jurisdiction ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci.

Concerning compatibility with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter, the Commission notes that in the present case, the Complainants seek the protection of their human rights, in this instance their rights under Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 and 20 of the African Charter. It so happens that one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, provided for in its Article 3(h), is the protection of human rights. Furthermore, nothing in the Complainants' allegations and application reveals any incompatibility with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter.

As regards the four aspects of jurisdiction, the Commission notes that the communication was submitted against Gabon, a State Party to the African Charter (jurisdiction ratione personae) and alleges the violation of rights enshrined in the African Charter, in this case Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14 and 20 of the Charter (jurisdiction ratione materiae). The complaint concerns facts that occurred in 2016 during the electoral and post-electoral period. The Respondent State became a party to the Charter on 20 February 1986 (jurisdiction ratione temporis); and the alleged violations were committed on the territory of the Respondent State (jurisdiction ratione loci). Thus, the Commission concludes that the four aspects of its jurisdiction are fulfilled. Consequently, this admissibility condition is respected.

Under Article 56(3), communications must not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the OAU. According to the Commission, the purpose of this clause is to ensure "diplomatic, courteous and respectful exchanges between the parties appearing before it and the need to preserve the integrity of State institutions, which are indispensable for the protection of human rights".

The Respondent State having presented no reply to the Complainants' arguments, and the Commission having noted no inappropriate language directed against it, the Commission considers that the condition provided for in Article 56(3) is fulfilled.

Article 56(4) provides that the communication must not be limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through the mass media. The Commission has interpreted this provision as requiring complainants to substantiate their communications with evidence.

The Commission notes that the Complainants relied on the judgments of the Gabonese Constitutional Court, the reports of the Gabonese Ministry of Justice, and numerous reports and other documents emanating from credible international institutions and organisations including the African Union, the United Nations, the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC, and the European Union Election Observation Mission.
Consequently, the Commission concludes that the requirement contained in Article 56(4) of the African Charter is indeed fulfilled.
In accordance with Article 56(5), communications may be considered only after exhaustion of local remedies, unless these remedies are unduly prolonged.

Since the case of Jawara v. The Gambia, the jurisprudence has crystallised the fact that the Commission requires complainants to exhaust local remedies only where these are "available, effective and sufficient to remedy the alleged violation". A remedy is available if "the petitioner can pursue it without impediment"; a remedy is effective if it "offers a prospect of success", while a remedy will be considered sufficient "if it is capable of redressing the complaint."
The Commission notes that the present communication concerns the results of the presidential election of 27 August 2016 and the post-electoral violence of 31 August and 4 September 2016.

As regards the election results, the Commission notes that under Article 121 of Law No. 07/96 of 12 March 1996, laying down provisions common to all political elections in the Gabonese Republic, "the Constitutional Court alone is competent to rule on claims relating to presidential, legislative, senatorial and referendum elections, and departmental and municipal council elections".

The Commission notes that Mr. Jean PING seized the Constitutional Court of Gabon on 8 September 2016, requesting a recount of the votes, and that his appeal was rejected on 24 September 2016. It also notes that the application for review lodged by Mr. Jean PING before the Constitutional Court on 3 November 2016 was rejected on 15 November 2016. The electoral dispute opening and closing before the Constitutional Court, the Commission considers that the remedies relating to the results of the presidential election have been exhausted.

The Commission notes, as regards the other allegations, that the Complainants have not presented evidence concerning the efforts made to obtain adequate redress from the judicial bodies of Gabon in respect of "the loss of human life, the numerous injured, the mass arrests of demonstrators by the security forces and the destruction of property". Such alleged violations should be submitted to the national courts for redress before being submitted to this Commission. The Commission recalls that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies dictates that the petitioner give the Respondent State the opportunity to remedy the violation committed before the case reaches an international judicial mechanism.

The Commission considers that upon the release of the report of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICC on 21 September 2016 indicating that this Court was incomplete, the Complainants should have brought the matter before the national courts in order to rule on the alleged violations. However, the Commission notes no initiative by the Complainants to this effect. It follows that local remedies were not exhausted with regard to the post-electoral violations.

Consequently, the Commission considers that the Communication partially satisfies the requirements of Article 56(5) of the African Charter. In other words, the requirements of Article 56(6) are satisfied as regards the electoral dispute but are not satisfied as regards the post-electoral violations.

Article 56(6) requires that a communication be submitted within a reasonable time from the exhaustion of local remedies or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter. Unlike the American Convention on Human Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which set a specific time limit of six months for the submission of communications, the Charter provides only that communications must be submitted within a reasonable time without, however, specifying its duration.

According to the jurisprudence of the Commission, notably in the case of Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe, time limits not exceeding 6 months are considered reasonable. However, in the interest of equity and justice, the Commission may depart from this usual 06-month norm "where there is a good and compelling reason" justifying that a complainant did not submit his complaint within that period, and grant him an opportunity to be heard.

The allegations relating to the post-electoral violations having been declared inadmissible, the Commission considers that it is not relevant to examine whether they were submitted within a reasonable time. The analysis is therefore limited to the allegations relating to the regularity of the presidential election.

The present complaint was submitted on 15 June 2023, that is six years and seven months after the rejection of the application for review by judgment of the Constitutional Court of 15 November 2016. To justify this long delay, the Complainants invoke the case of Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence & INTERIGHTS v. Cameroon, declared admissible although it had been filed 11 years after the facts. The Commission had adopted there a flexible conception of the admissibility criteria because the State of Cameroon had failed in "its obligation to administer on its territory a serene and diligent justice in order to give satisfaction to the Complainants as soon as possible, in accordance with the relevant provisions of the African Charter and the principles and guidelines on the right to a fair trial in Africa".

They also invoke the case of Association pour le progrès et la défense des droits des femmes maliennes and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Mali, in which the African Court held admissible a complaint submitted after a period of 4 years, 6 months and 24 days. The Court had taken into account two major contextual elements: on the one hand, the time taken by the applicants to assess the conformity of a new law with the international instruments ratified by the Respondent State; on the other hand, the climate of fear, intimidation and threats linked to an exceptional national crisis. Even the Respondent State acknowledged that this situation could be "fatal for peace, coexistence and social cohesion".

In the present Communication, the Complainants assert that they chose, initially, to verify whether Gabon was complying with its international obligations before resolving to seize the Commission. They thus invite the latter to assess the reasonable time criterion in light of the general context that prevailed in Gabon following the post-electoral violence.

The Commission notes that the Complainants indicate neither the verifications carried out after the close of the electoral dispute in November 2016, nor any threats that would have lasted for 6 years and 7 months. Consequently, the Commission considers that the present communication does not satisfy the requirement of Article 56(6).
Article 56(7) provides that a communication must not deal with cases that have been settled in accordance with the principles of the United Nations, the African Union or the African Charter.

In the case of Sudan Human Rights Commission and Another v. Sudan, the Commission considered that a case is considered settled if an international judicial body with a human rights mandate or jurisdiction has taken a decision on it and has given the complaint the authority of res judicata.

The Commission notes that the ICC was seized of the post-electoral violence alleged in the present communication but that it declared itself lacking jurisdiction ratione materiae to hear it. The Commission also notes that Jean Ping seized the Commission on 13 February 2018 to request, among other things, the reorganisation of the presidential election in the Haut-Ogoué province and the release of his five close associates imprisoned on account of their political opinions. This communication was declared inadmissible for non-compliance with Article 56(6). It follows that the ICC and the Commission have not settled the substantive questions submitted to it.

The Commission further notes that there is no evidence that this communication has been settled by another international judicial body. Consequently, the Commission considers that the communication satisfies the requirement of Article 56(7) of the African Charter. In view of all the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares this Communication inadmissible for failure to comply with the conditions provided for in Articles 56(1), 56(5) and 56(6) of the African Charter. ii. Notifies its decision to the Parties in accordance with Rule 118(4) of its Rules of Procedure.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat), received a complaint on 30 June 2013 from the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, Ali Askouri and Abdel-Hakeem Nasr (the Complainants), acting on behalf of persons affected by the construction of the Merowe and Kajbar Dams (the Victims).
The Complaint is submitted against the Republic of Sudan (Respondent State), State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

It is alleged that the Respondent State failed to engage in consultations with community elected representatives to obtain the free, prior and informed consent of the communities affected by the Merowe and Kajbar Dams. It is also claimed that no adequate compensation or resettlement site was provided for the communities around the Merowe Dam area. The Complainants add that the Respondent State is responsible for killings, systematic arrests, incommunicado detentions and torture of anti-dam activists and journalists in April 2006 (Merowe Dam) and June 2007 (Kajbar Dam).

The Complainants submit that construction of the Merowe Dam began in 2003 and was completed in 2009. They claim that the Dam's construction resulted in the displacement and forced eviction of over 50,000 people. They add that local communities affected by the construction (mainly the Amri, the Hamadab, and the Manasir) had been living on the land for centuries and practised a life inextricably linked to their ancestral land.

It is alleged that the Dams Implementation Unit (DIU), the authority responsible for the technical, administrative, and financial issues related to the construction of the Dams and the resettlement of the affected populations, refused to acknowledge the elected representatives of the affected communities as local partners. The Complainants aver that despite several community protests against the Merowe Dam, the affected areas were flooded without notice, causing irreparable harm to property, livestock, and cultural wellbeing as well as the environment around the Nile water (the species, plants, and soil). They add that in August 2006, the Respondent State, without issuing an appropriate warning, subjected the area inhabited by the Amri to heavy flooding, affecting 10,000 people and leading to the loss of houses, animals, and crops.

The Complainants aver that by Presidential Decree No. 353 (2002 Resettlement Act), an area of 6,364 km surrounding the site of the Merowe Dam was expropriated, including the area inhabited by the Amri, the Hamadab and Manasir communities. It is alleged that the affected communities were relocated to areas unsuitable for farming and herding and that the majority of the affected population has not received the promised compensation.

The Complainants submit that on 22 April 2006, armed militia, in the presence of police guards, killed at least three (3) anti-dam protestors during a peaceful gathering at a school courtyard and injured around 40 others. They add that perpetrators of the attack have not been prosecuted, and no formal investigations took place.

It is claimed that the Respondent State failed to conduct a proper impact assessment of the dam construction and that the flooded area contained more than 1,000 archaeological sites. The Complainants add that an independent Environmental Impact Assessment estimated that water loss due to evaporation from the reservoir storage could reach 2 percent of the total annual flow of the Nile River, and that it could have severe impacts downstream, reducing water flow below the Dam.

It is further submitted that the construction of the second dam, the Kajbar Dam, began in 2005 but was halted. The Complainants aver that, similar to the case of the Merowe Dam, the input of affected communities was not sought, despite a representative group having rejected plans to build a dam as far back as 1998. They add that if the Dam is constructed, an estimated 90 villages would be submerged, 10,000 Mahas, an indigenous Nubian community whose livelihood depends on their ancestral land would be displaced and 500 archaeological sites would be destroyed.

The Complainants allege that on 13 June 2007, heavily armed Sudanese security forces opened fire at a peaceful anti-dam demonstration, killing four (4) protestors and wounding more than 15 others. They state that 26 individuals, including journalists were arrested in the weeks that followed in relation to the protest. The Complainants add that perpetrators of the attacks were not prosecuted, despite numerous complaints and requests filed by aggrieved individuals.

The Complainants submit that on 27 August 2007, the United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on Adequate Housing expressed concern about "the situation of the communities affected by the hydro-electric projects in the Merowe and Kajbar areas in the Northern Nile Valley in Sudan" and requested that construction on the Dams stop. The Complainants further state that the UN Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights Situation in Sudan, in a 2008 report, noted that local communities had opposed the construction of the Dams, that some were forced to relocate, that community representatives were not consulted, and that Sudanese security forces used excessive force to suppress anti-dam protests.

It is averred that the adverse effects of the construction of the Merowe Dam continue to be felt by the affected population, even after its completion in 2009, making this an ongoing violation of the peoples' rights. The Complainants add that the Respondent State has recently expressed its intent to resume construction of the Kajbar Dam.
The Complainant alleges violation of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18,(1)(3) 19, 20, 21 and 22 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Commission) to: (i) Find the Respondent State in violation of the aforementioned Articles of the African Charter; (ii) Urge the Respondent State to halt the construction of the Kajbar Dam until the prior, free and informed consent of the affected communities is obtained; (iii) Urge the Respondent State to ensure restitution of the land of the Hamadab and Manasir communities where possible; (iv) Request the Respondent State to pay adequate compensation to individuals who lost their lands due to the construction of the Merowe Dam; (v) Request the Respondent State to provide adequate reparation for victims of torture and ill-treatment, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation and guarantees of non-repetition; (vi) Request the Respondent State to cease the use of and promptly amend legislation incompatible with the African Charter; and (vii) Call on the Respondent State to ensure the immediate prosecution of the perpetrators responsible for the killings, injuries and arbitrary detentions of the anti-dam protestors and activists.
The Secretariat received the Complaint on 30 June 2013 and acknowledged receipt of the same on 3 July 2013.

The Commission decided to be seized of the Communication during its 14 Extraordinary Session, held from July 20 to 24, 2013, in Nairobi, Kenya. Both parties were informed by respective correspondence dated 20 September 2013.

On 3 November 2013, the Complainants requested an extension of time within which to file their submissions on the admissibility. The request was granted in accordance with Rule 113 (2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure and communicated to the Complainants by letter dated 4 November 2014. The Respondent State was informed of this development by Note Verbale dated 11 November 2013.

On 20 December 2013, the Complainants transmitted their Submissions on Admissibility and requested the addition of Cairo Institute for Human Rights Studies and the Centre for the Study of Law, Justice and Society (Dejusticia), as legal representatives in the Communication. On 24 December 2013, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the Complainants' Submissions on Admissibility and informed them that the request to add 2 authors to the Communication will be tabled for consideration during the Commission's 15 Extra-Ordinary Session.

By Note Verbale dated 24 December 2013, the Complainants' Submissions on Admissibility were transmitted to the Respondent State, together with the Complainants' request for the addition of two more representatives.

On 20 January 2014, the Secretariat received a letter from Corbett & Co International Construction Lawyers (CCICL) indicating that CCICL was appointed to act on behalf of the Respondent State. By letter dated 30 January 2014, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the letter and informed CCICL that the Commission requires an official correspondence from the Respondent State, confirming the appointment.

By letter and Note Verbale dated 27 March 2014, the parties were informed of the Commission's decision to allow the addition of the 2 legal representatives. By the same correspondence the Secretariat also sought confirmation from the Respondent State on the appointment of CCICL as representatives. The Respondent State was also informed that the Commission would proceed to decide on Admissibility, as the time for submitting observations on the Complainants' arguments had elapsed.

On 5 May 2014, during the holding of the 55 Ordinary Session of the Commission in Luanda, Angola, the Secretariat hand-delivered copies of the above correspondence and documents to the Respondent State's delegates as receipt of the correspondence had not previously been acknowledged.
On 7 May 2014, the Secretariat received the Observations of the Respondent State on Admissibility, which were transmitted by courier to the Complainants on 16 May 2015 and delivered on 20 May 2014.
On 27 June 2014, the Complainants submitted their Reply to the Respondent State's Observations on Admissibility.

During its 19 Extraordinary Session, held from 16 to 25 February 2016, the Commission declared Communication 452/13 admissible. The decision on admissibility was transmitted to the parties by letter and Note Verbale dated 7 March 2016.

On 18 April 2016, the Complainants requested a one-month extension of time to file their Submissions on the Merits. The Commission granted the extension on 26 April 2016 under Rule 113(2) and notified both parties.

The Complainants submitted their Merits Submission on 5 June 2016, along with annexes. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 8 June 2016 and informed the Respondent State, transmitting the submission under Rule 108(1) for observations within sixty (60) days.
During its 59th Ordinary Session (21 October – 4 November 2016), the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication pending receipt of the Respondent State's submissions on merits

The Commission again deferred consideration of the matter during its 21st Extra-Ordinary Session, which was held from 23 February to 4 March 2017, citing the State's failure to submit observations on the merits.

During its 60th Ordinary Session, held from 8 to 22 May 2017, and later at the 22nd Extraordinary Session, held from 29 July to 7 August 2017, the Commission continued to defer the Communication to a later session, pending the State's response.

On 13 June 2018, the Complainants wrote to the Commission to inquire about the status of the Communication, noting that they had never received the Respondent State's submissions and requesting that the Commission proceed based on the State's failure to comply with Rules 108(1) and 11.

Despite being duly notified of the Complainants' submissions on the merits and given the requisite sixty (60) days under Rule 108(1) of the Commission's 2010 Rules of Procedure, the Respondent State failed to submit any response. The Commission deferred consideration of the Communication during multiple sessions, including the 59 and 60 Ordinary Sessions, as well as the 21st and 22nd Extraordinary Sessions. In the absence of a response from the State, the Commission decided to proceed with the determination of the Communication based on the Complainants' submissions alone as the only information at its disposal.

The Complainants submitted that the Admissibility requirements under Article 56(1), (2), (3), (4) and (7) of the Charter are clearly satisfied. Regarding Article 56(1) of the Charter, they state that the Authors of the Communication are clearly identified as Ali Askouri and Abdel-Hakeem Nasr, submitting the Communication for themselves and on behalf of other alleged victims. The three Non-Governmental Organisations represent them, and they provide full contact details. In terms of Article 56(2) of the Charter, they contend that the Communication alleges serious violations of rights guaranteed under the Charter and is, therefore, compatible with the Charter. They also aver that the language used is respectful and not disparaging or insulting, in compliance with Article 56(3) of the Charter. Furthermore, they argue that the allegations are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; therefore, the Communication complies with Article 56(4) of the Charter. In accordance with Article 56(7) of the Charter, they submit that the Communication does not deal with matters that have already been settled.

Regarding the requirement to exhaust local remedies under Article 56(5) of the Charter, the Complainants advance five main arguments, each supported by its arguments. They contend that the requirement is satisfied because "the [domestic] legal framework does not provide for available, effective or sufficient remedies for violations concerning lack of consultation, mass expulsion, destruction of property, inadequate resettlement and lack of reparation." In support of that argument, they aver, first, that Law 16 of 2002 on the 'Merowe Dam Resettlement and Compensation' establishes a Dams Implementation Unit (DIU) which is vested with the mandate to deal with compensation and relocation, among other issues. By Article 19 of Law 16 of 2002, all challenges to compensation or relocation shall be resolved before an Arbitration Committee. The Complainants state that the decision of the Arbitral Committee is final and not subject to appeal. The finality of the arbitral decision means that victims cannot access judicial remedies.

Further, the Complainants also aver that the Constitution does not provide for the right to shelter or housing or, indeed, the duty to consult prior to expropriation. They contend that this lack of legal provisions entails that there are no prospects of success in pursuing domestic remedies.

Secondly, in support of the first main argument, they contend that the DIU is immune from legal actions under several Sudanese laws. The DIU is institutionally under the Office of the President. As a result, its decisions have proved to be superior to all other government authorities. For example, during the construction of the Merowe Dam, the Governor of the Nile region, where the dam is located, agreed on a relocation plan with the affected people. The agreement was endorsed by the President under a decree and confirmed by the Federal Government. However, the DIU refused to implement the agreement, thereby effectively refusing to relocate the affected people. There were no legal sanctions against the DIU.

Thirdly, the Complainants contend that the domestic legal framework shields state agents from accountability and does not provide for effective and sufficient remedies for violations of the rights to life, liberty and security of the person, and the right to be free from torture and ill-treatment. They maintain that redressing violations of these rights requires the State to undertake effective investigations to establish facts, hold perpetrators accountable, and provide adequate reparations to the Complainants.

The Respondent State's police and national security forces (NISS) enjoy immunity from any criminal or civil legal action. For example, Section 45(2) of the Sudanese Police Act, 2008, provides that a police officer cannot be investigated for acts committed in the execution of their duties or pursuant to legal orders unless the responsible Minister or their delegate permits this. Similarly, Article 52 of the National Security Act provides that no NISS officer may be prosecuted without prior sanction of the Head of NISS.

There is no judicial procedure for victims to challenge the inaction of the Heads of those two institutions. The Complainants contend that, effectively, the police and NISS are allowed to determine for themselves whether and when to be held accountable for their acts. In practice, this happens very rarely, and as a result, it is virtually impossible for individual victims to access judicial remedies for violations committed by the police and NISS officers, such as those complained of in the present Communication.

Further, there are emergency laws under which people may be detained indefinitely without charge or trial. For example, Article 31 of the National Security Forces Act allows the security forces to detain people for up to nine months without access to judicial review. The Complainants aver that the Respondent State has not enacted any law that guarantees the right not to be arrested and detained arbitrarily, let alone the right to be brought before a court of law promptly.

The second main argument under Article 56(5) of the Charter is that attempts to utilise domestic remedies have been unduly prolonged and have revealed that such remedies are not available, adequate and sufficient. For example, after some protesters were killed, wounded, and detained in the June 2007 incident in respect of the Kajbar Dam, the victims and their families lodged a complaint with the public prosecutor. The federal parliament commissioned an inquiry into the shooting incident and a confidential report was submitted to the Minister of Justice in the same year 2007. However, despite numerous follow ups by victims and their families spanning until 2012, no further action has been taken by the authorities and no one has been prosecuted to date. The Complainants submit that the six years of inaction on the part of the State denotes that local remedies are unduly prolonged.

Similarly, with respect to the Merowe Dam, one Dr. Abdelrakeem Ahmed Ibn-Auf, one of the people affected, challenged the existing compensation scheme and sought a fairer scheme. His complaint was determined by the Adjudication Committee established under Article 19 of Law 16 of 2002. He was not satisfied with the Adjudication Committee's decision. Having thus exhausted the administrative remedies, he lodged his complaint before the regular civil courts, which refused to entertain the matter on the ground that they did not have jurisdiction. His appeals up to the Supreme Court were equally unsuccessful on that point.

The third main argument, advanced in the alternative, is that by repeatedly arresting anti-dam protesters, their elected representatives, and their lawyers, the Respondent State has created a climate of fear which renders any potential remedy unavailable, as pursuing remedies exposes the victims or their legal representatives to the risk of harassment. In this regard, the Complainants submit that local remedies need not be exhausted in the circumstances. Fourthly, the Complainants contend that the mass displacement of people to give way for the Merowe Dam is similar in nature and impact to the mass expulsion of individuals in that there was no prior consultation with the people to be displaced, and therefore no opportunity for them to challenge the displacement before the courts of law. The Complainants aver that the Commission has recognized mass expulsions as an exception to the exhaustion of local remedies rule. Accordingly, to the extent that the present Communication relates to mass displacement of people without prior consultation, and thus without affording them an opportunity to challenge the displacement, the requirement to exhaust local remedies should not apply.

The fifth and last main argument offered in the alternative is that the Communication falls under several exceptions to the requirement to exhaust local remedies. They contend that local remedies need not be exhausted because despite being fully aware of the serious violations alleged in the present Communication, the Respondent State has not taken any steps to remedy them. In this regard they rely on Amnesty International and others v Sudan, and Organisation Mondiale Contre La Torture v Rwanda in which the Commission stated that where the Respondent State has had ample notice of a situation of serious violations but has not taken steps to remedy the situation, local remedies need not be exhausted.

The Complainants also refer to the large and indeterminate number of victims and the nature of the violations, and contend that it is simply impracticable and undesirable for each of the numerous victims to litigate each of the massive and complex violations complained of.

Further, the Complainants aver that the Communication discloses an established pattern of administrative practices and legislative measures that are incompatible with the provisions of the Charter. They refer to the jurisprudence of the European Court to the effect that the rule of exhaustion is inapplicable where the administrative practice consisting of a repetition of acts incompatible with the Convention and official tolerance by the State authorities has been shown to exist, and is of such a nature as to make proceedings futile and ineffective, except where specific effective remedies against such legislation and practices exist. The Complainants contend that the exhaustion of local remedies rule is inapplicable to the extent that the present Communication discloses patterns of administrative practices and legislative measures.

Lastly, the Complainants state that the European Court of Human Rights adopts the position that in cases of violations which are continuing or likely to be repeated, the requirement to exhaust local remedies does not apply. They contend that the present Communication alleges continuing violations with respect to the Merowe Dam, which are also likely to be repeated with respect to the Kajbar Dam. Accordingly, they submit that Article 56(5) of the Charter is not applicable.

Regarding Article 56(6) of the Charter, which provides that Communications shall be considered on the merits if they are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted, the Complainants advance four arguments which can be briefly captured as follows.

They submit that the violations complained of and their effects are both of a continuing nature and are likely to recur with the planned construction of the Kajbar Dam. They submit that in cases of such violations, the timeliness requirement must be held to be satisfied, as to hold otherwise would allow future violations to occur. In support of the argument, they cite, among others, Moiwana Village v. Suriname in which the Inter-American Court of Human Rights considered whether it had competence to deal with the displacement of people which occurred before the State concerned had accepted the Court's jurisdiction. It held that "although this displacement supposedly occurred in 1986, their inability to return to those territories has allegedly continued. The Court, then, has competence to rule upon these alleged facts and their legal implications." The Complainants contend that, Collectif des veuves et ayants-Droit, Association mauritanienne des droits de l'Homme v Mauritania (2000) ACHPR para 85; Communications Nos. 48/90, 50/91, 89/93 - Amnesty International & others v Sudan (1999) ACHPR para. 39 Akdivar v. Turkey (1996) ECHR (Application no. 21893/93) para. 67; Cyprus v. Turkey (Application no. 25781/94) paras. 33, 99, among others. Moiwana Village v Suriname (2005) IACtHR (Series C No. 124) para. 43 to the extent the present Communication seeks to address the ongoing practice of violations that may lead to further violations if not addressed, it cannot be considered untimely.

The Complainants also contend that this Communication involves severe and massive violations against over 50,000 individuals. In the circumstances, it is impossible for each aggrieved individual to keep track of the time in which local remedies, if any, may be deemed to have been exhausted for each individual. Accordingly, Article 56(6) of the Charter must be applied flexibly to admit this Communication. Further, the Complainants state that where local remedies are found to be unavailable, ineffective, and insufficient, the requirement to submit a Communication within a reasonable period does not apply. Having earlier submitted that local remedies are unavailable, ineffective and insufficient, they contend that Article 56(6) of the Charter should not apply to the present Communication.

Furthermore, the Complainants aver that this Communication should be admitted because they engaged in good faith efforts over many years to exhaust local remedies in futility. They contend that the Commission should not punish them for the Respondent State's failure to provide effective remedies by finding the Communication untimely.

Lastly, the Complainants aver that remedies for the killing and assault of protesters in April 2006 and June 2007 can only be initiated by the State through investigation and prosecution of the perpetrators. They contend that by failing to initiate proper investigations and prosecutions despite promises to do so, the Respondent State is responsible for the delay, if any. The Complainants submit that they should not be punished for the Respondent State's failure in this regard.
For the foregoing reasons, the Complainants submit that the present Communication should be admitted for further consideration on the merits.

The Respondent State provides a detailed narrative of the steps taken at different stages of its dams project. The details in this regard are relevant for the merits stage. The details will not be reproduced at this stage. Regarding the admissibility of the Communication, the Respondent State submits, first, that the Communication is incompatible with the Charter under Article 56(2) of the Charter. It contends that the construction of irrigation and/or power generation dams does not per se violate the rights guaranteed under the Charter, as long as all necessary measures are taken to address and cure the negative impacts that some of its citizens are expected to be exposed to. It maintains that the construction of the dam is part of its responsibility to achieve development, welfare, and stability for its people in terms of the Charter.

Further, it contends that the claims regarding the planned construction of Kajbar Dam are premature, as the project is still in sketches and documents and has not been implemented yet. For these reasons, the Respondent State submits that the Communication is incompatible with the Charter and must be dismissed pursuant to Article 56(2) of the Charter.

Further, the Respondent State contends that this Communication contains disparaging language which renders it inadmissible under Article 56(3) of the Charter. It cites as examples of the disparaging language, expressions such as "... located in Nubia ...", "indigenous Nubians", "the Nubians qualify as an indigenous people ... given their self-identification as a specific group distinct from other Sudanese populations..." It states that in terms of Article 1 of its Constitution, "the Republic of the Sudan is an independent, sovereign state. It is a democratic, decentralized, multi-cultural, multilingual, multi-racial, multi-ethnic, and multi-religious country where such diversities co-exist. It categorically states that "there has never been a decentralised form of local government bearing the name 'Nubia'. The use of that term is contrary to Article 28 of the Charter, implies secessionist tendency, and touches on the integrity of the country contrary to Article 29(5) of the Charter.

Furthermore,, the Respondent State contends that the Communication must be declared inadmissible for failure to exhaust local remedies as required by Article 56(5) of the Charter. It refers to the five main arguments advanced by the Complainants and challenges them as follows.

There are legal and administrative frameworks for dealing with all issues relating to the dam projects, including the provision of adequate, sufficient and effective remedies; relocation of displaced people; and redressing complaints relating to compensation and relocation. The legal framework comprises the RIPAMD Act and the Regulations, Rules and Orders made thereunder.

The Supreme Political Committee established under the RIPAMD Act is a supervisory body. Its major assignment is to attract foreign funding and investment for the dams. It also endorses the findings and recommendations of the subordinate technical specialized committees. The affected people are represented in the SPC by their state governors who are elected through local elections conducted by the population of the respective states in accordance with the Constitution.

The Technical Specialised Committee, which initially had three representatives of the affected people (subsequently increased to four at its first meeting), identified the resettlement options and assessed compensation for land. It came up with a compensation scheme whereby a holder of 1 freehold feddan (=1.038 acres) in the affected area received 3 feddans in the resettlement area; 1 usufruct feddan was compensated with 1.5 feddans in the resettlement area.

In terms of remedies for complaints relating to compensation and relocation, there are two avenues under the RIPAMD Act. Section 14 of the RIPAMD Act provides for the right to apply for reconsideration of any decision or order made by the Commissioner relating to the assessment of compensation. The application is required to be lodged within 3 months of the issue of the decision or order. Secondly, section 19 of the RIPAMD Act provides for an Arbitration Tribunal composed of a judge as president, a representative of the Dams Implementation Unit (DIU), and a representative of the claimant. The arbitral award is final as far as the administrative hierarchy is concerned. Contrary to the Complainant's assertion, the RIPAMD Act does not state that arbitral awards are "...not subject to appeal".

The Respondent State explains that the finality of arbitral awards is with respect to the administrative hierarchy under the RIPAMD Act. Any decision taken under the RIPAMD Act is administrative and ordinarily is subject to challenge before the Administrative Court via mandamus or certiorari in accordance with the Administrative Adjudication Act of 2005.

The Respondent State avers that the motion challenging compensation lodged before ordinary civil courts by Dr. Abdelraheem Ahmed Ibn-Auf's was dismissed all the way to the Supreme Court because such courts have no jurisdiction to entertain administrative claims, such as relating to assessment of compensation under the RIPMAD Act. It further explains that having failed through the ordinary civil courts, Dr. Abdelraheem Ahmed Ibn-Auf's was free to lodge his claim before the appropriate administrative court, but he chose not to do so.

Further to the above avenues, the 2005 Constitution of Sudan protects the human and peoples' rights known in international instruments. Among others, Article 31 provides that All persons are equal before the law and are entitled without discrimination, as to race, colour, sex, language, religious creed, political opinion, or ethnic origin, to the equal protection of the law

Further, section 43 of the Constitution states that: 1. Every citizen shall have the right to acquire or own property as regulated by law. 2. No private property may be expropriated save by law in the public interest and in consideration for prompt and fair compensation. No private property shall be confiscated save by an order of a court of law. In terms of enforcement, Article 122 of the Constitution provides for the Constitutional Court, which has the competence to protect rights and adjudicate on the constitutionality of laws. Additionally, the rest of the judiciary is established under the Judiciary Act of 1986, and courts are arranged and organized under the Civil Procedure Act 1983 and the Criminal Procedure Act 1991.

The Respondent State also avers that its judiciary is completely independent of both the Executive and the Legislature. It refers to Article 128 of the Constitution, which provides that: 1. All Justices and Judges are independent in the performance of their duties and have full judicial competence with respect to their function; and they shall not be influenced in their judgments. 2. Justices and Judges shall uphold the Constitution and the rule of law and shall administer justice diligently, impartially and without fear or favour.

In respect of the shootings of March 2006 and June 2007, the Respondent State maintains that all necessary criminal proceedings were taken. The matter was ended by the injured and families of the deceased who freely waived their rights to continue prosecution in accordance with the Sudanese traditions of conciliation and provisions on compoundable offences in the Criminal procedure Act 1991. Deya (blood money) and compensation were paid to the victims and no further claims were made in respect of the incident.
In light of the foregoing, the Respondent State submitted that this Communication should be declared inadmissible.

Regarding the Respondent State's argument that the Communication is incompatible with the Charter, the Complainants maintain that the gist of this Communication is not a construction of dams per se. It is the lack of adequate prior consultations, forced expulsion and displacement of people, destruction of property, arbitrary killings and assault of the people that are impugned as violations of the Charter. In this regard, the Respondent State's argument is misplaced.

Besides, the Complainants contend that even though construction of Kajbar dam has not commenced, the mere fact that the Respondent State has already completed all technical preparations. There has not been adequate consultation entails that when construction commences, the violations are going to recur. This alone makes the case one of continuing violations, for which it must be declared admissible.

Concerning the contention that the reference to "Nubians" is contrary to Article 56(3) of the Charter, the Complainant insist that merely recognising a specific group of indigenous people who are or will be affected by the construction of a dam in the area they historically inhabit does not necessarily entail secessionist tendencies, let alone threaten the integrity of the Respondent State. Moreover, indigenous people are a widely recognised special group under international human rights law, and references to Nubians as indigenous people alone cannot properly be understood to convey secessionist intentions.

The Complainants further insist that there were no remedies for the lack of or inadequate consultations during the preparatory work of both the Merowe and Kajbar dams. They contend that the Governor, who allegedly represents the affected people in the Supreme Political Committee, is a public officer and an official of the Respondent State. Further, the technical committee only advises the Supreme Political Committee. Its recommendations are not binding. Moreover, the Respondent State does not indicate how the affected people's representatives to the Technical Committee were chosen, whether they included members of the committees elected by the affected communities, and whether the recommendations of the Technical Committee were implemented. The Complainants maintain that for all these irregularities, there are no local remedies.

Concerning the Respondent State's averments on remedies within domestic law, the Complainants contend, first, that recourse to Administrative Courts is an uncertain procedure as it is only permitted where: (a) the administrative body acted beyond its authority; (b) there is a procedural flaw in the administrative decision; (c) the administrative decision violates the law; or (d) the administrative body abused its authority. They contend that the appropriate remedies are not confined to challenging procedural improprieties. The relevant remedies relate to whether the entire system for awarding compensation and the grave violations resulting from the displacement of people are in accord with the rights of the affected people. For such remedies, recourse to administrative courts is an insufficient remedy.

The Complainants also maintain that the Constitutional framework is insufficient because the right to housing and shelter, and the duty to consult prior to expropriation are not provided for in the Constitution. Further, they observe that the claims of independence of the judiciary in principle are not supported by any evidence demonstrating independence in practice.

Concerning the killing and assault of protesters, the Complainants affirm that even though the Respondent State alleges that "all necessary criminal proceedings were taken", it neither discloses the results of the criminal inquiry, nor produces any evidence of the victims' waiver of the right to pursue criminal proceedings. Even if some victims had waived their rights, this would not have absolved the Respondent State from discharging its obligation to carry out an effective investigation and prosecution of the perpetrators of the violations. The Complainants contend that the payment of "blood money" as a reconciliatory form of settling grievances should accordingly not be regarded as a remedy that is available, effective, and sufficient. For the foregoing reasons, the Communication must be admitted for consideration on the merits.

This Communication is submitted under Article 55 of the Charter, which provides for "Communications other than those of State parties". As such, to be admitted for consideration on the merits, it must satisfy the threshold conditions laid down under Article 56 of the Charter.

The Commission notes that the parties do not join issues with respect to the conditions under Article 56(1), (4), (6), and (7) of the Charter. Nevertheless, as a threshold requirement for admissibility, the Commission examines compliance with all the conditions based on the information provided by the parties. In this regard, the Commission will first consider the uncontested conditions.

The authors of this Communication are clearly indicated as Ali Askouri and Abdel-Hakeem Nasr, who submitted it for themselves and on behalf of other alleged victims. Article 56(1) of the Charter, which requires that the authors of a Communication be identified, is clearly satisfied.

The Commission notes that the Communication is partly founded upon information in the personal knowledge of the two authors following their alleged involvement in the campaign against the Merowe and Kajbar Dam projects. In this regard, the Communication is not exclusively based on news disseminated through the mass media. Consequently, the Communication satisfies Article 56(4) of the Charter.

Regarding the requirement that Communications must be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted (Art. 56(6) of the Charter), the Commission notes that the question as to whether local remedies were exhausted also arises for consideration. Logically, the reasonable period would be reckoned from the time local remedies were exhausted, or as will be shown, from the time the Complainants realized or ought to have realized that local remedies are not available, or if available, that they are unduly prolonged, or ineffective, or insufficient. The Commission will consider the condition under Article 56(6) upon determining the requirements of exhausting local remedies.

Further, as the Complainants submit, which the Respondent State does not dispute and the Commission finds no reason to hold otherwise, the Communication complies with Article 56(7) of the Charter which requires that Communications must "not deal with cases which have been settled by the State involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter."

Reverting to the contested admissibility conditions, the first issue is whether, as argued by the Respondent State, the present Communication is incompatible with the Charter in terms of Article 56(2) thereof.

The Commission has expounded that compatibility with the Charter entails four main aspects, namely: the parties to the complaint; the subject matter of the complaint; the time the impugned events occurred relative to the time the Charter became applicable to the Respondent State; and the location or territorial jurisdiction where the impugned events occurred.

The Respondent State's argument evidently relates to compatibility with the Charter in terms of the subject matter. The Commission considers the Respondent State's argument untenable. This Communication does not per se challenge the mere act of building dams, which may indeed benefit the people in terms of development. Instead, it is sufficiently clear that the complaint concerns whether the Respondent State complied or is complying with its obligations under the Charter in the process of undertaking these critical development projects.
To the extent that the Communication pleads the violation of rights under the Charter, it is clearly compatible with the Charter in terms of subject matter.

Similarly, the argument that the complaint is premature in respect of the Kajbar dam cannot be accepted. The Respondent State itself states that in 2007 it already had field officers conducting studies for the dam in the intended location of the dam. which led to clashes with the protesting inhabitants, where some were killed, others injured, and yet others arrested. It is, as the Commission understands, precisely the manner in which the preparatory works for the dam have been conducted and the Respondent State's alleged response to people's expression of discontent with the projects that the Communication challenges as constituting violations of the provisions of the Charter. The subject matter is thus perfectly compatible with the Charter.

There do not appear to be any issues relating to personal, temporal, locational, or territorial compatibility. The Commission, accordingly, holds that the Communication is compatible with the Charter.

Regarding Article 56(3) of the Charter, the Commission notes that the words "located in Nubia ...", "indigenous Nubians", "the Nubians qualify as an indigenous people ... given their self-identification as specific group distinct from other Sudanese populations..." as used in the present Communication are meant to merely identify the alleged victims as a unique group that is indigenous to the location where the Kajbar dam is intended to be constructed. Indeed, the commendable diversity countenanced under section 1 of the Constitution cited by the Respondent State entails that multiple groups of people uniquely identify themselves as different from the others in one way or the other but coexisting peacefully as Sudanese under the jurisdiction of one State. Merely describing one of such groups as alleged victims cannot without more be understood to suggest secessionist tendencies. There is nothing beyond identifying the alleged victims as Sudanese indigenous to the Nubia location that suggests such tendencies.

For language to be deemed disparaging or insulting, it must clearly go beyond advancing a complaint and intend to bring an institution or officer or the State into disrepute. In this regard, it must be remembered that a complaint of human rights violations, by its very nature, negatively impacts the State. To offend Article 56(3) of the Charter, the language must clearly exceed the necessity of advancing the complaint. In the Commission's view, the words quoted above fall far short of such an intention. The Communication accordingly complies with Article 56(3) of the Charter.

Concerning the exhaustion of local remedies, it must be noted that this Communication joins a series of events which form the basis of the alleged violations. Although all these events relate to the dam's development projects, they can be isolated, disjoined and redressed through different domestic procedures if they exist. The measures complained of can reasonably be classified, for purposes of analysis, into two broad categories. The first category concerns all the measures (procedures) taken by the Respondent State to implement the dam's development projects. These measures include the alleged lack of consultation with the affected communities, forced mass displacement of people, flooding the areas without notice, the destruction of property resulting from the flooding, inadequate resettlement arrangements for the displaced people, and lack of reparations for the loss of land and other property.

The second category relates to those measures taken in reaction to the protests by the affected people. These measures include the killing and injuring of protesters; the alleged torture of anti-dam activists; and the alleged arrest and detention of anti-dam protestors, activists, journalists, and lawyers. Although related to the dams' development projects, these measures do not ordinarily constitute part of the steps taken for the construction of dams. They are generally reactionary, in response to concerted efforts by the local population to stop the projects.

The Commission will examine, in respect of each of these two categories, whether there are any remedies which the Complainants could have availed themselves to secure redress. It is not logical to disregard domestic remedies that may be available for one severable category of the measures on the basis that remedies are not in fact available in respect of the other category of measures.

Regarding the first category of measures, the Complainants assert that "effective and sufficient local remedies are not available" within the domestic legal framework. The Complainants cite four sub-arguments in support of this assertion which the Commission considers as follows.

In the first place the Complainants contend that access to judicial remedies is impeded by various laws adopted by the Respondent State. In this regard, they cited various provisions of Law No. 16 of 2002, "Law for the Resettlement and Compensation of People affected by the Merowe Dam" (Merowe Resettlement and Compensation Law). Among other things, they assert that this law requires a commissioner to assess resettlement options and compensation. They state that the Commissioner's decisions can only be challenged through arbitration. The arbitral decision is final and not subject to appeal. In the Complainants' view, this closes the door to judicial remedies.

The Commission notes the Respondent State's explanation that the finality of the arbitral decision merely relates to the mechanisms within the administrative hierarchy. Both the process before the Commissioner and the arbitration are administrative undertakings that can be challenged before formal administrative courts. This constitutes a judicial remedy. The Complainants, who in their submissions also categorize the arbitration as administrative, do not dispute the Respondent State's position. To the extent that individual recourse to administrative courts is available, the Complainant's argument that access to judicial remedies is closed is unfounded. It is open for the Complainants to challenge resettlement options and compensation after arbitration before the administrative courts.

Further, in their reply, Complainants contend that the remedies before administrative courts are uncertain because a judicial review by the administrative courts is only possible in the cases where (a) the administrative body which issues the impugned decision is legally incompetent; (b) there is a procedural flaw in the decision; (c) the decision is in violation of the law, and (d) the administrative body abused its authority. The Complainants surmise that a challenge to compensation would not succeed on these grounds.

The Commission considers that it is for the administrative courts to decide whether or not a challenge to compensation and resettlement falls under the recognised grounds for judicial review. Importantly, despite the impugned measures spanning some period of time from initial studies, construction of the Merowe dam, flooding of the area and the attendant destruction of property, and displacement of people, the Complainants do not cite a single instance when a proper recourse was made to the administrative courts concerning the alleged lack of consultations, destruction of property, mass displacement, inadequate resettlement and lack of reparations; and that the administrative courts declined to adjudicate on the basis that the complaints do not fall under the four recognised grounds for judicial review. As the Respondent State has submitted, and the Complainants' do not dispute, the single case of Dr Abdelraheem Ahmed Ibn-Auf was dismissed because it was filed before regular civil courts which have no jurisdiction over administrative matters instead of the administrative court.

The Commission has held that if a remedy has the slightest likelihood to be effective, the applicant must pursue it. Arguing that local remedies are not likely to be successful, without trying to avail oneself of them, will simply not sway the Commission.

In the present Communication, until an opportunity is given to the administrative courts, a mere surmise or apprehension that administrative court will not admit a complaint about under the recognised grounds of judicial review does not absolve the Complainants from attempting to have recourse to the administrative courts..

Furthermore, the Complainants asserted that the appropriate remedies for the violations in the first category (as classified under paragraph 83 above) would require the possibility of challenging the constitutionality of the very laws under which the dam's projects are implemented. They contend that such laws cannot be challenged because neither the 1988 nor the 2005 Constitutions provides for the right to housing and shelter and the duty to conduct prior consultations before expropriation.
