According to the Complainant, the abnormal prolongation is also characterised by 192 unjustified adjournments, causing the proceedings to last up to twelve years, whereas under Article 10(6) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing the Special Criminal Court, the latter is authorised only exceptionally to extend by 3 months the 6-month period allotted to it to render its decision.

The Complainant asserts that the absence of response to his requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013 and 11 December 2015 contravenes Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which stipulates in its Article 8 that "Where proof of restitution in cash is made before the examining magistrate, the latter shall draw up a record thereof, expressly mentioning the applicant's request for discontinuance of proceedings. A copy of the said record, accompanied by the payment receipt, shall be transmitted, within a maximum period of seventy-two (72) hours, to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court. The latter shall transmit the copy of the record and the copy of the payment receipt, together with his opinion, to the Minister in charge of justice, within the same period as above".

The Complainant also alleges that his habeas corpus applications (applications for immediate release), filed with the High Court of Mfoundi in Yaoundé on 13 October 2014 and 6 October 2016, were not followed up, in violation of Articles 584 and 585 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the CCP). He asserts that he is still detained on the basis of a warrant of pre-trial detention of 19 March 2012 which had a validity of 18 months in accordance with Article 221 of the CCP.

The Complainant asserts that the multiplication of proceedings against him is intended to keep him in detention. He illustrates this by his new indictment for forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal on 28 October 2014, at the time when he was awaiting the verdict of the Special Criminal Court on the charges of embezzlement of public funds and attempted escape. He argues that following the Order of partial dismissal and committal to the Special Criminal Court No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014, another identical procedure No. 021/RG-TCS/2015 was opened before the same court, abandoning the charge of embezzlement of public funds in favour of forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal.

The Complainant asserts that he is therefore held in detention on the basis of an expired warrant of pre-trial detention, issued by examining magistrate Dr Frédéric Placide Michel Batoum on 19 March 2012 for a maximum duration of 18 months in accordance with Article 221 of the CCP. The Complainant considers that an order of pre-trial detention should have been issued against him to regularise the proceedings.

The Complainant alleges that the Cameroonian courts lack independence and impartiality. In support of this assertion, he invokes Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a Special Criminal Court, which authorises an intrusion by the Minister of Justice after the seizure of the examining magistrate or the trial judges.

He also invokes correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 by which the Minister of Justice authorises the Madam Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court to discontinue the proceedings against five employees of Afriland First Bank while instructing her to maintain the proceedings against the Complainant for embezzlement of public funds, whereas the Order of partial dismissal and committal to the Special Criminal Court No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014 of the examining magistrate had removed the charge of embezzlement of public funds against the Complainant.

He further recalls the Commission's decision in Bakweri Lands Claims Committee v Cameroon, where it was held that "the President of the Republic exercises extraordinary powers so as to influence the organisation of the judiciary and that the judicial system is partial and lacks independence".

The Complainant alleges that his continued detention rests only "on the whims" of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court, who allegedly sent him on several occasions emissaries, namely Biyick Marcel, Ondao Jean Claude and Ngo Um Elisabeth, to demand from him the sum of 50 million CFA francs for his release. The denunciation of these facts to the Procurator General and the Minister of Justice and through the Cameroonian press did not, according to the Complainant, provoke the slightest reaction from the addressees.

The Complainant considers that it is within the register of these whims that his detention is abnormally prolonged, whereas his co-accused, all agents of Afriland First Bank, indicted and placed under a warrant of pre-trial detention on 13 January 2013, the day of the restitution of the sum of 1,738,013 CFA francs, were released after 24 hours of detention. The Complainant asserts that this constitutes "an extraordinary diligence that is equally questionable".

According to the Complainant, the exceeding of time limits generates a permanent fear of disciplinary proceedings among the magistrates and judicial police officers concerned. He asserts that, having largely exceeded the time limits, the magistrates handling his case are obliged to endorse the continued violation of his rights so as not to expose themselves to disciplinary sanctions.
In light of the foregoing, the Complainant requests the Commission to find that local remedies are abnormally prolonged.

On the use of disparaging or insulting language, the Respondent State alleges that the Complainant used the following insulting terms: "In reality, the continued detention of the complainant rests only on the whims of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court who sent, on several occasions, emissaries, namely Biyick Marcel, Ondao Jean Claude and Ngo Um Elisabeth, to demand from him the sum of fifty (50) million CFA francs tribulaire of his release...". "It is in this same register that the release (provisional release) of the complainant's eight (8) co-accused, all agents of Afriland First Bank, indicted and placed under a warrant of pre-trial detention, on 13 January 2013, from the Yaoundé Central Prison on 14 January 2013, the day of the restitution to the State coffers of the sum of 1,738,013 CFA francs, that is after 24 hours of detention, should be placed. An extraordinary diligence that is equally questionable".

The Respondent State alleges that such statements and defamatory imputations are groundless and bring discredit and opprobrium on the senior magistrates of the Special Criminal Court, on the judicial institution and even on the State of Cameroon. The Respondent State argues that the release of the Complainant's co-accused is not the result of corruption, insofar as the discontinuance of proceedings is a procedure governed by Articles 3 et seq. of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti.

The Respondent State recalls the Commission's jurisprudence in Kevin Ngwang Gumne v Cameroon, where the Commission held that "complainants should endeavour to be respectful in the language used in presenting their communications"; and Ilesanmi v Nigeria, where the Commission held that referring to the Head of State as "corrupt" and stating that he received bribes from drug traffickers was aimed at ridiculing and discrediting that institution and consequently constitutes the use of disparaging or insulting language. The Respondent State concludes that the terms used by the Complainant in the present Communication are in the same vein.

On the non-exhaustion of local remedies, the Respondent State alleges that local remedies are available and effective and recalls the remedies successfully pursued by the Complainant, namely his application to the Investigation Chamber of the Supreme Court, which suspended Order No. 283-SOG-12/C of 10 October 2012 of examining magistrate Dr. Frédéric Placide Michel Batoum on grounds of a defect in form; his application to the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé-centre administratif, who issued an order of 26 November 2012 authorising him to carry out all necessary attachments of the sum of 1,738,363,013 CFA francs in the accounts of Afriland First Bank held at the Bank of Central African States, the International Bank for Commerce and Savings of Cameroon and the General Bank Company of Cameroon; and his application before the Special Criminal Court, which resulted in Judgment No. 006/ADD-CRIM-TCS of 17 April 2015 ordering the joinder of proceedings No. 001/RG-TCS/2014 and proceedings No. 021/RG-TCS/2015.

Concerning the applications made by the Complainant for the discontinuance of proceedings, the Respondent State indicates that the decision to discontinue proceedings depends on the sole discretion of the Minister of Justice in accordance with Article 3(2) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which provides that "if the restitution occurs after the seizure of the Court, the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court may, on the authorisation of the Minister in charge of justice, discontinue the proceedings before any decision on the merits and the court shall pronounce the forfeitures of Article 30 of the Penal Code with an entry in the criminal record". According to the Respondent State, the Minister in charge of justice not being a judicial authority, the decision to discontinue proceedings cannot consequently be considered a local remedy within the meaning of Article 56(5) of the Charter.

In response to the Complainant's allegations that no action was taken on his habeas corpus applications, the Respondent State affirms that the habeas corpus application of 18 April 2018 was concluded by decision No. 130/HC of 20 September 2018 of the High Court of Mfoundi confirming the continued detention. It adds that the Complainant did not appeal against this decision and has therefore not exhausted local remedies.

In his reply, the Complainant refutes the Respondent State's arguments on the use of disparaging or insulting language, on the one hand, and on the exhaustion of local remedies, on the other. It is not necessary to repeat his arguments on local remedies insofar as the Complainant repeats the arguments initially submitted.

Concerning the use of disparaging or insulting language, the Complainant reiterates that his continued detention rests only on the whims of the Procurator General of the Special Criminal Court, who allegedly sent him on several occasions emissaries, namely Biyick Marcel, Ondao Jean Claude and Ngo Um Elisabeth, to demand from him the sum of 50 million CFA francs for his release. The denunciation of these facts to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court and to the Minister of Justice on 21 May 2015, and through the Cameroonian press, did not, according to the Complainant, provoke the slightest reaction from the addressees. He adds that the fact that neither the persons implicated nor the Respondent State brought any action for slanderous denunciation attests to the soundness of the denunciation.

For the Complainant, the Commission should ensure that the protection of the reputation of State institutions, guaranteed by Article 56(3) of the Charter, is not interpreted in a manner that violates or restricts the enjoyment of freedom of expression enshrined in Article 9 of the Charter.

The Complainant argues that the use of the terms "whims of the prosecutor" is neither in bad faith nor calculated to poison the mind of the public against the government and its institutions, and that the State has not proved otherwise.

To be declared admissible, a Communication submitted under Article 55 must fulfil the seven requirements set out in Article 56 of the Charter. The Commission's consistent position on the grounds of admissibility is that the requirements set out in Article 56 are cumulative, meaning that if one of them is not met, the communication will be declared inadmissible.

The Commission notes from the parties' arguments that five of the seven admissibility criteria are not disputed. It is the requirement relating to the prohibition of disparaging or insulting language and that of the exhaustion of local remedies that are strongly contested by the parties. That observation having been made, it falls to the Commission to examine whether all the requirements are met, while devoting substantial discussion to the requirements disputed between the parties.
Article 56(1) provides that "Communications relating to human and peoples' rights ... received by the Commission shall be considered if they indicate their authors".

According to the Commission's jurisprudence, complainants or authors of complaints must indicate their identity and contact details. The present Communication is submitted by Kaptue Tagne Serges Bruces (the Complainant) assisted by Mandela Center International (Representative). The Complainant and his representative provided their names, as well as their physical, telephone and electronic addresses. Consequently, the Complainant and his representative have adequately identified themselves for the purposes of the processing of the Communication. The Commission concludes that the requirement prescribed in paragraph 1 of Article 56 has been met.

Article 56(2) provides that "communications ... received by the Commission shall be considered if they are compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter." The Commission's consistent interpretation of this provision is that the compatibility of a communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the Charter means the possibility for the Commission to hear the matter before it without violating the provisions of these two instruments, as well as conformity with the four aspects of its jurisdiction, namely jurisdiction ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci.

Concerning compatibility with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the Charter, the Commission notes that in the present case the Complainant seeks the protection of his human rights, namely his rights under Articles 6 and 7 of the Charter. It happens that one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, provided for in its Article 3(h), is the protection of human rights. Furthermore, nothing in the Complainant's allegations and application reveals any incompatibility with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the Charter.

With regard to the four aspects of jurisdiction, the Commission notes that the communication was submitted against Cameroon, a State Party to the Charter (jurisdiction ratione personae) and alleges the violation of rights enshrined in the Charter, in this case the violation of Articles 6 and 7 of the Charter (jurisdiction ratione materiae). The complaint concerns facts that occurred from 19 March 2012, the date on which the Complainant's pre-trial detention began. The Respondent State became a party to the Charter on 20 June 1989 (jurisdiction ratione temporis); and the alleged violations were committed on the territory of the Respondent State (jurisdiction ratione loci). Thus, the Commission concludes that the four aspects of its jurisdiction are met. Consequently, this admissibility requirement is met.

The rule of this provision is that "communications [...] received by the Commission shall be considered if they are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or to the Organization of African Unity". According to the Commission, the purpose of this clause is to ensure "diplomatic, courteous and respectful exchanges between the parties appearing before it and the need to preserve the integrity of State institutions, which are indispensable to the protection of human rights."

The Commission has previously held that "in determining whether a certain remark is disparaging or insulting and has undermined the integrity of the judiciary, the Commission must be satisfied that the said remark or language is aimed at unlawfully and intentionally damaging the dignity, reputation or integrity of a judicial officer or body, and that it is used in a manner calculated to pollute the minds of the public or any reasonable man to cast aspersions on the Administration of justice and weaken public confidence in it. The language must be aimed at undermining the integrity and status of the institution and discrediting it."

In the present Communication, the Respondent State alleges that the Complainant used the following insulting terms: "In reality, the continued detention of the complainant rests only on the whims of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court who sent, on several occasions, emissaries, namely Biyick Marcel, Ondao Jean Claude and Ngo Um Elisabeth, to demand from him the sum of fifty (50) million CFA francs tribulaire of his release...". "It is in this same register that the release (provisional release) of the complainant's eight (8) co-accused, all agents of Afriland First Bank, indicted and placed under a warrant of pre-trial detention, on 13 January 2013, from the Yaoundé Central Prison on 14 January 2013, the day of the restitution to the State coffers of the sum of 1,738,013 CFA francs, that is after 24 hours of detention, should be placed. An extraordinary diligence that is equally questionable".

The Commission notes that the expression "whim" is not in itself an insult against the institution of the Public Prosecutor, since what is aimed at is denouncing the ambiguous attitudes of that judicial authority regarding his case, in light of the relevant law applicable to the case. In concreto, it is a matter of highlighting the unpredictable behaviour of a judicial authority from which integrity and objectivity are expected in the handling of cases. The use of this expression aims simply at denouncing the unjustified persistence of a judicial authority against a person subject to the law.

The Commission notes that by letter of 21 May 2015, the Complainant denounced the allegations of corruption by the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court to the same Procurator General and to the Minister of Justice. The Complainant also provided copies of local newspapers reproducing the same allegations. The Commission observes that in his denunciation, the Complainant provided the names of three persons presenting themselves as emissaries of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court to extort fifty (50) million CFA francs from him in exchange for his release. The Respondent State does not deny having received these denunciations.

The Commission notes that the Respondent State's observations contain no information even on the opening of an investigation to determine whether the facts denounced by the Complainant were true or unfounded. The Commission also notes that the substance of the Complainant's allegations in the present Communication is similar to the content of his denunciation with regard to the allegations of corruption. In these circumstances, allegations that have been the subject of a denunciation at the national level cannot constitute insulting language or discredit directed at the Respondent State.

The Commission also does not detect any insulting terms in the Complainant's remarks on the "extraordinary and questionable" diligence leading to the release of his eight co-accused after only 24 hours of detention. Given that the eight co-accused received an expeditious handling of their cases, the Complainant, who has been in detention for more than 12 years, whose case had experienced 192 adjournments as of 19 April 2024 and whose four applications for release of 28 January 2013, 13 October 2014, 11 December 2015 and 6 October 2016 had not been followed up, is justified in questioning the reasons for the expeditious procedure for the benefit of his co-accused and in criticising the judicial bodies handling his case.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission considers that the Complaint complies with the requirement of Article 56(3).

In Article 56(4), the Charter requires that "communications relating to human and peoples' rights ... shall be considered if they are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media". Under this rule, the Commission cannot consider communications based solely on information disseminated by the media. The Commission has interpreted this provision as requiring complainants to support their communications with evidence.

In the present communication, the Complainant attached various forms of evidence to his observations, including judicial decisions and applications for release. The Commission therefore considers that the communication complies with Article 56(4).

In this provision, the Charter stipulates that "communications relating to human and peoples' rights ... shall be considered if they are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged". Since the Jawara v. The Gambia case, jurisprudence has confirmed that the Commission requires complainants to exhaust local remedies only where these are "available, effective and sufficient to remedy the alleged violation". A remedy is available if "the applicant can pursue it without impediment"; a remedy is effective if it "offers a prospect of success", while a remedy will be considered sufficient "if it is capable of redressing the complaint".

In the present communication, the Complainant alleges that the failure to respect reasonable time limits in the handling of the case of Public Prosecutor and State of Cameroon v. Kaptue Tagne Serges Bruces and others, the absence of responses to his three habeas corpus applications, the interference of the executive in judicial proceedings, and the multiplication of proceedings intended to keep him in detention are dependent on the unavailability and ineffectiveness of local remedies. For its part, the Respondent State alleges that local remedies are available and effective.

The Commission notes that the law organising the Special Criminal Court lays down procedural time limits which may be extended exceptionally. It also notes that the case of Public Prosecutor and State of Cameroon v. Kaptue Tagne Serges Bruces and others was transferred to the Special Criminal Court on 10 October 2012 whereas the said Court was established in December 2011, which suggests that the Special Criminal Court was not yet overloaded at the time of the committal. The Commission observes that the Respondent State has provided no justification for holding the first hearing two weeks after the expiry of the statutory 30-day period provided for by Article 10(1) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a Special Criminal Court, which provides that "The President of the Court shall determine, after consultation with the Procurator General, the date of the hearing, which must be set no later than thirty days after notification of the committal order ...". This provision provides for no exception, which means that the exceeding of time limits is justified only in case of force majeure, which is not the case in the present matter.

As of 19 April 2024, the case of Public Prosecutor and State of Cameroon v. Kaptue Tagne Serges Bruces and others had been subject to 192 adjournments over more than 11 years of proceedings before the Special Criminal Court. The parties' pleadings indicate no investigative act carried out by the Special Criminal Court to bring the case to a state ready for judgment following the Supreme Court Judgment No. 017/SSP/CS of 22 August 2017 dismissing the Complainant's appeal seeking to invalidate certain evidence of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court.

It therefore appears that, as of the date of submission of the Complainant's reply, a period of 6 years, 7 months and 27 days (from 22/8/2017 to 19/4/2024) had elapsed without notable diligence on the part of the Special Criminal Court. This passivity is notoriously excessive in light of Article 10(6) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a Special Criminal Court, which stipulates that "the Court has a maximum period of six (6) months to render its decision. This period may be extended by a maximum of three (3) months by order of the President of the Court. This order is not subject to appeal. Any appeal, in this case, shall be placed on the file".

It emerges from the parties' arguments that the first complaint transferred to the Special Criminal Court on 10 October 2012 and the two other complaints set before the same Court on 8 August 2014 were still pending as of 19 April 2024, well beyond the maximum period of 9 months laid down by Article 10(6) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011. In the absence of any justification for the delay in handling these complaints, the Commission concludes that the domestic judicial proceedings are abnormally prolonged.

With regard to the applications for release, the Commission notes that following the restitution of the corpus delicti of the embezzlement, the Complainant addressed two requests for discontinuance of proceedings to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013 and 11 December 2015. The Respondent State does not contest this allegation by the Complainant but argues that recourse to the Minister of Justice is not a remedy to be exhausted within the meaning of Article 56(5) of the Charter.

The Commission recalls that the remedies to be exhausted before it is seized are judicial remedies. The characterisation as a judicial remedy depends on the powers exercised by the institution or authority concerned. Thus, in Patrick Okiring and Another v. Uganda, the Commission held that "the Uganda Human Rights Commission, endowed with judicial powers comparable to those of traditional courts, can be considered a remedy to be exhausted". It emerges from the file and the texts governing the Special Criminal Court that the Minister of Justice exercises judicial powers. The Respondent State itself affirms that the decision to discontinue proceedings depends on the sole discretion of the Minister in charge of justice in accordance with Article 3(2) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which provides that "if the restitution occurs after the seizure of the Court, the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court may, on the authorisation of the Minister in charge of justice, discontinue the proceedings before any decision on the merits and the court shall pronounce the forfeitures of Article 30 of the Penal Code with an entry in the criminal record". The Minister of Justice also participates in the exercise of judicial power, as evidenced by the Written Authorisation No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 of the Minister of Justice given to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court for the discontinuance of proceedings against Fotie Dzudie Gilles Gabriel, Fokam Pauline, Kuate Pierre, Guela Simo Célestin and Dadjeu Kengne Olivier, for the facts of complicity in embezzlement of public funds, by virtue of Article 2 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti.

The remedies pursued by the Complainant before the Minister of Justice are therefore judicial remedies. The absence of response to the two requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013 and 11 December 2015 consequently amounts to the ineffectiveness of these remedies.

As regards the three habeas corpus applications, filed with the High Court of Mfoundi on 13 October 2014, 6 October 2016 and 18 April 2018 respectively, the Commission notes that in Cameroon, the habeas corpus procedure is governed by Articles 584 to 588 of the CCP. These provisions place particular emphasis on the exceptional nature of detention and the speed of the procedure without, however, specifying the time limit for the procedure at first instance. Under Article 586, the time limit for appeal is five (5) days from the day after the date of the order maintaining detention. Article 587 provides that the appellate court shall rule within 10 days.

The Commission notes that the habeas corpus application of 18 April 2018 was concluded by decision No. 130/HC of 20 September 2018 of the High Court of Mfoundi confirming the continued detention, that is after a period of five (5) months and two (2) days. This period is abnormally long having regard to the requirement of speed arising from the CCP. The Commission also notes that the Complainant did not appeal against this decision. On the other hand, the High Court of Mfoundi took no action on the habeas corpus applications of 13 October 2014 and 6 October 2016, whereas Articles 584 and 585 of the code of procedure oblige the court seized to rule on them promptly.

The Commission recalls its jurisprudence, notably in the Communication SERAC v. Nigeria, where it concluded that remedies were ineffective following the inaction of the Respondent State despite the fact that it had been amply informed of the alleged violations. More pertinently, in the Communication Article 19 v. Eritrea, the Commission held that, faced with the inaction of the Respondent State, one may consider either that local remedies do not exist or, if they exist, that they are ineffective [...]. It follows that the habeas corpus applications filed by the Complainant with the High Court of Mfoundi proved to be ineffective.

The Commission observes that the Respondent State did not react to the Complainant's allegation that proceedings No. 021/RG-TCS/2015 for forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal were opened against him in order to keep him in detention, after having benefited from an abandonment of proceedings for embezzlement of public funds by Order No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014. The Commission notes that Order No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014 of partial dismissal and committal to the Special Criminal Court maintains the charges of embezzlement of public funds against the Complainant and his alleged accomplices, namely Fotie Dzudie Gilles Gabriel, Fokam Pauline, Kuate Pierre, Guela Simo Célestin and Dadjeu Kengne Olivier. The Commission also notes that the Complainant has not demonstrated the impact of proceedings No. 021/RG-TCS/2015 for forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal on the duration of the judicial proceedings. Consequently, this ground of the Complainant, unsupported by evidence, cannot succeed.

From all of the foregoing, the Commission concludes that 192 unjustified adjournments, and the inaction of the Respondent State in the face of the two requests for discontinuance of proceedings to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court, and of the two habeas corpus applications before the High Court of Mfoundi, amply demonstrate the ineffectiveness and abnormal prolongation of local remedies. Consequently, the Communication satisfies the requirements of Article 56(5) of the Charter.

Article 56(6) of the African Charter stipulates that communications relating to human and peoples' rights ... shall be considered if they are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter.

Although the African Charter does not specify the meaning of the notion of "reasonable period" for submitting a complaint after exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission, drawing inspiration from the practice in the Inter-American and European human rights systems, decided in the Majuru v. Zimbabwe case that the six-month period may be considered a "usual standard". That said, the Commission has affirmed on several occasions, notably in the above-cited Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe case and later in the Samuel T. Muzerengwa and 110 Others (represented by Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights) v. Zimbabwe case, that the "reasonable period" is determined on a case-by-case basis and "where there is a valid and compelling reason why a complainant was late, the Commission may consider the complaint in order to ensure fairness and justice".

It emerges from the parties' submissions that the case was characterised by three separate complaints involving the Complainant and several agents of Afriland First Bank. The proceedings were joined by the Special Criminal Court on grounds of indivisibility by Judgment No. 006/ADD-CRIM/TCS of 7 April 2015. At that time, the case was still under investigation.

Since the joinder of 7 April 2015, the Complainant has undertaken several judicial steps to obtain justice and recover his freedom. These include in particular the request for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 11 December 2015, the appeal on points of law of 1 July 2016 seeking to invalidate exhibits and two habeas corpus applications, filed on 6 October 2016 and 18 April 2018. In parallel, the Complainant continued to take part in the hearings of the Special Criminal Court.

The file reveals that the last act taken by the Complainant before the seizure of the Commission is the habeas corpus application of 6 October 2016. The Commission notes that the CCP does not lay down a fixed period within which the court seized must rule on the habeas corpus application, and given the recurrent exceeding of procedural time limits by the Cameroonian judicial authorities already noted, the Commission considers that the Complainant should logically wait a certain time before concluding that his remedy was ineffective.

The Commission also notes that the communication was submitted on 19 April 2017, that is 6 months and 12 days after the habeas corpus application of 6 October 2016. Even though the Commission has referred to the six-month period established by the European Court of Human Rights and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the consistent rule is that the reasonable period is determined on a case-by-case basis.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant remained combative from the beginning of the proceedings until the seizure of the Commission on 19 April 2017 and even afterwards, as evidenced by the habeas corpus application of 18 April 2018. Fairness and justice require that a Complainant not be penalised for the ineffectiveness and abnormal prolongation of local remedies attributable to the Respondent State, as already established above. Moreover, nothing in the file reveals any negligence on the part of the Complainant.
Consequently, the Commission considers that the Communication was submitted within a reasonable period in accordance with Article 56(6).

Article 56(7) of the African Charter stipulates that "communications relating to human and peoples' rights ... shall be considered if they do not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter".

In the Sudan Human Rights Commission and Another v. Sudan case, the Commission held that a matter is considered settled if an international judicial body with a human rights mandate or competence has taken a decision on it and has conferred on the complaint the authority of res judicata. In the present case, there is no evidence that this communication has been settled by another international judicial body. The Commission therefore considers that the communication satisfies the requirement of Article 56(7).
For these reasons, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights decides to declare the present Communication admissible.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State treats him differently from his co-accused without objective and reasonable justification and that there is no proportionality between the aim pursued and the means employed.

He alleges the absence of follow-up to his six applications for provisional release whereas his five co-accused, namely FOTI DZUDIE Gilles Gabriel, FOKAM Pauline, KUATE Pierre, GUELA SIMO Célestin and DADJEU KENGNE Olivier, benefited from release within 24 hours. He argues that the lack of diligence led to more than 200 unjustified and fanciful adjournments.

He also alleges that instead of benefiting from provisional release following the restitution to the State coffers of the embezzled sum in accordance with the law, he was kept in detention by the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on the instruction of the Minister of Justice through correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016, requesting the discontinuance of the proceedings brought against the other accused and his continued detention for embezzlement of public funds.

The Complainant alleges that he is the victim of a difference in treatment in similar legal situations, where all his co-accused have been free since 14 January 2013 whereas he is still in arbitrary detention, 12 years later.

He invokes the provisional release of his eight (08) co-accused on the day of the restitution to the State coffers of the sum of 1,738,363,013 CFA francs, that is after only 24 hours of detention. For the Complainant, this extraordinary diligence for the benefit of his co-accused constitutes discriminatory treatment.

The Complainant considers his conviction by the Special Criminal Court on 21 March 2021 unjust, whereas the embezzled sum had been entirely restituted to the Cameroonian Public Treasury on 13 January 2013 and his 08 co-accused were acquitted.

According to the Complainant, the State of Cameroon failed in its duty of judicial protection of the citizen insofar as he has been and continues to be subjected to discrimination in the handling of his case, with his six applications for release of 28 January 2013, 13 October 2014, 11 December 2015, 6 October 2016, 18 April 2018 and 16 August 2019 remaining without follow-up, and following an attempted fraud by the agents sent by the Procurator General, his complaint has not been the subject of any investigation to date, although the judicial authorities were under an obligation to do so.

The Complainant alleges that his long arbitrary detention, his discriminatory treatment by the judicial authorities, his separation from his family, and his conditions of detention constitute psychological, psychic and moral violence. The Complainant alleges that he suffered a particularly severe psychiatric impairment, exempting him from any future undertaking in the context of his business.

The Complainant argues that the judicial authorities' failure to grant the habeas corpus applications and the more than 200 adjournments of his case before the Special Criminal Court plunged him into total depression and suicidal feelings.

The Complainant also argues that he did not bring a complaint against State agents for acts of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment because all his remedies before the judicial authorities never succeeded and there is no point in bringing a remedy that proves to be unavailable, inaccessible and ineffective.

Referring to Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the Complainant argues that there is an arbitrary deprivation of liberty when the ground for the arrest is unlawful; the victim was not informed of the reasons for his arrest; the victim's procedural rights were not respected; or the victim was not brought before a judge within a reasonable time.

According to the Complainant, his continued detention was no longer lawful after the restitution of the embezzled amount in 2013, and he should have been released within six days in accordance with Article 8 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti.

The Complainant argues that the Cameroonian judicial authorities made abusive use of detention without any need to prevent his flight, to prevent him from putting pressure on witnesses or tampering with evidence. According to the Complainant, the prolonged detention was made possible particularly through excessive and abusive adjournments not provided for by law; the lack of relevance of the refusal of the habeas corpus applications by the High Court of Yaoundé, and the absence of response to his requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice.

The Complainant argues that his pre-trial detention of 12 years is arbitrary and violates Article 6 of the African Charter in that it far exceeds the maximum legal duration of eighteen (18) months provided for by Article 221 of the code of criminal procedure. In this regard, he cites Communication 232/99 Ouko v. Kenya, in which the Commission held that detention of 10 months without trial was arbitrary.

The Complainant reiterates that his continued detention rests only on the whims of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court, who sent emissaries, namely Biyick Marcel, Ondoia Jean Claude and Ngo Um Elisabeth, to demand from him the sum of fifty (50) million CFA francs, tributaire of his release.

The Complainant emphasises that local remedies are unavailable, ineffective, abnormally prolonged and have been characterised by an absence of guarantees of independence and impartiality, non-compliance with procedural time limits, unjustified adjournments, the interference of the Minister of Justice in the proceedings before the Special Criminal Court and the absence of response to his applications for release filed with the High Court of Mfoundi on 28 January 2013, 13 October 2014, 11 December 2015, 6 October 2016, 18 April 2018 and 16 August 2019; and to three requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013, 11 December 2015 and 2 August 2019. The Complainant also denounces the multiplication of proceedings against him in order to keep him in detention.

He reiterates that his continued detention rested only on the whims of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court. He argues that the letter denouncing the prosecutor's attitude, addressed to the Procurator General and the Minister of Justice on 21 May 2015, never received the slightest reaction from the addressees.

The Complainant argues that he was sentenced without evidence to a heavy prison sentence of 15 years without suspension whereas the corpus delicti was restituted and all his co-accused were acquitted following the sole will of the Minister of Justice.

For the Complainant, the terms "theft", "embezzlement of public funds", "remain maintained" and "offences of forgery and use of forged documents in public and authentic documents" used by the Minister of Justice in his correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 denote a presumption of guilt, especially since this statement was made before the final judgment.

The Complainant alleges the impossibility for his counsel to access the file and the notification of a new indictment in their absence at one stage of the proceedings. He argues that his counsel were able to access the investigation file only several months after his incarceration.
The Complainant alleges the failure to respect reasonable time and the lack of independence of the trial court.

On the first branch of his argument, the Complainant alleges that he is unjustly detained beyond the 18 months prescribed in Article 221 of the CCP, and that the trial was organised with excessive delay in violation of Article 10(1) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a Special Criminal Court, laying down a maximum period of six (06) months to render its decision, that is until 10 April 2013, a period which could be exceptionally extended by three (03) months by order of the President of the Special Criminal Court.

He also alleges that the absence of response to his requests for discontinuance of proceedings to the Minister of Justice and the Procurator General on 28 January 2013, 11 December 2015 and 2 August 2019 affects the right to have his case heard within a reasonable time.

The Complainant further alleges the multiplication of procedural acts to keep him in detention. He denounces, on the one hand, his new indictment on 28 October 2014 for forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal at the time when he was awaiting the verdict before the Special Criminal Court. He alleges, on the other hand, that following the Order of partial dismissal and committal to the Special Criminal Court No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014, another procedure No. 021/RG-TCS/2015, identical to the first, was opened before the trial court.
He finally alleges unjustified adjournments and the intrusion of the Minister of Justice in the proceedings before the Special Criminal Court.

On the second branch relating to the impartiality of the trial court, the Complainant argues that the right to a fair trial includes equality of arms, the right to have one's case heard, to be informed of the reasons and to seek an appropriate remedy, and the right to present one's case and evidence appropriately. The Complainant invites the Commission to verify whether the proceedings as a whole were fair within the meaning of Article 7(1) of the African Charter.

The Complainant alleges that his relatives suffered too much from his unlawful detention and had to seek treatment outside Cameroon at their own expense, notably in West Africa. He alleges that those who remained in Cameroon received no assistance from the State of Cameroon.

He alleges that, as head of a single-parent family, his offspring have been totally disrupted owing to the lack of financial, psychological and social support. He argues that some have dropped out of school and find themselves drifting into delinquency in the streets of the various cities of the country.

He alleges that his partner, with whom he was in a marriage, had to leave Cameroon not only for health care, but also to flee, abandoning the activities that provided her with income to support her children, and who also finds herself disabled.
He alleges that these events undermine the physical and moral health of his family.

The Complainant alleges that the Special Criminal Court allows an improper intrusion by the Minister of Justice after the seizure of the examining magistrates or trial judges. He recalls the correspondence of the Minister of Justice No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 addressed to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court asking him to discontinue the proceedings brought against his co-accused.

The Complainant argues that in these conditions, it would be a fiction to believe that persons arrested and prosecuted for the offences of embezzlement of public funds falling within the jurisdiction of the Special Criminal Court will be brought before an independent judge who will conduct the gathering of evidence. He alleges that for this reason, violations of the rights of the defence are endorsed during the preliminary investigation.

According to the Complainant, the facts of this communication are similar to those denounced in the Bakweri Lands Claims Committee v. Cameroon case, where the Commission held that "the President of the Republic exercises extraordinary powers so as to influence the organisation of the judiciary and that the judicial system is partial and lacks independence".

The Complainant argues that all magistrates work under orders and under permanent pressure from the Minister of Justice, and considers that in these conditions, the invocation of irregularities and procedural defects by counsel becomes a professional act that would irritate the judge, who is hurried and bound by time limits, and over whom hangs the threat of disciplinary proceedings. He adds that the provisions providing for disciplinary proceedings against magistrates and judicial police officers who have not respected procedural time limits generate a permanent fear that no longer enables the magistrate to honour his oath.
The Complainant argues that this psychological state led the Special Criminal Court to convict him by exactly every means, as the Minister of Justice had requested.

The Complainant further argues that the fact that the proceedings undertaken before the courts of the Respondent State did not result in credible convictions violates the right of access to justice and attests to the lack of independence of the courts in Cameroon.

The Complainant alleges that his ordeal is also linked to the multiplication of proceedings against him, non-compliance with procedural time limits, unjustified adjournments and the absence of response to his applications for release and to his requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court.

The Complainant alleges that the obligation imposed by Article 1 is not an obligation of due diligence, but rather an obligation of result. The Complainant argues that the violation of the rights mentioned above entails the violation of Article 1 insofar as it attests to the inability of the State Party to adopt adequate measures to give effect to the provisions of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission to find and declare that the Respondent State violated Articles 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 18 and 26 of the African Charter, and consequently to recommend that the State of Cameroon: • Put an urgent end to the said violations; • Order his immediate release; • Sanction the perpetrators of the violations found; • Take measures of guarantees of non-repetition, including amending its legislation to guarantee the non-intrusion of the Executive in the Judiciary and to make the discontinuance of proceedings mandatory in case of restitution of the corpus delicti in order to bring it into conformity with the provisions of the Charter; • Present apologies to the Complainant, as an acknowledgement of the violation of his rights, and ensure that their acts are not repeated; • Pay the Complainant the sum of twenty-five billion (25,000,000,000) CFA francs or 39 million euros), as damages for the twelve years of abusive and arbitrary detention, broken down as follows: 15 billion CFA francs for moral prejudice and 10 billion CFA francs for economic and financial prejudice.

On the assessment of the quantum of monetary reparation, the Complainant explains that until his incarceration, he was a very prosperous economic operator and that he had created in France several companies including ELLIOS SA employing about fifty French people. He alleges that in the course of 2005, he decided to return to Cameroon and sold all his companies for a value of a little over two billion CFA francs and was then 29 years old. He alleges that at the time of his arrest he headed eight companies (CAMDEV SA, CAMDEV TELECOM, TVC, EDUC TAGNE, HELLIOS SA, S. MEKAM SARL, TAGNE Business Corporation SA, and KAPT MEDIA SA) which had won contracts worth several billion CFA francs, and that he aspired to take over the public telecommunications company, Camtel.

He alleges that his prolonged detention ruined all his companies and his reputation because of the presumption of guilt to which he was subjected among the public. He alleges that he suffers from profound irreversible psychological conditions that constantly drive him into a depressive state with a regular urge to commit suicide, and that consequently he will no longer be able to undertake anything for the rest of his life.
With regard to the suffering endured by his family, the Complainant argues that his former fiancée and his children suffered emotional anguish because of his incarceration.
The Complainant requests the Commission to order total compensation of twenty-five billion CFA francs (25,000,000,000) or 39 million euros.

The Respondent State requests the Commission to exclude from its examination on the merits the new violations alleged by the Complainant and to limit itself to examining Articles 6 and 7 of the African Charter.

The Respondent State alleges that the grounds for the Complainant's deprivation of liberty and the related conditions are determined by the Penal Code and the CCP, notably Article 218-1 of the CCP, referred to in the warrant of pre-trial detention, which provides that: "Detention is an exceptional measure which may be ordered only in case of a misdemeanour or a felony. Its purpose is to preserve public order, the security of persons and property and to ensure the preservation of evidence as well as the appearance in court of the accused".

It considers that embezzlement of public funds being a felony within the meaning of Articles 21(a) and 184(a) of the Penal Code, the Complainant was rightly placed under a warrant of pre-trial detention after his indictment. It adds that the committal order does not invalidate the warrant of pre-trial detention in accordance with Article 262-2 of the CCP, which stipulates that "Where the accused who is detained or placed under judicial supervision is committed for trial before the Court for a felony, the committal order does not terminate pre-trial detention". Thus, the Respondent State continues that the order of 10 October 2012 committing the Complainant for trial did not terminate his detention, which remained lawful.
The Respondent State argues that the Complainant, prosecuted for a felony punishable by life imprisonment, cannot benefit from release in accordance with Article 224-2 of the CCP.

On the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the courts which would impede the effectiveness of local remedies, the Respondent State alleges that the Constitution of Cameroon enshrines the independence of the judiciary. It adds that the CCP (Articles 591 et seq.) sets out the grounds for recusal and determines the related procedure and that the Penal Code (Article 126) punishes representatives of the executive power who give "orders or prohibitions" to the courts.

The Respondent State alleges that by refraining from bringing a recusal action or initiating criminal proceedings on the basis of Article 126 of the Penal Code, the Complainant ipso facto admitted the self-evident facts that are the independence and impartiality of the judicial system of Cameroon.

On the point relating to the authorisation to discontinue proceedings, the Respondent State alleges that independence applies only to judges and that the letter of the Minister of Justice authorising the discontinuance of proceedings is not addressed to the President of the Special Criminal Court, but to the Procurator General, who decided on the discontinuance of proceedings. It alleges that the request of a litigant for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice, who is not a judicial authority, does not constitute a judicial remedy requiring a response.

On the right to the presumption of innocence, the Respondent State argues that the letter of the Minister of Justice authorising the discontinuance of proceedings contains no term likely to suggest the guilt of the Complainant.

On the right to defence, the Respondent State alleges that the investigation files (of the Examining Magistrates of the High Court of Mfoundi and of the Special Criminal Court) were made available to the counsel of all the indicted persons before their interrogation on the merits, in accordance with Article 172-3 of the CCP, which provides that "The procedural file shall be kept at the disposal of counsel at the investigation chambers, twenty-four (24) hours before each interrogation or confrontation".

The Respondent State also alleges that the Complainant deliberately did not rely on Article 3 of the CCP, which provides that: "(1) The violation of a rule of criminal procedure shall be sanctioned by absolute nullity where it: a) Prejudices the rights of the defence defined by the legal provisions in force; b) Infringes a principle of public policy. (2) The nullity provided for in paragraph 1 of this article cannot be cured. It may be invoked at any stage of the proceedings by the parties, and must be raised ex officio by the trial court".

On the right to be tried within a reasonable time, the Respondent State alleges that the assessment of reasonable time takes into account the complexity of the proceedings, what is at stake and the conduct of the actors.

It argues that in the present case, the stakes are eminently significant in that the Complainant and his accomplices are accused of having diverted 1,738,363,013 CFA francs from the "HIPC Funds", exposing Cameroon, beyond the serious financial loss, to the loss of financing from international donors.

According to the Respondent State, the proceedings opened against the Complainant are of proven complexity owing to the high number of persons involved, the origin of the funds concerned (World Bank and International Monetary Fund) and the sophisticated fraudulent schemes that enabled their diversion; all of which necessitated multiple acts of inquiry, investigation and trial.

The Respondent State argues that the conduct of the Complainant and his counsel contributed to lengthening the proceedings opened. It alleges that in addition to multiple refusals to make depositions, the Complainant regularly changed counsel to slow down the course of the proceedings and the latter in turn multiplied obstacles to the proceedings, notably through fanciful requests for adjournment and the exercise of dilatory remedies.

To prove this fact, the Respondent State cites the appeal on points of law of August 2013, concluded by a judgment of 15 May 2014; the appeal of 1 July 2016, concluded by the judgment of 20 August 2017, declaring the said appeal inadmissible; the application to the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé-Centre Administratif, concluded by the order of 26 November 2012; the request for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013; the request for discontinuance of proceedings withdrawn on 11 November 2015; and the multiple habeas corpus applications addressed to the President of the High Court of Mfoundi.

The Complainant invites the Commission to admit his additional submissions in accordance with its jurisprudence developed notably in Communications 433/12 Albert Bialufu Ngandu v. Democratic Republic of Congo, 416/12 Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Cameroon, and 318/06 Open Society Justice Initiative v. Côte d'Ivoire. The Complainant alleges that in these precedents, the Commission held that additional claims are admitted provided that they are based on the same facts, do not call into question matters settled at admissibility, that their author can substantiate them and that the opposing party cannot successfully contest them. The Complainant argues that his additional claims do not call into question matters settled at admissibility and invites the Commission to defeat the Respondent State's claims.
With regard to Articles 6 and 7, the Complainant largely repeats the grounds and arguments contained in his earlier submissions. Thus, the present exposition is limited to the new arguments.

On the allegation of arbitrary detention (Article 6), the Complainant argues that the charge of attempted escape and that of forgery and use of forged documents invoked to justify the extension of his detention did not convince the trial judge, who found him not guilty on these charges. The Complainant reiterates that his continued detention after restitution of the embezzled amount is arbitrary. He recalls that it was on his own application pursued before the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé that Afriland First Bank paid the embezzled amount to the Treasury, and that he cannot be required to pay back the same alleged embezzled amount when the State of Cameroon has already received it in full.

On the alleged violation of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter, the Complainant argues that in the history of Cameroonian justice, no action seeking to recuse or to initiate criminal proceedings against representatives of the executive power who give "orders or prohibitions" to the courts has ever succeeded and that persevering in this route without any outcome would be like trying to determine the sex of angels. The Complainant considers his sentence to 15 years' imprisonment without suspension unjust, whereas the corpus delicti was restituted and all his co-accused were acquitted, following the sole will of the Minister of Justice. He alleges that a conviction not based on solid evidence violates the presumption of innocence. In this regard, he cites the judgment of the African Court in Application No. 019/2018, Mohamed Abubakari v. Tanzania.

The Complainant alleges that the Special Criminal Court, in its flawed Judgment No. 007/CRIM/TCS of 31 March 2021, used ingenious and subjective quibbles to acquit his 08 co-accused. He observes that, relying on the provisions of Article 184 paragraph 1 of the Penal Code, which defines embezzlement, the Special Criminal Court concluded that there is no need to examine as an autonomous offence the facts initially characterised as forgery and use of forged documents in public and authentic documents, charged against the accused FOTI DZUDIE Gilles Gabriel, FOKAM Pauline, KUATE Pierre, GUELA and DADJEU KENGNE Olivier, these facts in reality constituting the fraudulent means of the crime of embezzlement of public property. The Complainant requests the Commission to assess whether the process used by the Special Criminal Court to reach its conclusions respected the right to have one's cause heard in accordance with the requirements of Article 7(1), and whether the proceedings as a whole were fair within the meaning of Article 7(1).

On the alleged violation of Article 7(1)(b) of the Charter, the Complainant argues that the purpose of the presumption of innocence is to avoid influencing the decision of the trial court. The Complainant reiterates that correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of the Minister of Justice, of 27 January 2016, asking Madam Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court to discontinue the proceedings brought against the other accused and to maintain the complainant in detention for "embezzlement of public funds", violates the presumption of innocence.

On the alleged violation of Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter, the Complainant maintains that his counsel found themselves unable to access the file and invites the Commission to request the Respondent State to provide the slightest evidence of access to the investigation file at the investigation chambers by his lawyers. The Complainant also alleges that the nullity remedy stipulated in Article 3 of the CCP is of no use in that all local remedies proved ineffective owing to the lack of response from the judicial authorities.

On the alleged violation of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter, the Complainant argues that he showed irreproachable diligence and that the facts of the case reveal no element of fact or law that would make the proceedings complex so as to justify a relatively long duration. The Complainant alleges that the 200 recorded adjournments were fanciful and arbitrary and aimed only at keeping him in detention, by all means, and at destroying his rich career as a businessman.

The Complainant considers that whatever the circumstances, a period of ten (10) years of pre-trial detention without final judgment cannot manifestly be considered reasonable. He refers notably to General Comment No. 13 of the United Nations Human Rights Committee (HRC), in which the HRC affirms that the right to have one's case heard within a reasonable time includes not only the time within which the trial must begin, but also the time within which it must end, as well as the judgment rendered both at first instance and on appeal.

The Respondent State requests the Commission to exclude from its examination on the merits the new violations alleged by the Complainant and to limit itself to examining Articles 6 and 7 of the African Charter.

The Commission notes that, in addition to the grounds developed at the admissibility stage, namely on the allegation of violation of Articles 6 and 7 of the Charter, the Complainant alleges the violation of his rights protected by Articles 1, 2, 3, 5, 18 and 26 of the African Charter. These additional grounds being the subject of new claims, it is for the Commission to rule on them prior to examining the merits.

In this regard, the Commission considers that additional substantive submissions are admissible provided that they are not based on new facts, do not call into question matters settled at admissibility, that their author can substantiate them and that the opposing party cannot successfully contest them.

On the facts, the Commission notes on the one hand that those related to the course of the domestic proceedings up to its seizure do not vary between admissibility and the merits. The submissions relating to Articles 1, 2, 3 and 26 of the Charter are based on the same facts and cannot therefore be considered new facts. However, the submissions seeking to call into question the reasoning of judgment No. 007/CRIM/TCS of 31 March 2021 which resulted in the Complainant's conviction at first instance and the acquittal of his co-accused will be excluded from the analysis insofar as the Complainant can appeal his conviction and the Commission is not an appellate court.

The Commission notes on the other hand that the facts relating to torture and the disruption of the Complainant's family are invoked for the first time at the merits stage of the present communication. The Commission therefore considers that the grounds based on the violation of Articles 5 and 18 are based on new facts.

As regards the satisfaction of the admissibility requirements, the facts underlying the allegations of violation of Articles 1, 2, 3 and 26 are intimately linked to those reported concerning the violation of Articles 6 and 7. Indeed, the facts alleged at the admissibility stage related to the prolonged pre-trial detention, the differential treatment with his co-accused, the lack of integrity of the prosecutor at the Special Criminal Court and the intrusion of the Minister of Justice in the proceedings, allegations which were the subject of remedies before the domestic courts. Moreover, the Complainant sufficiently substantiates the allegations of violation of Articles 1, 2, 3 and 26. Finally, the Commission, in ruling on the merits, ensures the soundness of the grounds put forward by the Complainant.

As a consequence of the foregoing, the Commission receives the Complainant's additional grounds and claims based on Articles 1, 2, 3 and 26 of the Charter and excludes from the examination on the merits the additional claims based on Articles 5 and 18 of the African Charter.

Article 2 of the African Charter provides that "Every individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as race, ethnic group, color, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status."

The Commission considers that public officials, including prosecutors and judges, must "perform their functions impartially and avoid any political, social, racial, ethnic, religious, cultural, sexual, gender or any other form of discrimination".

In its jurisprudence, the Commission interprets Article 2 of the African Charter as prohibiting discrimination on a prohibited ground, notably ethnic affiliation, colour, sex, language and national origin.

The Commission notes that the Complainant's submissions raise the question of whether his continued detention after the provisional release of his co-accused constitutes discriminatory treatment. The Commission notes that the Complainant did not indicate the prohibited ground of discrimination of which the Respondent State would have been guilty. It also notes that such a ground does not emerge from the parties' submissions and concludes that Article 2 of the Charter is not violated.
Article 3 of the African Charter provides that: "1. Every individual shall be equal before the law. 2. Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law."

The Commission considers that equal protection of the law means that "no person or class of persons shall be denied the same protection of the laws which is enjoyed by other persons or classes of persons in like circumstances in their lives, liberty, property and in the pursuit of happiness".

The African Commission has also held that a violation of Article 3(2) of the African Charter must demonstrate that "the Respondent State did not accord the complainant the same treatment it accorded to others, or that the Respondent State accorded favourable treatment to other persons in the same situation as the complainant".
The Commission notes the Complainant's allegation that he is a victim of a difference in treatment compared with his co-accused who are in similar legal situations.

In the present communication, the Complainant alleges differential treatment with regard to the provisional release granted to his co-accused FOTI DZUDIE Gilles Gabriel, FOKAM Pauline, KUATE Pierre, GUELA SIMO Célestin and DADJEU KENGNE Olivier.

The first question to be settled is whether the Complainant and his five co-accused are in similar legal situations. It emerges from the documents in the file that the Complainant is a signatory of the tripartite agreement with the State of Cameroon, within the framework of the RIGC Project. He is also a signatory of the operations on the account CAMDEV/PROJET RIGC No. 00910191001-83 held in the books of Afriland First Bank for the purpose of receiving the funds intended to finance the RIGC Project.

The Commission notes that the sums withdrawn from account No. 00910191001-83 were paid into a new account No. 00910191002-92 under the same title CAMDEV/PROJET RIGC, opened and pledged by the Complainant. The judgment of the Special Criminal Court notes that at all stages of the proceedings, the Complainant admitted his participation in the financial scheme that facilitated the embezzlement. The admission and the fact that the Complainant was undoubtedly a beneficiary of the embezzled amounts constitute a very serious indication of his guilt.

With regard to the Complainant's five co-accused, who are all agents of Afriland First Bank, it emerges from the submission of the Public Prosecutor before the Special Criminal Court that the incriminated term deposits took place on 4 January 2007, 8 January 2007, 15 January 2008 and 15 December 2008; and that the five agents were prosecuted for their alleged involvement in the fraudulent operations: 1) KUATE Pierre as business fund manager who proceeded to open the CAMDEV-Projet RIGC account in June 2005; 2) FOTI DZUDIE Gilles Gabriel as business fund manager who allowed the opening of the second account in January 2007 in the absence of all the required signatures and as manager of the renewals of the term deposits and the pledging of the funds; 3) DADJEU KENGNE Olivier as head of the Afriland First Bank branch from January 2006 to March 2016 and manager of the said account who received the documents alleged to be forged; 4) FOKAM Pauline as head of the Afriland First Bank-Yaoundé branch, hierarchical superior of the three preceding agents in 2009; and 5) GUELA SIMO Célestin as deputy director of Afriland First Bank and hierarchical superior of the account managers.

The Commission considers that the prosecuted agents of Afriland First Bank could have been negligent or complicit in the fraudulent operations insofar as the procedure for renewing term deposits and pledging consisted of giving the client forms for reading and approval, and in case of agreement these, once signed, were returned to the bank. The records of interrogation placed in the file show that all the indicted agents consistently pleaded not guilty. In addition, no document in the file indicates that the bank's agents were individually beneficiaries of the embezzled amounts. The Commission therefore considers that the indications of guilt with regard to them were less evident compared to the Complainant.

It emerges from Judgment No. 007/CRIM/TCS of 31 March 2021 that the restitution of the embezzled amount was made on 13 January 2013 by Afriland First Bank on behalf of its agents and that this bank had the Complainant's property seized to be reimbursed.

Moreover, contrary to the Complainant's claims, the discontinuance of proceedings after restitution of the embezzled amount is an option and not an imperative, having regard to Article 3(1) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which provides that "In case of restitution of the corpus delicti before the seizure of the Court by committal order of the examining magistrate or by judgment of the Investigation Chamber of the Supreme Court, the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court may, on the authorisation of the Minister in charge of justice, discontinue the proceedings". The Commission notes that the restitution of the embezzled amount was made before the seizure of the Special Criminal Court on 5 November 2014.

In these circumstances, the legal situation of the Complainant is different from that of his co-accused. The Commission deduces from this that the differential treatment between the Complainant and his co-accused is justified. It must therefore be concluded that Article 3 of the African Charter has not been violated.

Under Article 6 of the African Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The Commission recalled the importance of these provisions in the Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa (Luanda Guidelines, 2014), which provide that no one shall be deprived of liberty except on the grounds and in accordance with the procedures established by law.

The Commission has observed that a deprivation of liberty that does not fall within the strict limits of the law or is for unacceptable or simply arbitrary reasons constitutes a violation of Article 6 of the Charter.

The Commission notes the Complainant's allegation that his continued detention was no longer lawful after restitution of the embezzled amount in 2013 by virtue of Article 3 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti. For its part, the Respondent State argues that the complainant's detention complies with Cameroonian procedural law.

As noted above, the discontinuance of proceedings after restitution of the embezzled amount is an option and not an imperative, having regard to Article 3 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti. The Complainant's arguments on this point therefore cannot succeed.

As regards the prolonged pre-trial detention, the Commission notes that in Cameroonian criminal law, the duration of pre-trial detention before judgment is governed by Article 221 of the CCP, which provides that: "(1) The duration of pre-trial detention shall be fixed by the Examining Magistrate in the warrant. It may not exceed six (6) months. However, it may be extended by reasoned order, for at most twelve (12) months in case of a felony and six (6) months in case of a misdemeanour. (2) Upon expiry of the period of validity of the warrant of pre-trial detention, the Examining Magistrate must, on pain of disciplinary proceedings, immediately order the release of the accused, unless he is detained on another ground".

The Commission notes in the present communication that the High Court of Mfoundi issued a warrant of pre-trial detention against the Complainant on 19 March 2012. This warrant was extended by order of the same court on 21 September 2012.

The first complaint was transferred to the Special Criminal Court on 10 October 2012 whereas the two other complaints were transferred to that court on 5 November 2014. The joinder of the three proceedings by the Special Criminal Court took place on 7 April 2015. The Commission notes that the Special Criminal Court ruled at first instance on the case on 31 March 2021, more than 9 years after the first transfer of the case to that court, whereas Article 10(6) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a special criminal court stipulates that "the Court has a maximum period of six (6) months to render its decision. This period may be extended by a maximum of three (3) months by order of the President of the Court. This order is not subject to appeal. Any appeal, in this case, shall be placed on the file".

The Commission notes the Complainant's allegation that his new indictment on 28 October 2014 for forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents as co-principal and the opening of proceedings No. 021/RG-TCS/2015, identical to that concluded by the Order of partial dismissal and committal to the Special Criminal Court No. 44/CI2/TCS/2014 of 5 November 2014, were intended only to keep him in detention.

The Commission takes note of the judgment of the Special Criminal Court holding that the facts of forgery of public and authentic documents and use of forged documents are a constituent element of the crime of embezzlement. The Commission considers that such facts cannot validly constitute a separate offence justifying a new indictment and the continued detention of the Complainant. It also notes that the Respondent State did not respond to the allegation relating to proceedings No. 021/RG-TCS/2015 and concludes that these proceedings had no legal relevance.

The Commission notes that following the restitution of the embezzled amount on 13 January 2013, the Complainant addressed three requests for discontinuance of proceedings to the Minister of Justice and to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court on 28 January 2013, 11 December 2015 and 2 August 2019. No action was taken on these requests, as acknowledged by the Respondent State, which considers that such remedies do not require a response. In this regard, the Commission has already concluded that the law governing the Special Criminal Court confers judicial powers on the Minister of Justice, and considers that the requests for discontinuance of proceedings addressed to him are judicial remedies requiring a response.
