The Commission also notes that the Complainant filed six habeas corpus applications with the High Court of Mfoundi on 28 January 2013, 13 October 2014, 11 December 2015, 6 October 2016, 18 April 2018 and 16 August 2019 respectively. Of these six habeas corpus applications, the High Court of Mfoundi ruled only on that of 18 April 2018, by decision No. 130/HC of 20 September 2018 confirming the continued detention of the Complainant. This decision was made after more than 6 years of pre-trial detention of the Complainant. This attests to a notable lack of speed in the handling of habeas corpus applications.

In total, the Complainant was kept in pre-trial detention for more than 9 years, well beyond the 18-month limit stipulated in Article 221 of the CCP, without any objective justification. It must therefore be concluded that Article 6 of the Charter has been violated.

Article 7(1) of the African Charter provides that: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal."

Under the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force".

The right to appeal to national courts recognises for every person the right to bring a civil, criminal or other action to vindicate his rights or obtain reparation. The Commission has also interpreted the right to appeal to national courts under Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter as the right to appeal to a higher court.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that local remedies are unavailable, ineffective, abnormally prolonged and were characterised by the intrusion of the Minister of Justice in the proceedings before the Special Criminal Court and the lack of integrity of the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court.

The Commission notes that the Complainant's arguments do not reveal any element establishing that he was prevented from appealing to national courts or from appealing against his conviction. Consequently, the Commission finds that the allegation of violation of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter has not been proved.

Under the provisions of Article 7(1)(b) of the Charter, "Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal". The question that the Commission must settle in the present case is whether the content of correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of the Minister of Justice, of 27 January 2016, addressed to Madam Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court, violates the right to the presumption of innocence.

The Commission considers that the purpose of the presumption of innocence is to avoid passing judgment on the suspect even before the competent institution can rule and to avoid influencing the decision of the trial court. The presumption of innocence requires that "all public authorities refrain from prejudging the outcome of a trial" and that "State representatives must refrain from any statement or measure that would amount to regarding the accused person as already guilty or imputing his guilt, before a competent and impartial court has ruled duly to that effect".

The Commission notes that the decision to discontinue proceedings depends on the sole discretion of the Minister of Justice in accordance with Article 3(2) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which provides that "if the restitution occurs after the seizure of the Court, the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court may, on the authorisation of the Minister in charge of justice, discontinue the proceedings before any decision on the merits and the court shall pronounce the forfeitures of Article 30 of the Penal Code with an entry in the criminal record".

It is by virtue of this power that the Minister of Justice gave Authorisation No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 to the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court for the discontinuance of proceedings against five co-accused for the facts of complicity in embezzlement of public funds. This letter indicated that "the prosecution for embezzlement of public funds remains maintained against Kaptue Tagne Serges Bruces". The Commission considers that the terms used with regard to the Complainant describe a charge and cannot in themselves constitute a violation of the presumption of innocence.
As a consequence of the foregoing, the Commission considers that the Respondent State did not violate Article 7(1)(b).

Article 7(1)(c) of the African Charter provides that: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice;

The State must provide "effective procedures and adequate mechanisms enabling every person living on its territory and subject to its jurisdiction, without distinction of any kind". This applies to criminal as well as civil cases. In criminal proceedings, the accused must have the right to defend himself or be informed of his right to legal representation. The right to defence includes the possibility of communicating with a lawyer and having access to documents, as well as the obligation not to proceed with the trial without the lawyer being informed of the date of the trial and of the charges brought against him.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges without the slightest evidence that his counsel were able to access the investigation file only several months after his incarceration and that the notification of a new indictment was made in their absence at one stage of the proceedings. The Commission notes the Complainant's request to require the Respondent State to prove compliance with the adversarial principle. The burden of proof lying with the applicant, the Commission can reverse the burden of proof only where the means of proof are under the control of the Respondent State. The Commission considers that evidence may be adduced by means of correspondence addressed to the prosecuting authority or the trial court, testimonies or any other means of proof.
Consequently, the Commission considers that the violation of Article 7(1)(c) of the Charter is not established.

Article 7(1)(d) of the African Charter provides that: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal." By the grounds based on the violation of these provisions, the Complainant alleges a duration of proceedings beyond reasonable limits and a lack of fairness of the proceedings. The Commission first examines the grounds based on the failure to be tried within a reasonable time (first branch) before turning to the allegation of partiality (second branch).

On the first branch, the Commission notes that it emerges from the wording of the above-mentioned provisions that there is a right to a judgment and a right to have that judgment delivered without excessive delay. In Article 19 v. Eritrea, the Commission adopts three factors for assessing reasonable time: the complexity of the case, the conduct of the Complainant and that of the authorities of the Respondent State.

In Pagnoule (on behalf of Mazou) v. Cameroon, the Commission decided that two (2) years of proceedings without judgment and without valid reason justifying such a delay constituted a violation of the right to be tried within a reasonable time. In Centre for Free Speech v. Nigeria, concerning a period of detention of two (2) years without trial, the Commission placed particular emphasis on the need to try the case with the greatest speed in cases of pre-trial detention.

In Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Cameroon, the Commission considered that pre-trial detention of (7) years was not reasonable. In that case, the Complainant had been the subject of six (6) orders or warrants of pre-trial detention, four (4) severance orders, four (4) committal orders without any of the successive charges being different from those already covered by the first indictment, and the violation of a judicial decision ordering the release of the Complainant after four (4) years of pre-trial detention.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant filed six habeas corpus applications with the High Court of Mfoundi on 28 January 2013, 13 October 2014, 11 December 2015, 6 October 2016, 18 April 2018 and 16 August 2019 respectively. The Commission notes that in Cameroon, the habeas corpus procedure is governed by Articles 584 to 588 of the CCP. These provisions place particular emphasis on the exceptional nature of detention and the speed of the procedure without, however, specifying the time limit for the procedure at first instance.

The Commission notes that the habeas corpus application of 18 April 2018 was concluded by decision No. 130/HC of 20 September 2018 of the High Court of Mfoundi confirming the continued detention, that is after a period of five (5) months and two (2) days. This period is abnormally long having regard to the requirement of speed arising from the CCP. On the other hand, the High Court of Mfoundi took no action on the other habeas corpus applications.

Three requests for discontinuance of proceedings to the Minister of Justice and the Procurator General on 28 January 2013, 11 December 2015 and 2 August 2019, after the restitution of the embezzled amount, likewise received no follow-up.

From the warrant of pre-trial detention issued against the Complainant by the High Court of Mfoundi on 19 March 2012 to the date of the judgment of 31 March 2021, a period of nine (9) years and twelve (12) days elapsed. Yet, Article 221 of the CCP provides that the maximum period of pre-trial detention is 18 months.

The Commission notes that the first complaint was transferred to the Special Criminal Court before 10 October 2012 whereas the two other complaints were transferred to that court on 5 November 2014. It also notes that from the joinder of the proceedings by the Special Criminal Court on 7 April 2015 to the admissibility of the present Communication, the case had been subject to 192 unjustified adjournments. According to the Complainant, the number of adjournments reached 200 at the date of submission of the brief on the merits. The Special Criminal Court ruled on the case by Judgment No. 007/CRIM/TCS of 31 March 2021.

The Commission notes that the Respondent State provides no material elements justifying such lengthy proceedings. It also does not explain to what extent the Complainant's multiple applications for release and changes of lawyers affected the duration of the proceedings.

The Commission considers that the proceedings were prolonged beyond reasonable limits, having regard to Article 10(6) of Law No. 2011/028 of 14 December 2011 establishing a Special Criminal Court, stipulating that "the Court has a maximum period of six (6) months to render its decision. This period may be extended by a maximum of three (3) months by order of the President of the Court. This order is not subject to appeal. Any appeal, in this case, shall be placed on the file". In these circumstances, the Complainant did not enjoy the right to be tried within a reasonable time. Consequently, the Commission considers that the violation of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter is established.

On the second branch relating to impartiality, the Commission notes that the question of impartiality may arise from internal and external elements relating both to the judge himself and to other authorities having competence in the organisation of the judicial system. The principle covers both the subjective impartiality of the judge and the objective impartiality of the court. The Commission considers that "the fairness of proceedings implies the absence of any influence, pressure, intimidation or interference, direct or indirect, from anyone and for any reason". The burden of proving impartiality falls on the party alleging it.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Minister of Justice intervened in the proceedings to authorise the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court to release the Complainant's five co-accused in accordance with Article 3 of Decree 2013/288 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti.

In these circumstances, the Commission considers that the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court lacks independence from the Minister of Justice in the granting of provisional release to persons prosecuted for embezzlement of public funds
From the foregoing, the Commission concludes that there is a violation of Article 7(1)(d) of the African Charter.

Article 26 of the African Charter provides that: "States parties to the present Charter shall have the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts and shall allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter."

Article 26 concerns the independence of the courts and the establishment of national human rights institutions. In the present case, the Complainant alleges the lack of independence of the Special Criminal Court and of the magistrates from the executive power in general and the Minister of Justice in particular. This calls on the Commission to assess the independence of the Special Criminal Court and the attitude of the magistrates in the domestic judicial proceedings at the origin of this communication.

The independence of the courts comprises institutional independence and individual independence. Institutional independence is determined by reference to factors such as the legal establishment of the judiciary as a body distinct from the executive and legislative powers with exclusive jurisdiction in judicial matters, administrative independence in its day-to-day management, functioning without inappropriate and unjustified interference, and adequate resources to enable the judiciary to properly discharge its functions. The Commission has held that the judiciary must be independent of any external influence, notably executive.

Individual independence relates to the personal independence of judges and their ability to discharge their functions without fear of reprisals. The State must "refrain from taking any measure likely to threaten, directly or indirectly, the independence and security of judges and magistrates". The African Court on Human Rights has held that "individual independence is reflected mainly in the mode of appointment and security of tenure of judges, in particular the existence of clear criteria for selection, appointment, term of office, and the availability of adequate guarantees against external pressures. Individual independence further requires that States ensure that judges are not transferred or removed from office at the whim or discretion of the executive or any other governmental or private authority". The Commission also considers that independence is linked to the "real or apparent impartiality" of the court.

At the admissibility stage of this communication, the Respondent State indicated that the decision to discontinue proceedings depends on the sole discretion of the Minister of Justice in accordance with Article 3(2) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti, which provides that "if the restitution occurs after the seizure of the Court, the Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court may, on the authorisation of the Minister in charge of justice, discontinue the proceedings before any decision on the merits and the court shall pronounce the forfeitures of Article 30 of the Penal Code with an entry in the criminal record".

It is in the exercise of this power that the Minister of Justice, by correspondence No. 017/CF/CAB/ME/MJ/GDS of 27 January 2016 addressed to Madam Procurator General at the Special Criminal Court following a working session in his office, asked her to discontinue the proceedings brought against the other accused in this case while maintaining the Complainant KAPTUE TAGNE in detention for embezzlement of public funds.

The Commission considers that Article 3(2) of the above-mentioned Decree No. 2013/288 enshrines a stranglehold of the Minister of Justice over prosecutors in the matter of discontinuance of proceedings against persons prosecuted for embezzlement of public property. This implies that even in the absence of indications of guilt, the prosecutor cannot provisionally release a defendant until he has received the authorisation of the Minister of Justice. The Commission considers that this power granted to the Minister of Justice is likely to negatively influence the enjoyment of the right to liberty of the accused and flagrantly violates the independence of prosecutors. The Commission also notes that the Respondent State admits that the independence of the judiciary does not apply to prosecutors. It must therefore be concluded that Article 26 of the Charter has been violated.

With regard to the other aspects of the proceedings, the Commission recalls that procedural defects committed by the investigating body may constitute a violation of Article 26 if they affect the final decision. It notes, however, that in the present case, the Complainant did not submit evidence establishing that the magistrates involved in the investigation and trial of his case were "under orders and under permanent pressure from the Minister of Justice" and the impact of their failings on his conviction. It must therefore be concluded that the Complainant's allegation has not been proved.

Consequently, the Commission concludes that Article 3(2) of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti violates Article 26 of the African Charter and dismisses the Complainant on his allegations relating to the pressure exerted on the magistrates involved in the investigation and trial of his case.

Article 1 of the African Charter provides that: "The Member States of the Organization of African Unity parties to the present Charter shall recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in this Chapter and shall undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them." The Complainant requests the Commission to find the violation of Article 1 as a consequence of the other violations mentioned in this communication.

The Commission's consistent jurisprudence considers that the violation of any provision of the African Charter automatically entails the violation of Article 1. According to the Commission, this attests to the failure of the State Party to adopt adequate measures to give effect to the provisions of the African Charter. The African Court reached the same conclusion in the Thomas v. Tanzania case, holding that the obligation set out in Article 1 of the Charter is not complied with or is violated when any of the rights, duties or freedoms enshrined in the Charter has been restricted, violated or not applied. It must therefore be concluded that Article 1 of the African Charter has been violated.

In its now consolidated jurisprudence, the Commission considers that any violation of the rights enshrined in the Charter gives rise to a right to reparation, including monetary reparation. This is the case, for example, in Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Cameroon, where the Commission indicated that reparation may take various forms depending on the rights violated and the circumstances of the case, ranging from administrative, legislative and judicial actions to monetary compensation.
The Commission also considers that "the right to reparation encompasses not only the right to an effective remedy, but also to adequate, effective and full reparation".

The Commission reiterates that it is incumbent on the applicant to provide evidence to substantiate his claims, notably in the matter of material damage. The Commission recalls that there is an irrebuttable presumption of moral prejudice in favour of victims of violations of the rights guaranteed by the African Charter and that reparation for moral prejudice is based on equity, taking into account the seriousness of the victim's suffering, the duration and consequences of the human rights violations.
In the present case, the Complainant makes a series of claims for reparation. The Commission proposes to analyse them as follows.

On the declaration of the violation of the provisions of the Charter, the Complainant requests the Commission to find the violation of Articles 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7(1)(a), 7(1)(b), 7(1)(c), 7(1)(d), 18(1) and 26 of the Charter. As already developed, the Commission concluded that Articles 1, 6, 7(1)(d) and 26 of the Charter were violated. It is therefore appropriate for the Commission to make a declaration to that effect.
Concerning his request to enjoin the State of Cameroon to put an urgent end to the said violations, the Commission has not found any ongoing violations and dismisses the request.

On the request to order the immediate release of the Complainant, the Commission notes that the latter has not proved how the procedural defects had an impact on his conviction and dismisses the request.

On the sanctioning of the perpetrators of the violations found, the Commission considers that the Respondent State has an obligation to make reparation for the violation of Articles 1, 6, 7(1)(d) and 26 of the African Charter. The Respondent State should also urgently amend Article 3 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti in order to guarantee the independence of prosecutors at the Special Criminal Court.

With regard to apologies, the Commission considers that apologies are one of the forms of satisfaction, normally ordered in the context of violations jeopardising the honour and reputation of the victim, or of massive violations of a certain level of gravity. In the present case, the Complainant does not demonstrate the need for apologies. Thus, the Commission considers that there is no need to recommend apologies.
On monetary reparation, the Complainant requests reparation of twenty-five billion (25,000,000,000) CFA francs or 39 million euros, as damages for the twelve years of abusive and arbitrary detention.

The Commission considers that the Complainant suffered material prejudice as a result of his prolonged pre-trial detention, notably by bearing his lawyers' fees. However, the Complainant provided no evidence enabling this prejudice to be assessed nor the scales used to calculate the amount claimed. Consequently, the Commission is not in a position to rule on reparation for material prejudice and refers the Complainant to the national courts for the assessment of the quantum of the prejudice suffered, in accordance with its jurisprudence.

The Commission also considers that the Complainant's long pre-trial detention caused him moral damage which should be repaired on grounds of equity. The Commission notes that in criminal proceedings, the accused person may be placed in pre-trial detention under the conditions determined by law. It follows that reparation concerns only the prejudice resulting from detention carried out outside the requirements of the law.

With regard to the assessment of the moral damage caused by the prolonged pre-trial detention, the Complainant requests the Commission to apply the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in the case of Apicella v. Italy. In that case, the ECHR held that "a sum varying from 1,000 to 1,500 euros per year of duration of the proceedings is a starting basis for the calculation to be made. The outcome of the national proceedings has no importance as such on the moral damage suffered as a result of the duration of the proceedings. The overall amount will be increased by 2,000 euros if what is at stake in the dispute is significant, notably in matters of labour law, status and capacity of persons, pensions, proceedings that are particularly serious in relation to the health or life of persons".

In the present case, the Commission considers that the Complainant's pre-trial detention beyond the maximum period of 18 months provided for by Article 221 of the CCP must be repaired. From the Complainant's arrest on 9 March 2012 to the judgment of the Special Criminal Court on 21 March 2021, 9 years 12 days elapsed. After subtracting the 18 months of pre-trial detention authorised by law, there remain 7 years 6 months and 12 days. The ECHR judgment recalled above concerned a succession case whereas the present communication concerns a case of embezzlement of public property. Given that the Complainant admitted his guilt and that he was convicted, the Commission finds it just to award him moral reparation of five hundred (500) euros per year of pre-trial detention beyond the legal time limits, that is five hundred (500) Euros multiplied by seven, that is three thousand five hundred (3,500) Euros. The Commission considers that this amount should be paid to the Complainant within one year, given that the State budget is adopted every year.

For these reasons, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares that: a) Articles 2, 3, 7(1)(a), 7(1)(b), and 7(1)(c) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights have not been violated. b) Articles 1, 6, 7(1)(d) and 26 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights have been violated.

Consequently, the Commission recommends that the Republic of Cameroon: a) Revise Article 3 of Decree No. 2013/288 of 4 September 2013 laying down the modalities for the restitution of the corpus delicti in order to make it compatible with Articles 7 and 26 of the African Charter; b) Pay the Complainant moral reparation of three thousand five hundred (3,500) Euros or its equivalent in CFA francs within one year from notification; c) Pay material reparation to the Complainant, to be assessed in accordance with domestic judicial procedure; d) Report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of notification of the present decision, on the measures taken with a view to implementing the present decision. Done at the 83rd Ordinary Session, held from 2 to 22 May 2025 in Banjul, The Gambia. SECRETARY

Le 29 décembre 2023 le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples a reçu une Plainte introduite par Landry Angelo ADELAKOUN, Romaric ZINSOU, Miguèle HOUETO, Fréjus ATTINDOGLO, et Conaïde AKOUEDEDENOU DJE (les Plaintants), contre la République du Bénin (Etat défendeur), Etat ayant ratifié la Charte africaine le 20 janvier 1986.

Les Plaintants exposent que par décision N°23-031/HAAC du 08 août 2023 portant mesure conservatoire contre le Groupe de Presse " La gazette du Golfe ", le Président de la Haute Autorité de l'Audiovisuel et de la Communication (HAAC) a suspendu tous les moyens de communication de masse du groupe (Golfe Télévision, Golfe FM, l'hebdomadaire Gazette du Golfe et leurs canaux digitaux), jusqu'à nouvel ordre.

Ils affirment que ladite décision fait référence au communiqué 23/HAAC/PT/SG/SCS du 03 août 2023 invitant les acteurs des médias à faire preuve de plus de professionnalisme et au respect scrupuleux des dispositions constitutionnelles et légales dans le traitement de l'information relative à l'apologie des coups d'Etat en Afrique et dans la sous-région.

Les Plaintants ajoutent que la HAAC a considéré que le groupe de presse " à travers ses moyens de communication de masse ne s'est pas exécuté" et que considérant la " gravité des faits et l'urgence", des mesures conservatoires doivent d'être prises. Ces mesures étant la suspension jusqu'à nouvel ordre des activités du groupe.
Les Plaintants précisent que cette suspension est intervenue suite à l'actualité relative au coup d'Etat au Niger.

Les Plaintants soutiennent que si tel que rappelé dans le premier considérant de la décision N°23-031/HAAC du 08 août 2023, toute tentative de renversement d'un régime constitutionnel est un crime dont l'apologie est inadmissible, intolérable dans toute société démocratique, il appert de relever que loin d'être une réponse à la promotion des principes et valeurs démocratiques, cette décision est plutôt attentatoire aux libertés fondamentales et surtout au droit à l'information et la liberté de presse pierres angulaires de toute démocratie sérieuse.

Les Plaintants affirment qu'ils ont initié un recours en inconstitutionnalité de la décision du Président de la HAAC devant la Cour constitutionnelle sur le fondement des articles 3 ; 117 ; 120 et 121 de la loi N° 2019 - 40 du 07 Novembre 2019 portant révision de la loi n° 90- 32 du 11 décembre 1990 portant Constitution de la République du Bénin, et 28 de la loi 2022-09 du 27 juin 2022 portant loi organique sur la Cour constitutionnelle.
Ils allèguent que par décision DCC 23-234 du 02 novembre 2023 la Cour constitutionnelle a dit et jugé qu'« il n'y a pas violation de la Constitution ».

Sans citer les dispositions pertinentes de la Charte, les Plaintants allèguent la violation de la liberté expression et du droit à l'information. Se référant à la Charte, les droits allégués avoir été violés renvoient à l'article 9.

Les Plaintants demandent à la Commission d'accorder les mesures suivantes : i. Se déclarer compétente ii. Déclarer la plainte recevable Dire que le Bénin à travers la décision N°23-031/HAAC du 08 août 2023 portant mesure conservatoire contre le Groupe de Presse " La gazette du Golf " a violé les dispositions de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples.
La plainte a été reçue au Secrétariat de la Commission le 29 décembre 2023.

Par lettre du 15 avril 2024, le Secrétariat a informé les plaignants de la décision d'admission de la plainte et les a également requis de soumettre leurs arguments sur la recevabilité et le fond dans un délai de soixante (60) jours conformément à la règle 116 (1) du règlement intérieur de la Commission.

Par Note Verbale du 15 avril 2024, le Secrétariat a informé l'État Défendeur de la décision d'admission de la plainte et l'a également informé que les Plaignants ont été invités à soumettre leurs arguments sur la recevabilité et le fond.
Par mail du 20 juin 2024, les Plaignants ont transmis à la Commission leurs observations sur la recevabilité et le fond.
Par lettre du 27 juin 2024, la Commission a accusé réception des observations des plaignants sur la recevabilité et le fond.
Par Note Verbale du 08 aout 2024, la Commission a transmis à l'Etat défendeur les arguments et preuves des plaignants sur la recevabilité et le fond.
Par lettre du 04 septembre 2024, l'Etat a transmis son mémoire en défense à la Commission.

Par Note Verbale du 05 septembre 2024, la Commission a accusé réception du mémoire en réponse de l'Etat défendeur et constaté qu'il ne contenait pas des observations sur le fond et lui a accordé un délai supplémentaire de trente (30) jours pour soumettre un mémoire en réponse contenant des observations sur la recevabilité et le fond.

Par lettre du 16 octobre 2024, l'Etat défendeur a déposé un mémoire en réponse contenant des observations sur la recevabilité et le fond. La Commission en a accusé réception par Note verbale du même jour. Ce mémoire a été transmis aux Plaignants le même jour.
La Commission n'a pas reçu de dupliche de la part des Plaignants. Les moyens des Plaignants sur la recevabilité de la Communication

Dans la présente Communication, les Plaignants affirment avoir épuisé tous les recours internes car ils ont saisi la Cour constitutionnelle qui, par Décision DCC 24-040 du 14 mars 2024, avait dit qu'« il n'y a pas violation de la Constitution » et que conformément à l'article 114 de la Constitution, "les décisions de la Cour sont sans recours et s'imposent aux pouvoirs publics".
S'agissant des autres conditions de recevabilité prévues à l'article 56 de la Charte africaine, les Plaignants n'ont développé aucun argumentaire.

L'Etat du Bénin, Etat défendeur, sollicite de la Commission le rejet de la plainte au motif que les requérants ne disposent pas de la qualité pour agir en l'espèce et qu'ils n'ont pas épuisé les voies de recours internes.

L'Etat défendeur rappelle qu'en droit, la recevabilité de l'action est essentiellement subordonnée du point de vue de la personne du plaideur à deux conditions : la qualité et l'intérêt, et que la qualité à agir se ramène à justifier d'un intérêt direct et personnel.

L'Etat défendeur soutien que les Plaignants n'ont pas indiqué à quel titre ils ont saisi la Commission et qu'ils ne démontrent nullement le lien qui les rattache au groupe de presse "La Gazette du Golfe" et en vertu duquel ils auraient l'habilitation légale pour agir contre la décision de la HAAC.

L'Etat défendeur affirme que les Plaignants, en se fondant sur la décision de la Cour constitutionnelle ont conclu à tort à l'épuisement de tous les recours internes. Il ajoute qu'il subsiste au plan interne au moins un recours non encore épuisé.

L'Etat défendeur relève que l'action des requérants est dirigée contre la décision n° 23-031/HAAC du 08 aout 2023 du Président de la HAAC du Benin, entérinée par la décision n° 23-032/HAAC prise par les conseillers de la HAAC et qu'étant une décision administrative, elle est susceptible de recours devant le juge administratif au sens des dispositions des articles 43 et 54 de la loi n° 2022-13 du 05 juillet 2022 portant loi organique sur la HAAC ainsi que celles de l'article 818 de la loi n° 2008-07 portant Code de procédure civile, commerciale, sociale, administrative et des comptes.

L'Etat défendeur soutient qu'en dehors du recours en inconstitutionnalité exercé par les requérants, la décision querellée devait être soumise au préalable à la censure de ce juge avant d'être déférée à la Commission et que n'ayant pas procédé ainsi, les requérants n'ont pas épuisé tous les recours internes.

La recevabilité des communications introduites auprès de la Commission africaine est régie par les conditions stipulées dans l'article 56 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples. Cet article prévoit 7 conditions qui doivent cumulativement être remplies par le Plaignant pour que sa communication puisse être déclarée recevable.
L'article 56(1) de la Charte exige qu'une communication indique l'identité de ses auteurs, même si ceux-ci demandent l'anonymat.
La présente communication a été introduite par Landry Angelo ADELAKOUN, Romaric ZINSOU, Miguèle HOUETO, Fréjus ATTINDOGLO, et Conaïde AKOUEDENOUDJE.

L'Etat défendeur ne remet pas en cause l'identité des auteurs, mais conteste leur qualité de représentants du groupe La Gazette du Golfe. Il soutient que les Plaignants ne fournissent aucune preuve établissant l'existence d'un mandat officiel ou d'un consentement permanent des victimes pour agir en leur nom.

La Commission souhaite rappeler que, s'agissant du locus standi, elle a adopté une approche libérale quant à la qualité pour agir de ceux qui peuvent la saisir sur la base des droits consacrés par la Charte.

Dans la présente Communication, la Commission observe que l'Etat défendeur remet en cause devant elle, une qualité procédurale pourtant reconnue aux Plaignants par sa propre juridiction nationale. En effet, ainsi qu'il ressort tant des observations de l'Etat défendeur que de celles des Plaignants, la Cour constitutionnelle du Bénin a admis leur plainte et statué sur le fond de leurs prétentions. Il en découle que l'Etat défendeur, ayant omis de contester la qualité des Plaignants au stade interne, ne saurait valablement soulever cette exception devant la Commission. Dès lors, l'argument selon lequel les Plaignants n'auraient pas qualité pour agir au nom du groupe de presse concerné est inopérant.

La Commission souhaite également rappeler que l'article 56 (1) exige seulement que l'auteur ou les auteurs d'une communication soient identifiés. Les auteurs de cette communication étant clairement identifiés et au vu des précédents développements, la Commission considère que cette condition est remplie.
L'article 56(2) de la Charte exige que la communication soit compatible avec la Charte de l'OUA (Acte constitutif de l'Union africaine) ou avec la Charte africaine elle-même.

Dans la communication Michael Majuru c. Zimbabwe, la Commission avait explicité que « compatibilité » signifie « conforme » ou « en conformité avec » ou « non contraire » ou « non contre », de même qu'elle a dit que « selon la jurisprudence de la Commission, il n'est pas nécessaire que les plaignants précisent quels articles de la Charte ont été violés, ni même quel droit est invoqué, pour autant qu'ils aient soulevé le fond du problème en question. »

La Commission a interprété l'article 56(2) de la Charte comme exigeant la compatibilité avec l'Acte constitutif de l'Union africaine ou la Charte, et avec les quatre (4) aspects de sa compétence, à savoir la compétence ratione personae, materiae, temporis et loci. En ce qui concerne le premier aspect, la Commission note que cette communication vise la protection des droits de l'homme, qui est l'un des objectifs de l'Acte constitutif de l'Union africaine, prévu à l'article 3 (h) de celui-ci. En outre, aucun élément des observations et de la plainte des requérants ne révèle une incompatibilité avec la Charte. En ce qui concerne la compétence, la Commission note que l'État défendeur est partie à la Charte (compétence ratione personae), que la plainte allègue des violations primafacie des droits protégés par la Charte en l'occurrence la liberté d'expression et le droit à l'information (compétence ratione materiae). La communication a par ailleurs été introduite pour des violations qui ont eu lieu après la ratification de la Charte par l'État défendeur, sur le territoire de ce dernier (compétence ratione loci) et que les faits ont eu lieu après que l'État défendeur est devenu parti à la Charte le 20 janvier 1986 (compétence ratione temporis).
La Commission considère dès lors la condition de l'article 56(2) satisfaite.
En vertu de l'article 56 (3), les communications ne doivent pas contenir des termes outrageants ou insultants à l'égard de l'État mis en cause, de ses institutions ou de l'OUA (UA).

Dans sa jurisprudence subséquente et notamment dans Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe c. République du Zimbabwe, la Commission avait affirmé que les termes outrageants ou insultants « doivent être dirigés contre l'État partie concerné, ses institutions ou l'Union africaine ».

La Commission est d'avis que les termes utilisés dans la Communication ne sont pas outrageants ou insultants à l'égard de l'État mis en cause, de ses institutions ou de l'UA et pour ces raisons, la Commission estime que la condition de l'article 56(3) de la Charte africaine a été remplie.

L'article 56(4) prévoit que la communication ne doit pas se limiter à rassembler exclusivement des nouvelles diffusées par des moyens de communication de masse. Dans la présente communication, les plaignants ont fourni des preuves documentaires constituées des décisions de la HAAC et de la Cour constitutionnelle du Bénin. Par ailleurs, aucun élément de leurs soumissions n'indique que les allégations qu'elle contient reposent exclusivement sur des informations diffusées par des moyens de communication de masse. En conséquence, la Commission estime que la condition énoncée à l'article 56(4) de la Charte africaine est remplie.
L'article 56(5) exige que les communications ne soient examinées qu'après épuisement des voies de recours internes, à moins que ces voies de recours ne soient indûment prolongées.

La Commission rappelle que « La règle exigeant l'épuisement des voies de recours internes comme condition de la présentation d'une réclamation internationale est fondée, entre autres principes, sur l'affirmation selon laquelle l'État défendeur doit d'abord avoir la possibilité de réparer par ses propres moyens, dans le cadre de son propre système juridique interne, le tort prétendument causé à l'individu. ».

Pour l'Etat défendeur, les plaignants ont eu tort de considérer la saisine de la Cour constitutionnelle et la décision de cette dernière comme l'ultime recours, censé satisfaire la condition de l'épuisement des recours internes. Il ajoute que la décision querellée était susceptible de recours devant le juge administratif et la Cour suprême car émanant d'un organisme administratif à caractère juridictionnel.

La Commission souhaite ici rappeler la décision de la Cour constitutionnelle sur le recours en inconstitutionnalité introduit par les Plaignants, telle que rapportée par ces derniers ainsi que par l'Etat défendeur : « EN CONSÉQUENCE, Article 1 : Dit qu'elle est incomplète pour connaître de la violation du code de l'information et de la communication et du code de déontologie de la presse. Article 2 : Se déclare compétente pour statuer sur la violation du droit à l'information, la liberté de presse, la liberté d'opinion, la liberté d'expression, le droit au travail ainsi que sur celle des dispositions de l'article 35 de la Constitution. Article 3 : Dit qu'il n'y a pas violation de la Constitution. ».

La Commission reconnaît que, dans certains cas, l'exigence d'épuisement des voies de recours internes peut être satisfaite même si toutes les voies théoriquement disponibles n'ont pas été empruntées, à condition que le Plaignant ait exercé les recours qui apparaissent comme les plus pertinents, efficaces et suffisants dans les circonstances de l'espèce.

En effet, dans Sir Dawda K. Jawara c. Gambie, la Commission a précisé que les recours doivent être effectifs et ne pas être indûment prolongés et que pour être conformes à l'article 56(5), ces recours doivent être disponibles, efficaces et satisfaisants.

En l'espèce, les plaignants n'ont pas démontré que la saisine du tribunal administratif, et en cas d'insatisfaction, l'exercice d'un pourvoi devant la Cour suprême, plus haute juridiction de l'ordre judiciaire du Benin, aurait été excessivement long ou inefficace. Ils n'ont pas non plus démontré leur futilité comme l'avait dit la Commission dans Cudjoe c. Ghana.

Si le contrôle de constitutionnalité et des droits fondamentaux relève de la Cour constitutionnelle, la Commission est d'avis avec l'Etat défendeur que d'autres voies de recours étaient disponibles pour les requérants tenant compte de la qualité de l'autorité ayant pris la décision querellée et de l'organisation judiciaire de l'Etat défendeur.

Dans ses précédentes décisions, la Commission avait déjà établi que les recours internes sont les recours ordinaires de droit commun qui existent dans les juridictions et sont normalement accessibles aux personnes en quête de justice et qu'ils s'appliquent aux tribunaux de nature judiciaire. Sur cette question la Commission reste guidée par et réaffirme sa position adoptée dans l'affaire Jean-Claude Roger Gbago c. Côte d'Ivoire, selon laquelle l'absence de recours à une voie judiciaire disponible entraîne l'irrecevabilité d'une communication. Par ailleurs, la Cour constitutionnelle n'avait pas vidé tout le fond de l'affaire, s'étant déclarée incomplète pour connaître de la violation du code de l'information et de la communication et du code de déontologie de la presse. La Commission estime que les Plaignants auraient dû au préalable s'adresser au tribunal administratif puis à la Cour suprême avant de la saisir. Dans Selemabothoko Magdeline Rachidi c. Afrique du sud, la Commission avait conclu au défaut d'épuisement des voies de recours internes car « la Commission reconnaît que la décision de la Haute Cour de radier sa plainte du rôle des affaires urgentes n'était pas une décision définitive. Comme l'a fait valoir l'Etat défendeur, la plaignante pouvait encore réinscrire son affaire au rôle normal. Au lieu de cela, la requérante a décidé de s'adresser à la Cour constitutionnelle où sa plainte a été rejetée en raison de l'absence de fondement et d'urgence. Il est donc clair pour la Commission, comme le soutient l'Etat défendeur, que la requérante dispose d'autres voies de recours internes dans le cadre de la législation nationale ».

En l'espèce, les Plaintants se sont abstenus de saisir les mécanismes internes compétents et n'ont pas apporté la preuve de l'indisponibilité, de l'inefficacité ou de l'insuffisance de ces recours, telle qu'exigée par l'article 56(5) de la Charte. La Commission considère en définitive que cette communication ne remplit pas le critère de recevabilité tel que prévu par l'article 56(5) de la Charte

L'article 56(6) exige qu'une communication soit présentée dans un délai raisonnable après l'épuisement des voies de recours internes. S'agissant de cette condition, ni le plaignant ni l'État défendeur n'ont présenté d'observations.

Dans des affaires antérieures, la Commission, a généralement estimé qu'un délai de six mois était un délai raisonnable pour présenter une communication. La Commission a également jugé qu'en l'absence de délai spécifique dans la Charte, ce qui constitue un "délai raisonnable" doit être évalué au cas par cas, en tenant compte des circonstances de la plainte, de la nature de la procédure nationale et du fait que le requérant justifie ou non tout retard. Il s'ensuit que le Plaignant doit justifier tout délai excédant six (6) mois.

La Commission estime que, lorsque le Plaignant n'a manifestement pas épuisé les recours internes disponibles, efficaces et suffisants, il est inutile d'analyser la condition relative au respect du délai raisonnable. En effet, le point de départ du calcul de ce délai ne saurait être fixé qu'à compter de l'épuisement effectif des voies de recours internes ou de la démonstration convaincante de leur indisponibilité ou inadéquation. En l'absence de cette condition préalable, l'examen du délai raisonnable est prématuré et dénué de pertinence.

L'article 56(7) dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) ne pas concerner des cas qui ont été réglés conformément soit aux principes de la Charte des Nations Unies, soit de la Charte de l'Organisation de l'Unité Africaine et soit des dispositions de la présente Charte. ».

Dans l'affaire Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) c. Sudan, la Commission a estimé qu'une question est considérée comme réglée si un organe juridictionnel international doté d'un mandat ou d'une compétence en matière de droits de l'homme a pris une décision à ce sujet et a conféré à la plainte l'autorité de la chose jugée.

Dans la présente communication, rien dans le dossier indique que l'affaire a déjà été réglée par un organe juridictionnel international. La Commission conclut que la condition posée à l'article 56(7) est satisfaite.

A la lumière de ce qui précède, la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples : i. Déclare la communication irrecevable pour non-conformité aux dispositions de l'article 56(5) de la Charte africaine. ii. Informe les parties de sa décision conformément à l'article 118(4) de son Règlement intérieur (2020). Adoptée à la 84 session ordinaire de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples tenue virtuellement du 21 au 31 juillet 2025.

On 29 December 2023, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights received a Complaint submitted by Landry Angelo ADELAKOUN, Romaric ZINSOU, Miguèle HOUETO, Fréjus ATTINDOGLO, and Conaïde AKOUEDEDENOU DJE (the Complainants), against the Republic of Benin (Respondent State), a State that ratified the African Charter on 20 January 1986.

The Complainants state that by decision No. 23-031/HAAC of 8 August 2023 imposing a provisional measure against the Press Group "La gazette du Golfe", the President of the High Authority for Audiovisual and Communication (HAAC) suspended all the mass media outlets of the group (Golfe Télévision, Golfe FM, the weekly Gazette du Golfe and their digital channels), until further notice.

They assert that the said decision refers to communiqué 23/HAAC/PT/SG/SCS of 3 August 2023 inviting media actors to show more professionalism and scrupulous respect for constitutional and legal provisions in the handling of information relating to the apology of coups d'état in Africa and in the sub-region.

The Complainants add that the HAAC considered that the press group "through its mass media outlets has not complied" and that, considering the "gravity of the facts and the urgency", provisional measures must be taken. These measures being the suspension until further notice of the activities of the group.
The Complainants specify that this suspension occurred following the news relating to the coup d'état in Niger.

The Complainants argue that although, as recalled in the first recital of decision No. 23-031/HAAC of 8 August 2023, any attempt to overthrow a constitutional regime is a crime whose apology is inadmissible and intolerable in any democratic society, it is apparent that, far from being a response to the promotion of democratic principles and values, this decision rather infringes fundamental freedoms and above all the right to information and freedom of the press, cornerstones of any serious democracy.

The Complainants assert that they initiated an action for unconstitutionality of the decision of the President of the HAAC before the Constitutional Court on the basis of Articles 3, 117, 120 and 121 of Law No. 2019-40 of 7 November 2019 revising Law No. 90-32 of 11 December 1990 on the Constitution of the Republic of Benin, and Article 28 of Law 2022-09 of 27 June 2022 on the organic law on the Constitutional Court.
They allege that by decision DCC 23-234 of 2 November 2023 the Constitutional Court stated and held that "there is no violation of the Constitution".

Without citing the relevant provisions of the Charter, the Complainants allege the violation of freedom of expression and the right to information. Referring to the Charter, the rights alleged to have been violated refer to Article 9.

The Complainants request the Commission to grant the following measures: i. Declare itself competent ii. Declare the complaint admissible Declare that Benin, through decision No. 23-031/HAAC of 8 August 2023 imposing a provisional measure against the Press Group "La gazette du Golf", violated the provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.
The complaint was received at the Secretariat of the Commission on 29 December 2023.

By letter of 15 April 2024, the Secretariat informed the complainants of the decision to admit the complaint and also requested them to submit their arguments on admissibility and the merits within a period of sixty (60) days in accordance with Rule 116(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

By Note Verbale of 15 April 2024, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State of the decision to admit the complaint and also informed it that the Complainants had been invited to submit their arguments on admissibility and the merits.
By email of 20 June 2024, the Complainants transmitted to the Commission their observations on admissibility and the merits.
By letter of 27 June 2024, the Commission acknowledged receipt of the complainants' observations on admissibility and the merits.
By Note Verbale of 8 August 2024, the Commission transmitted to the Respondent State the complainants' arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits.
By letter of 4 September 2024, the State transmitted its brief in defence to the Commission.

By Note Verbale of 5 September 2024, the Commission acknowledged receipt of the Respondent State's brief in response and noted that it did not contain observations on the merits and granted it an additional period of thirty (30) days to submit a brief in response containing observations on admissibility and the merits.

By letter of 16 October 2024, the Respondent State filed a brief in response containing observations on admissibility and the merits. The Commission acknowledged receipt by Note Verbale of the same day. This brief was transmitted to the Complainants on the same day.
The Commission did not receive a rejoinder from the Complainants. The Complainants' arguments on the admissibility of the Communication

In the present Communication, the Complainants assert that they have exhausted all local remedies as they seized the Constitutional Court, which, by Decision DCC 24-040 of 14 March 2024, had stated that "there is no violation of the Constitution" and that in accordance with Article 114 of the Constitution, "the decisions of the Court are not subject to appeal and are binding on public authorities".
As regards the other admissibility requirements provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter, the Complainants have developed no argument.

The State of Benin, Respondent State, requests the Commission to dismiss the complaint on the ground that the applicants do not have standing in this case and that they have not exhausted local remedies.

The Respondent State recalls that in law, the admissibility of an action is essentially subject, from the standpoint of the person of the litigant, to two conditions: standing and interest, and that standing to act comes down to justifying a direct and personal interest.

The Respondent State argues that the Complainants did not indicate in what capacity they seized the Commission and that they in no way demonstrate the link that connects them to the press group "La Gazette du Golfe" and by virtue of which they would have the legal authority to act against the decision of the HAAC.

The Respondent State asserts that the Complainants, relying on the decision of the Constitutional Court, wrongly concluded that all local remedies had been exhausted. It adds that at least one remedy not yet exhausted remains at the domestic level.

The Respondent State notes that the applicants' action is directed against decision No. 23-031/HAAC of 8 August 2023 of the President of the HAAC of Benin, endorsed by decision No. 23-032/HAAC taken by the HAAC councillors and that, being an administrative decision, it is subject to appeal before the administrative judge within the meaning of the provisions of Articles 43 and 54 of Law No. 2022-13 of 5 July 2022 on the organic law on the HAAC as well as those of Article 818 of Law No. 2008-07 on the Code of civil, commercial, social, administrative and accounts procedure.

The Respondent State argues that, apart from the action for unconstitutionality brought by the applicants, the impugned decision should have been submitted beforehand to the scrutiny of this judge before being referred to the Commission and that, not having done so, the applicants have not exhausted all local remedies.

The admissibility of communications submitted to the African Commission is governed by the requirements stipulated in Article 56 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. This article provides for 7 requirements which must cumulatively be fulfilled by the Complainant for his communication to be declared admissible.
Article 56(1) of the Charter requires that a communication indicate the identity of its authors, even if the latter request anonymity.
The present communication was submitted by Landry Angelo ADELAKOUN, Romaric ZINSOU, Miguèle HOUETO, Fréjus ATTINDOGLO, and Conaïde AKOUEDENOUDJE.

The Respondent State does not call into question the identity of the authors, but contests their capacity as representatives of the group La Gazette du Golfe. It argues that the Complainants provide no evidence establishing the existence of an official mandate or of a standing consent of the victims to act on their behalf.
The Commission wishes to recall that, with regard to locus standi, it has adopted a liberal approach as to the standing of those who may seize it on the basis of the rights enshrined in the Charter.

In the present Communication, the Commission observes that the Respondent State calls into question before it a procedural capacity that was nevertheless recognised for the Complainants by its own national court. Indeed, as emerges from both the Respondent State's observations and those of the Complainants, the Constitutional Court of Benin admitted their complaint and ruled on the merits of their claims. It follows that the Respondent State, having failed to contest the Complainants' standing at the domestic stage, cannot validly raise this objection before the Commission. Consequently, the argument that the Complainants would not have standing to act on behalf of the press group concerned is ineffective.

The Commission also wishes to recall that Article 56(1) requires only that the author or authors of a communication be identified. The authors of this communication being clearly identified and in view of the preceding developments, the Commission considers that this requirement is met.
Article 56(2) of the Charter requires that the communication be compatible with the OAU Charter (Constitutive Act of the African Union) or with the African Charter itself.

In the communication Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe, the Commission had explained that "compatibility" means "in accordance with" or "in conformity with" or "not contrary to" or "not against", just as it said that "according to the jurisprudence of the Commission, it is not necessary for complainants to specify which articles of the Charter have been violated, or even which right is invoked, provided that they have raised the substance of the issue in question."

The Commission has interpreted Article 56(2) of the Charter as requiring compatibility with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the Charter, and with the four (4) aspects of its jurisdiction, namely jurisdiction ratione personae, materiae, temporis and loci. As regards the first aspect, the Commission notes that this communication seeks the protection of human rights, which is one of the objectives of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, provided for in Article 3(h) thereof. In addition, no element of the applicants' observations and complaint reveals an incompatibility with the Charter. As regards jurisdiction, the Commission notes that the Respondent State is a party to the Charter (jurisdiction ratione personae), that the complaint alleges prima facie violations of rights protected by the Charter, in this case freedom of expression and the right to information (jurisdiction ratione materiae). The communication was moreover submitted for violations that took place after the ratification of the Charter by the Respondent State, on the territory of the latter (jurisdiction ratione loci) and the facts took place after the Respondent State became a party to the Charter on 20 January 1986 (jurisdiction ratione temporis).
The Commission therefore considers the requirement of Article 56(2) satisfied.
Under Article 56(3), communications must not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the OAU (AU).

In its subsequent jurisprudence and notably in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe v. Republic of Zimbabwe, the Commission had affirmed that disparaging or insulting language "must be directed against the State Party concerned, its institutions or the African Union".

The Commission is of the view that the language used in the Communication is not disparaging or insulting towards the State concerned, its institutions or the AU and for these reasons, the Commission considers that the requirement of Article 56(3) of the African Charter has been fulfilled.

Article 56(4) provides that the communication must not be limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through mass media. In the present communication, the complainants provided documentary evidence consisting of the decisions of the HAAC and of the Constitutional Court of Benin. Moreover, no element of their submissions indicates that the allegations it contains are based exclusively on information disseminated through mass media. Consequently, the Commission considers that the requirement set out in Article 56(4) of the African Charter is fulfilled.
Article 56(5) requires that communications be considered only after exhaustion of local remedies, unless these remedies are unduly prolonged.

The Commission recalls that "The rule requiring the exhaustion of local remedies as a condition for the presentation of an international claim is based, among other principles, on the assertion that the respondent State must first have the opportunity to redress by its own means, within the framework of its own domestic legal system, the wrong allegedly done to the individual.".

For the Respondent State, the complainants were wrong to consider the seizure of the Constitutional Court and the decision of the latter as the ultimate remedy, supposed to satisfy the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies. It adds that the impugned decision was subject to appeal before the administrative judge and the Supreme Court as it emanated from an administrative body of a jurisdictional nature.

The Commission wishes here to recall the decision of the Constitutional Court on the action for unconstitutionality brought by the Complainants, as reported by the latter as well as by the Respondent State: "CONSEQUENTLY, Article 1: Finds that it is incomplete to hear the violation of the information and communication code and the press code of ethics. Article 2: Declares itself competent to rule on the violation of the right to information, freedom of the press, freedom of opinion, freedom of expression, the right to work as well as that of the provisions of Article 35 of the Constitution. Article 3: Finds that there is no violation of the Constitution.".

The Commission acknowledges that, in certain cases, the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies may be satisfied even if not all the theoretically available remedies have been pursued, provided that the Complainant has pursued the remedies that appear to be the most relevant, effective and sufficient in the circumstances of the case.

Indeed, in Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission specified that remedies must be effective and not unduly prolonged and that to comply with Article 56(5), these remedies must be available, effective and satisfactory.

In the present case, the complainants have not demonstrated that seizing the administrative court, and in case of dissatisfaction, lodging an appeal on points of law before the Supreme Court, the highest court of the judicial order of Benin, would have been excessively long or ineffective. Nor have they demonstrated their futility as the Commission had said in Cudjoe v. Ghana.

While the review of constitutionality and of fundamental rights falls within the competence of the Constitutional Court, the Commission is of the view, with the Respondent State, that other remedies were available to the applicants taking into account the capacity of the authority that took the impugned decision and the judicial organisation of the Respondent State.

In its previous decisions, the Commission had already established that local remedies are the ordinary common law remedies that exist in the courts and are normally accessible to persons seeking justice and that they apply to courts of a judicial nature. On this question the Commission remains guided by and reaffirms its position adopted in the case Jean-Claude Roger Gbago v. Côte d'Ivoire, according to which the failure to have recourse to an available judicial remedy renders a communication inadmissible. Moreover, the Constitutional Court had not disposed of the whole merits of the case, having declared itself incomplete to hear the violation of the information and communication code and the press code of ethics. The Commission considers that the Complainants should have first applied to the administrative court and then to the Supreme Court before seizing it. In Selemabothoko Magdeline Rachidi v. South Africa, the Commission had concluded that local remedies were not exhausted because "the Commission acknowledges that the decision of the High Court to strike her complaint off the urgent roll was not a final decision. As the Respondent State argued, the complainant could still have re-enrolled her case on the normal roll. Instead, the applicant decided to apply to the Constitutional Court where her complaint was dismissed for lack of foundation and urgency. It is therefore clear to the Commission, as the Respondent State argues, that the applicant has other local remedies available under national legislation".

In the present case, the Complainants refrained from seizing the competent domestic mechanisms and did not provide proof of the unavailability, ineffectiveness or insufficiency of these remedies, as required by Article 56(5) of the Charter. The Commission ultimately considers that this communication does not meet the admissibility requirement as provided by Article 56(5) of the Charter

Article 56(6) requires that a communication be submitted within a reasonable time after exhaustion of local remedies. With regard to this requirement, neither the complainant nor the Respondent State presented observations.

In earlier cases, the Commission has generally considered that a period of six months was a reasonable time for submitting a communication. The Commission has also held that in the absence of a specific time limit in the Charter, what constitutes a "reasonable time" must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the circumstances of the complaint, the nature of the domestic proceedings and whether or not the applicant justifies any delay. It follows that the Complainant must justify any delay exceeding six (6) months.

The Commission considers that, where the Complainant has manifestly not exhausted the available, effective and sufficient local remedies, it is pointless to analyse the requirement relating to compliance with reasonable time. Indeed, the starting point for calculating this period can be fixed only from the actual exhaustion of local remedies or the convincing demonstration of their unavailability or inadequacy. In the absence of this precondition, the examination of reasonable time is premature and devoid of relevance.

Article 56(7) provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission and relating to human and peoples' rights shall (...) not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter.".

In the case of Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan, the Commission held that a matter is considered settled if an international judicial body with a human rights mandate or competence has taken a decision on it and has conferred on the complaint the authority of res judicata.

In the present communication, nothing in the file indicates that the case has already been settled by an international judicial body. The Commission concludes that the requirement set out in Article 56(7) is satisfied.

In light of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares the communication inadmissible for non-compliance with the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter. ii. Informs the parties of its decision in accordance with Rule 118(4) of its Rules of Procedure (2020). Adopted at the 84th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held virtually from 21 to 31 July 2025.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received a Complaint on 16 February 2022 from Maselina Mathabela (the Complainant), represented by Adv. Shadrack Tebeile, against the Republic of South Africa (the Respondent State), a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complainant alleges that she was born on 26 April 2000 in Springs, Gauteng Province, South Africa, and has lived in the country her entire life. Even so, she added that she is undocumented due to her parents' Mozambican nationality and their inability to provide the necessary documentation for her to acquire a South African identity card.

The Complainant further alleges that despite having a clinic card issued at her birth, she has been unable to obtain an official birth certificate or identity document. Additionally, her immunization card incorrectly lists her name as "Marselina Mathebula" instead of "Maselina Mathabela."

It is alleged that in 2017, the Complainant approached the Department of Home Affairs for an identity document but was informed that she would need to provide documentation from her undocumented parents, who had already returned to Mozambique.

The Complainant alleges further that this situation has resulted in significant barriers to her accessing education, employment, and other vital services. She alleged that in 2018, after completing Grade 12—the final year of secondary education in South Africa, culminating in the National Senior Certificate ("matric") issued by the Department of Basic Education—she was unable to pursue higher education due to the lack of a valid identity document.

The Complainant further alleges that, in November 2021, she filed an urgent application before the High Court of South Africa (Mpumalanga Division) seeking an order compelling the Department of Home Affairs to issue her with an identity document. The application was struck off the roll on the ground of lack of urgency, and the Court did not address the substantive merits of the claim.

Subsequently, the Complainant filed an application for direct access to the Constitutional Court of South Africa, again raising the urgency of her predicament. On 6 December 2021, the Constitutional Court dismissed the application for direct access, holding that it was not in the interests of justice to hear the case at that time, and expressly indicating that there was no reason the applicant could not pursue her proceedings in the High Court.

The Complainant avers that her inability to obtain identification documents, despite meeting the criteria set forth in South Africa's Citizenship Act, constitutes a violation of several rights guaranteed by the African Charter.
The Complainant alleges violations of Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 12(2), 13, 17(1), and 22(1) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights by the Respondent State.

The Complainant prays that the Commission: (a) Declare that the Respondent State has violated the Complainant's rights under Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7(1)(a), 12(2), 13, 17(1), and 22(1) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. (b) Order that the Complainant be recognized as a South African citizen by birth in terms of Section 2(2)(a) and (b) of the South African Citizenship Act 88 of 1995. (c) Order that the Complainant be granted South African citizenship in terms of Section 4(3)(a) and (b) of the South African Citizenship Act 88 of 1995. (d) Direct the Respondent State to register the Complainant's birth, enter her details into the South African population register, and assign her a South African identity number. (e) Order that the Respondent State issue the Complainant with a birth certificate and identity document within ten (10) days from the date of the order. (f) Order the Respondent State to compensate the Complainant for legal costs incurred in the High Court and Constitutional Court of South Africa, including the costs of two counsel in both courts. (g) Order the Respondent State to pay the Complainant compensation in the amount of R2,000,000.00 (Two Million South African Rands) within three (3) months from the date of the order. (h) Grant any further orders the Commission deems fit in the circumstances.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received the Complaint from Maselina Mathabela (the Complainant), represented by Advocate Shadrack Tebeile, on 16 February 2022.

On 13 June 2022, the Commission considered the Complaint and decided to be seized of the matter in accordance with Rule 115(5) of its Rules of Procedure, 2020. The Secretariat subsequently notified both parties of this decision by letter and Note Verbale.

In the same correspondence, the Respondent State was informed of its obligation to submit its arguments and evidence on both admissibility and merits within sixty (60) days of notification, pursuant to Rule 116(1) of the Rules of Procedure, 2020. The Secretariat also communicated the Commission's decision to dismiss the Complainant's request for Provisional Measures, noting that the Complainant had failed to demonstrate a risk of irreparable harm and that granting the measures sought—namely, the issuance of a temporary South African birth certificate and identity number—would pre-empt the outcome of the proceedings on the merits.

On 21 June 2022, the Respondent State addressed a Note Verbale to the Secretariat requesting the complete set of annexures, noting that certain attachments to the Complaint were missing. On the same day, the Secretariat acknowledged this request and transmitted the complete set of missing documents to the Respondent.

On 26 April 2023, the Respondent State submitted a formal request for an extension of thirty (30) days to file its observations on admissibility and merits, citing the need for additional time to compile and prepare the necessary documentation. By letter dated the same day, the Secretariat granted the requested extension, allowing the Respondent until 6 June 2023 to submit its observations.

On 26 May 2023, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the Respondent State's submission on admissibility. However, it observed that the submission did not include arguments on the merits. The Secretariat accordingly issued a Note Verbale granting the Respondent a further thirty (30) days to submit its observations on the merits.

On 19 June 2023, the Respondent State addressed a communication to the Secretariat requesting an oral hearing on admissibility and merits, or admissibility alone, so as to clarify the applicable domestic legal framework. This request was transmitted to the Bureau of the Commission for consideration in accordance with Rule 102(3) of the Rules of Procedure, 2020, and was never granted.

On the same date, 19 June 2023, the Secretariat notified the Respondent State that its observations on admissibility had been transmitted to the Complainant for rejoinder within thirty (30) days, pursuant to Rule 116(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure. The Complainant never filed a rejoinder.
The Complainant submits that the present Communication satisfies all the admissibility requirements set out under Article 56 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.

In compliance with Article 56(1), the Complainant avers that her identity is fully disclosed. She states that she is an adult female, born on 26 April 2000 in Springs, Gauteng Province, Republic of South Africa, and has resided in South Africa her entire life. The Complainant further attaches a clinic card and documentation affirming her place of birth to support her assertion of identity and victim status within the meaning of the Charter.

With respect to Article 56(2), the Complainant contends that the Communication is compatible with the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. She submits that the rights alleged to have been violated are protected under the African Charter and that the relief sought does not challenge the sovereignty or territorial integrity of the Respondent State. The Complainant maintains that the Communication raises legal claims of a human rights nature and seeks only to vindicate rights secured under the Charter.

With regard to Article 56(3), the Complainant affirms that the language of the Communication is respectful and devoid of any disparaging or insulting expressions. She stresses that the pleadings are formulated in the tone and style of a legal petition and do not improperly attack the institutions of the Respondent State or the African Union.

In relation to Article 56(4), the Complainant submits that the Communication is not based exclusively on information disseminated through the media. Rather, she relies upon first-hand testimony and verifiable documentation, including a clinic card, official correspondence, and the record of domestic judicial proceedings. The Complainant further states that the facts alleged are supported by her affidavit and by the annexed materials submitted to the Commission.

As to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies under Article 56(5), the Complainant submits that she approached the High Court of South Africa, seeking urgent relief in relation to her lack of identity documentation. The High Court, however, struck out her application on 18 November 2021 for lack of urgency.

Subsequently, she applied to the Constitutional Court of South Africa, which dismissed her application on 6 December 2021. The Complainant contends that these steps constituted an exhaustion of available and effective domestic remedies. She appends copies of the relevant High Court and Constitutional Court processes and decisions to her affidavit.

The Complainant further argues that, in any event, the domestic remedies available to her were ineffective and incapable of providing adequate redress. She submits that her repeated efforts over a prolonged period to regularize her status with the Department of Home Affairs proved unsuccessful, notwithstanding her eligibility for documentation. The Complainant further contends that the legal avenues she pursued failed to provide timely and effective relief, thereby rendering the available remedies inadequate in the circumstances of her case. She particularly notes that the lack of documentation precluded her from enrolling in university, and that the harm occasioned was of a continuing and urgent nature, which domestic processes were incapable of remedying.

Concerning Article 56(6), the Complainant avers that the Communication was submitted within a reasonable time following the Constitutional Court's dismissal of her application on 6 December 2021. The Communication was filed before the African Commission on 16 February 2022, a period of approximately two months. The Complainant contends that this interval is reasonable in the circumstances and does not amount to undue delay, particularly given the seriousness of the violations alleged.

Finally, with regard to Article 56(7), the Complainant affirms that the matter has not been submitted to any other international mechanism of settlement and that no parallel proceedings are pending before any other international or regional forum.
