Les Etats parties à la présente Charte s'engagent à prendre les mesures nécessaires en vue de protéger la santé de leurs populations et de leur assurer l'assistance médicale en cas de maladie. » De son côté, l'article 14 du Protocole de Maputo assure « le respect et la promotion des droits de la femme à la santé, y compris la santé sexuelle et reproductive ».

Le droit au meilleur état de santé s'entend de l'existence des soins, services et conditions de santé, leur accessibilité, leur acceptabilité et la qualité et impose à l'Etat le devoir de le respecter, de le réaliser et de le protéger.

Dans son Observation Générale n° 2 (Observation Générale N ° 2 sur l'Article 14.1 (a), (b), (c) et (f) et Article 14. 2 (a) et (c)) du Protocole à la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples relatif aux Droits de la Femme en Afrique), la Commission considère que le droit, pour la femme, de maîtriser sa fécondité impose à l'Etat des obligations générales de respect, de protection, de promotion et de réalisation, notamment : s'abstenir d'interférer avec ou de restreindre le contrôle des femmes sur leur fertilité ; veiller à ce qu'aucun tiers n'interfère avec le droit conféré par l'article 14(1)(a) ; veiller à ce que les femmes soient en mesure d'exercer un contrôle sur leur fertilité., y compris en prenant des mesures pour que les femmes soient conscientes de leurs droits et soient en mesure de les faire valoir et adopter des lois, des politiques, des directives et des programmes pour permettre aux femmes d'exercer leur droit de maîtriser leur fécondité.

L'article 14 (1) (b), du Protocole de Maputo impose à l'Etat l'obligation générale de respecter, de protéger, de promouvoir et de mettre en œuvre les droits conférés concernant la décision d'avoir ou non des enfants, le nombre d'enfants et l'espacement des naissances. Les Etats ne peuvent donc pas imposer aux femmes l'obligation d'avoir des enfants, d'avoir un certain nombre d'enfants (ou de limiter le nombre d'enfants) ou dicter l'espacement des enfants.

En l'espèce, la Plaignante a été victime d'un viol, perpétré par un représentant de l'Etat. Ce crime a produit des conséquences négatives permanentes sur sa santé physique, mentale et sexuelle. En outre, son droit de contrôler sa capacité reproductive et celui d'exercer un contrôle sur sa fécondité ont également été violés, car suite à cette agression, elle est tombée enceinte et a accouché en aout 2015.

A l'analyse des faits , les obligations à la charge de l'Etat n'ont pas été respectées, car aucune des recommandations formulées par la jurisprudence de la Commission y compris ses commentaires généraux, mais particulièrement l'Obligation Générale relative à l'article 1 de la Charte africaine et 2 du Protocole de Maputo qui impose aux États parties à la Charte africaine et au Protocole de reconnaître les droits qui y sont garantis et d'adopter des mesures législatives et autres pour donner effet à ces droits, devoirs et libertés, n'a été prise en charge par l'Etat partie. Il est avéré que l'Etat défendeur est défaillant en ce qui concerne la protection des droits garantis aux articles 16 de la Charte africaine et 14 du Protocole de Maputo.

Par conséquent, la Commission conclut que l'Etat congolais a failli à ses obligations découlant des dispositions de l'article 16 de la Charte africaine ainsi que de l'article 14 du Protocole de Maputo.

L'article 18(1) de la Charte africaine consacre la famille comme étant l'élément naturel et la base de la société, et devant par conséquent être protégée par l'Etat, qui veille à sa santé physique et morale.

La Commission a clairement énoncé que la séparation des membres d'une famille constitue une violation au droit contenu à l'article 18(1). Elle a également rappelé que l'Etat a une obligation positive à l'égard de la famille, qu'il se doit d'assister dans la satisfaction de ses besoins et de ses intérêts, et de protéger des abus de toute sorte de ses propres agents et organes et de parties tierces. Il doit empêcher la survenance de tout acte visant à violer les droits ainsi consacrés.

Au-delà des dispositions contenues dans la Charte africaine il est unanimement accepté que la famille constitue le socle de la société, particulièrement en Afrique où elle revêt un caractère sacré. Ainsi, assurer la protection de la famille c'est préserver l'équilibre de la nation. Il est donc primordial de s'assurer que cette protection se fasse selon les normes établies.

En l'espèce, dans le contexte socio-culturel de la région de la RDC, largement décrit et documenté, où se trouve la plaignante, il ressort des pièces du dossier de procédure que le viol et la stigmatisation conséquente à son endroit ont porté une atteinte grave à sa vie familiale en endommageant gravement sa réputation. Cela a conduit à la rupture de l'unité familiale, la détérioration de ses conditions de vie, de sa santé physique et psychologique. Et tout cela sans aucune protection ou prise en charge par l'Etat.

L'obligation d'assurer la sécurité, physique et morale de la famille implique la protection des droits sociaux économiques pour sa réalisation. Le viol subi par la victime et la grossesse qui s'en est suivie ont fait éclater la cellule familiale de la victime, du fait de sa répudiation par son époux, qui a refusé d'assumer la prise en charge de l'enfant à naître, et du rejet de sa famille biologique.

Compte tenu de ce qui précède, il ne fait aucun doute que l'Etat a failli à sa mission de protection de la vie familiale de la victime, en ne garantissant par l'unité de celle-ci. La Commission constate donc la violation effective de l'article 18(1) par l'Etat défendeur. L'article 1 de la Charte africaine impose aux États parties à la Charte africaine de reconnaître les droits qui y sont garantis, et d'adopter des mesures législatives et autres, pour donner effet à ces droits, devoirs et libertés. La même obligation est implicitement contenue dans l'article 24 du Protocole de Maputo.

La jurisprudence de la Commission a établi que toute violation de l'une des dispositions de la Charte africaine, entraîne automatiquement la violation de l'article 1. En d'autres termes, si un État partie n'assure pas le respect des droits contenus dans la Charte africaine, cela constitue une violation de l'article 1 de la Charte africaine.

Pour ce qui est de l'article 24 du Protocole de Maputo, traite de la protection spéciale des femmes en situation de détresse, et s'applique par conséquent à la situation de la plaignante. Néanmoins, dans le cas d'espèce, bien que cet article contienne une obligation implicite pour l'Etat de protéger, du point de vue structurel et substantiel, la Commission estime que c'est l'article 26 du Protocole est le pendant de l'article 1 de la Charte en termes de mise en œuvre et de suivi.

À cet égard, et après avoir constaté que l'Etat défendeur a violé plusieurs articles de la Charte africaine à savoir les articles 2 lu conjointement avec l'article 18(3), 5, 7 (1) lu conjointement avec l'article 26, 16, 18 (1) tous lus conjointement avec l'article 1 de la Charte africaine, ainsi que des articles 2, 3, 4, 8, 14, 24 et 25 du Protocole de Maputo, la Commission conclut à la violation des articles 1 de la Charte et 26 du Protocole de Maputo.

La plaignante demande à la Commission d'ordonner à la République Démocratique du Congo de lui offrir une réparation intégrale appropriée incluant des mesures d'indemnisation financière pour les préjudices matériels et immatériels causés, une réhabilitation psychologique gratuite et des mesures de réinsertion sociale et économique.

Dans sa résolution n°60/147 du 16 décembre 2005 relative aux Principes fondamentaux et directives concernant le droit à un recours et à réparation des victimes de violations flagrantes du droit international des droits de l'homme et de violations graves du droit international humanitaire, l'Assemblée Générale des Nations Unies prévoit en l'article IX ce qui suit : « Le but d'une réparation adéquate, effective et rapide est de promouvoir la justice en remédiant aux violations flagrantes du droit international des droits de l'homme ou aux violations graves du droit international humanitaire. La réparation devrait être à la mesure de la gravité de la violation et du préjudice subi. Conformément à sa législation interne et à ses obligations juridiques internationales, l'Etat assure aux victimes la réparation des actes ou omissions qui peuvent lui être imputés et qui constituent des violations flagrantes du droit international des droits de l'homme ou des violations graves du droit international humanitaire. Dans les cas où la responsabilité de la réparation incombe à une personne physique, à une personne morale ou à une autre entité, la personne ou l'entité devrait assurer réparation à la victime ou indemniser l'État lorsque celui-ci a déjà assuré réparation à la victime. »[...].« Conformément à la législation interne et au droit international, et compte tenu des circonstances de chaque cas, il devrait être assuré aux victimes de violations flagrantes du droit international des droits de l'homme et de violations graves du droit international humanitaire, selon qu'il convient et de manière proportionnée à la gravité de la violation et aux circonstances de chaque cas, une réparation pleine et effective, comme l'énoncent les principes 19 à 23, notamment sous les formes suivantes : restitution, indemnisation, réadaptation, satisfaction et garanties de non-répétition. »

Dans l'affaire IHRDA et autres c/ République du Burundi, la Commission a considéré qu'« une indemnisation devrait être accordée pour tout dommage résultant de violations flagrantes du droit international des droits de l'homme et de violations graves du droit international humanitaire, qui se prête à une évaluation économique, selon qu'il convient et de manière proportionnée à la gravité de la violation et aux circonstances de chaque cas, tel que : (a) le préjudice physique ou psychologique ;(b) les occasions perdues, y compris en ce qui concerne l'emploi, l'éducation et les prestations sociales ;(c) les dommages matériels et la perte de revenus, y compris la perte du potentiel de gains ;(d) le dommage moral et ;(e) les frais encourus pour l'assistance en justice ou les expertises, pour les médicaments et les services médicaux et pour les services psychologiques et sociaux. »

Dans le cas présent, le rapport médical de la plaignante indique notamment que de ce qu'elle a subi, il a résulté une incapacité de travail de 100 jours, une incapacité partielle permanente de 20%, une souffrance endurée très forte (-/7) et un préjudice esthétique léger. A cela s'ajoutent des conséquences psychologiques, caractérisées par une forte anxiété, de la peur et une tendance à la dépression. Par ailleurs, la situation familiale et sociale de la victime s'est également détériorée, car elle a été repudiée par son mari et a perdu sa dignité au sein de la communauté suite au viol. Pour tout cela, la plaignante s'est vu proposer un règlement à l'amiable consistant en une somme de 100 USD, une chèvre, une pièce de tissu et la reconnaissance du viol par le Lieutenant-Colonel.

Dans ses directives concernant la justice transitionnelle, le Haut-Commissariat aux droits de l'homme dit que les victimes ont droit à réparation et que ce droit se traduit par des mesures visant à tenter de remédier aux violations des droits de l'homme, en offrant aux victimes ou à leur famille, ainsi qu'aux communautés touchées, un certain nombre d'avantages, matériels et symboliques. La réparation doit être adéquate, efficace, rapide, et devrait être à la mesure de la gravité des violations et du préjudice subis.

L'analyse des faits et des preuves fournies par la plaignante, montre clairement que la réparation qui lui a été proposée ne se rapproche guère des critères précédemment cités, et ne saurait être considérée comme étant adéquate et satisfaisante au regard du préjudice subi.

En conséquence, la Commission recommande que l'Etat défendeur prenne les mesures nécessaires afin de s'assurer que la victime puisse jouir d'une indemnisation juste et équitable. 217 La Commission a déjà établi dans sa jurisprudence que les excuses publiques participent de « l'admission par l'Etat de sa qualité non seulement de civilement responsable des agissements de ses préposés, mais encore de son manquement à son obligation générale de protection de ses citoyens. » En l'espèce, l'Etat est responsable de ne pas avoir su apporter la protection nécessaire à la victime, qui a été agressée sexuellement par l'un de ses représentants. La Commission considère que les motifs sont pertinents, et dit la plaignante fondée sur ce moyen, et décide donc que l'Etat défendeur est tenu de présenter ses excuses à la victime. 218 L'article 1 de la Charte africaine impose aux Etats parties à la Charte africaine de reconnaître les droits qui y sont garantis et d'adopter des mesures législatives et autres pour donner effet à ces droits, devoirs et libertés. La même obligation est contenue dans l'article 24 du Protocole de Maputo. La prise en charge des mesures de garanties de non répétition, participe au respect de cette obligation par les Etats parties. Par ailleurs, la Résolution 22/10 du Conseil des Droits de l'Homme « (§10) engage [...] les Etats et, s'il y a lieu, les autorités gouvernementales compétentes à assurer une formation adéquate aux agents des forces de l'ordre et au personnel militaire et à promouvoir une formation adéquate dans le cas du personnel privé agissant pour le compte d'un Etat, notamment dans le domaine du droit international des droits de l'homme [...] ». Les faits ci-dessus analysés ont démontré qu'il est plus que nécessaire pour l'Etat défendeur d'acter dans le sens de la recommandation de la Résolution 22/10. La Commission, Par ces motifs, 1. Dit que la République démocratique du Congo a violé les articles 1, 2, 5, 7/1, 16, 18 et 26 de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples, ainsi que les articles 2, 3, 4, 8, 14, 24, 25 et 26 du Protocole de Maputo. 2. En conséquence, recommande à la République démocratique du Congo de bien vouloir :i. Mener une enquête prompte, approfondie et efficace sur le viol subi par la victime et les autres violations subies, par des organes judiciaires indépendants et impartiaux aux fins d'engager des poursuites pénales contre les auteurs et de les sanctionner ; ii. Offrir une réparation intégrale appropriée à la victime, incluant des mesures d'indemnisation financière pour les préjudices matériels et immatériels causés à une réhabilitation psychologique gratuite et des mesures de réinsertion sociale et économique ; iii. Mettre en place des garanties de non-répétition, en particulier par le biais d'excuses publiques adressées à la victime et d'un message fort condamnant de tels actes ; iv. Publier la décision le moment venu, dans les règles établies par la Charte 3 La Commission prie la République Démocratique du Congo de lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, les mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée lors de la 82 Session ordinaire de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples tenue virtuellement du 25 février au 11 mars 2025

This Communication is submitted by Ms. Aline BAHOGWERHE (the Complainant) against the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), a State Party to the African Charter (ratified on 20 July 1987), pursuant to Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (African Charter); the Complainant is represented by the NGO TRIAL.

The Complainant states that on 15 December 2014, at around 5:00 in the morning, in the village of Sebele, located in the territory of Fizi, in South Kivu province, where she lived with her husband, Mr. Djombo Mafutano, a Sergeant-Major 1 in the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), and their three children, someone knocked on the door of their home, calling for Mr. Mafutano, her husband. As the person knocking at the door introduced himself as Sergeant Loketo, a colleague of Mr. Mafutano, the latter opened the door. Sergeant Loketo then told him that Lieutenant-Colonel Kyatula Muke, commander of the 1 Battalion from the 3301 - Regiment of the FARDC based at Sebele, had instructed him to come and fetch him, without disclosing the reason. The Complainant's husband therefore went to the place where he had been summoned.

The Complainant indicates that at around 14:00 on the same day of 15 December 2015, worried and without news of her husband, she went to the military base and found her husband in detention, on the order of the Lieutenant-Colonel. However, the latter had not yet communicated the reasons to her. This detention at the military base lasted five (5) days without the reason for his arrest being communicated. The Complainant adds that during the five days of her husband's detention, Lieutenant-Colonel Kyatula Muke regularly passed in front of their house, on his way to visit a house under construction about 500 metres from their home.
The Complainant states that on 17 December 2014, while she was doing housework in front of her home, she saw Lieutenant-Colonel Muke walk past her house; the latter greeted her for the first time.

The Complainant adds that on 19 December 2014, in the morning, she saw Lieutenant-Colonel Muke pass in front of her house a second time; she then decided to ask him the reasons for her husband's detention; in response, he asked her to prepare a meal for him and said that he would explain on his return. The Complainant did not see him again that day.

The Complainant states that on 20 December 2014, at around 9:00 in the morning, while she was working in front of her house, Ms. Safi, a woman living in the neighbourhood, invited her to her home to look at clothes offered for sale. Interested, she went there, the latter's home being about thirty minutes' walk away. On the premises, Ms. Safi invited her to go and sit in the living room and, on entering, she saw Lieutenant-Colonel Muke and became frightened. Ms. Safi then admitted to her that in reality she had no clothes to sell, but that she had called her for the Lieutenant-Colonel.

The Complainant further adds that, despite the fear she felt, she had tried to reassure herself by thinking that she might obtain information about her husband's detention, but this was not the case. Finally feeling in danger in the presence of Lieutenant-Colonel Muke, she tried to leave the house, but Lieutenant-Colonel Muke grabbed her forcefully by her skirt and told her that he had made her come in order to have sexual intercourse with her and that it was only by this means that she could hope to obtain the release of her husband. The Complainant alleges that Lieutenant-Colonel Muke ultimately raped her and that, despite her efforts to call for help, no one intervened, and that Ms. Safi, who heard everything from outside, did not come to her rescue.

The Complainant mentions that at around 19:00, she went to the place where her husband was detained to give him food, and informed him of the situation. However, he asked her not to say anything until his release.

The Complainant states that she went to the hospital on 20 December 2014 but did not inform the nurses of the facts of the rape; she specifies that she confined herself to mentioning the pains she felt in her body in a general way. It was in early January that she decided, with her husband's consent, to go to the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) hospital, where she was taken in charge by a specialised unit.

The Complainant asserts that, paradoxically, Lieutenant-Colonel Muke lodged a complaint against her, her husband and Mr. Bosembe, a Chaplain of the FARDC unit, before the Bureau 5 of the unit, accusing them of spreading false information against him.

The Complainant adds that, having become aware of the existence of the NGO Arche d'Alliance, she decided to consult this organisation in order to obtain advice and assistance; Arche d'Alliance then suggested to her the possibility of reporting Lieutenant-Colonel Muke; it was thus that she decided to bring a legal action against him.

The Complainant specifies that in the course of January 2015, with the support of Arche d'Alliance, she seized the Civil Public Prosecutor's Office of Fizi, which then seized the Garrison Military Prosecutor's Office of Baraka, the competent authority.
The Complainant alleges that after several hearings, the military prosecutor's office proposed to her that she accept a settlement with the alleged perpetrator, which she refused.

The Complainant further alleges that on 27 November 2015, the Senior Prosecutor sent her a letter informing her that the file concerning her case was being transmitted for communication to the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office in Bukavu; however, no information has been communicated to her on her file to date, despite the requests and reminders of her lawyer.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 5, 7, 16, 18 and 26 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, as well as Articles 2, 3, 4, 8, 14, 24 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainant requests the Commission to: - Grant provisional measures to the victim and the witnesses; - Register this communication and declare it admissible; - Find that the violation of the above-mentioned provisions, read in conjunction with Article 1 of the African Charter; - Find that the facts before the Commission also reveal a violation by the State Party of the above-cited provisions of the Maputo Protocol; - Order the Democratic Republic of Congo, in application of Articles 7(1) and 26 of the African Charter, to conduct a prompt, thorough and effective investigation into the rape suffered by the victim and the other violations suffered, by independent and impartial judicial bodies, with a view to instituting criminal proceedings against the perpetrators and punishing them; - Order the Democratic Republic of Congo to provide appropriate full reparation to the victim, including measures of financial compensation for the material and non-material harm caused, free psychological rehabilitation and measures of social and economic reintegration; - Require the Democratic Republic of Congo to provide guarantees of non-repetition, in particular through a public apology addressed to the victim and a strong message condemning such acts; - Request the Democratic Republic of Congo to publish the Commission's findings; - Order the Democratic Republic of Congo to report, within a period of three months, on the follow-up it will have given to the Commission's conclusions.
The Complaint was received by the Secretariat of the Commission on 16 May 2016 and the Secretariat acknowledged receipt thereof.

During its 59 Extraordinary Session held from 21 October to 04 November 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Complaint and admitted it while rejecting the provisional measures requested by the Complainant, in that the request to that effect does not contain sufficient and satisfactory elements as required by Rule 98 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure. The Parties were informed of this decision and the Secretariat requested the Complainants to submit their observations on Admissibility.
The Secretariat received the Complainant's arguments on the admissibility of the Communication on 18 January 2017.

By Note Verbale Ref: CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/608/19 of 7 June 2019, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State that the Commission, during its 64 Ordinary Session held from 24 April to 14 May 2019, decided to defer consideration of Communication 622/16 – Aline BAHOGWERHE v. Democratic Republic of Congo to a later session in order to await its arguments. The Secretariat at the same time transmitted to the Respondent State the Complainant's arguments on admissibility while requesting it to submit its arguments pursuant to Rule 105(2) of the 2010 Rules of Procedure.

By Note Verbale Ref: CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/1129/19 of 11 September 2019, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State that the Commission had, once again, decided at its 26 Extraordinary Session held from 16 to 30 July 2019, to defer consideration of the Communication to a later session in order to await its arguments on admissibility.

Having received no response from the Respondent State until then, the Secretariat, by Note Verbale Ref: CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/599/20 of 4 September 2020, informed the State that the Commission, at its 66 Ordinary Session held from 13 July to 7 August 2020, had decided to defer consideration of the communication to a later session in order to allow the State to submit its statement in defence.

During the 73 Ordinary Session of the Commission held from 21 October to 10 November 2022, a decision on admissibility was adopted and communicated to the parties with a request to the Complainant to submit her arguments on the merits.
The Complainant submitted her arguments on the merits by letter of 13 April 2023, which arguments were transmitted to the State by Note Verbale ACHPR/STC/COMM/622/16/492/23 of 20 April 2023.
During its subsequent sessions, the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication as it had still not received the arguments of the Respondent State.

The State having largely exceeded the time limit granted to it and having moreover made no request for an extension of that time limit, the Commission instructed the Secretariat to prepare a decision on the merits by default.
The Complainant alleges that the Communication should be declared admissible as it fulfils all the conditions set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.

The Complainant maintains that the Communication indicates its authors, namely TRIAL International as Representative of the Requêteante, and Aline Bahogwerhe as the Requêteante; in accordance with Article 56 para 1 of the African Charter.
The Complainant alleges that this complaint is compatible with the Charter as well as with the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity as required by Article 56 para 2 of the Charter.

The Complainant further alleges that, in accordance with Articles 55 et seq. of the Charter, the Commission is competent to receive and consider individual communications submitted against any State Party, from the date on which the Charter entered into force for that State. She specifies that this Complaint is directed against the Democratic Republic of Congo, which is a State Party to the Charter, in force for it since 28 October 1987, that is 3 months after the deposit of the instruments of ratification. It is also specified that the facts that are the subject of this Communication took place in December 2014 and took place on Congolese territory. She therefore concludes that the Commission has full jurisdiction ratione temporis and loci to receive this Communication.

The Complainant alleges that the Communication demonstrates a prima facie violation of the provisions of Article 2 read in conjunction with Article 18 para 3; Article 5; Article 7 para 1 read in conjunction with Article 26; Article 16 and Article 18 para 1, all read in conjunction with Article 1 of the African Charter, in respect of the Requêteante who is Aline Bahogwerhe. Consequently, the Commission has jurisdiction ratione personae and materiae to hear this communication.

The Complaint also reveals the violation, in respect of Aline Bahogwerhe, of Articles 2, 3, 4, 8, 14, 24 and 25 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol), ratified by the DRC on 9 June 2008. Article 32 of the Maputo Protocol as well as Article 60 of the African Charter, which provides that the Commission shall draw inspiration from international law on human and peoples' rights, particularly from the provisions of various African instruments on human and peoples' rights, give the Commission jurisdiction to rule on violations of the said Protocol. The Complainant therefore concludes that the Commission may also find the violations of the Maputo Protocol contained in this communication.
The Complainant maintains that the Communication is not written in disparaging or insulting language as prescribed by Article 56 para 3 of the African Charter.

The Complaint maintains that the information contained in the file of this Communication is not exclusively based on news disseminated through the mass media, in accordance with Article 56 para 4 of the African Charter. It maintains that the information comes directly from the account of the Requêteante and from documents in her possession and that the text of the Communication is corroborated by reports of credible non-governmental organisations and international organisations.

With regard to local remedies, the Complainant, while reaffirming the principle recognised in Article 56 para 5 that the communication must be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure of those remedies is unduly prolonged; also recalls that this principle admits of exceptions developed by the Commission. She maintains that the existing local remedies were activated to obtain justice, but that they proved futile and ineffective and that they were unduly prolonged. She further maintains that taking further steps would not be realistic for the complainant, given her indigence and the fact that she is without legal aid.

Referring to the jurisprudence of the Commission, the Complainant recalled that, according to the Commission itself, for the purposes of the admissibility of a complaint, only the exhaustion of available, effective and sufficient local remedies can be required. She recalls that, according to the Commission, "a remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment. It is effective if it offers a prospect of success, is adequate to accomplish a purpose and can produce the result sought or expected" and it is sufficient when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the complainants.

She recalls that, according to the Commission, a remedy that has no chance of success does not constitute an effective remedy. She also notes that "the existence of a remedy must be sufficiently certain, not only in theory but also in practice, failing which it will lack the requisite accessibility and effectiveness".

The Complainant alleges that in the present case, the Requête, as soon as the facts occurred on 20 December 2014, denounced the crimes by activating all the local remedies available in order to obtain the opening of a prompt and effective investigation with a view to the prosecution of the alleged perpetrators and reparation of the harm suffered.

The Complainant considers that the procedure opened before the FARDC bureau cannot be considered effective, the reason being that this bureau has no independence, the alleged perpetrator of the violations being a hierarchical superior of the members of the bureau. As to the procedures opened before the Garrison Military Prosecutor's Office of Baraka in December 2014 and the Senior Prosecutor's Office of Bukavu in April 2015, these procedures, according to the Complainant, are not effective in view of the fact that the prosecuting authorities in question are not independent and impartial.

The Complainant further maintains that jurisprudence has established the principle that the jurisdiction of military courts must be limited to purely military offences committed by military personnel, for the proper administration of justice. She maintains in addition that the lack of independence of the prosecuting authorities in the case is apparent from the unlawful attempts at an amicable settlement of the crime of rape suffered by her, which clearly cannot be considered a sufficient remedy given that an amicable settlement is not capable of giving satisfaction and repairing the alleged violations in the case in question, and this is a manifest expression of a lack of respect towards the victim.

The Complainant maintains that, on the list of elements that demonstrate the ineffectiveness of the local remedies activated, there are other elements such as the lack of financial means alleged by the military prosecutor's office to justify the absence of thorough investigations at the scene of the crime, the impossibility of hearing the witnesses and even the alleged perpetrator of the violations given that his hearing was conditional on authorisation by the military command.

The Complainant further maintains that important rules of Congolese criminal procedure on sexual violence were not respected. By way of example, contrary to Article 7 bis of Law No. 06/019 of 20 July 2006 amending and supplementing the Decree of 06 August 1959 on the Congolese Code of Criminal Procedure, the complainant was not assisted by counsel during all phases of the procedure. Likewise, contrary to Article 14 of the same law, the judicial authorities did not require "a doctor and psychologist in order to assess the condition of the victim of sexual violence and to determine the appropriate care as well as to evaluate the extent of the harm suffered by the victim and its subsequent aggravation".

The Complainant concludes by affirming that it is clear that remedies were activated but proved ineffective and that, given the general climate of impunity of perpetrators of crimes of sexual violence and the passivity of the prosecuting authorities, it is obvious that at present, the pending judicial remedies have absolutely no chance of success. She adds that this has only been confirmed over time since, since the submission of the Communication in April 2016, the continuous steps taken informally by her lawyer to revive the proceedings have led to no concrete result and no progress has been recorded in the file. She affirms that, on the contrary, there was an attempt to intimidate her, since, on 4 June 2016, on the orders of Lt-Colonel Kyatula Muke, an individual attempted to end the life of the Requêteuse. The Complainant recalls that an urgent request for an immediate provisional measure had been addressed to the Commission to that effect.

She also maintains that the remedies were unduly prolonged, insofar as there was a delay in the initiation of the investigation and a delay is observed in the overall duration of the pending procedure. She further notes that the requirement of local remedies is not realistic because of the indigence of the Requêteuse, and explains that she is in a very precarious economic situation.
The Complainant maintains that this Communication was submitted within a reasonable time, which ran from the moment she realised that local remedies were ineffective.
The Complainant maintains that the file of this complaint has not been submitted to any other international procedure of investigation or settlement.

The Commission notes that while the Complainant has provided arguments on the admissibility of her Complaint, the Respondent State, despite the multiple notifications and reminders by Notes Verbales Ref: CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/608/19 of 7 June 2019, CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/1129/19 of 11 September 2019 and CADPH/COMM/622/16/RDC/599/20 of 4 September 2020 respectively, sent by the Secretariat of the Commission, has provided no arguments.

The jurisprudence of the Commission in such circumstances provides that it rules on admissibility by default. The Commission will then conduct its analysis solely on the basis of the elements presented by the Complainant.
The present case is brought under Article 55 of the Charter and, as such, must satisfy the seven (7) cumulative conditions of Article 56 of the Charter for the admissibility of communications.
Article 56(1) of the African Charter provides that Communications must indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity.

The Commission agrees with the Complainant that the identity of the author of the Communication is indicated. It notes that all the information establishing this identity is contained in the Communication. These are Aline BAHOGWERHE, of Congolese nationality, represented by the NGO TRIAL. The authors of the Communication are clearly identified and, a fortiori, do not request anonymity. Consequently, the Commission considers that this admissibility condition is satisfied.
In accordance with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Communication must be compatible with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter.

The Commission affirmed in the case of Law Society of Zimbabwe v. Zimbabwe that the compatibility of a Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union rests on its compatibility with the objectives and principles enshrined in the Act, and more precisely on the question whether the claims of the Communication would not contravene the objectives or principles expressed in the Act. In this sense, the Commission considers that no aspect of this communication could be considered contrary to any of the objectives or principles of the Constitutive Act.

As to the criterion of compatibility with the African Charter, it should be noted that a Communication against a State is admissible on condition that the State is a party to the Charter and that the alleged violations of rights concern rights guaranteed by the African Charter. In addition, the alleged violations must have been committed on the territory or under the jurisdiction of the State concerned, and after the entry into force of the Charter for that particular State.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that the Communication is directed against the Democratic Republic of Congo, a State Party to the African Charter, which entered into force for it on 28 October 1987. The rights whose violation the Complainant alleges are protected by Article 2 read in conjunction with Article 18 para 3, Article 5, Article 7 para 1 read in conjunction with Article 26, Article 16 and Article 18 para 1, all read in conjunction with Article 1 of the African Charter.

After analysis of the foregoing, the Commission concludes that the alleged violations took place on the territory of the Respondent State, and that the State concerned is indeed a party to the African Charter. It also notes that the facts did indeed occur after the entry into force of the Charter for the DRC

Article 56(3) of the African Charter provides that Communications shall be considered if they are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the Organisation of African Unity.

The Complainant maintains that the Communication is written in respectful language, and consequently meets the requirement of Article 56(4) of the African Charter, which prohibits the use of insulting and disparaging language.

The Commission, having thoroughly reviewed the entire file of this Communication, is convinced that it contains no disparaging or insulting language directed against the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. It therefore concludes that the admissibility condition laid down in Article 56(3) of the Charter is met by the Complainants.

Article 56(4) of the African Charter prohibits Complaints brought before the Commission under Article 55 of the same Charter from being "limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through the mass media".

The Commission considers that there is nothing to suggest that the statements contained in this communication are limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through the mass media. In addition, the Complainant has assured the Commission that the facts refer to a direct account by the victim of the violations and to documents in her possession. She also adds that the text of the Communication is corroborated by reports published by credible non-governmental and international organisations; although she has not provided proof to establish this.
Nevertheless, given the facts established above by the Complainant, the Commission considers that the condition of Article 56(4) of the African Charter is sufficiently fulfilled.
Communications are considered only if they are "sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged."

However, it emerges from the jurisprudence of the Commission that, for the purposes of the admissibility of a Communication, only the exhaustion of available, effective and sufficient local remedies is required.

In the case of Anuak Justice Council v. Ethiopia, the Commission established that a remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment and it is effective if it offers a prospect of success, is adequate to accomplish a purpose and can produce satisfaction for the complainant.

The Commission has also established that "a remedy which has no chance of success does not constitute an effective remedy" and that "the existence of a remedy must be sufficiently certain, not only in theory but also in practice.

In the present case, the Complainant alleges that the local remedies proved ineffective and unsatisfactory, that they were unduly prolonged and that they are not realistic because of the indigence of the victim.

She alleges that the procedure opened before the FARDC unit could not be considered an effective remedy in view of the fact that the members of that body were hierarchical subordinates of the alleged perpetrator of the crime.

The Commission agrees with the Complainant that this fact does not respect the principles of proper administration of justice since it offers no guarantee of independence, impartiality and neutrality.

Concerning the judicial remedies pursued, the Complainant maintains that the procedures activated before the Garrison Military Prosecutor's Office of Baraka in December 2014 and before the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office of Bukavu in April 2015 are not effective for lack of independence and impartiality of the prosecuting authorities.

This lack of independence is further evident at the level of the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office of Bukavu, which needed to obtain the prior authorisation of the military command in order to be able to hear the alleged perpetrator, which would also have prevented any progress in the file.

The Commission recognises that its jurisprudence establishes that the principle of exhaustion of local remedies may admit of exceptions and that complainants are required to exhaust such remedies only insofar as they are available, effective and sufficient.

However, the Commission is not of the view, in its jurisprudence as established in the case of Kenya and Kituo Cha Sheria v Kenya, that mere apprehension about the independence of the judicial system of a Respondent State would be a valid argument for setting aside the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies.

The Commission therefore reiterates that unless the Complainants are able to demonstrate a personal situation that would render local remedies unavailable or ineffective in their particular case, arguments relating to the general state of the judicial system are not sufficient.

Accordingly, the Commission confines itself to analysing the elements that could constitute the personal situation that would have rendered local remedies unavailable or ineffective, as presented above.

The Commission does not consider well founded the argument of the complainants that the military courts have no jurisdiction to hear this case for the sole reason that the offence in question is an ordinary law offence. It considers that the judicial organisation and the distribution of jurisdiction among courts fall within the exclusive domain of States and that it is a matter of their sovereignty.

However, the Commission, examining the personal elements that could effectively justify the independence of the military courts before which the file is pending, finds on the one hand that the step taken with a view to achieving an amicable settlement was tainted by an irregularity, insofar as it clearly appears that the consent of the victim was absent, knowing that the consent of both parties is one of the necessary conditions for contemplating an amicable settlement. On the other hand, the Commission considers that the justifications, such as the lack of financial means, put forward by the prosecuting authorities in support of their inaction, in particular for not having conducted investigations at the scene of the rape, clearly demonstrate the ill will of these authorities to pursue the file. The facts of attempted intimidation alleged by the Complainant in her additional information also largely bear this out.
The Commission concludes that the personal situations that are cited and that have been analysed are sufficiently strong to justify the unavailability and ineffectiveness of local remedies.

However, as regards the Complainant's lack of means and the absence of legal assistance in accordance with Article 7 bis of Law No. 06/019 of 20 July 2006 amending and supplementing the Congolese Code of Criminal Procedure, the Commission considers that the Complainant has not established whether she initiated all relevant procedures to obtain legal assistance before it was refused to her, and consequently, this does not sufficiently establish a justified argument concerning the need to exhaust local remedies under Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

The Commission also considers that the fact that the Court did not prescribe a medical examination for the Complainant as a victim of sexual violence, in accordance with Article 14 of the same law, does not sufficiently justify the need to exhaust local remedies.

On the question of the undue prolongation of local remedies, the Commission recalls that the notion of undue prolongation has not been circumscribed, but that its jurisprudence provides certain indications relating to the promptness of the initiation of investigations and the overall duration of the pending procedure.

In the case of Abdel Hadi, Ali Radi and Others v. Republic of Sudan, the Commission held that "allegations of torture against public officials place on the State the immediate obligation to open a prompt, impartial and effective investigation in order to establish the truth of these allegations and to bring the perpetrators to justice if the allegations are well founded". The Commission also stated that "what is important is whether the Respondent State had knowledge of these allegations and whether it took steps to investigate these allegations".

In the present case, which is a case of rape, the victim was heard only more than a month after the occurrence of the facts, and with the aim of proceeding to an amicable settlement without her having previously given her consent. Moreover, no measure was taken by the prosecuting authorities to document the sexual violence.

The Commission notes that Congolese legislation provides that "the preliminary investigation in matters of sexual violence shall be carried out within a maximum period of one month from the seizure of the judicial authority and that the investigation and the delivery of judgment shall take place within a period of 3 months from the seizure of the judicial authority." The Commission observes that neither the time taken to initiate the investigations nor the overall duration of the procedure complies with the legislative provisions in force, since until the submission of the complaint before the Commission on 25 April 2016, there was no prospect of the file being brought to a conclusion.

To conclude, the Commission considers, after analysis, that the Complainant faced considerable obstacles that constituted a hindrance to her obtaining redress. It therefore considers that the remedies were neither effective nor satisfactory for the victim.

According to the wording of Article 56(6) of the Charter, the Commission must not take up Communications that are not "submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter".

The Complainant alleges that this period is 6 months according to the jurisprudence of international bodies such as the European Court of Human Rights, but that the autonomous 6-month rule must be adapted to each specific context.

The Commission affirms that the notion of reasonable time has not been circumscribed by it. It also agrees with the Complainant that the reasonable time must be determined on a case-by-case basis, and recalls that it had already established this principle.

The Complainant maintains that from the occurrence of the facts in December 2014 to the seizure of the Commission on 25 April 2016, time did indeed elapse, but this time is justified insofar as actions were ongoing throughout that period. She affirms that it was in the face of the apparent blockage of the file and after the multiple attempts to revive it to enable the prosecuting authorities to restore her rights, that she considered at the beginning of 2016 that local remedies had no chance of success. She explains that, as a final attempt to revive the file, she filed yet another follow-up letter with the Senior Military Prosecutor in charge of the file on 12 April 2016, correspondence that allegedly again remained unanswered. It was then that she contemplated recourse to the Commission and the actual submission of her complaint took place on 25 April 2016, which according to her falls within a reasonable time.

The Commission maintains that as a general rule, where local remedies are unavailable or ineffective, complainants must submit their complaint to the Commission as soon as they realise or should have realised that local remedies are unavailable or ineffective.

The Commission notes the multiple actions undertaken by the Complainant with the aim of obtaining follow-up from the prosecuting authorities, including the last procedural act dated 12 April. It considers that the period between that date and 25 April, the date on which the Complaint was received, is a reasonable time and considers that this time could have been used for the overall preparation of the file, including the search for representatives, the drafting of the file, the setting up of the strategy, etc. Consequently, the Commission considers that the condition laid down in Article 56(6) is met.

Article 56(7) of the Charter obliges the Commission not to admit as admissible any complaint that concerns "cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter".

The Commission found in this Communication no element or evidence contrary to the Complainant's assertion that her Complaint satisfies the admissibility conditions provided for in Article 56(7) of the Charter and does not fall within the category of cases already settled. Thus, for the Commission, this admissibility condition contained in Article 56(7) of the Charter must also be considered satisfied.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares this Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the African Charter.

The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 2 read in conjunction with Article 18(3), 5, 7(1) read in conjunction with Article 26, 16, 18(1), all read in conjunction with Article 1 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, as well as Articles 2, 3, 4, 8, 14, 24 and 25 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol).

The Complainant maintains that the provisions of Article 2 of the African Charter entitle every individual to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognised and guaranteed in the Charter without distinction of any kind, in particular [...] that based on sex".

That according to Article 18(3) of the African Charter, "the State shall ensure the elimination of every discrimination against women and also ensure the protection of the rights of the woman and the child as stipulated in international declarations and conventions". This obligation is reinforced by Article 2(1) of the Maputo Protocol, which requires States to combat discrimination against women in all its forms by adopting appropriate measures at the legislative, institutional and other levels. States must in particular undertake to adopt and effectively implement appropriate legislative and regulatory measures, including those prohibiting and curbing all forms of discrimination and harmful practices that endanger the health and general well-being of women.

The Complainant indicates that the Commission in its jurisprudence has considered that the principle of non-discrimination enshrined in Articles 2 and 18(3) ensures protection against discrimination against women; That the Commission has indicated that "discrimination may be defined as the application of any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference based on (...) sex and having the purpose or effect of nullifying or impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by all persons, on an equal footing, of all rights and freedoms."

The Complainant also adds that the Maputo Protocol defines discrimination as "any distinction, exclusion or restriction or any differential treatment based on sex and whose objectives or effects compromise or destroy the recognition, enjoyment or the exercise by women, regardless of their marital status, of human rights and fundamental freedoms in all spheres of life".

The Complainant further cites the provisions of General Recommendation No. 19 of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), which emphasises that the "definition of violence against women includes gender-based violence, that is, violence that is directed against a woman because she is a woman or that affects women disproportionately. It includes acts that inflict physical, mental or sexual harm or suffering, threats of such acts, coercion and other deprivations of liberty. Gender-based violence may breach specific provisions of the Convention, regardless of whether those provisions expressly mention violence".

She adds in particular that the Commission has already been confronted with the application of Articles 2 and 18(3) to a case of violence of a sexual nature and that Article 1 of the Maputo Protocol, in affirming that the definition of acts of violence against women includes "all acts perpetrated against women which cause or could cause them physical, sexual, psychological, and economic harm"

The complainant further submits that the crime of rape of which she was a victim was committed by a representative of the Congolese State and constitutes an act of sexual violence against her, particularly because she was unable to benefit from any protection either before or after the violence suffered, in a social context of discrimination against women that has had profound negative repercussions on her, physically, psychologically and economically. As determined by the Commission, there was no reasonable criterion that could justify the discrimination suffered in a case of sexual violence and, in this instance, this was made possible because of the situation of vulnerability in which she was already placed. In addition, the rape is part of the context of widespread and systematic sexual violence committed against women in the East of the Democratic Republic of Congo by members of the army

Finally, the complainant considers that the Congolese State did not take adequate measures to prevent and punish these forms of discrimination that endanger the health and general well-being of women; consequently she asks the Commission to find the violation by the State of Articles 2 and 18(3) of the African Charter as well as of Article 2(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainant submits the following: Article 5 of the African Charter provides that "every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited".

Likewise, Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol affirms that "every woman shall have the right to dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition and protection of her human and legal rights". Moreover, Article 4(1) of the same Protocol declares that "every woman shall be entitled to respect for her life and the integrity and security of her person. All forms of exploitation, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited."

She also indicates that Article 5 prohibits "not only torture, but also cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment", which therefore includes acts causing severe physical or psychological suffering as well as those that humiliate the individual or force him or her to act against his or her will or conscience". She adds that the Commission has specified that "the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment is to be interpreted as widely as possible to encompass the widest possible array of physical and mental abuses."

The complainant further submits that it is fundamental to emphasise that rape is considered a form of torture by international jurisprudence, notably in the jurisprudence of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (AKayezu case, 1992), which concluded that "[l]ike torture, rape is used for such purposes as intimidation, degradation, humiliation, discrimination, punishment, control or destruction of a person. Like torture, rape is a violation of personal dignity, and rape in fact constitutes torture when inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity."
Moreover, several medical studies conducted on rape have confirmed that "the trauma suffered in terms of physical symptoms and emotional distress is similar to that of other victims of torture."

The complainant finally adds that the Commission has characterised rape as a form of torture and ill-treatment contrary to Article 5 of the African Charter, notably in a case concerning the Democratic Republic of Congo; it had also considered that "the rape of women and girls (...) is also a violation of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women."

The Complainant also cites the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, the United Nations Human Rights Committee, as well as the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which have likewise considered rape as "a particularly grave and abhorrent form of ill-treatment", "a form of extreme gender-based sexual violence" and specified that "rape may constitute torture even when it is based on a single act and takes place outside public establishments, for example in the victim's home (...)".

The complainant considers that she was the victim of a sexual assault of extreme gravity, namely the crime of rape. In particular, she was forced and thrown to the ground, the perpetrator of the crime violently spread her legs, got on top of her and penetrated her by force. She no longer remembers how long he spent on top of her; She cried out loudly calling for help but no one came to her aid. This crime caused acute suffering and even today, a serious impact on her health, both physical and psychological. These allegations are supported by a medical report that confirms the consistency of the account, including the behaviour of the victim (anxiety, fear, depressive tendency) and the presence of a pregnancy. The consequences of the assault of which she was a victim have resulted in permanent physical and psychological damage.

Finally, she indicates that the perpetrator of the crime is a representative of the Congolese State, namely a Lieutenant-Colonel in the army whom she knew. Taking into account the course of events, it emerges that these actions were premeditated and intentional and carried out with the help of an accomplice after the victim's husband had first been placed in detention in order to remove him from his wife so that he could not protect her.

As regards obligations, the Complainant submits that by virtue of Article 5 of the African Charter and Articles 3 and 5 of the Maputo Protocol, States have obligations, in particular that of taking measures aimed at preventing the occurrence of such acts by putting in place "effective solutions in a transparent, independent and effective legal system" and by conducting effective and independent investigations into these allegations. States must also punish the perpetrators of acts of torture and guarantee full reparation to the victims.

The effective implementation of Articles 3(4) and 4(2) of the Maputo Protocol presupposes that States have the obligation to adopt and implement "appropriate measures to ensure the protection of every woman's right to respect for her dignity and protection of women from all forms of violence, particularly sexual violence (...)." and that the State must "punish the perpetrators of violence against women and implement programmes for the rehabilitation of women victims."

The complainant submits that the Commission analysed the obligation to conduct effective investigations into allegations of sexual violence in a case concerning Egypt, referring to the Guidelines and Measures for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture, Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment in Africa (Robben Island Guidelines), which provide that "in the event of an allegation of torture or ill-treatment, an impartial and effective investigation must be opened without delay and conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the United Nations Manual on the Effective Investigation and Documentation of Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment."

She also cites the jurisprudence of the Human Rights Committee, which imposes an obligation to conduct prompt, impartial, independent and effective investigations into allegations of serious human rights violations. In this regard, the Committee has affirmed that "these obligations arise notably in respect of those violations recognised as criminal under either domestic or international law, notably torture and similar cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (article 7), summary and arbitrary killing (article 6) and enforced disappearance (articles 7 and 9 and, frequently, 6).

She indicates that she reported the violations of which she was a victim in January and April 2015 and has since undertaken numerous steps with the various national institutions in order to advance the proceedings. However, in the face of the slowness of the Congolese judicial system, she showed diligence and pro-activity for more than a year, but in vain.

She emphasises that the procedure opened before the Bureau 5 of the FARDC Unit based at Sebele is not an effective and adequate remedy to bring those responsible to justice and guarantee reparation for the victim in her case. Indeed, despite the numerous reminders to the various bodies in charge of her file, the authorities are in flagrant violation of the time limits set by national legislation, which is compounded by the generalised context of impunity for the perpetrators of crimes of sexual violence and of stigmatisation of victims in the DRC.

In conclusion, the complainant asks the Commission to find the violation of Article 5 of the African Charter as well as Articles 3 and 4 of the Maputo Protocol and the failure to comply with the positive obligations arising from these articles by the Respondent State. Of the violation of Articles 7(1)(a), Article 26 of the African Charter and Articles 8 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol on the right to an effective remedy before independent courts

Under Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter "every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: [...] the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force."

Moreover, Article 26 of the African Charter requires States "to guarantee the independence of the Courts and [to] allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter", an essential component for guaranteeing victims an effective remedy before domestic judicial institutions.

The complainant submits that the Commission has interpreted this article as recognising the right of complainants to have "unimpeded access to a competent court or tribunal to hear their case." According to the jurisprudence developed, a competent body is a body that holds the power by law to investigate the case and to try the person subject to prosecution.

She also indicates that the protection granted by Article 7(1)(a) is not limited to persons arrested and detained but "it includes the right of everyone to have access to the relevant judicial bodies with the competence to hear their case and to grant them adequate reparation, as well as to any other individual"

She adds that the Commission has specified that "[u]nder Article 7(1) of the African Charter, anyone who feels that his or her rights have been violated has the right to bring his or her case before the competent national courts. The position or status of the victim or of the alleged perpetrator is therefore immaterial. This means that a person whose rights have been violated, including by persons acting in their official capacity, should have an effective remedy before a competent, impartial judicial body and enjoy the right to have his or her cause heard without any discrimination".

The Commission has also considered that where victims are prevented from accessing the courts to have their case heard, State authorities violate Article 7(1) of the African Charter. It has also considered that "where the competent authorities place obstacles in the way of victims' access to the courts, they must be held responsible".

The Complainant then adds that the Commission has already read Articles 7(1) and 26 of the African Charter together, affirming that "Article 7 is based on the right to be heard by impartial courts, and Article 26 stresses the independence of courts; the Commission notes that it is the duty of States to establish credible institutions that can enable the promotion and protection of human rights. Article 26 being thus the necessary appendage of Article 7, one can only hope for a fair trial before impartial tribunals and courts". With regard to the independence of a court, the Commission specified that "in all cases, the independence of a court must be assessed in relation to the degree of independence of the judiciary from the executive. This implies that account be taken of the manner in which its members are appointed, the duration of their term of office, the existence of protection against external pressures and whether or not there is an appearance of independence, according to the adage that justice must not only be done, it must also be seen to be done".

The Complainant also emphasises that the Maputo Protocol confers special protection on women by affirming in Article 8 that "women and men are equal before the law and shall have the right to equal protection and benefit of the law. States shall take all appropriate measures to ensure: a) effective access by women to legal and judicial assistance and services." Article 25 of the Protocol adds that "[s]tates undertake to guarantee appropriate reparation to any woman whose rights and freedoms, as recognised in this Protocol, are violated".

The complainant indicates that she undertook several steps to report the crime suffered, to obtain justice and reparation. She reported the perpetrator of the crime before the Garrison Military Prosecutor's Office of Baraka and the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office of Bukavu, the competent authorities for these allegations. She reports having been heard in the absence of any legal assistance and was offered an amicable settlement far below the minimum required for the purposes of justice and reparation for a rape victim and moreover totally unlawful. Indeed, she was offered a sum of 100 USD, a goat, a piece of cloth and the Lieutenant-Colonel's acknowledgment of the rape.

As regards the criminal complaint lodged with the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office in Bukavu, the authorities were unable to carry out a single act of investigation effectively, even having to obtain the authorisation of the military command in order to be able to hear the alleged perpetrator of the violations. The complainant explains that despite the multiple reminders, the authorities did nothing, thereby violating the time limits prescribed by law and, several years after the crime, they have not taken any effective investigative step; the facts therefore remain unpunished and she has never received reparation.
All these acts combined contributed to the violation of the complainant's right to effective access to and an effective remedy before the national courts.

In view of the foregoing, she therefore asks the Commission to find the violation by the Respondent State of Articles 7(1)(a) and 26 of the African Charter as well as Articles 8 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainant submits that Article 16 of the African Charter provides that "every individual shall have the right to enjoy the best attainable state of physical and mental health" and that "States Parties to the present Charter shall take the necessary measures to protect the health of their people and to ensure that they receive medical attention when they are sick".

The Commission has affirmed that "the enjoyment of the right to health as widely understood is vital to all aspects of a person's life and well-being, and is crucial to the realisation of all the other fundamental human rights and freedoms."

She also adds that the Maputo Protocol in its Article 14 ensures "the respect and promotion of women's right to health, including sexual and reproductive health". These rights include in particular the right to control their fertility, the right to decide whether to have children and the right to self-protection and to be protected against sexually transmitted infections.

The Complainant indicates that the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights has specified that "the right to health, like all human rights, imposes three types or levels of obligations on States parties: the obligations to respect, protect and fulfil. [...] The obligation to respect requires States to refrain from interfering directly or indirectly with the enjoyment of the right to health".

The Complainant also submits that in a case concerning Egypt, the Commission found that the sexual assaults perpetrated against the victims caused physical, psychological and sexual harm and trauma. This violence affected their physical and psychological health in violation of the article of the Charter. She therefore respectfully asks the Commission to apply, mutatis mutandis, these criteria and arguments to the facts described in this communication.

She indicates, indeed, that her right to physical, psychological and sexual health was violated. She suffered a crime of sexual violence, namely a rape, perpetrated by a representative of the State. This crime had permanent negative consequences for her physical, mental and sexual health. Her medical report indicates in particular that she received an incapacity for work of 100 days, a permanent partial incapacity of 20%, very severe suffering endured (-/7) and a slight aesthetic prejudice.

To this are added the psychological consequences characterised by strong anxiety, fear and a tendency towards depression. Moreover, the family and social situation of the victim also deteriorated because she was repudiated by her husband and lost her dignity within the community following the rape.

Her right to control her reproductive capacity and that of exercising control over her fertility were also denied to her because as a result of the assault, she became pregnant and gave birth to a child presumed to be the result of the rape in August 2015.
The complainant therefore asks the Commission to find the violation of Article 16 of the African Charter as well as of Article 14 of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainant indicates that Article 18(1) of the African Charter provides that "the family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral".

To that end, she cites the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which has specified the scope of the right to protection of the family provided for in Articles 17 and 23 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, affirming in particular that "the protection of this right must be guaranteed against all such interferences and attacks on the protection of this right." It also added that "[t]his right is violated, for example, where a woman's sexual history is taken into consideration in deciding the extent of her legal rights and protection, including protection against rape".

The European Court of Human Rights has also considered rape and other forms of sexual abuse as serious interferences with the private and family life of the victims in violation of Article 8 of the European Convention. The Inter-American Court has also found a violation of the right to family life in the case of a girl raped by State agents in a context of armed conflict.

The complainant submits that in the present case, the socio-cultural context of the region of the DRC where she is located, the rape and the resulting stigmatisation of her have seriously impaired her family life by gravely damaging her reputation. This led to the breakdown of the family unit and the deterioration of her living conditions and of her physical and psychological health. And all this without any protection or support from the State.
She therefore asks the Commission to find the violation of Article 18(1) of the African Charter by the Respondent State in respect of her.

The complainant recalls the obligation of protection contained in Article 1 of the African Charter and Article 24 of the Maputo Protocol, in particular that of adopting all necessary measures for their respect.

The Maputo Protocol, in Article 24, obliges States to take specific protective measures in respect of women in distress, including pregnant women and women in situations of need, particularly with regard to their physical, economic and social condition.
The complainant further emphasises that the Commission has already clarified that "any violation of any of its provisions is [therefore] automatically a violation of Article 1"

She also added that the obligations resting on States parties are threefold: the respect, protection and fulfilment of rights. In this regard, the Commission has defined them as follows: "[a] State complies with the obligation to respect recognised rights by avoiding violating them. To protect is to take the necessary measures, in accordance with its constitutional rules and the provisions of the relevant treaty (in this case the African Charter), to adopt the legislative or other measures that are necessary to give effect to these rights; To fulfil rights means that every person whose rights are [violated] is entitled to an effective remedy, since rights without reparation have little value."

The complainant also indicates that the Commission has also added the positive obligation to promote human rights: "at the first level, the obligation to respect human rights requires the State to refrain from interfering in the enjoyment of all fundamental rights; it must respect right holders, protected against political, economic and social interference. Protection generally requires the creation and maintenance of an environment or framework of effective interaction of laws and regulations so that individuals are able to freely exercise their rights and freedoms. This is very closely linked to the third obligation of the State to promote the enjoyment of all human rights. The State should make sure that individuals are able to exercise their rights and freedoms, for example, by promoting tolerance, raising awareness, and even building infrastructure. The last level of obligation of the State requires it to fulfil rights and freedoms in accordance with the various human rights instruments to which it has freely consented. It is more a positive expectation on the part of the State to direct its system towards the effective realisation of rights."

Finally the complainant submits that the Commission has had occasion to recall that, while "aware that States may be confronted with difficult situations, the Charter does not provide for general provisions allowing States to derogate from their responsibilities in situations of emergency, especially where so-called non-derogable rights are concerned, "such as the right to life or the right not to be subjected to torture."

In conclusion, the complainant indicates that several rights and freedoms protected by the African Charter were violated by the Democratic Republic of Congo, because the State did not comply with its obligations to respect, protect, guarantee and promote the rights and freedoms of the victim who was raped by State agents and despite her heightened need for protection, in particular due to her vulnerability, the authorities carried out no effective investigation into the facts that could have enabled the prosecution of the perpetrators and reparation for the victim.
The complainant therefore asks that the Commission find the violation of Article 1 of the African Charter and Article 24 of the Maputo Protocol against her.

As the procedure indicates, despite the time elapsed well beyond the time limits prescribed by the Rules of Procedure of the Commission, the Respondent State has not transmitted its observations on the merits.
The Commission will proceed to analyse the merits of this case solely on the basis of the Complainant's arguments and the information available to it (Rules of Procedure, 120-2)

According to the provisions of Article 2 of the African Charter, "every individual shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the present Charter without distinction of any kind such as [...] sex." Article 18(3) requires the State to "[...] ensure the elimination of every discrimination against women and also ensure the protection of the rights of the woman and the child as stipulated in international declarations and conventions".

Article 2(1) of the Maputo Protocol enjoins States to combat discrimination against women in all its forms, by adopting appropriate measures at the legislative, institutional and other levels. States must in particular undertake to adopt and effectively implement legislative and regulatory measures prohibiting and curbing all forms of discrimination and harmful practices that endanger the health and general well-being of women.
