Elle se prononce dans les mêmes conditions sur les décisions non susceptibles d'appel rendues par toute juridiction des États Parties dans les mêmes contentieux. En cas de cassation, elle évoque et statue sur le fond. La Commission fait observer que la présente Communication concerne une affaire qui rentre dans le cadre des Actes Uniformes OHADA. A cet égard, la Commission a déjà conclu que la CCJA est un recours interne au sens de l'article 56(5). Cette position est confirmée par la législation et la jurisprudence tant internes qu'internationales.

En l'espèce, la Commission constate que les faits allégués n'ont été portés que devant les juridictions nationales qui ont connu des plaintes y afférentes et rendu des décisions. En outre, l'affaire n'est pendante devant aucun autre organe visé aux dispositions du même article. Enfin, et par conséquent, il n'y a pas lieu de craindre que l'Etat défendeur puisse faire l'objet d'une double poursuite encore moins d'une condamnation dans cette même cause. La Commission en conclut que la Communication respecte la condition examinée. La Commission constate par conséquent qu'il s'agit d'une Communication qui n'a pas été réglée suivant les termes de l'article 56(7) de la Charte et en conclut qu'elle respecte le critère posé par les dispositions dudit article.
Pour ces motifs, la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples déclare la présente Communication recevable conformément à l'Article 56 de la Charte africaine.

Le Plaignant allègue que le service de Greffe de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun ainsi que celui du secrétariat particulier de son Premier Président ont catégoriquement refusé d'enregistrer une nouvelle requête de Dame ETOUMAN et la SARL METIS aux fins de sursis à exécution de l'Arrêt N°171/REF rendu le 09 mars 2018 par la Cour d'Appel du Centre.
Il indique que ladite requête trouvait son juste fondement dans le recours en cassation introduit devant la CCJA, et auquel la Haute juridiction s'était déclarée incompetent rationae materiae.

Le Plaignant indique en outre que face à ces refus inattendus et illégaux, les conseils des victimes avaient entrepris de rencontrer le Premier Président de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun afin de dénoncer directement cette situation abusive de son greffe, mais tout accès leur avait été refusé par le responsable du service du Protocole de son Cabinet.

Il rapporte qu'afin de ne pas compromettre les délais impartis en l'espèce, la requête aux fins de sursis à exécution a été transmise par les services de courriers urgents de la poste au Secrétariat du Premier Président contre décharge valant accusé de réception.

Il allègue que malgré ladite décharge, les victimes se sont toujours vues refuser la délivrance du certificat de dépôt sollicité de droit et, n'ont jamais su quel sort avait été réservé à ladite requête.

Le Plaignant allègue également qu'un tel manquement grave avait conforté la partie adverse, dame Marie MINLEND NYOBE, à poursuivre l'exécution de l'arrêt de la Cour d'Appel du Centre, conduisant ainsi à l'expulsion abusive des victimes, avec la bonne couverture du Greffe de la Cour Suprême qui avait à dessein refusé d'enregistrer la requête et par ricochet, la délivrance du certificat de dépôt.

Le Plaignant allègue en outre qu'après l'arrêt N°210/2019 rendu par la CCJA en date du 27 juin 2019, annulant et cassant l'arrêt numéro 171/REF du 09 mars 2018 de la Cour d'Appel du Centre, tant querellé et qui avait quand même été exécuté, les victimes ont saisi le Greffier en Chef de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun via Monsieur le Premier Président de ladite Cour, en application des textes en vigueur, en vue de l'apposition de la formule exécutoire sur la décision de la CCJA. Ils déplorent que cette demande soit restée sans suite jusqu'à la saisine de la Commission.

Aux dires du Plaignant, le comportement de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun s'assimile à une volonté manifeste d'obstruer toute action, pourtant encadrée par la loi, visant à restaurer les victimes dans leurs droits.

Le Plaignant rappelle qu'en vertu des dispositions de la Charte Africaine, tout Etat qui reconnaît à ses citoyens le droit à un accès à la justice, doit prendre des dispositions dans son système judiciaire afin que ces voies de recours soient toujours ouvertes à ses justiciables.

Il expose que face à une telle attitude manifestement illégale, violant les droits humains d'accès à la justice, les victimes se sont retrouvées dépourvues de tout rempart, n'ayant plus aucun autre moyen de recours national pour les protéger de l'attitude tant irrégulière qu'illégale de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun.

Il conclut que dans le cas d'espèce, l'Etat du Cameroun ne prévoit aucun mécanisme de recours contre les décisions de justice irrégulières de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun à telle enseigne que les décisions de cette Cour sont insusceptibles de tout recours.

Le Plaignant indique que la loi numéro 92/008 du 14 aout 1992 fixant certaines dispositions relatives à l'exécution des décisions de justice modifiée par celle numéro 97/018 du 07 août 1997 dispose en son article 2 (1) qu' « en matière non répressive, l'exercice d'une voie de recours, a l'exception du pourvoi devant la Cour Suprême suspend l'exécution de la décision de justice attaquée ».
Il soutient que selon le législateur camerounais, toute demande de sursis à exécution devant la Cour Suprême du Cameroun est de droit admise pour examen et ne saurait faire l'objet de refus de dépôt.

Il allègue cependant que l'Etat du Cameroun n'a prévu aucune voie de recours en cas de refus d'enregistrer une requête de ce genre au greffe de la Cour Suprême, alors qu'il s'agit d'une garantie fondamentale pour le droit à un procès équitable.

Le Plaignant indique que les victimes ont saisi la CCJA après la décision de la Cour Suprême de déclarer irrecevable la première demande de sursis à exécution. Selon le Plaignant, c'est à la suite de la décision de rejet et savamment motivée de la CCJA s'agissant du sursis à exécution des décisions rendues par l'Etat partie que les victimes ont saisi de nouveau la Cour Suprême pour les mêmes fins.

Il allègue que la Cour Suprême n'a même pas daigné enregistrer ladite requête pour en donner une chance d'être examinée pour se rendre compte de l'élément nouveau dans la procédure. Il allègue en outre que le zèle subi par les conseils des Plaignantes tant du service du Greffe de la Cour Suprême que du service de Protocole du Premier Président de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun, constitue une attitude manifestement illégale, abusive et irrégulière faisant obstacle au droit à une voie de recours.

Il indique que par une telle abstention, l'Etat du Cameroun ne garantit pas à ses justiciables un droit à un procès équitable, violant par cette occasion les dispositions de l'article 7 de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples.

Il rapporte que conformément au Décret N° 2002/299 du 3 décembre 2002, le Greffier en Chef de la Cour Suprême est l'autorité chargée d'apposer la formule exécutoire sur les arrêts rendus par la CCJA. Il allègue que la non détermination par le texte sus évoqué du délai d'examen de ladite requête sur ordonnance aux fins d'apposition de la formule exécutoire se justifie sans doute par le caractère formaliste de cette procédure dénuée de toute appréciation au fond de l'objet de la décision et donc, l'examen de la requête ne devrait pas prendre plus de temps que cela ; rien ne devant par conséquent expliquer que la requête des plaignantes pour se voir apposer la formule exécutoire ait connu des difficultés de traitement.

Le Plaignant indique qu'en date du 29 août 2019, les plaignantes ont saisi le Greffier en Chef de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun d'une requête aux fins d'apposition de la formule exécutoire sur l'arrêt de la CCJA N° 210/2019 du 27 juin 2019 lequel cassait et annulait l'arrêt d'expulsion de la Cour d'appel pour lequel le sursis à exécution avait refusé d'être enregistré par la Cour Suprême.

Il allègue que bien que l'article 46 du Règlement de Procédure de la Cour Suprême de la CCJA énonce que la formalité de l'apposition de la formule exécutoire qui est effectuée est faite « sans autre contrôle que celui de vérification de l'authenticité du titre par l'autorité nationale », ladite formalité n'a pas été réalisée pendant plusieurs mois jusqu'à la saisine de la Commission.

Le Plaignant allègue que le non traitement par la Cour Suprême du sursis à exécution déposé en son temps par les victimes par devant celle-ci, a valu à ces dernières une expulsion abusive, mais aussi, le refus d'apposer dans un délai raisonnable la formule exécutoire sur la décision de la CCJA qui annulait celle de la Cour d'Appel qui a semblé être protégée par la Cour Suprême. De ce qui précède, il conclut que les victimes n'ont pas bénéficié du droit à un procès juste et équitable.

Le Plaignant indique que la violation de l'article 7 de la Charte Africaine emporte également manquement par l'Etat du Cameroun, du respect de ses engagements contractés en vertu des articles 1, 25 et 26 de la Charte.

Bien que le Secrétariat ait invité l'Etat défendeur à présenter ses arguments et ses éléments de preuve sur le fond, conformément aux dispositions pertinentes du Règlement intérieur de la Commission, aucune réponse n'a été reçue de la part de l'Etat défendeur en dépit des délais qui lui ont été accordés à cet effet.

La Commission a établi dans sa pratique l'examen par défaut d'une affaire lorsque l'Etat défendeur n'a pas soumis ses observations à l'expiration des délais requis. Sur la base de sa jurisprudence, des constatations faites à la procédure et tirant les conséquences de ce que l'Etat défendeur, bien qu'ayant été invité à le faire, n'a pas présenté ses observations sur le fond, l'analyse de la Commission se fera sur la base des éléments en sa possession.

La Commission note que le Plaignant allègue la violation des articles 3, 7(1), 25 et 26 lus conjointement avec l'article 1 de la charte africaine. Cependant, lors de la soumission des arguments sur le fond, il n'a pas soumis d'arguments sur la violation alléguée de l'article 3 de la Charte africaine. L'analyse de la Commission va par conséquent, se limiter aux allégations de violation des dispositions des articles aux articles 1, 7(1), 25 et 26 de la Charte.

L'article 7(1)(a) de la Charte stipule que « 1. Toute personne a droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue. Ce droit comprend : (a) le droit de saisir les juridictions nationales compétentes de tout acte violation les droits fondamentaux qui lui sont reconnus et garantis par les conventions, les lois, règlements et coutumes en vigueur ».

Les moyens invoqués par le Plaignant sur ce point tendent à faire conclure que le refus du service de Greffe de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun et celui du secrétariat particulier de son Premier Président d'enregistrer une nouvelle requête aux fins de sursis à exécution de l'arrêt de la Cour d'Appel du Centre ainsi que leur refus de délivrer le certificat de dépôt de celle transmise par les services de courriers urgents de la poste viole le droit à l'accès à la justice.

La Commission note que la disposition ainsi rappelée comporte une série de droits liés au procès équitable. Il s'agit tout d'abord du droit de voir sa cause être entendue par un tribunal. Sont en outre protégés par cette disposition, le droit d'accès à la justice. A cet égard, la Commission renvoie à ses Directives et principes sur le droit à un procès équitable et à l'assistance judiciaire en Afrique pour rappeler que chaque individu a droit à un recours effectif devant les tribunaux compétents contre des actes attentatoires aux droits garantis par la constitution, la loi ou la Charte, même lorsque les actes ont été commis par des personnes dans le cadre de leurs fonctions officielles. Le droit à un recours effectif comporte nécessairement l'accès à la justice ;
En outre, dans Amnesty International c. Zambie, la Commission a considéré le droit à l'appel comme composante du droit protégé à l'article 7(1)(a) de la Charte.

En l'espèce, la Commission note que la première requête du Plaignant à la Cour Suprême aux fins de sursis à exécution de l'Arrêt n°171/REF de la Cour d'Appel du 09 mars 2018 a été déclarée irrecevable par Ordonnance du 4 juillet 2018.

La Commission note en outre que les services compétents de la Cour Suprême ont refusé d'enregistrer une nouvelle requête de sursis déposé dans les délais par le Plaignant après le dépôt devant la CCJA du pourvoi en cassation contre l'arrêt de la Cour d'appel. Elle fait observer que lesdits services n'ont pas non plus livré aux victimes un certificat de dépôt de la requête déposée par service de courrier alors que la Cour Suprême était la seule juridiction compétente à fournir aux victimes, ledit acte pouvant suspendre l'exécution de l'Arrêt de Cour d'Appel du Centre. Cette situation a abouti à l'expulsion des victimes de l'immeuble en exécution de l'arrêt rendu par la Cour d'appel et qui faisait l'objet d'un pourvoi en cassation.

En effet, le sursis à exécution des arrêts des Cours d'appel faisant application des Actes uniformes, de la CCJA en l'espèce, sont de la compétence exclusive de la Cour suprême, en application de la loi n°97/018 du 14 aout 1992 fixant certaines dispositions relatives à l'exécution des décisions de justice, modifiée par la loi n°97/018 du 7 août 1997.

La Commission note que les victimes n'ont jamais été informées du sort réservé à ladite requête. Elle fait observer que la Cour Suprême saisie n'a pas examiné la demande pour pouvoir se rendre compte de l'élément nouveau dans la procédure, notamment la saisine de la CCJA pour un pourvoi en cassation.

Sur le fondement de ce qui précède, la Commission conclut que le refus de la Cour suprême d'enregistrer la nouvelle requête aux fins de sursis à exécution de l'arrêt de la Cour d'Appel du centre et le défaut de délivrance du certificat de dépôt de la requête reçue par services courrier, viole le droit d'accès à la justice, notamment le droit d'être entendu par une juridiction compétente, protégé aux termes des dispositions de l'article 7(1)(a) de la Charte.

Aux termes des dispositions de l'article 7(1)(d), toute personne a droit à un jugement dans un délai raisonnable par une juridiction impartiale. Le Plaignant allègue le retard accusé par le Greffe de la Cour Suprême pour apposer la formule exécutoire sur l'Arrêt n°210/2019 du 27 juin 2019 de la CCJA.

Dans sa jurisprudence sur le délai raisonnable d'administration de la justice, la Commission procède à une évaluation au cas par cas, notamment sur la base de facteurs tels que les faits de la cause, la situation du Plaignant et le droit interne de l'Etat défendeur. En tout état de cause, c'est à l'aune des circonstances de l'espèce et de la complexité des questions portées devant les tribunaux que devrait se déterminer le caractère raisonnable ou non du délai d'administration de la justice.

La Commission note que les victimes ont saisi le Greffier en chef de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun le 29 août 2019 d'une requête aux fins d'apposition de la formule exécutoire sur l'Arrêt n°210/2019 du 27 juin 2019 de la CCJA.

Il ressort des informations contenues au dossier que le Premier Président de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun, a ordonné l'apposition de la formule exécutoire sur l'Arrêt susmentionné suivant Ordonnance n°633 du 10 décembre 2019 exécutoire sur minute. La question qu'il revient à la Commission de régler en l'espèce est de savoir si le délai dans lequel la formule exécutoire a été apposée peut être considéré comme raisonnable dans les circonstances de la cause.

A cet égard, la Commission note qu'entre le 29 août 2019 et le 10 décembre 2019, un délai de trois mois et 10 jours s'était écoulé depuis la saisine par les victimes de l'autorité compétente, qu'est le Greffier en chef de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun.

La Commission note que le Règlement de Procédure de la CCJA ne prescrit pas des délais pour l'apposition de la formule exécutoire sur ses arrêts. Elle note cependant que son article 46 énonce que la formalité de l'apposition de la formule exécutoire est faite « sans autre contrôle que celui de vérification de l'authenticité du titre par l'autorité nationale ».

La Commission note en outre que bien que le Décret n°2002/299 du 3 décembre 2002, désigne le Greffier en chef de la Cour Suprême du Cameroun comme autorité chargée d'apposer la formule exécutoire sur les arrêts de la CCJA et sur les sentences arbitrales rendues en application du règlement d'arbitrage de ladite Cour et de l'Acte Uniforme relatif au droit de l'arbitrage, l'Etat défendeur ne prescrit pas des délais pour le faire.

La Commission fait observer cependant que l'exequatur des sentences arbitrales de la CCJA est accordé dans les quinze jours du dépôt de la requête, par une ordonnance du Président de la Cour ou du juge délégué à cet effet et confère à la sentence un caractère exécutoire dans les Etats parties.

La Commission constate que l'acte de vérification de l'authenticité de l'arrêt de la CCJA a duré plus de trois mois. Sur la base de ces constatations, elle conclut que l'apposition de la formule exécutoire, trois mois et 10 jours après le dépôt de la requête n'a pas été faite dans un délai raisonnable. En conséquence, il y a lieu de conclure à la violation des dispositions de l'article 7(1)(d) de la Charte.

L'article 25 de la Charte africaine établit pour les Etats parties le devoir de promouvoir et d'assurer, par l'enseignement, l'éducation et la diffusion, le respect des droits et des libertés contenus dans la présente Charte, et de prendre des mesures en vue de veiller à ce que ces libertés et droits soient compris de même que les obligations et devoirs correspondants. Quant à l'article 26, il édicte aux Etats parties le devoir de garantir l'indépendance des tribunaux et de permettre l'établissement et le perfectionnement d'institutions nationales appropriées chargées de la promotion et de la protection des droits et libertés garantis par la présente Charte.

La Commission note que les victimes allèguent le manquement par l'Etat défendeur au respect de ses engagements en vertu des articles 1, 25 et 26 de la Charte du fait de la violation de l'article 7 de la Charte Africaine. Au soutien de cette allégation, elles avancent que la violation du droit à un procès équitable emporte automatiquement celle des articles susmentionnés. La Commission note qu'elles ne fournissent pas d'arguments et encore moins des preuves contingentes. En conséquence, la Commission ne peut recevoir les victimes en leurs moyens tendant à faire conclure automatiquement à la violation des dispositions des articles 25 et 26 de la Charte.

L'Article 1er de la Charte africaine impose aux Etats parties de reconnaître les droits, les devoirs et les libertés énoncés dans la Charte et d'adopter des mesures législatives ou autres pour les appliquer.

Dans sa jurisprudence constante, la Commission a conclu que la violation d'une disposition quelconque de la Charte africaine entraîne automatiquement la violation de l'article 1. La Cour africaine a abouti à la même conclusion dans la Requête n°005/2013 – Alex Thomas c. Tanzanie en jugeant que l'obligation énoncée à l'article 1 de la Charte n'est pas respectée ou est violée lorsque l'un quelconque des droits, des devoirs ou des libertés inscrits dans la Charte a été restreint, violé ou non appliqué.

Dans la présente Communication, la Commission est arrivée à la conclusion que l'Etat défendeur a violé les dispositions de l'article 7(1)(a) et (d) de la Charte. En conséquence des violations de droits substantiels ainsi établies, la Commission conclut qu'il y a eu violation de l'Article 1 de la Charte.
La Commission ayant reçu le Plaignant en certains de ses moyens, il y a lieu d'examiner les demandes y afférentes.

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission de constater la violation des droits des victimes par l'Etat défendeur, notamment la violation de l'article 7. Il sollicite en outre une réparation de 2.000.000.000 (deux milliards) FCFA au titre de réparation de tous préjudices confondus du fait des multiples violations, par l'Etat du Cameroun, des droits humains consacrés dans la Charte africaine.
S'agissant de la première demande, sur la base de son analyse à cet égard, la Commission conclut à la violation des dispositions des articles 1 et 7(1)(a) et (d) de la Charte.

Concernant la demande de réparation pour les préjudices soufferts du fait de la violation des droits garantis par la Charte, la Commission note que le Plaignant les a évalués à la somme de deux milliards (2.000.000.000) FCFA, en tenant compte de la gravité des faits en ce que les victimes ont perdu d'importants investissements, notamment une habitation dont la seule valeur vénale de l'immeuble a été évaluée par un expert à un montant de 370.000.000 (trois cent soixante-dix millions) FCFA ; un fonds de commerce dont l'activité avait pignon sur rue dans la Capitale Yaoundé; d'importants moyens pour financer toutes les procédures soit en défense, soit en attaque pour le respect de leurs droits ; les grands investissements effectués sur le fonds de commerce pendant de nombreuses années pour une activité commerciale florissante ; le manque à gagner engrangé depuis l'expulsion abusive ; le tort moral ; la perte de toute une vie, notamment le décès de dame ETOUMAN dont l'enquête a conclu à un assassinat, à cause de ses combats judiciaires dans cette affaire.

Conformément à la jurisprudence établie de la Commission, la violation des droits protégés par la Charte ouvre droit à réparation, y compris une réparation monétaire. La Commission ayant conclu à la violation des dispositions sus-énumérées de la Charte, il y a lieu de faire suite aux demandes en réparation.

La Commission note que le Plaignant produit un inventaire des préjudices subis par les victimes. S'il avance le montant de deux milliards (2.000.000.000) FCFA, il n'en produit cependant ni les chiffres détaillés ni les preuves des pertes alléguées d'investissements et dépenses encourues pour financer les procédures judiciaires relatives à la présente affaire.

Elle note en outre que les pièces versées au dossier en guise de justification de l'indemnisation comprennent notamment les conclusions d'une expertise indiquant la valeur vénale de l'immeuble exploité par les victimes, la copie du registre de commerce et du crédit mobilier de la Société Metis ainsi que la copie du contrat de bail commercial entre Messieurs Minlend et Cazade, toutes choses qui ne permettent pas l'évaluation des dommages subis par les victimes en vue de la détermination de la valeur des réparations demandées.

Elle note par ailleurs que le Plaignant n'apporte aucune preuve du lien entre les violations constatées et le décès de dame ETOUMAN. Il n'apporte pas non plus la preuve du manque à gagner du fait de l'expulsion et des frais de procédure.

La Commission fait observer qu'en l'absence de preuves permettant de déterminer et de quantifier les dommages subis, elle ne peut pas s'y prononcer dans cette affaire. Par conséquent, conformément à sa jurisprudence, elle renvoie le calcul des dommages et intérêts aux juridictions nationales. A cet égard, elle recommande qu'une réparation juste, adéquate, efficace, suffisante, appropriée, orientée vers la victime et proportionnelle au préjudice souffert soit accordée aux victimes, notamment aux ayant-droit de Feue Madame ETOUMAN Hélène Adèle.
Pour ces motifs, la Commission dit que la République du Cameroun n'a pas violé les dispositions des articles 25 et 26 de la Charte.

Déclare en revanche que la République du Cameroun a violé les dispositions des articles 1 et 7(1)(a) et (d) de la Charte. En conséquence, la Commission demande à la République du Cameroun de: i. Exécuter l'Arrêt n°210/2019 du 27 juin 2019 de la CCJA et en tirer toutes les conséquences juridiques. ii. Accorder aux victimes une réparation adéquate et suffisante du préjudice causé par les violations constatées. iii. Adopter des mesures législatives en vue de prescrire les délais légaux d'apposition de la formule exécutoire des arrêts et sentence arbitrales de la CCJA. iv. Lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingts jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée par la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peupleslors de sa 84 Session Ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 21 au 30 juillet 2021

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received a Complaint filed on 1 November 2019 by Maître Nchankou Njindam, hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant", on behalf of Sarl METIS and the rightful claimants of the late Mrs ETOUMAN Hélène Adèle, hereinafter referred to as "the victims".

The Complaint was filed against the Republic of Cameroon (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent State or Cameroon), a State that ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) on 20 June 1989.

The Complainant indicates that there was an eviction of Sarl METIS and the late Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle from the leased premises, as a result of the execution of a commercial lease contract signed between the lessor, Mr Minlend Nyobe Joseph Alexandre and the lessee, Mr Alain Christian Georges Cazade, promoter of the Company METIS SARL.

The Complainant reports that on 9 March 2018, the Court of Appeal of the Centre in Yaoundé, by Judgment 171/REF, upheld Order 122/C handed down on 16 February 2016 by the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé Centre administratif ordering the said eviction.

The Complainant reports that the victims lodged an appeal on points of law (pourvoi en cassation) before the Common Court of Justice and Arbitration (CCJA) so that it would rule on the violation of the law, the distortion of the facts of the case, lack of jurisdiction and the violation of the forms prescribed by law on pain of nullity, which vitiated Judgment 171/REF.

The Complainant stresses that the victims filed a first application for a stay of execution of the said Judgment before the Supreme Court, and notification was made to the opposing party as well as to Maître EMBOLO MESSINA Martine, the bailiff in charge of the matter.

The Complainant indicates that the first application was declared inadmissible by Order of 4 July 2018 on the ground that it was based on an inadmissible appeal on points of law because it raised issues relating to the application of the Uniform Act of the Organization for the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa (OHADA) on General Commercial Law in its Articles 118, 133 and 134.

The Complainant stresses that in order to correct this ground of inadmissibility invoked by the Supreme Court of Cameroon, the CCJA was seized of an appeal on points of law dated 12 July 2018. Being still within the time limits for seizure, a new application was initiated before the Supreme Court of Cameroon for a stay of execution of the challenged Judgment of the Court of Appeal of the Centre in Yaoundé pending the forthcoming decision of the CCJA.

The Complainant alleges that the registry service of the Supreme Court of Cameroon as well as that of the registry of the Private Secretariat of the First President of the said court categorically refused to receive the said application and consequently to issue the related certificate of filing, without any legal ground. He also alleges the refusal to grant the victims a hearing by the head of the protocol service of this high court.

The Complainant indicates that none of the various requests for intervention filed with the Minister of Justice and with the President of the Republic helped to see the victims' rights respected despite the acknowledgment of receipt by the Prosecutor General asking him to specify the subject matter of the said requests.

The Complainant specifies that following the refusal of the Secretary of the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon to receive the application for a stay of execution and to issue the related certificate of filing, Judgment No. 171/REF of 9 March 2018 handed down by the Court of Appeal was to be executed and the victims were illegitimately evicted from the premises on 6 July 2018, thereby causing immeasurable prejudice to Sarl METIS and to the late Mrs Etouman.

The Complainant stresses that the consequences of this injustice are all the more serious because the CCJA by Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 annulled Judgment No. 171/REF handed down by the Court of Appeal which had upheld the solution of Order No. 122/C of the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé Centre-administratif terminating the lease and ordering the eviction of the victims from the leased premises and also annulled the aforementioned Order, restoring the case and the parties to the same and sensitive state in which they were before the annulled decision.

The Complainant adds that in Judgment 211/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA, in application of its jurisprudence, the CCJA declared itself incompetent to order a stay of execution of a decision emanating from a national court of an OHADA member State; and that it thus clearly appears that the Supreme Court of Cameroon was the victims' last bulwark to spare them a grave injustice and enormous prejudice.

The Complainant indicates that on 29 August 2019, the victims seized the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court of Cameroon with an application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA; and that since that date, that is, more than two months after the filing of this application, this formality has not been carried out; yet Article 46 of the CCJA Rules of Procedure states that the formality of affixing the enforcement formula is carried out without any other control than verification of the authenticity of the title by the national authority.

The Complainant indicates that while the victims had fought all these judicial battles, abandoned by all, and found themselves at the end of the tunnel through the request for the affixing of the enforcement formula on Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA because they had definitively emerged victorious from this judicial struggle, Mrs Etouman Hélène (aged 35) was strangely found dead at her home.
The Complainant states that the case has not been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or of similar competence.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 3, 7(1), 25 and 26 read together with Article 1 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission to: a. Receive the complaint and declare it well-founded; b. Find the denial of justice of which the State of Cameroon has been guilty and which it continues to display; c. Find that the victims suffered immeasurable prejudice, which SARL METIS continues to suffer, as a result of the unjust and inequitable conduct of the State of Cameroon; d. Find the violation by the State of Cameroon of its commitments under the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights; e. Order the State of Cameroon to pay the sum of 2,000,000,000 (two billion CFA francs) to the victims, on account of their unlawful eviction and the financial and moral prejudice suffered as a result of the State of Cameroon.
The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission on 30 December 2019. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 15 January 2020.

At its 27 Extraordinary Session held from 19 February to 4 March 2020 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission examined the complaint and decided to admit it. By letter and Note Verbale of 6 March 2020, the parties were informed of this decision. The Secretariat, on the same occasion, invited the Complainant to submit the evidence and arguments on the admissibility of the Communication within 2 months following notification, in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Rules of Procedure.

By correspondence of 13 April 2020, the Complainant transmitted the evidence and arguments on the admissibility of the Communication to the Secretariat. The latter acknowledged receipt and transmitted them to the Respondent State in order to enable it to present its observations on the said arguments, in accordance with Rule 105(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2010).

At its 67 Ordinary Session held virtually from 13 November to 3 December 2020, the Commission examined the Communication and decided to defer its decision in order to await the Respondent State's observations on admissibility. The Parties were informed on 4 September 2020 and a reminder was sent to the Respondent State.

At its 68 Ordinary Session held from 14 April to 4 May 2021, the Commission examined the Communication and decided to defer its decision in order to await the Respondent State's observations on admissibility. The Parties were informed on 10 May 2021 and the Respondent State's submissions were requested.

On 12 October 2022, the Respondent State transmitted its observations in response to the Complainant's brief on Admissibility. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 16 November 2022 and transmitted them on the same day to the Complainant in order to enable him to present his reply brief, in accordance with Rule 105(3) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure 2010.

On 8 February 2023, the Complainant sent the reply brief to the Respondent State's observations on the admissibility of the Communication. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt by letter of 9 February 2023 and transmitted it to the Respondent State on the same day. This brought the exchange of pleadings between the parties to an end.

On 5 June 2023, by letter and Note Verbale, the parties were informed of the decision taken by the Commission at the 75 Ordinary Session held from 3 to 23 May in Banjul, The Gambia, to defer the examination of the Communication on admissibility to a later session due to time constraints.

At its 77 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 20 October to 9 November 2023, in Arusha, Tanzania, the Commission examined the Communication and declared it admissible. The Parties were informed on 11 November 2024 and the Complainant's observations on the merits were requested within the time limits provided for by the Rules of Procedure.

On 16 November 2024, the Secretariat of the Commission received the Complainant's e-mail acknowledging receipt of the notification letter as well as the request for transmission of his observations on the merits.

On 4 January 2025, the Complainant transmitted his observations on the merits to the Secretariat. On 21 January 2025, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt and transmitted the said observations to the Respondent State on the same day and requested its response within a period of sixty (60) days.
At the expiry of the time limits and until the day of examination of the Communication on the merits, the Secretariat had still not received the Respondent State's observations on the merits.
The Complainant states that he has fulfilled all the admissibility requirements stipulated in Article 56 of the Charter.

Concerning the first requirement on the identity of the author of the Communication, he indicates that his identity is well known in his capacity as representative of the victims since the proceedings followed in Cameroon and before the CCJA of OHADA. The Complainant further indicates that the identity of the victims is also clearly indicated from the submission of the initial complaint. They are "METIS SARL", a limited liability company, whose registered office is in Yaoundé, at the place called camp sic Hippodrome, PO Box 16385 Yaoundé (Cameroon), with a share capital of FCFA 1,000,000 (one million), registered in the RCCM under number: RC/YAO/2006/B/912, represented by its legal representative; and the late Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle Hélène, a trader now deceased. He concludes in this regard that the communication satisfies the first requirement of Article 56 of the Charter and that it should be declared admissible.

On the second requirement relating to the compatibility of the Communication with the African Charter and the Constitutive Act, the Complainant also states that the communication is in conformity with the principles and values enshrined in the African Charter. He indicates that his complaint aims to denounce the violations, by the State of Cameroon, of the rights proclaimed and guaranteed by the African Charter to its citizen, in particular the violation of Articles 3, 7(1), 25 and 26 read together with Article 1 of the African Charter. He explains that the African Commission is competent whenever a signatory State fails in one of its obligations prescribed by the African Charter, and where its citizens and he himself find themselves affected by virtue of this violation.

The Complainant reports that the present communication fully satisfies the admissibility requirement laid down in paragraph 3. He states that he has always shown, in all his written submissions relating to the present case, absolute respect and deference in the vocabulary used both towards the State of Cameroon and towards the institutions of the African Union. He concludes that the communication cannot be reproached for the use of the slightest disparaging and still less insulting term to describe either the Supreme Court of Cameroon or the State of Cameroon, or the institutions of the African Union.

Regarding compliance with the 4 requirement, the Complainant indicates that the Communication is in no way based on news disseminated through the mass media because the Complaint was filed on the basis of edifying, relevant and established evidence and legal arguments, as illustrated by the chronology of the judicial battles waged by the Complainant as well as the schedule of administrative and judicial documents that accompany the present communication.

He cites in particular Judgment No. 171/REF of 9 March 2018 of the Court of Appeal of the Centre upholding the solution of Order No. 122/C handed down on 16 February 2016, by the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé Centre - administratif; the copy of the certificate of filing of the appeal on points of law lodged before the CCJA; the application for a stay of execution of the said judgment before the Supreme Court; the copy of the order of 4 July 2018 handed down by the Supreme Court of Cameroon, the various requests for intervention filed with the Minister of Justice and with the President of the Republic, the copy of the writ of demand served by the bailiff in Yaoundé; the copy of Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA annulling the Judgment of the Court of Appeal of the Centre; the copy of Judgment No. 221/2019 of the CCJA which dismissed the Complainants' application for a stay of execution; as well as the copy of the application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA.

On the requirement laid down in paragraph 5, the Complainant submits that the Communication both post-dates the exhaustion of local remedies under Cameroonian law, and concerns a procedure that has been unduly prolonged.

On the exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant indicates that the victims have indeed exhausted the remedies available under Cameroonian procedural law, which provides for a two-tier court system with, after the decision of the judge of first instance, an appeal before the competent Court of Appeal and then either an appeal on points of law before the Supreme Court of Cameroon for matters falling strictly under domestic law, or an appeal before the CCJA for matters governed by OHADA uniform acts.

He explains that the victims respected the two-tier court system and exhausted local remedies because after the President of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé Centre administratif handed down order No. 122/C of 16 February 2016, ordering the eviction of SARL METIS and the late Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle, they appealed to the Court of Appeal of the Centre and then, after its confirming judgment of 9 March 2018, they lodged an appeal on points of law before the CCJA.

The Complainant explains that in parallel to the proceedings on the merits, the victims filed an application for a stay of execution of the judgment of the Court of Appeal of the Centre upholding their eviction, which placed them before an insurmountable procedural obstacle, the State of Cameroon having provided no remedy in the event of refusal by the Supreme Court to receive an application for a stay of execution.

The Complainant submits that after having rejected the victims' request for a stay of execution for the first time, the latter seized the same court a second time with a second application for a stay of execution but the registry service and the protocol service of the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon refused to receive the correspondence.

Referring to the Commission's decision in Communication 218/98 - Civil Liberties Organisation, Legal Defence Centre, Legal Defence and Assistance Project v. Nigeria which held that recourse to a court whose decisions cannot be appealed is a violation of the right to a fair trial, the Complainant submits that the State of Cameroon has not provided any remedy against manifestly unlawful and irregular decisions, actions or omissions of the Supreme Court of Cameroon.

The Complainant explains that despite the judgment of the CCJA of 27 June 2019 annulling the judgment of the Court of Appeal No. 171/REF of 9 March 2018 which ordered the eviction of SARL METIS and the late Mrs ETOUMAN, the Supreme Court of Cameroon, through the jurisdiction of its First President which was, from the outset, the only one competent to rule on the stay of execution of the said judgment, did not do so.

The Complainant concludes that the decisions of the CCJA and of the Supreme Court as the highest courts of the Cameroonian judicial order give rise to no remedy and in themselves reflect the exhaustion of remedies.

On the undue prolongation of the procedure, the Complainant, invoking the Commission's opinion in the case of RADDHO v. Zambia, indicates that when it is proved that local remedies are ineffective, unavailable or unduly prolonged, national justice may be set aside and the examination of the merits of the communication admitted.

The Complainant explains that after Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA by which the CCJA set aside Judgment No. 171/REF of 9 March 2018 of the Court of Appeal of the Centre, the enforcement formula was to be affixed to it for its implementation. He reports that on 29 August 2019, the victims seized the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court of Cameroon with an application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on Judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 of the CCJA. He alleges that although the enforcement formula procedure is a simple act, more than four months elapsed without this crucial formality being carried out in order to restore the applicants to their rights, which prompted them to seize the Commission on 5 January 2020.

Regarding compliance with the requirement laid down in paragraph 6, the Complainant indicates that Judgment No. 171/REF of the Court of Appeal of the Centre confirming the eviction of SARL METIS and the late Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle from the TPI of Yaoundé Centre - administratif was delivered on 9 March 2018. He adds that the victims lodged an appeal with the CCJA and an application for a stay of execution against the Judgment of the Court of Appeal of the Centre with the Supreme Court of Cameroon on 12 July 2018. He alleges that the latter refused to receive the said application and to issue them with a certificate of filing which would have been necessary to stop the eviction procedure that unjustly threatened them.

The Complainant further explains that the victims seized the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court of Cameroon on 29 August 2019 with an application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on the Judgment of the CCJA of 27 June 2019 annulling the Judgment of the Court of Appeal and restoring them to their rights. He submits that paragraph 6 of Article 56 of the African Charter has been complied with because the complaint was filed on 1 November 2019, that is, two months after the filing of the application for the affixing of the enforcement formula, a formality which had not been carried out when the complaint was filed with the Commission.

On compliance with the requirement laid down in paragraph 7, the Complainant indicates that the victims have not seized any other international or community court or institution in relation to the facts of the present case. He submits that the communication has in no way been settled in accordance with either the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or of the Charter of African Unity, or the provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.

Before demonstrating the inadmissibility of the Communication under examination, the Respondent State recalled the facts of the case as set out by the Complainant and then restated the reality of the facts.

In its response brief, the Respondent State stresses that the Company METIS SARL, represented by Mr CAZADE Alain Christian, of French nationality, was brought before the Judge of summary proceedings of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé-Centre Administratif for the purposes, on the one hand, of termination of the lease contract for non-payment of rent and, on the other hand, of eviction from the building located in Yaoundé at the place called "Camp Sic Hippodrome".

According to the Respondent State, the late Mrs ETOUMAN voluntarily intervened in this procedure, claiming to have acquired the business operated by Mr CAZADE, and stating that she had paid the rent arrears.

The Respondent State explains that, disposing of the matter by Order No. 122/C of 16 February 2016, the Judge of summary proceedings, on the one hand, declared the voluntary intervention inadmissible, on the other hand noted the termination of the lease contract for non-payment of rent by this company and finally, ordered the eviction of Sarl METIS and Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle from the premises as well as of all occupants deriving their rights from her.

It reports that the late Mrs ETOUMAN having appealed this decision, the Court of Appeal of the Centre, by Judgment No. 171/REF of 9 March 2018, annulled this Order for violation of the law (non-reproduction of the operative parts of the pleadings in the recitals). On evocation, it declared the voluntary intervention admissible but ill-founded, then noted the termination of the lease contract for failure to pay rent by the company METIS SARL and ordered the eviction of its promoter and of all occupants deriving their rights from him.

The Respondent State indicates that by Order of 4 July 2018, the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon declared "inadmissible" the application for a stay of execution of this Judgment, filed on 29 May 2018 by the late Mrs ETOUMAN. It further indicates that the registers of the Registry of this high court do not mention the filing of any other application for the same purposes.

The Respondent State also indicates that by Order No. 633 of 10 December 2019 enforceable on the original, the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon, seized by an application of 29 August 2019 from the late Mrs ETOUMAN, ordered the affixing of the enforcement formula on Judgment No. 210/2019 handed down on 27 June 2019 by the CCJA.

On the admissibility of the Communication, the Respondent State submits that the Communication is not admissible because it does not satisfy the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies as set out in Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

The Respondent State first raises the irrelevance of the Communication's author's argument on the exhaustion of local remedies. It recalls that it is an established principle of general international law, supported by the Commission's jurisprudence and doctrine, that the local remedies pursued must be capable of ensuring reparation of the alleged violations of Human Rights. And that the latter generally takes the form of restitution, compensation, "satisfaction" and guarantees of non-repetition.

The Respondent State notes that the author of the Communication alleges the violation of Articles 3(1 and 2) and 7 of the Charter on equality before the law and the right to a fair trial, in that the services of the Supreme Court of Cameroon allegedly refused not only to receive a second application for a stay of execution but also to affix the enforcement formula on a Judgment handed down by the CCJA.

The Respondent State further notes that in claiming to have exhausted domestic judicial remedies, the Complainant invokes not judicial actions for reparation of the alleged violations but rather the eviction action brought by Mrs MINLEND as well as the subsequent proceedings mentioned above, namely the appeal before the Court of Appeal of the Centre, the appeal on points of law before the CCJA, the requests for a stay of execution and for the affixing of the enforcement formula.

For the Respondent State, contrary to the above-stated principle, the said proceedings were therefore not aimed at obtaining reparation for the alleged violations, hence the irrelevance of the Communication's author's argument on the exhaustion of local remedies, which are however available, effective and capable of being pursued without hindrance.
In its conclusions on the question of the exhaustion of local remedies, the Respondent State submits that they are available, effective and can be pursued without hindrance.

On the availability of local remedies in relation to the alleged violations, the Respondent State observes that the alleged violations of Articles 3(1 and 2) and 7 of the Charter would result from alleged refusals by the services of the Supreme Court of Cameroon to receive a second application for a stay of execution and to affix the enforcement formula on a judgment handed down by the CCJA. It submits that in criminal terms, such conduct, if by extraordinary chance it were proven, could be characterised as refusal of a due service and abuse of office, offences provided for and punished by the Cameroonian Penal Code, in particular Articles 148 and 140.

It indicates that on the remedies available in criminal matters, the CPP offers the person who considers himself a victim a host of possibilities including the complaint, direct summons and the complaint with civil party application. The CPP provides that the decision handed down is subject to appeal, then to an appeal on points of law.

The Respondent State further sets out the remedies available in civil matters. It indicates that the alleged violations could be analysed as a service fault (faute de service), which is such as to engage the responsibility of the State of Cameroon before the Administrative Court, seized by way of an application initiating proceedings pursuant to Article 32 of Law No. 2006/022 of 29 December 2006 on the organisation and functioning of Administrative Courts.

On the effectiveness of local remedies, the Respondent State indicates that Cameroonian courts have heard or are hearing judicial proceedings relating to the facts of abuse of office, refusal of a due service or service fault. By way of recent illustration regarding abuse of office, it reports that the Court of First Instance of Douala-Bonanjo, by judgment of 5 August 2021, found a defendant guilty of this offence and awarded the civil party the sum of 3 2000 000 000 CFA francs, that is, 47 292 851, 20 dollars, as reparation for the prejudice suffered. It further reports that in several cases, the administrative court has established the service fault attributable to the State of Cameroon and entailing the obligation to make reparation for the prejudice suffered, among others, the poor functioning of the public service, the delay shown by the Administration or its abstention.

On the capacity of local remedies to be pursued without any hindrance, the Respondent State indicates that beyond the case of the complaint which is subject to the principle of being free of charge (Art. 135-4 CPP), direct summons, the complaint with civil party application and the application initiating proceedings entail a modest cost. By way of example, the application initiating proceedings before the Administrative Court gives rise to a deposit of 20,000 CFA francs, that is, 29.56 dollars.

The Respondent State submits that these local remedies involve flexible procedures set by the CCP and are examined within a reasonable time. It explains that under Law No. 2009/004 of 14 April 2009 on the organisation of legal aid, indigent litigants may request and obtain, where appropriate, exemption from all or part of the procedural costs.

The Respondent State concludes that the Communication is inadmissible because the Complainant has not exhausted local remedies although they are available, effective and can be pursued without obstacle.

In his supplementary observations in response to the Respondent State's arguments on admissibility, the Complainant reports that while the various civil (judicial and administrative) and criminal procedures listed by the State of Cameroon exist in the texts in Cameroon, the essential question arises of their effectiveness for the present case. He thus developed arguments on the ineffectiveness of the remedies available in Cameroonian legislation for the present case, and on the ineffectiveness of local remedies linked to legal obstacles.

According to the Complainant, it appears from the State of Cameroon's above-mentioned submissions that it is content to list the various procedures that were carried out in Cameroon without acknowledging the human rights violations that resulted from them, both from the irregular eviction of the victims and from the refusal by the Supreme Court to give legal effect to the decisions emanating from the CCJA in their favour. By way of illustration, the Complainant cites the application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on the Judgment of the CCJA which took an abnormally long time even though it was only a procedure falling within the purely administrative functions of the registry of the Supreme Court, falling within the public service of justice.

He submits that there was therefore no need for a local remedy because the decision of the local remedy, namely the appeal for the facts in this case, does exist, namely judgment No. 171/REF handed down on 9 March 2018 by the Court of Appeal of the Centre annulled by judgment No. 210/2019 of 27 June 2019 handed down by the CCJA.

Relying on the Commission's jurisprudence in the case of RADDHO v. Zambia, the Complainant recalls that when it is proved that local remedies are ineffective, unavailable or unduly prolonged, national justice may be set aside and the examination of the merits of the communication admitted.
In the present case, the question of reasonable time, constituting a human rights violation, is highlighted, which justifies the seizure of the Commission.

Moreover, it is established that the victims were faced with a situation of impossibility of pursuing remedies having regard to the status of the persons concerned, rendering ineffective the local remedies theoretically referred to by the State of Cameroon, which makes it possible to invoke the Commission's established jurisprudence on the ineffectiveness of local remedies in order to retain the Commission's jurisdiction.

As a reminder, the institution at issue is indeed the Supreme Court of Cameroon, a supranational Court whose Head, who is the First President, is the body vested with the power to have the appropriate procedure implemented to sanction one of his defaulting collaborators.

Indeed, under Article 629 paragraph 1 of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure, "when a judge of the judiciary is liable to be charged with an offence, the competent Prosecutor General shall submit an application to the President of the Supreme Court who shall designate a judge to investigate the case and three others, of a rank at least equal to that of the person accused, with a view to the eventual trial of the case at first instance."

Paragraph 2 of the above-mentioned article continues by specifying that "The President of the Supreme Court shall also indicate the town where the case will be tried". This is, where applicable, the privilege of jurisdiction enjoyed by a judge under investigation.

Also, Article 630 of the same Code provides that "the provisions of Article 629 are also applicable when the injured party addresses a complaint with civil party application against a judge to the President of the Supreme Court".

Article 633 of the Code of Criminal Procedure clearly specifies that "when the judge accused is the most senior in the highest grade, his case is examined by the Supreme Court sitting in Plenary Assembly"

Yet the plenary assembly, which was the second autonomous institution of the Supreme Court in 1972, underwent modifications with Law No. 2006/016 of 29 December 2006 on the organisation and functioning of the Supreme Court, amended and supplemented by Law No. 2017/014 of 12 July 2017, and is still chaired by the First President in accordance with Article 18 of the above-referenced 2006 law.

However, it should be noted that the powers set out above fall to the President of the Supreme Court who has national jurisdiction; even though the law did not envisage the hypothesis where the President of the Supreme Court himself would be accused in the context of criminal proceedings.

For the Complainant, an essential obstacle thus appears here which the victims faced, consequently preventing them from pursuing a remedy, where applicable, having regard to the status of the person concerned; it being understood that the latter would not have been able to authorise the initiation of proceedings against himself.

On the cases of jurisprudence, the Complainant observes that they are not illustrative of the present case since none of these decisions relates to any conviction of the "First President of the Supreme Court" to serve effectively as an example. The same applies to the offences that the State of Cameroon merely cites without however characterising them in the present case. The State of Cameroon develops a fallacious argument by making it appear that the Cameroonian judge is a civil servant within the meaning of decree No. 94/199 of 7 October 1994 on the General Statute of the Public Service even though he enjoys a special status which derogates from that of other civil servants.

According to the Complainant, it therefore goes without saying that local remedies are deemed to have been exhausted owing, on the one hand, to the abnormally long time taken to affix the enforcement formula on the CCJA's judgment and, on the other hand, owing to the ineffectiveness of local remedies given the impossibility of pursuing remedies in relation to the status of the persons concerned, as decided in the case of RADDHO v. Zambia, communication 71/92.

On the ineffectiveness of local remedies linked to legal obstacles, it appears to the Complainant that the remedies referred to by the State of Cameroon could not have succeeded given the legal impossibility of bringing a criminal action against the First President of the Supreme Court in view of his prerogatives that are exorbitant under ordinary law and the blocking of the administrative appeal brought by the victims owing to a correspondence from the State of Cameroon assuring that appropriate actions would be set up, which has had no follow-up to date.

For the Complainant, the State of Cameroon's argument on the existence and effectiveness of remedies should be rejected as unfounded because the alleged local remedies presented by the State of Cameroon are manifestly impossible to pursue owing to the multiple and serious legal obstacles linked to the status of the person concerned in the present case.

The Complainant points out that until the date of his supplementary submissions (more than three years later), no "appropriate action" had been initiated as indicated in the correspondence which came one year after the filing of the appeal.

Also, it should be noted that the aforesaid correspondence bound the proceedings of the prior administrative appeal (recours gracieux) such that the applicants could not have initiated other proceedings since the Minister had already said that the appeal filed had been transmitted to the Prosecutor General for appropriate action except that this correspondence still has not been followed up; rendering the time for examination of the administrative appeal abnormally long. This highlights the question of reasonable time which makes the present Commission competent in this case.

The present Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights which gives the Commission competence to receive and consider "Communications other than those of States Parties". Such communications must, in order to be declared admissible, fulfil the requirements provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter.

The examination of the grounds invoked and the facts set out above reveals an agreement between the parties on all the admissibility requirements listed in Article 56 of the African Charter, with the exception of the exhaustion of local remedies. The Commission will address the Admissibility proper of the Communication under examination.

Article 56(1) of the African Charter provides that the identity of the author of the Communication must be clearly indicated, even if he requests the Commission to keep his anonymity. In the present case, the Commission notes that the identity of the author is clearly indicated. He is Maître Nchankou Njindam who represents Sarl METIS and the rightful claimants of the late Mrs ETOUMAN Hélène Adèle. The Complainant's full address is also contained in all his submissions. The Commission considers that he is sufficiently identified and that the Communication consequently meets the requirement under examination.

With regard to Article 56(2) of the African Charter which provides that Communications must be compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter, the Commission observes that the compatibility of a communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter should be understood as the possibility for the Commission to hear the case before it without violating the provisions of the instruments referred to. In other words, the verification of compatibility must consist, for the Commission, in ensuring that all the grounds and claims contained in the Communication are compatible ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci with the instruments mentioned above. That said, the Commission is of the view that under the provisions of Article 56(2), the examination of compatibility ratione materiae must also be established with the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

The Commission notes that in this case, the Communication is submitted against Cameroon, a State Party to the African Charter and that the Complainant has standing. In addition, the Complainant alleges the violation, on the territory of the Respondent State, of rights protected by the Charter. The Commission also notes that the Charter was in force in Cameroon at the time of the facts. Finally, it is manifest that neither the grounds nor the claims contained in the Communication infringe any of the principles adopted under the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

As regards Article 56(3) of the African Charter which requires that Communications do not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the OAU/AU. On examination of the Complaint, the Commission notes that the Communication does not contain insulting or disparaging language directed against the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. The Communication therefore fulfils the requirement under examination.

Under Article 56(4) of the African Charter, Communications must not be limited to gathering exclusively news disseminated through the mass media. On this point, the Commission finds that the information submitted by the Complainant contains, among others, the victims' judicial applications and official documents produced by the institutions of the Respondent State including judgments handed down by national courts and by the CCJA. It concludes that the requirement under examination has been met.

As to the conformity of the Communication with the provisions of Article 56(5), the Commission notes that the Complainant had, by way of judicial proceedings, challenged the order of the Court of First Instance of Yaoundé-Centre Administratif before the courts.

It is the established jurisprudence of the Commission that the objective of this requirement is to enable the State concerned to settle in priority, according to its domestic law, the alleged human rights violation before its examination by an international body, to prevent such a body from being used as a court of first instance but rather as a body of last resort.

In its application by the Commission, Article 56(5) has been the subject of abundant jurisprudence which confirms this interpretation and broadens it. The leading decision on the question is undoubtedly that rendered in the famous case of Jawara v. The Gambia, in which the Commission elucidates the nature and quality of the local remedies whose exhaustion is required of the complainant. The Commission thus stated that within the meaning of Article 56(5) of the Charter, the remedies to be exhausted must be "available, effective and sufficient". The Commission continues by setting out the meaning of these criteria as follows: A remedy is considered available when it can be pursued without hindrance by the applicant, it is effective if it offers prospects of success and it is sufficient when it is capable of redressing the complaint.

On examination of the parties' submissions, it appears to the Commission that local remedies were available since judicial proceedings were indeed initiated by the Complainant. However, the Commission must establish whether these remedies were exhausted as well as their effectiveness and their sufficiency since the Complainant alleges a denial of justice on the part of the Respondent State.

On the question of the exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission notes that for the redress of the alleged violations, the victims attempted to pursue existing judicial remedies by appealing to the Court of Appeal against the judgment handed down by the Court of First Instance, and also lodged an appeal on points of law before the CCJA against the judgment of the Court of Appeal upholding that of the Tribunal de Grande Instance. The Commission also notes that the victims, in parallel to the proceedings on the merits, seized the Supreme Court with an application for a stay of execution which was not received by the competent services. It also notes that the victims subsequently seized the Supreme Court once again with an application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on the CCJA judgment setting aside that of the Court of Appeal.

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has observed that the provisions of Article 14 of the OHADA Treaty recognise the CCJA's full competence to hear appeals on points of law against decisions rendered by national courts in all cases raising questions relating to the application of a Uniform Act and of the Regulations provided for in this Treaty, with the exception of decisions applying criminal sanctions. The Commission concludes in this regard that the CCJA's judgment entailed the exhaustion of local remedies, given that the present communication concerns a case that falls within the scope of the OHADA Uniform Acts.

On the Respondent State's argument setting out the non-exhaustion of local remedies concerning the allegation of denial of justice, the Commission finds, on examination of the parties' submissions, that although the Penal Code provides for criminal proceedings against the Judge concerned for refusal of a due service and abuse of office, the person concerned is the First President of the Supreme Court, who is also the head of the body vested with the power to set in motion the appropriate procedure to sanction defaulting judges.

The Commission further observes that denial of justice does not constitute a violation separate from the Complainant's allegations, given that it concerns the execution of a domestic decision which, once executed, could have remedied the violations alleged by the victims, after exhaustion of the existing remedies.

Having concluded that local remedies were exhausted, the Commission considers that there is no longer any need to examine the question of the undue prolongation of the procedure, which constitutes an exemption factor from the exhaustion of local remedies. The Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the requirement of Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

Article 56(6) of the African Charter requires the submission of the Communication within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter. Although the African Charter does not specify the meaning of the notion of "reasonable period" for submitting a complaint after the exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission, drawing inspiration from the practice in the inter-American and European human rights systems, decided in the case of Majuru v. Zimbabwe that the period of six months may be considered a "usual standard".

In the present Communication, it appears from the evidence put forward by the Complainant that the judgment of 9 March 2018 handed down by the Court of Appeal of the Centre, upholding that of the TPI of Yaoundé Centre - administratif on the eviction of SARL METIS and the late Mrs ETOUMAN Adèle, was the subject of an appeal lodged in July 2018 with the CCJA which handed down its judgment on 27 June 2019 annulling the Judgment of the Court of Appeal. The Commission notes that the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court of Cameroon was seized on 29 August 2019 with an application for the affixing of the enforcement formula on the CCJA Judgment.

The Commission further notes that the present Communication was submitted on 1 November 2019, that is, within a period of two months after the filing of the application for the affixing of the enforcement formula. The Commission finds that such a time limit for seizure is reasonable and that the Communication consequently fulfils the requirement laid down by the Charter in this regard.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Communication must not deal with matters which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata; of non-lis pendens; and of non bis in idem.

In this case, the Commission notes that, apart from the actions undertaken before the national courts, the Complainant brought this case before the CCJA, the common court established by the OHADA treaty, as court of cassation to hear all decisions rendered by the appellate courts of the States Parties in all cases raising questions relating to the application of the uniform acts but also decisions not subject to appeal rendered by any court of the States Parties and of the regulations provided for in this Treaty with the exception of decisions applying criminal sanctions. It rules under the same conditions on decisions not subject to appeal rendered by any court of the States Parties in the same disputes. In the event of cassation, it evokes and rules on the merits. The Commission observes that the present Communication concerns a case that falls within the scope of the OHADA Uniform Acts. In this regard, the Commission has already concluded that the CCJA is a local remedy within the meaning of Article 56(5). This position is confirmed by both domestic and international legislation and jurisprudence.

In this case, the Commission finds that the alleged facts were brought only before the national courts which heard the related complaints and rendered decisions. Furthermore, the case is not pending before any other body referred to in the provisions of the same article. Finally, and consequently, there is no reason to fear that the Respondent State may be subject to double prosecution, still less to a conviction in this same cause. The Commission concludes that the Communication respects the requirement under examination. The Commission therefore finds that this is a Communication which has not been settled within the terms of Article 56(7) of the Charter and concludes that it respects the criterion laid down by the provisions of the said article.
For these reasons, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter.

The Complainant alleges that the Registry service of the Supreme Court of Cameroon as well as that of the private secretariat of its First President categorically refused to register a new application by Mrs ETOUMAN and SARL METIS for a stay of execution of Judgment No. 171/REF handed down on 9 March 2018 by the Court of Appeal of the Centre.

He indicates that the said application had its proper basis in the appeal on points of law lodged before the CCJA, and in respect of which the High court had declared itself incompetent ratione materiae.

The Complainant further indicates that faced with these unexpected and unlawful refusals, the victims' counsel had undertaken to meet the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon in order to directly denounce this abusive situation of his registry, but all access had been denied to them by the head of the Protocol service of his Office.

He reports that so as not to compromise the time limits allotted in this case, the application for a stay of execution was transmitted by the urgent mail services of the post office to the Secretariat of the First President against a receipt serving as acknowledgment of receipt.

He alleges that despite the said receipt, the victims were always refused the issuance of the certificate of filing requested as of right and never knew what fate had been reserved for the said application.

The Complainant also alleges that such a grave failure had emboldened the opposing party, Mrs Marie MINLEND NYOBE, to pursue the execution of the Judgment of the Court of Appeal of the Centre, thus leading to the abusive eviction of the victims, with the good cover of the Registry of the Supreme Court which had deliberately refused to register the application and, by ricochet, the issuance of the certificate of filing.

The Complainant further alleges that after Judgment No. 210/2019 handed down by the CCJA on 27 June 2019, annulling and setting aside judgment number 171/REF of 9 March 2018 of the Court of Appeal of the Centre, so much disputed and which had nevertheless been executed, the victims seized the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court of Cameroon via the First President of the said Court, in application of the texts in force, with a view to the affixing of the enforcement formula on the CCJA decision. They lament that this request remained without follow-up until the seizure of the Commission.
According to the Complainant, the conduct of the Supreme Court of Cameroon amounts to a manifest will to obstruct any action, yet provided for by law, aimed at restoring the victims to their rights.

The Complainant recalls that under the provisions of the African Charter, any State which recognises for its citizens the right of access to justice must take measures in its judicial system so that these remedies are always open to its litigants.

He explains that faced with such a manifestly unlawful attitude, violating the human right of access to justice, the victims found themselves deprived of any bulwark, having no other national remedy to protect them from the irregular and unlawful attitude of the Supreme Court of Cameroon.

He concludes that in the present case, the State of Cameroon provides no mechanism for remedy against irregular judicial decisions of the Supreme Court of Cameroon to such an extent that the decisions of this Court are not subject to any remedy.

The Complainant indicates that law number 92/008 of 14 August 1992 laying down certain provisions relating to the execution of judicial decisions amended by number 97/018 of 7 August 1997 provides in its Article 2(1) that "in non-criminal matters, the exercise of a remedy, with the exception of an appeal before the Supreme Court, suspends the execution of the challenged judicial decision".

He submits that according to the Cameroonian legislator, any application for a stay of execution before the Supreme Court of Cameroon is admitted as of right for examination and cannot be subject to refusal of filing.

He alleges, however, that the State of Cameroon has provided no remedy in the event of refusal to register an application of this kind at the registry of the Supreme Court, whereas this is a fundamental guarantee for the right to a fair trial.

The Complainant indicates that the victims seized the CCJA after the decision of the Supreme Court to declare the first application for a stay of execution inadmissible. According to the Complainant, it was following the rejection decision, learnedly reasoned, of the CCJA regarding the stay of execution of decisions rendered by the State Party that the victims seized the Supreme Court again for the same purposes.

He alleges that the Supreme Court did not even deign to register the said application to give it a chance to be examined so as to take note of the new element in the proceedings. He further alleges that the zeal suffered by the counsel of the Complainants both from the Registry service of the Supreme Court and from the Protocol service of the First President of the Supreme Court of Cameroon, constitutes a manifestly unlawful, abusive and irregular attitude obstructing the right to a remedy.

He indicates that by such abstention, the State of Cameroon does not guarantee to its litigants a right to a fair trial, thereby violating the provisions of Article 7 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.

He reports that in accordance with Decree No. 2002/299 of 3 December 2002, the Chief Registrar of the Supreme Court is the authority responsible for affixing the enforcement formula on judgments handed down by the CCJA.
