The Gauteng Division of the High Court of South Africa's ruling in this case was to the effect that the Order which was appealed against did not dispose of any issue; neither was it final or definitive of the parties' rights.

In light of this, the Respondent State submits that the Complainant could not successfully appeal against the Order in terms of Section 17(1) of the Superior Court Act, No. 10 of 2013. However, the Respondent State notes that the Complainant still had the option to set the matter down again for hearing, but with stricter compliance with the rules and procedures of the South African courts. If this avenue had failed, he still had the option to appeal a decision on the merits to the Supreme Court of Appeal or the Full Bench of the High Court and, subsequently, the Constitutional Court, if the appeal had been rendered unsuccessful.

The Respondent State further argues that the Complainant had the prerogative to enroll his application on the normal court roll in terms of the practice manual of the Polokwane High Court and set his matter down for hearings as the merits were not yet determined.

The Respondent State submits that in addition to the Complainant having the option to set the matter on the normal court roll, the South Africa Uniform Rules of Court grant a Respondent in a motion proceeding to enroll a matter for hearing on the Roll if the Applicant in a matter fails to apply for the date, before approaching the Constitutional Court on an urgent basis to set aside the order handed down by Polokwane High Court.

Lastly, the Respondent State argues that the Complainant could seek redress from the Labour Court for an order to unblock his Persal Number in terms of the Basic Conditions of Employment Act No. 75 of 1997.

The Respondent State submits that the Commission needs to be guided by the principle of the primacy of domestic remedies in reaching its decision. The Respondent State also submits that it has adequately demonstrated the availability of judicial remedies that the Complainant could have utilised before filing the complaint.
The Respondent State contends that the Commission has sufficient grounds to render the complaint inadmissible as it does not meet the requirements of Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

Article 56 of the African Charter provides that communications submitted under Article 55 of the African Charter shall be considered if they satisfy the seven (7) conditions of admissibility set out therein. The requirements are conjunctive and should be viewed cumulatively, such that a failure to meet any of the requirements renders a communication inadmissible.
The Commission considers the submissions of the parties in light of these requirements as follows:

Article 56(1) of the African Charter requires that a communication 'indicate its authors even if the latter request anonymity.' The practice and jurisprudence of the Commission posits that the provision requires the Complainants to provide their identity and contact details so that the communication is processed adequately. This also provides an avenue for communication with the parties to ensure continued interest in the matter or to request additional information that may be required pertaining to the communication. In the present case, Mashilo Alfred Sako is identified as the complainant, represented by Advocate Shadrack Tebeile. Therefore, the parties are sufficiently identified, and the communication duly complies with Article 56 (1) of the African Charter.

Article 56(2) of the African Charter requires a Communication to be compatible with the Charter of the African Union or the Charter. Furthermore, the Commission has interpreted this provision to include compatibility with the four (4) aspects of its competence, namely competence ratione personae, materiae, temporis and loci. The Commission is satisfied that this communication satisfies the four aspects necessary to establish jurisdiction. The Commission notes that the communication was introduced against the Respondent State, a party to the African Charter (competence ratione personae), alleges the violation of rights provided for in the Charter, in particular Articles 7(1), 7(1)(a), 13(2), 13(3) and 15 (competence ratione materiae) of the African Charter, alleges that the violation was committed in the territory of the Respondent State (competence ratione loci) and that the alleged violation occurred after the Respondent State ratified the African Charter (competence ratione temporis).

Additionally, the Commission notes that the communication seeks the protection of human rights and is, in turn, compatible with Article 3(h) of the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Therefore, nothing in the Complainant's submissions reveals any incompatibility with the African Union Constitutive Act or the African Charter. In view of the foregoing, the Complainant has satisfied Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

Regarding the language used, Article 56(3) of the African Charter provides that communications shall not contain disparaging or insulting language directed to the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. In Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe v Republic of Zimbabwe, the Commission held that "in determining whether a certain remark is disparaging or insulting and whether it has dampened the integrity of the judiciary, the Commission has to satisfy itself whether the said remark or language is aimed at unlawfully and intentionally violating the dignity, reputation or integrity of a judicial officer or body and whether it is used in a manner calculated to pollute the minds of the public or any reasonable man to cast aspersions on and weaken public confidence on the administration of justice." The Commission has satisfied itself that in the present case, the Complainant did not use any language undermining the integrity and status of the institution being complained against and bringing it into disrepute. Consequently, this condition of admissibility is fulfilled.

Article 56(4) of the African Charter provides that communications should not be 'based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media.' In interpreting this provision, the Commission has acknowledged the importance of mass media as a source of information and reiterated that the issue of concern is whether the information obtained from the media is correct and the veracity of the allegations from it. The Complainant produced court documents as evidence and has not relied exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media. Thus, this communication satisfies the provisions of Article 56(4) of the African Charter.

Concerning the exhaustion of domestic remedies, Article 56(5) of the African Charter provides that communications may only be admitted after 'exhaustion of local remedies if they exist unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged.'

The rationale behind Article 56(5) of the African Charter is to give state parties the first responsibility to resolve allegations of human rights violations using their domestic remedies and within their domestic legal system. This is informed by the principle of the subsidiarity of the international adjudicatory system. The settled jurisprudence of the Commission shows that this is one of the most important conditions for the admissibility of communications.

The Commission has further established that these domestic remedies must be available, in that they can be used by the Complainant without impediment; effective, because they offer a prospect of success; and sufficient, because it is capable of fully redressing the alleged violations.
The Complainant argues that he exhausted all available local remedies because he utilised the legal system up to the apex court, that is, the Constitutional Court.

On the other hand, the Respondent State submits that while the Complainant filed a case in the Constitutional Court, the matter was dismissed on a technicality. Thus, the Complainant still had the opportunity to file an application on the normal roll from the High Court and appeal, if the outcome was undesirable, up to the Constitutional Court.

The Respondent State further submits that according to the domestic legal system of the Republic of South Africa, it is trite law that when a case is struck off the roll, it is unappealable per the Thembane Cleaning Services judgment referenced above. Therefore, the procedure to approach the Constitutional Court of South Africa was misplaced and premature.

In this Communication, the Commission concurs with the Respondent State's assertions and notes that after the urgent application was struck off the roll, the Complainant did not take the necessary steps to file the application on the normal court roll and allow the necessary court processes to unfold. This would have allowed for the matter to be adjudicated on the merits, which, if dismissed, could have been appealed against at the Supreme Court of Appeal. However, the Complainant did not do so.

In Jawara v The Gambia, the Commission highlighted that in determining the availability of a remedy, it will consider whether the Complainant knows of the remedy and can pursue it without impediment. The Complainant is legally represented and should therefore have effectively exhausted all known and available local remedies through the assistance of his representatives.

The Commission notes that, indeed, according to the South African legal system, the Complainant had the option of approaching the Labour Court for relief to get his Persal Number unblocked. However, he did not utilise this procedure.

Furthermore, the South African Uniform Rules of Court grant a Respondent in a motion proceeding to enroll a matter for hearing on the roll if the Applicant in a matter fails to apply for the date. While this may be an unlikely occurrence on the part of the Respondent, who may not have any direct interest in ensuring the finalisation of this matter, it buttresses the notion that there were other available avenues the Complainant could have benefited from, in exhausting domestic remedies, before approaching the Commission.

In any event, the Commission takes cognisance of the fact that the Complainant did not actively prosecute his claim from the beginning to justify his cases being heard on an urgent basis. This situation arose after his dismissal in 2004. However, the Complainant did not actively and urgently prosecute the matter until 2021. Instead, he relied on unofficial information from third parties as opposed to following due process. The Complainant should have followed the proper court proceedings and exhausted all local remedies. There was no apprehension of any injustice in exhausting local remedies, which would warrant an exception to the mandatory rule.

In Obert Chinhamo v Zimbabwe, the Commission drew inspiration from the UN Human Rights Committee which stated that "the mere fact that a domestic remedy is inconvenient or unattractive, or does not produce a result favourable to the petitioner does not, in itself, demonstrate the lack or exhaustion of all effective remedies." While the Complainant sought his cases to be heard on an urgent basis, the fact that proceeding on the normal court roll would not have been favourable to him, as this would not be as expeditious as he had hoped, did not render the local remedies unavailable or duly exhausted. The dismissal of both cases in the High Court and the Constitutional Court was done on procedural as opposed to substantive grounds.

Finally, the Commission reiterated in Rencontre Africaine pour la défense des droits de l'homme v Zambia that when a government 'argues that the Communication should be declared inadmissible because local remedies have not been exhausted, this government has the responsibility of proving the existence of such remedies.' The Commission contends that the Respondent State has successfully proven the existence of remedies at the Complainant's disposal.

In view of the above, the Commission concludes that the Complainant has not exhausted domestic remedies and that this Communication fails to meet the requirements of Article 56 (5) of the African Charter.

With regards to the time limit for lodging a complaint, Article 56(6) of the African Charter provides that communications are to be admitted if they are submitted within a reasonable time, following the exhaustion of domestic remedies or the date set by the Commission for the counting of the time limit for admissibility before the Commission itself.

In Promoting Justice for Women and Children (PROJUST NGO) vs. Democratic Republic of Congo, the Commission noted that the requirement in Article 56(6) is tied to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies so much so that the point of departure of the reasonable time is from the date of exhaustion of local remedies. It is not worthwhile to analyse Article 56(6) of the African Charter when failure to exhaust local remedies has been established. In this communication, the Commission has established that the Complainant failed to exhaust local remedies. Consequently, the need to analyse the condition of Article 56(6) of the African Charter in the present Communication also falls away.

Finally, Article 56(7) of the African Charter states that 'Communications relating to human and Peoples' Rights... shall be considered if they do not deal with cases which have been settled by the states involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter.' This condition codifies the principle of non bis in idem or res judicata by requiring that the matter referred to it should not be pending before another body on the merits.

In Luke Munyandu Tembani and Benjamin John Freeth (represented by Norman Tjombe) v Angola and Thirteen Others, the Commission averred that the provision requires that a case "no longer be under consideration under an international dispute-settlement procedure" Additionally, the case must have been decided on the merits and a 'final settlement' given by that body. The settlement must be from an 'adjudication mechanism with a human rights mandate. In the present case, there is no evidence to suggest that this matter was settled by another international adjudicatory body. Thus, the Communication complies with Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

In view of the above, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares the Communication inadmissible for lack of compliance with the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter; ii. Notifies the Parties of its decision in accordance with the provisions of Rule 118(4) of its Rules of Procedure. Done at the 83 Ordinary Session of the Commission held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 2 to 22 May 2025.

Le 26 juillet 2023, la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (la Commission) a reçu à travers son secrétariat une plainte déposée par Monsieur Jean Paul BELFIS ci-après « Plaignant » contre la République du Congo ci-après « Etat défendeur », ayant ratifié la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (la Charte africaine) le 30 décembre 2009. Monsieur BELFIS est représenté par Me Claudio COELHO DE CARVALHO ci-après « Représentant ».

Monsieur BELFIS est un citoyen français résidant à Pointe noire en République du Congo et actionnaire et président du conseil d'administration de la société GESTION NOUVELLE DES CHANTIERS ET ATELIERS DU CONGO en sigle GNCAC S.A.

Le Plaignant allègue que la SOCIETE CIVILE IMMOBILIERE GABY SARL en sigle SCI GABY est actionnaire de la société GNCAC S.A, avec Conseil d'Administration, créée le 08 juillet 1987. Elle détient 17,2% d'action ; que Monsieur Jean Paul BELFIS est le Président du Conseil d'Administration et Monsieur Armand TESTI, le Directeur Général.

Il soutient que Monsieur Gabriel NZAMBILA avant de créer la SCI GABY était actionnaire en son nom propre et c'est en sa qualité d'administrateur qu'il a saisi le Tribunal de Commerce de Pointe-Noire le 21 mai 2015 aux fins d'obtenir un audit extérieur global de la société GNCAC et de sa filiale la SIAC pour la période allant de l'année 2010 à 2014 sur le fondement de l'article 159 de l'Acte Uniforme OHADA portant sur les sociétés commerciales et du Groupement d'intérêt économique (GIE).

Il allègue que, par ordonnance du 18 mai 2015, le Président du Tribunal de Commerce de Pointe-Noire, Juge des référés, a ordonné l'audit des activités et comptes de la société GNCAC pour les années 2010 à 2014 et désigné Monsieur Vincent PENA PITRA YOBA Expert-Comptable, pour y procéder. Sur appel de la société GNCAC, la Chambre Commerciale de la Cour d'appel de Pointe-Noire a, rôle n° 168, répertoire 39 du 22 décembre 2015, annulé la décision du juge du Tribunal de commerce en toutes ses dispositions et évoquant et statuant à nouveau, a désigné le Cabinet RAINBOW FINANCES S.A à l'effet de procéder à l'audit en remplacement de Monsieur Vincent PENA PITRA YOBA Expert-Comptable.

Le Plaignant fait observer que la Cour Commune de Justice et d'Arbitrage de l'OHADA, saisie par la société GNCAC a, par arrêt n° 138/2017 du 14 décembre 2017, cassé et annulé l'arrêt de la Chambre Commerciale de la Cour d'Appel rôle n° 168, répertoire 39 du 22 décembre 2015. Nonobstant cet arrêt, Monsieur Gabriel NZAMBILA, en sa qualité d'administrateur de la SCI GABY, mécontent du rapport du Cabinet d'expertise RAINBOW, qui avait continué sa mission, la saisine de la CCJA n'étant pas suspensive, a confié unilatéralement la mission d'expertiser les comptes de la société GNCAC pour la période du 1er janvier 2010 au 31 décembre 2016, au Cabinet d'audit et Conseils GRANT THORTON.

Ce Cabinet a présenté à Monsieur Gabriel NZAMBILA en exécution de la mission qui lui a été confiée le compte rendu de sa mission d'expertise. Au vu de ce rapport d'expertise, la SCI GABY a saisi le Tribunal de Commerce de Pointe-Noire, motif pris des anomalies constatées dans la gestion de la société GNCAC par le Cabinet d'Audit et de Conseils GRANT THORTON aux fins de mise sous administration judiciaire de la société GNCAC.

Par ordonnance du 24 février 2017, rôle commercial n° 482, la société GNCAC a été mise sous administration judiciaire pour une durée de 6 mois avec possibilité de renouvellement et le Cabinet ABB VISION, représenté par Monsieur André Blaise BOLLE, a été nommé Administrateur Provisoire. Le 10 novembre 2017, par ordonnance rôle commercial n° 596, cette administration provisoire a été prorogée d'une durée de 6 mois.

Le Plaignant allègue que le 20 décembre 2017, l'Administrateur Provisoire a notifié son rapport au Président du Conseil d'Administration de la société GNCAC et suggéré de réunir sans délai un Conseil d'Administration aux fins de prendre des décisions qui s'imposent dans l'intérêt supérieur de la société. Le Président du Conseil d'Administration devant ces injonctions a dû convoquer un Conseil d'Administration, puis une Assemblée Générale Ordinaire qui se sont tenus le 06 janvier 2018.

Le Plaignant soutient que l'actionnaire, le représentant légal de la SCI GABY, alors que les résolutions ont été votées et adoptées par 83% de l'actionnariat, a émis des réserves infondées et a refusé de signer la minute du procès-verbal de l'Assemblée Générale Ordinaire du 06 janvier 2018. Des suites, il a saisi le Tribunal Correctionnel de Pointe-Noire, par citation directe, le 21 juin 2018, pour entendre Monsieur Jean Paul BELFILS, en sa qualité de Président du Conseil d'Administration, pour être poursuivi de délit de dissimulation de la véritable situation de la société et d'abus de biens sociaux.

Par jugement correctionnel répertoire n° 147 RP n° 1090/2018 du 02 juillet 2019, le plaignant en sa qualité de Président du Conseil d'Administration a été déclaré coupable de délit de dissimulation de la véritable situation de la société et d'abus de biens sociaux. Il a été donc condamné à une peine de 24 mois assortie de sursis et à payer à la SCI GABY, représentée par Monsieur Gabriel NZAMBILA la somme de 784.193.250 FCFA et celle de 300.000.000 de FCFA à titre de dommages-intérêts, soit un total de 1.084.193.250 FCFA.

Le 03 juillet 2019, le plaignant a interjeté appel de cette décision. Par arrêt correctionnel du 16 juillet 2020, la Première Chambre Correctionnelle de la Cour d'appel de Pointe-Noire a confirmé le jugement entrepris en toutes ses dispositions. Sur le pourvoi du plaignant, la Deuxième Chambre Pénale de la Cour Suprême du Congo a rejeté ledit pourvoi par arrêt n° 34/GCS-21 du 30 juillet 2021. Cet arrêt a été servi au plaignant le 06 août 2021.
Le Plaignant allègue la violation des article 3 (1) et 7 (1)(C) de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission : a) De le déclarer recevable et bien fondé en sa requête ; b) De constater la violation du principe du procès équitable par la Première Chambre Correctionnelle de la Cour d'Appel de Pointe-Noire et la Chambre Pénale de la Cour Suprême du Congo, notamment l'article 3 alinéa 1 et l'article 7 alinéa 1er -c de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples ; c) D'ordonner le réexamen de cette procédure afin de remédier à la situation générée par les dispositions de l'arrêt n° 34/GCS-21 de la Chambre Pénale de la Cour Suprême de Brazzaville du 30 juillet 2021 et celles de la Première Chambre Correctionnelle de la Cour d'Appel de Pointe-Noire du 16 juillet 2020, rôle 003, répertoire n° 006.

La plainte initiale a été reçue au Secrétariat de la Commission le 26 juillet 2023. Un accusé de réception a été adressé au Plaignant le 18 août 2023, l'informant des insuffisances relevées dans sa soumission, notamment l'absence d'indications claires sur la partie mise en cause. Il lui a alors été suggéré de reformuler sa plainte en utilisant le formulaire prévu à cet effet.
Le 28 août 2023, le Plaignant a transmis une version corrigée de sa plainte, dont la réception a été confirmée par courrier daté du 30 août 2023.

Par lettre en date du 22 septembre 2023, la Commission a informé le Plaignant de sa décision de se saisir de la plainte. Par Note Verbale du même jour, elle a informé l'État défendeur de cette saisine, précisant que les observations et éléments de preuve relatifs à la recevabilité et au fond, une fois transmis par le Plaignant, lui seraient communiqués.

Par courriel du 8 juillet 2024, la Commission a attiré l'attention du Plaignant sur le risque de radiation de sa plainte, en raison de l'absence de soumission, dans les délais impartis, des arguments relatifs à la recevabilité et au fond.

Par courriel daté du 19 août 2024, le plaignant a présenté ses arguments et preuves sur la recevabilité et le fond, indiquant que même en l'absence de telles observations supplémentaires, la Commission ne peut pas radier la plainte car elle contenait tous les éléments nécessaires à la décision et s'attend à ce que la Commission examine la communication.

Par lettre datée du 25 septembre 2024, la Commission accusait réception des observations du Plaignant sur la recevabilité et le fond. Ces observations ont été communiquées à l'État défendeur par Note Verbale le même jour.
À ce jour, l'État défendeur n'a soumis aucune réplique aux arguments du Plaignant.
Les moyens invoqués par le Plaignant au regard de la recevabilité de sa communication se fondent sur les dispositions de l'article 56(2) et (5) de la Charte.

S'agissant de l'article 56(2) de la Charte, relatif à la compatibilité de la communication avec la Charte de l'Organisation de l'Unité Africaine (aujourd'hui Acte constitutif de l'Union africaine) ou avec la Charte africaine, le Plaignant soutient que sa plainte vise à obtenir réparation pour la violation de ses droits à l'égalité devant la loi et à un procès équitable, tels que garantis par les articles 3 et 7 de ladite Charte.

S'agissant de l'article 56(5) de la Charte, relatif à l'épuisement des voies de recours internes, le Plaignant affirme que le rejet de son pourvoi par la Cour suprême du Congo marque la fin des recours internes disponibles.
La Commission n'a pas reçu de réponse de la part de l'Etat défendeur quant aux arguments du Plaignant.

La règle 118(2) du Règlement intérieur de 2020 de la Commission dispose ce qui suit : « Lorsqu'aucune observation sur la recevabilité n'a été reçue de l'Etat défendeur dans le délai fixé, la Commission procède à l'adoption d'une décision par défaut fondée sur les informations dont elle dispose. »

En conséquence, et au regard du fait que l'Etat défendeur, bien qu'informé de la plainte, n'a soumis aucune observation, l'analyse de la Commission se fondera exclusivement sur les éléments de preuve présentés par le Plaignant.

De prime abord, la Commission souhaite rappeler que l'article 56 de la Charte énonce sept (7) conditions de recevabilité que toute plainte soumise en vertu de l'article 55 de la Charte doit remplir cumulativement. Le non-respect de l'une de ces conditions entraîne le rejet de la communication. C'est à la lumière de ces conditions que sera examinée la recevabilité de la présente communication.

L'article 56(1) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) indiquer l'identité de leur auteur même si celui-ci demande à la Commission de garder l'anonymat ».
La Commission note que la présente Communication a été introduite devant elle par Monsieur Jean Paul BELFIS, représenté par Me Claudio COELHO DE CARVALHO.
Les adresses complètes et les coordonnées de contact du Plaignant et de son représentant étant bien précisées, la Commission conclut que la Communication respecte cette condition.

L'article 56(2) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) être compatibles avec la Charte de l'Organisation de l'Unité Africaine ou avec la présente Charte ».

La Commission a affirmé dans l'affaire Law Society of Zimbabwe c Zimbabwe que la compatibilité d'une Communication avec l'Acte Constitutif de l'Union africaine repose sur sa compatibilité avec les objectifs et les principes consacrés par l'Acte, et plus précisément sur la question de savoir si les requêtes de la Communication ne contreviendraient pas aux objectifs ou aux principes exprimés dans l'Acte. A cet égard, la Commission constate que ni les moyens ni les demandes contenus dans la Communication n'enfreignent aucun des objectifs et principes adoptés aux termes dudit Acte ou la Charte.

En ce qui concerne le critère de compatibilité des communications avec la Charte africaine, la Commission doit s'assurer que les moyens invoqués ainsi que les demandes formulées dans la communication relèvent de sa compétence, tant sur le plan personnel (ratione personae), matériel (ratione materiae), temporel (ratione temporis) que territorial (ratione loci).

En l'espèce, la Commission note que la communication est introduite contre la République du Congo, Etat partie à la Charte africaine (compétence ratione personae). En outre, les Plaignants allèguent que les violations ont eu lieu sur le territoire de l'Etat défendeur (compétence ratione loci), de droits protégés par les articles 3 (1) et 7 (1)(C) de la Charte (compétence ratione materiae). La Commission note par ailleurs que la Charte était en vigueur en République du Congo à l'époque des faits (compétence ratione temporis). En conséquence, la Commission conclut que la Communication respecte les dispositions de l'article 56(2) de la Charte.

L'article 56(3) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) ne pas contenir des termes outrageants ou insultants à l'égard de l'Etat mis en cause, de ses institutions ou de l'OUA (UA) ».

Dans l'affaire Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe c. la République du Zimbabwe, la Commission a déclaré que "pour déterminer si une certaine remarque est outrageante ou insultante et si elle a porté atteinte à l'intégrité du pouvoir judiciaire, la Commission doit s'assurer que ladite remarque ou ledit terme vise à porter illégalement et intentionnellement atteinte à la dignité, à la réputation ou à l'intégrité d'un fonctionnaire ou d'un organe judiciaire et qu'il est utilisé de manière intentionnelle pour manipuler l'opinion publique ou toute personne raisonnable afin de jeter le discrédit sur l'administration de la justice et d'affaiblir la confiance du public à son égard."

Après analyse de la plainte, la Commission relève que le Plaignant n'a utilisé aucun langage qui viserait à porter indûment atteinte à l'estime de l'Etat défendeur ou de l'Union africaine. À la lumière de ce qui précède, la Commission estime que l'article 56 (3) de la Charte est respecté.

L'article 56(4) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) ne pas se limiter à rassembler exclusivement des nouvelles diffusées par des moyens de communication de masse ».

L'interprétation de cette disposition issue des affaires Jawara et Ahmed Ismael et 528 autres c. République arabe d'Égypte est que « la question n'est pas de savoir si l'information provient des médias, mais plutôt si elle est exacte » et si le requérant a tenté d'en vérifier la véracité.

En l'espèce, la Plaignant a produit divers éléments de preuve, notamment la Grosse certifiée conforme de l'arrêt n° 34/GCS-21 de la Chambre Pénale de la Cour Suprême du 30 juillet 2021, l'Expédition certifiée conforme de l'arrêt de la Première Chambre Correctionnelle rôle n° 003, répertoire n°006 de la Cour d'appel de Pointe-Noire du 16 juillet 2020, le Procès-verbal du Conseil d'Administration du 6 janvier 2018 ou encore le Procès-verbal constant que le Sieur Jean Paul BELFILS est Président du Conseil d'Administration et non Directeur Général du 17 février 2018. La Commission considère, dès lors, que le Plaignant ne s'est pas du tout fondé sur des informations médiatiques et que la présente communication satisfait aux exigences de l'article 56(4) de la Charte.

L'article 56(5) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) être postérieures à l'épuisement des recours internes s'ils existent, à moins qu'il ne soit manifeste à la Commission que la procédure de ces recours se prolonge d'une façon anormale ».

La Commission rappelle que l'exigence d'épuisement des recours internes constitue un principe fondamental en droit international, en particulier devant les juridictions et mécanismes internationaux de protection des droits de l'homme. Ce principe implique que le requérant doit avoir utilisé, sans succès, tous les recours disponibles et effectifs devant les juridictions nationales avant de saisir une instance internationale. Il repose sur la reconnaissance de la souveraineté des États et sur le respect du principe de subsidiarité, selon lequel la responsabilité première de la protection des droits de l'homme incombe aux États eux-mêmes. Ce principe vise également à éviter l'encombrement des juridictions internationales par des affaires qui auraient pu trouver une solution au niveau national, et à encourager le renforcement des systèmes judiciaires internes.

La jurisprudence de la Commission reconnaît que l'exigence d'épuisement ne s'applique qu'aux recours internes qui sont disponibles, efficaces et suffisants, seuls ceux-ci pouvant raisonnablement être exigés des Plaignants. Un recours est considéré comme disponible si le requérant peut l'exercer sans entrave, il est considéré comme efficace s'il offre une perspective de succès, et il est jugé suffisant s'il est capable de redresser la situation.

La jurisprudence de la Commission a également établi, notamment dans Human Rights Council et autres c. Éthiopie, que le défaut d'épuisement des recours internes disponibles rend une communication irrecevable.

Dans la présente communication, le Plaignant a indiqué avoir été déclaré coupable de délit de dissimulation de la véritable situation de la société GNCAC et d'abus de biens sociaux le 02 juillet 2019 par le Tribunal Correctionnel de Pointe-Noire. Il avait été condamné à 24 mois de prison avec sursis et à payer à la SCI GABY, représentée par Monsieur Gabriel NZAMBILA la somme de 784.193.250 FCFA et celle de 300.000.000 de FCFA à titre de dommages-intérêts, soit un total de 1.084.193.250 FCFA.

La Commission note que le Plaignant a interjeté appel de ce jugement le 03 juillet 2019 et que le 16 juillet 2020, la première chambre correctionnelle de la Cour d'Appel de Pointe-Noire a confirmé le jugement entrepris en toutes ses dispositions
La Commission note que le 30 juillet 2021, la 2 chambre pénale de la Cour suprême du Congo a rejeté le pourvoi du Plaignant en cassation.

La Cour suprême étant la plus haute juridiction de l'État défendeur et ayant statué sur le fond de l'affaire, la Commission considère que le Plaignant dans la présente communication a effectivement épuisé les recours internes disponibles en République du Congo, et que sa communication satisfait aux exigences de l'article 56(5) de la Charte.

L'article 56(6) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) être introduites dans un délai raisonnable courant depuis l'épuisement des recours internes ou depuis la date retenue par la Commission comme faisant commencer à courir le délai de sa propre saisine ».

Dans la communication en examen, le délai raisonnable sera examiné à partir de l'épuisement des recours internes. La Commission relève que la décision de la Cour suprême rejetant le pourvoi a été rendu le 30 juillet 2021 et notifiée au Plaignant le 06 août 2021. Le Plaignant a saisi la Commission le 26 juillet 2023, soit une (1) année et 349 jours plus tard. La question qui se pose est celle de savoir si ce délai est raisonnable.

La Commission rappelle sa jurisprudence constante, à commencer par l'affaire Majuru, selon laquelle, en général, le délai raisonnable pour déposer une plainte est de six (6) mois. Dans cette décision, la Commission a estimé que si la plainte n'est pas déposée dans ce délai, l'appréciation du délai raisonnable doit être effectuée au cas par cas. Pour cela, la Commission doit tenir compte des circonstances de la plainte, de la nature de l'affaire au niveau national et de la justification éventuelle du plaignant. Il s'ensuit que le plaignant doit justifier tout retard excédant six mois.

Dans la communication ARTICLE 19 et autres c. Zimbabwe, la Commission a conclu que la communication n'avait pas été introduite dans un délai raisonnable après l'épuisement des voies de recours internes, les plaignants l'ayant soumise un peu moins de deux ans après l'arrêt définitif de la Cour suprême, et que « la raison avancée par les plaignants concernant la saisine tardive n'est ni bonne ni impérieuse ».

Par ailleurs, le Comité des droits de l'homme dans sa décision relative à la communication no 3049/2017 avait noté que : « ... l'auteur n'a pas expliqué pourquoi il avait soumis sa communication tardivement. En l'absence de toute autre information ou explication pertinente dans le dossier, le Comité considère que le retard est déraisonnable... ».

Après examen des soumissions du Plaignant, la Commission constate que celui-ci n'a fourni aucune justification valable quant au retard accusé dans le dépôt de sa communication. En l'absence d'éléments explicatifs suffisants, la Commission est dans l'obligation de conclure que la condition énoncée à l'article 56(6) de la Charte n'est pas remplie

L'article 56(7) de la Charte dispose que « les communications visées à l'article 55 reçues à la Commission et relatives aux droits de l'homme et des peuples doivent (...) ne pas concerner des cas qui ont été réglés conformément soit aux principes de la Charte des Nations Unies, soit de la Charte de l'Organisation de l'Unité Africaine et soit des dispositions de la présente Charte. »

Dans l'affaire Sudan Human Rights Commission and Another c. Sudan, la Commission a estimé qu'une question est considérée comme réglée si un organe juridictionnel international doté d'un mandat ou d'une compétence en matière de droits de l'homme a pris une décision à ce sujet et a conféré à la plainte l'autorité de la chose jugée.

Dans la présente communication, le Plaignant n'a pas donné d'information à ce propos et la Commission ne relève dans sa narration aucun fait de nature à prouver que l'affaire ait déjà été réglée par un organe juridictionnel international. La Commission conclut que la condition posée à l'article 56(7) de la Charte est satisfaite.

Compte tenu de ce qui précède, la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples : i. Déclare la présente Communication irrecevable pour défaut de conformité aux exigences de l'article 56(6) de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples. ii. Instruit le Secrétariat à notifier sa décision aux Parties conformément à la règle 118(4) de son Règlement intérieur. Fait lors de la 84ème Session ordinaire de la Commission tenue virtuellement du 21 au 30 juillet 2025.

On 26 July 2023, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) received through its secretariat a complaint filed by Mr Jean Paul BELFIS hereinafter the "Complainant" against the Republic of the Congo hereinafter the "Respondent State", which ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) on 30 December 2009. Mr BELFIS is represented by Counsel Claudio COELHO DE CARVALHO hereinafter the "Representative".

Mr BELFIS is a French citizen residing in Pointe Noire in the Republic of the Congo and a shareholder and chairman of the board of directors of the company GESTION NOUVELLE DES CHANTIERS ET ATELIERS DU CONGO abbreviated GNCAC S.A.

The Complainant alleges that the SOCIETE CIVILE IMMOBILIERE GABY SARL abbreviated SCI GABY is a shareholder of the company GNCAC S.A, with a Board of Directors, created on 8 July 1987. It holds 17.2% of the shares; that Mr Jean Paul BELFIS is the Chairman of the Board of Directors and Mr Armand TESTI, the Managing Director.

He maintains that Mr Gabriel NZAMBILA before creating SCI GABY was a shareholder in his own name and it is in his capacity as director that he seized the Commercial Court of Pointe-Noire on 21 May 2015 in order to obtain a comprehensive external audit of the company GNCAC and of its subsidiary SIAC for the period from the year 2010 to 2014 on the basis of Article 159 of the OHADA Uniform Act on commercial companies and Economic Interest Groups (EIG).

He alleges that, by order of 18 May 2015, the President of the Commercial Court of Pointe-Noire, Judge in summary proceedings, ordered the audit of the activities and accounts of the company GNCAC for the years 2010 to 2014 and appointed Mr Vincent PENA PITRA YOBA, Chartered Accountant, to carry it out. On appeal by the company GNCAC, the Commercial Chamber of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire, in docket no. 168, register 39 of 22 December 2015, annulled the decision of the judge of the Commercial Court in all its provisions and, taking up the case and ruling anew, appointed the firm RAINBOW FINANCES S.A to carry out the audit in replacement of Mr Vincent PENA PITRA YOBA, Chartered Accountant.

The Complainant observes that the Common Court of Justice and Arbitration of OHADA, seized by the company GNCAC, by judgment no. 138/2017 of 14 December 2017, quashed and annulled the judgment of the Commercial Chamber of the Court of Appeal docket no. 168, register 39 of 22 December 2015. Notwithstanding this judgment, Mr Gabriel NZAMBILA, in his capacity as director of SCI GABY, dissatisfied with the report of the expert firm RAINBOW, which had continued its mission, the seizure of the CCJA not being suspensive, unilaterally entrusted the mission of auditing the accounts of the company GNCAC for the period from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2016, to the audit and advisory firm GRANT THORTON.

This firm presented to Mr Gabriel NZAMBILA in execution of the mission entrusted to it the report of its audit mission. In view of this expert report, SCI GABY seized the Commercial Court of Pointe-Noire, on the ground of the anomalies found in the management of the company GNCAC by the Audit and Advisory firm GRANT THORTON with a view to placing the company GNCAC under judicial administration.

By order of 24 February 2017, commercial docket no. 482, the company GNCAC was placed under judicial administration for a period of 6 months with the possibility of renewal and the firm ABB VISION, represented by Mr André Blaise BOLLE, was appointed Provisional Administrator. On 10 November 2017, by order commercial docket no. 596, this provisional administration was extended for a period of 6 months.

The Complainant alleges that on 20 December 2017, the Provisional Administrator notified his report to the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company GNCAC and suggested convening without delay a Board of Directors in order to take the decisions necessary in the best interests of the company. The Chairman of the Board of Directors, faced with these injunctions, had to convene a Board of Directors, then an Ordinary General Meeting which were held on 6 January 2018.

The Complainant maintains that the shareholder, the legal representative of SCI GABY, although the resolutions were voted on and adopted by 83% of the shareholding, raised unfounded reservations and refused to sign the original minutes of the Ordinary General Meeting of 6 January 2018. Subsequently, he seized the Criminal Court of Pointe-Noire, by direct summons, on 21 June 2018, to have Mr Jean Paul BELFILS, in his capacity as Chairman of the Board of Directors, prosecuted for the offence of concealing the true situation of the company and misuse of corporate assets.

By criminal judgment register no. 147 RP no. 1090/2018 of 2 July 2019, the complainant in his capacity as Chairman of the Board of Directors was found guilty of the offence of concealing the true situation of the company and misuse of corporate assets. He was therefore sentenced to a term of 24 months suspended and to pay to SCI GABY, represented by Mr Gabriel NZAMBILA the sum of 784,193,250 CFA francs and that of 300,000,000 CFA francs as damages, a total of 1,084,193,250 CFA francs.

On 3 July 2019, the complainant appealed this decision. By criminal judgment of 16 July 2020, the First Criminal Chamber of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire upheld the judgment under appeal in all its provisions. On the complainant's appeal on points of law, the Second Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Congo dismissed the said appeal by judgment no. 34/GCS-21 of 30 July 2021. This judgment was served on the complainant on 6 August 2021.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 3 (1) and 7 (1)(C) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights

The Complainant requests the Commission: a) To declare his application admissible and well-founded; b) To find the violation of the principle of the fair trial by the First Criminal Chamber of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire and the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Congo, notably Article 3 paragraph 1 and Article 7 paragraph 1-c of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights; c) To order the review of this procedure in order to remedy the situation generated by the provisions of judgment no. 34/GCS-21 of the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of Brazzaville of 30 July 2021 and those of the First Criminal Chamber of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire of 16 July 2020, docket 003, register no. 006.

The initial complaint was received at the Secretariat of the Commission on 26 July 2023. An acknowledgement of receipt was sent to the Complainant on 18 August 2023, informing him of the deficiencies noted in his submission, notably the absence of clear indications on the party complained against. It was then suggested to him to reformulate his complaint using the form provided for that purpose.
On 28 August 2023, the Complainant transmitted a corrected version of his complaint, the receipt of which was confirmed by letter dated 30 August 2023.

By letter dated 22 September 2023, the Commission informed the Complainant of its decision to be seized of the complaint. By Note Verbale of the same day, it informed the Respondent State of this seizure, specifying that the observations and evidence relating to admissibility and the merits, once transmitted by the Complainant, would be communicated to it.

By email of 8 July 2024, the Commission drew the Complainant's attention to the risk of striking out of his complaint, owing to the failure to submit, within the time limits set, the arguments relating to admissibility and the merits.

By email dated 19 August 2024, the complainant presented his arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits, indicating that even in the absence of such additional observations, the Commission cannot strike out the complaint because it contained all the elements necessary for the decision and expects the Commission to examine the communication.

By letter dated 25 September 2024, the Commission acknowledged receipt of the Complainant's observations on admissibility and the merits. These observations were communicated to the Respondent State by Note Verbale the same day.
To date, the Respondent State has submitted no reply to the Complainant's arguments.
The arguments invoked by the Complainant with regard to the admissibility of his communication are based on the provisions of Article 56(2) and (5) of the Charter.

Regarding Article 56(2) of the Charter, relating to the compatibility of the communication with the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity (now the Constitutive Act of the African Union) or with the African Charter, the Complainant maintains that his complaint seeks to obtain reparation for the violation of his rights to equality before the law and to a fair trial, as guaranteed by Articles 3 and 7 of the said Charter.

Regarding Article 56(5) of the Charter, relating to the exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant affirms that the rejection of his appeal by the Supreme Court of the Congo marks the end of the available local remedies.
The Commission has not received a response from the Respondent State regarding the Complainant's arguments.

Rule 118(2) of the Commission's 2020 Rules of Procedure provides as follows: "Where no observations on admissibility have been received from the Respondent State within the time limit set, the Commission shall proceed to adopt a decision by default based on the information available to it."

Consequently, and in view of the fact that the Respondent State, although informed of the complaint, has submitted no observations, the Commission's analysis will be based exclusively on the evidence presented by the Complainant.

At the outset, the Commission wishes to recall that Article 56 of the Charter sets out seven (7) admissibility conditions that any complaint submitted under Article 55 of the Charter must fulfil cumulatively. Failure to comply with any one of these conditions leads to the rejection of the communication. It is in light of these conditions that the admissibility of the present communication will be examined.

Article 56(1) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) indicate their authors even if the latter request the Commission to keep their identity anonymous".
The Commission notes that the present Communication was submitted before it by Mr Jean Paul BELFIS, represented by Counsel Claudio COELHO DE CARVALHO.
The full addresses and contact details of the Complainant and his representative being clearly specified, the Commission concludes that the Communication meets this requirement.

Article 56(2) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) are compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter".

The Commission affirmed in the case Law Society of Zimbabwe v. Zimbabwe that the compatibility of a Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union rests on its compatibility with the objectives and principles enshrined in the Act, and more precisely on the question whether the requests in the Communication would not contravene the objectives or principles expressed in the Act. In this regard, the Commission finds that neither the arguments nor the requests contained in the Communication infringe any of the objectives and principles adopted under the said Act or the Charter.

As regards the criterion of compatibility of communications with the African Charter, the Commission must ensure that the arguments invoked as well as the requests formulated in the communication fall within its jurisdiction, whether personal (ratione personae), material (ratione materiae), temporal (ratione temporis) or territorial (ratione loci).

In the present case, the Commission notes that the communication is submitted against the Republic of the Congo, a State party to the African Charter (jurisdiction ratione personae). Furthermore, the Complainants allege that the violations took place in the territory of the Respondent State (jurisdiction ratione loci), of rights protected by Articles 3 (1) and 7 (1)(C) of the Charter (jurisdiction ratione materiae). The Commission further notes that the Charter was in force in the Republic of the Congo at the time of the facts (jurisdiction ratione temporis). Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the Charter.

Article 56(3) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the OAU (AU)".

In the case Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights & Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe v. Republic of Zimbabwe, the Commission stated that "in determining whether a certain remark is disparaging or insulting and whether it has undermined the integrity of the judiciary, the Commission must be satisfied that the said remark or term is aimed at unlawfully and intentionally dishonouring or discrediting or insulting the dignity, reputation or integrity of a judicial officer or body and that it is used intentionally to manipulate public opinion or any reasonable person in order to discredit the administration of justice and weaken public confidence in it."

After analysis of the complaint, the Commission notes that the Complainant did not use any language that would aim to unduly undermine the esteem of the Respondent State or of the African Union. In light of the foregoing, the Commission considers that Article 56 (3) of the Charter is complied with.

Article 56(4) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media".

The interpretation of this provision arising from the cases Jawara and Ahmed Ismael and 528 Others v. Arab Republic of Egypt is that "the question is not whether the information comes from the media, but rather whether it is accurate" and whether the applicant tried to verify its veracity.

In the present case, the Complainant produced various pieces of evidence, notably the certified true copy (grosse) of judgment no. 34/GCS-21 of the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court of 30 July 2021, the certified true copy (expedition) of the judgment of the First Criminal Chamber docket no. 003, register no. 006 of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire of 16 July 2020, the Minutes of the Board of Directors of 6 January 2018 or the Minutes of 17 February 2018 recording that Mr Jean Paul BELFILS is Chairman of the Board of Directors and not Managing Director. The Commission considers, therefore, that the Complainant did not at all rely on media information and that the present communication satisfies the requirements of Article 56(4) of the Charter.

Article 56(5) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged".

The Commission recalls that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies constitutes a fundamental principle in international law, in particular before international human rights courts and mechanisms. This principle implies that the applicant must have used, without success, all available and effective remedies before national courts before seizing an international body. It is based on the recognition of State sovereignty and on respect for the principle of subsidiarity, according to which the primary responsibility for the protection of human rights lies with States themselves. This principle also aims to avoid the congestion of international courts with cases that could have found a solution at the national level, and to encourage the strengthening of domestic judicial systems.

The jurisprudence of the Commission recognises that the exhaustion requirement applies only to local remedies that are available, effective and sufficient, only these being reasonably required of Complainants. A remedy is considered available if the applicant can pursue it without impediment, it is considered effective if it offers a prospect of success, and it is deemed sufficient if it is capable of redressing the situation.

The jurisprudence of the Commission has also established, notably in Human Rights Council and Others v. Ethiopia, that failure to exhaust available local remedies renders a communication inadmissible.

In the present communication, the Complainant indicated that he was found guilty of the offence of concealing the true situation of the company GNCAC and misuse of corporate assets on 2 July 2019 by the Criminal Court of Pointe-Noire. He had been sentenced to 24 months' imprisonment suspended and to pay to SCI GABY, represented by Mr Gabriel NZAMBILA the sum of 784,193,250 CFA francs and that of 300,000,000 CFA francs as damages, a total of 1,084,193,250 CFA francs.

The Commission notes that the Complainant appealed this judgment on 3 July 2019 and that on 16 July 2020, the first criminal chamber of the Court of Appeal of Pointe-Noire upheld the judgment under appeal in all its provisions
The Commission notes that on 30 July 2021, the 2nd criminal chamber of the Supreme Court of the Congo dismissed the Complainant's appeal on points of law.

The Supreme Court being the highest court of the Respondent State and having ruled on the merits of the case, the Commission considers that the Complainant in the present communication has effectively exhausted the available local remedies in the Republic of the Congo, and that his communication satisfies the requirements of Article 56(5) of the Charter.

Article 56(6) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter".

In the communication under examination, the reasonable time will be examined from the exhaustion of local remedies. The Commission notes that the decision of the Supreme Court dismissing the appeal on points of law was rendered on 30 July 2021 and notified to the Complainant on 6 August 2021. The Complainant seized the Commission on 26 July 2023, that is one (1) year and 349 days later. The question that arises is whether this period is reasonable.

The Commission recalls its constant jurisprudence, starting with the case Majuru, according to which, in general, the reasonable period for filing a complaint is six (6) months. In that decision, the Commission considered that if the complaint is not filed within this period, the assessment of reasonable time must be made on a case-by-case basis. For this, the Commission must take into account the circumstances of the complaint, the nature of the case at the national level and the possible justification of the complainant. It follows that the complainant must justify any delay exceeding six months.

In the communication ARTICLE 19 and Others v. Zimbabwe, the Commission concluded that the communication had not been submitted within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of local remedies, the complainants having submitted it a little less than two years after the final judgment of the Supreme Court, and that "the reason advanced by the complainants for the late seizure is neither good nor compelling".

Moreover, the Human Rights Committee in its decision on communication no. 3049/2017 had noted that: "... the author has not explained why he submitted his communication late. In the absence of any other relevant information or explanation in the file, the Committee considers that the delay is unreasonable...".

After examination of the Complainant's submissions, the Commission finds that he has provided no valid justification for the delay incurred in filing his communication. In the absence of sufficient explanatory elements, the Commission is obliged to conclude that the condition set out in Article 56(6) of the Charter is not fulfilled

Article 56(7) of the Charter provides that "communications referred to in Article 55 received by the Commission, relating to human and peoples' rights, shall be considered if they (...) do not deal with cases which have been settled by these States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter."

In the case Sudan Human Rights Commission and Another v. Sudan, the Commission considered that a matter is considered settled if an international judicial body with a mandate or jurisdiction in human rights has taken a decision on it and has given the complaint the authority of res judicata.

In the present communication, the Complainant gave no information in this regard and the Commission notes in his narrative no fact capable of proving that the case has already been settled by an international judicial body. The Commission concludes that the condition set out in Article 56(7) of the Charter is satisfied.

In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares the present Communication inadmissible for failure to comply with the requirements of Article 56(6) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights. ii. Instructs the Secretariat to notify its decision to the Parties in accordance with Rule 118(4) of its Rules of Procedure. Done at the 84th Ordinary Session of the Commission held virtually from 21 to 30 July 2025.

Le 02 juin 2022, le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu une Communication introduite par José Marius Mboyo Makpma Kavr, ci-après dénommé « le Plaignant ».

La plainte a été déposée contre la République centrafricaine (ci-après dénommée « l'État défendeur » ou « RCA »), un État qui a ratifié la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine) le 24 avril 1986.

La Plainte porte sur des violations des droits de l'homme commises à l'encontre de M. José Marius Mboyo Makpma Kavr, ressortissant de la République centrafricaine résidant dans la commune de Bimbo, à Bangui (RCA), et Responsable juridique de Morrisson Groupe, une société à responsabilité limitée dont le Plaignant a hérité de feu Maurice MBOYO MAKPAMA.

Le Plaignant déclare avoir été détenu arbitrairement en 2018 et en décembre 2021. Bien qu'il n'ait pas expliqué les raisons de sa détention, la décision du Procureur général du 23 décembre 2021, indique qu'il a été détenu pour une audience dans le cadre d'une procédure pénale devant le Tribunal de Grande Instance de Bangui.

Le Plaignant affirme avoir hérité de deux biens immobiliers situés Martys Avenue et dans le quartier Benz-Vi, qui ont été vendus illégalement. La décision du Tribunal de Grande Instance de Bangui dans l'affaire civile n° 008/2020, jointe par le Plaignant, indique que l'un des biens a été vendu par Ecobank.

Selon le Plaignant, l'autre bien a été vendu par un membre de sa famille. Il a intenté une action en justice contre la vente de la propriété située Martys Avenue et Benz-Vi district, qui était toujours en cours au niveau national au moment du dépôt de la plainte.
Le Plaignant allègue la violation des articles 2, 3, 4, 6, 7(1)(d) et (2) de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine).

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission : a. de déclarer que les droits du Plaignant en vertu des articles 2, 3, 4, 6, 7(1)(d) et (2) de la Charte ont été violés ; b. de condamner à l'État défendeur à verser 50 000 000 FCFA au titre du préjudice moral résultant de l'arrestation illégale et de la détention arbitraire du Plaignant, ainsi que 250 000 000 FCFA au titre du préjudice financier résultant de l'achat frauduleux de son bien immobilier loué par M. Jack NABIL MROUE ; c. d'ordonner au Défendeur de restituer les deux propriétés situées à l'Avenue Martys, vendues à M. NABIL MROUE Jack, Directeur de la société Auto Star, et l'autre propriété située dans le quartier Benz-Vi, vendue à M. HAÏTHAM SROU YOUSSEF
Le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine a reçu la Plainte le 02 juin 2022.
Le 9 août 2022, la Commission s'est saisie de l'affaire, vu qu'elle remplissait toutes les conditions requises par la Règle 115(5) du Règlement intérieur de 2020.

Le 13 août 2022, les Parties ont été informées que la Plainte avait été saisie et le Plaignant a été invité à présenter ses arguments et des éléments de preuve sur la recevabilité et le fond de l'affaire dans un délai de soixante (60) jours, conformément à la Règle 116(1) du Règlement intérieur de 2020.

Le 6 août 2024, un e-mail a été envoyé pour attirer l'attention du Plaignant sur l'expiration du délai de soixante (60) jours qui lui avait été accordé et pour lui signaler la possibilité de radiation de la Communication pour défaut de poursuite diligente.

Le 24 août 2025, un dernier e-mail a été envoyé au Plaignant pour l'informer que la Commission examinerait le dossier en vue de le retirer de sa liste, conformément à la règle 124(2) du Règlement intérieur de 2020.

La règle 116(1) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission (2020) dispose : lorsque la Commission est saisie d'une Plainte, elle demande au Plaignant de présenter ses arguments et des éléments de preuve sur la recevabilité et le fond de l'affaire dans les soixante (60) jours suivant sa réception.

Dans la présente Communication, le Plaignant a été invité, le 13 août 2022, à présenter ses arguments et des éléments de preuve sur la recevabilité et le fond de la communication dans un délai de soixante (60) jours à compter de la date de notification. Le délai prescrit de soixante (60) jours a expiré le 13 octobre 2022, mais aucun argument et aucun élément de preuve n'ont été présentés dans le délai imparti.

La Commission note que deux (2) e-mails ont été envoyés successivement au Plaignant, le premier pour attirer son attention sur l'expiration du délai de soixante (60) jours qui lui avait été accordé, et le second pour lui indiquer que la Commission examinerait l'affaire en vue de la retirer de sa liste, conformément à la règle 124(2) du Règlement intérieur de 2020. À ce jour, le Plaignant n'a pas réagi à cette correspondance.

La Commission rappelle que la Communication 407/11 – Artur Margaryan et Artur Sargsyan c/ République du Kenya ; les Communications 637/16 et 639/16 – M. Mohammed Abdel Hay Faramawy et 2 autres (représentés par Dr Abdel Hay Faramawy et 4 autres) c/ République arabe d'Égypte ; et la Communication 387/10 – Kofi Yamagnane c/ Togo, ont été radiées pour défaut de poursuite diligente, les Plaignants n'ayant pas transmis leurs observations sur la recevabilité.

Dans la présente Communication, la Commission constate que le Plaignant n'a pas manifesté d'intérêt pour la poursuite de cette Communication et qu'elle ne dispose donc pas d'informations suffisantes pour se prononcer sur la recevabilité de ladite Communication.

Compte tenu de ce qui précède, la Commission décide de radier la présente Communication pour défaut de poursuite diligente, conformément à la règle 124(2) du Règlement intérieur (2020). Adopté lors de la 85 Session ordinaire de la Commission africaine, tenue du 01 au 30 octobre 2025

On 2 June 2022, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received a Communication submitted by José Marius Mboyo Makpma Kavr, hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant".

The Complaint was filed against the Central African Republic (hereinafter referred to as "the Respondent State" or "CAR"), a State that ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) on 24 April 1986.

The Complaint concerns human rights violations committed against Mr José Marius Mboyo Makpma Kavr, a national of the Central African Republic residing in the commune of Bimbo, in Bangui (CAR), and Legal Representative of Morrisson Groupe, a limited liability company which the Complainant inherited from the late Maurice MBOYO MAKPAMA.

The Complainant states that he was arbitrarily detained in 2018 and in December 2021. Although he did not explain the reasons for his detention, the decision of the Prosecutor General of 23 December 2021 indicates that he was detained for a hearing in the context of criminal proceedings before the Tribunal de Grande Instance of Bangui.

The Complainant claims to have inherited two real estate properties located on Martys Avenue and in the Benz-Vi district, which were sold illegally. The decision of the Tribunal de Grande Instance of Bangui in civil case No. 008/2020, attached by the Complainant, indicates that one of the properties was sold by Ecobank.

According to the Complainant, the other property was sold by a member of his family. He brought a legal action against the sale of the property located on Martys Avenue and in the Benz-Vi district, which was still pending at the domestic level at the time the complaint was filed.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 2, 3, 4, 6, 7(1)(d) and (2) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complainant requests the Commission: a. to declare that the Complainant's rights under Articles 2, 3, 4, 6, 7(1)(d) and (2) of the Charter have been violated; b. to order the Respondent State to pay 50,000,000 CFA francs for the moral prejudice resulting from the Complainant's unlawful arrest and arbitrary detention, as well as 250,000,000 CFA francs for the financial prejudice resulting from the fraudulent purchase of his real estate property rented by Mr Jack NABIL MROUE; c. to order the Respondent to return the two properties located on Martys Avenue, sold to Mr NABIL MROUE Jack, Director of the company Auto Star, and the other property located in the Benz-Vi district, sold to Mr HAÏTHAM SROU YOUSSEF
The Secretariat of the African Commission received the Complaint on 2 June 2022.
On 9 August 2022, the Commission seized itself of the matter, as it met all the requirements of Rule 115(5) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure.

On 13 August 2022, the Parties were informed that the Complaint had been seized and the Complainant was requested to submit his arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits of the case within sixty (60) days, in accordance with Rule 116(1) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure.

On 6 August 2024, an e-mail was sent to draw the Complainant's attention to the expiry of the sixty (60) day time limit granted to him and to inform him of the possibility of the Communication being struck out for failure to prosecute diligently.

On 24 August 2025, a final e-mail was sent to the Complainant to inform him that the Commission would consider the file with a view to striking it off its list, in accordance with Rule 124(2) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure.

Rule 116(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure (2020) provides: when the Commission is seized of a Complaint, it shall request the Complainant to submit his arguments and evidence on admissibility and the merits of the case within sixty (60) days of receipt.

In the present Communication, the Complainant was requested, on 13 August 2022, to submit his arguments and evidence on the admissibility and the merits of the communication within sixty (60) days from the date of notification. The prescribed time limit of sixty (60) days expired on 13 October 2022, but no arguments and no evidence were submitted within the time limit.

The Commission notes that two (2) e-mails were sent successively to the Complainant, the first to draw his attention to the expiry of the sixty (60) day time limit granted to him, and the second to inform him that the Commission would consider the case with a view to striking it off its list, in accordance with Rule 124(2) of the 2020 Rules of Procedure. To date, the Complainant has not responded to this correspondence.

The Commission recalls that Communication 407/11 – Artur Margaryan and Artur Sargsyan v. Republic of Kenya; Communications 637/16 and 639/16 – Mr Mohammed Abdel Hay Faramawy and 2 others (represented by Dr Abdel Hay Faramawy and 4 others) v. Arab Republic of Egypt; and Communication 387/10 – Kofi Yamagnane v. Togo, were struck out for failure to prosecute diligently, the Complainants not having submitted their observations on admissibility.

In the present Communication, the Commission finds that the Complainant has not shown any interest in pursuing this Communication and that it therefore does not have sufficient information to rule on the admissibility of the said Communication.

In view of the foregoing, the Commission decides to strike out the present Communication for failure to prosecute diligently, in accordance with Rule 124(2) of the Rules of Procedure (2020). Adopted at the 85 Ordinary Session of the African Commission, held from 1 to 30 October 2025

The Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (Ethiopia) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter), since 15 June 1998. Ethiopia also ratified the Protocol on the Rights of Women in Africa (The Maputo Protocol) on 18 July 2018.

Ethiopia submitted its Initial to 4th Periodic Report to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) at the latter’s 46th Ordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 11 to 25 November 2009.

Subsequently, Ethiopia has since submitted its 5th-6th Combined Periodic Report (2009-2013), considered by the Commission during its 56th Ordinary Session, held in Banjul (The Gambia) from 21 April to 7 May 2015. The related Concluding Observations were adopted at the Commission’s 18th Extraordinary Session held in Nairobi (Kenya) from 29 July to 7 August 2015.

On 19 January 2024, Ethiopia submitted to the Commission its 7th and 10 combined Periodic Report on the implementation of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and Initial Report under the Maputo Protocol (the Report under review). While it was scheduled to be reviewed at the Commission’s 79 Ordinary Session (May 2024), the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs requested the postponement of the review to the 81 Ordinary Session (October 2024), then to the 83 Ordinary Session (May 2025).
The Report was reviewed on 9 and 11 May 2025, in the framework of the Commission’s 83 Ordinary public Session, held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 2 to 22 May 2025.

A high-level Ethiopian Delegation, led by H.E. Mr. Belayihun Yirga Kifle, State Minister, Ministry of Justice, represented the State Party during the review, which was marked by a frank and constructive dialog with the members of the Commission.
At the end of the interactive dialog, the Ethiopian Delegation undertook to provide the Commission with more information in writing and sent a written contribution on 11 June 2025.

The Periodic Report covers developments in Ethiopia in the promotion and protection of human rights during the period under review. The Commission takes note with appreciation of the participatory and inclusive process that led to the preparation of the Periodic Report, by an inter-ministerial team coordinated by the Ministry of Justice, and including officials from the Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Women and Social Affairs, the Central Statistics Service and Federal Prisons Commission (Paragraph 25).

In addition, the Report has the merit of focusing on the challenges faced by the Ethiopian authorities in their quest to implement the rights enshrined in the African Charter, inter alia, security problems including the conflict in the north of the Country, health and education challenges and negative social practices.

The present Concluding Observations reflect positive aspects and factors limiting the enjoyment of human rights in Ethiopia. They also highlight the areas of concern identified through the review of the Report and the additional information provided subsequently.

Finally, the Commission presents recommendations to Ethiopia on measures necessary to strengthen the enjoyment of human rights, as guaranteed by the African Charter, the Maputo Protocol, the Kampala Convention, as well as other relevant regional and international instruments. Recommandations : Ethiopia should : - Continue the State Party's commitment to the submission of Periodic Reports, in accordance with the relevant ACHPR Guidelines on State Reporting. - Include in the next periodic report a section on the implementation of the Kampala Convention, ratified by Ethiopia in June 2020. - Include in the next periodic report a section on the implementation of the Protocols on the Rights of Older Persons, ratified by Ethiopia in June 2020, following its recent entry into force. Cooperation with the Commission Recommendation: Ethiopia should report to the Commission on the measures taken to implement the decisions of the Commission in finalized communications, namely: - Communication 301/05 Haregewoin Gabre-Selassie and IHRDA (on behalf of former Dergue Officials) v Ethiopia (adopted in November 2011); - Communication 341/07 Equality Now and Ethiopian Women Lawyers Association (EWLA) v Ethiopia (adopted in November 2015); - Communication 419/12 The Indigenous Peoples of the Lower Omo (represented by Survival International Trust) v Ethiopia (adopted in August 2022); - Communication 461/13 Eskinder Nega Fenta and Reyoot Alemu (represented by Media Legal Defence Initiative and Freedom Now) v Ethiopia (adopted in August 2022); - Communication 455/13 Abubaker Ahmed Mohamed et al. v Ethiopia (adopted in March 2023); - Communication 599/16 Ethiopian Electorate (represented by Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights and IHRDA) v Ethiopia (adopted in November 2023). General recommendations Ratifications

The Commission commends the Government of Ethiopia for ratifying during the reporting period the Kampala Convention and the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Older Persons, in June 2020.

Furthermore, the Delegation informed that efforts are underway to accede to the International Convention on the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of their Families and that a comprehensive diagnostic study to thoroughly assess the legal and practical implications of ratifying the Convention on Enforced Disappearance.

The Delegation also informed that ratification of international instruments is primarily linked to national priorities, the condition of the domestic legal framework, and the readiness of relevant institutions to implement them. Recommendations: Ethiopia should: - Strengthen its efforts to ratify the International Convention on the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of their Families and the Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance. - Engage consultations on the ratification of the following instruments: • At the African Union level: o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (Signed on 6 June 1998); o The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa; o Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security; o The Protocol on the Court of Justice of the African Union (Signed on 1 June 2004); o The Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights; o African Charter on the Values and Principles of Decentralisation, Local Governance and Local Development. o Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Specific Aspects of the Right to a Nationality and the Eradication of Statelessness in Africa, adopted in February 2024; o The African Union Convention on Ending Violence against Women and Girls (adopted in February 2025). • At the United Nations level : o The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons as well as the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness o The Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture; o The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; o The Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights aiming to the abolition of the death penalty; o The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; o The Optional protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; o The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child; o The Optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. National human rights framework

The Delegation informed that the GoE has decided to revise the draft of the Third National Human Rights Action Plan to ensure the inclusion of a broader range of rights and to guarantee the meaningful participation of the public and remains committed to allocating sufficient funding for its implementation.
The Commission takes note of the newly established institutional set-up called the National Implementation, Monitoring, Reporting, and Follow-up Mechanism (NIMRFM).

Furthermore, the Delegation informed that both federal and regional declarations of a state of emergency are constitutionally regulated to limit discretionary power.
